finding_statement: Enterprise agility -- the ability to thrive in a continuously changing business environment -- can be operationalized as a repeating four-phase cycle: establishing and adjusting strategic and operative goals for both business and IT, (re-)engineering the enterprise architecture accordingly, implementing and running the enterprise, and continuously monitoring for adaptation needs that restart the cycle.
mechanism: Because enterprise engineering is not a one-time greenfield design but an ongoing redesign of a running enterprise, a structured Plan-Do-Check-Act style cycle ensures that changes triggered from either the business side (e.g., altered strategy) or the technology side (e.g., new IT capabilities) are captured, modeled, implemented, and then monitored for further necessary adaptation, rather than being addressed as one-off projects that leave the architecture stale until the next major initiative.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether the organization's enterprise or IT architecture practice follows an explicit, recurring goal-setting, re-engineering, implementation, and monitoring cycle (rather than only doing architecture planning at the start of major projects), and whether monitoring explicitly feeds back into the next goal-setting phase.
page_or_section: Section 4.1: Modelling procedure for continuous business-IT alignment, p. 82

finding_statement: The extreme-case study reports higher business-IT alignment maturity in organizations applying a more mature mix of governance structures, processes, and relational mechanisms, and lower maturity in poorly aligned cases. It treats the level-two observation as exploratory.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Sections 6.3, 7: Exploring the relationship between IT governance and business/IT alignment; Conclusions, pp. 7-9

finding_statement: A Delphi panel of industry experts first identified a ten-practice minimum baseline of IT governance practices by consensus; cross-referencing this baseline against actual maturity differences between the high- and low-alignment extreme-case organizations narrowed it to a key minimum baseline of seven practices -- IT steering committee, IT project steering committee, portfolio management, IT budget control and reporting, CIO reporting to the CEO/COO, project governance/management methodologies, and IT leadership -- that were both expert-endorsed and empirically differentiating.
mechanism: Delphi experts rated all 33 candidate practices on perceived effectiveness and ease of implementation across three consensus-building rounds (final Kendall's W = 0.53, moderate agreement) and nominated a top-10 minimum baseline; comparing this expert-derived baseline against the extreme-case maturity data confirmed that seven of these ten practices were clearly and consistently more mature (above level 2) in the high-performing organizations, providing convergent evidence from two independent methods (expert consensus and empirical case comparison).
operationalisation_hint: Use this seven-practice key minimum baseline, and the broader ten-practice Delphi baseline, as candidate starting points for IT governance implementation, cross-checked against the closely overlapping but not identical eleven-practice list identified through pure extreme-case comparison in the companion 2009 paper.
page_or_section: Sections 6.2-6.3: Delphi minimum baseline; key minimum baseline, pp. 6, 8-9

finding_statement: Prioritizing which IT governance practices to implement first should account for two independent dimensions -- perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation -- since some practices are both highly effective and easy to implement (e.g., IT steering committees, CIO reporting to the CEO/COO), while others are perceived as highly effective but comparatively hard to implement (e.g., benefits management and reporting, charge-back arrangements), and still others (e.g., COBIT, IT governance assurance and self-assessment) may be valuable at a higher level of abstraction without scoring highly on either dimension individually.
mechanism: A panel of 22 senior IT, business, and consulting experts rated all 33 candidate IT governance practices independently on a 0-5 scale for perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation; because these two dimensions do not always move together, treating important practice as a single undifferentiated concept risks either underinvesting in high-effectiveness-but-harder practices or overinvesting effort in easy-but-lower-value practices; frameworks like COBIT, which operate at a higher level of abstraction, can still be valuable because many of the individually-rated effective detailed practices are integral parts of such frameworks even when the framework itself does not score as high individually.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting which IT governance practices to roll out first, plot or rank candidate practices on both perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation (via expert panel or similar structured elicitation) rather than a single combined priority score, and sequence early efforts toward practices that are both effective and easy, while planning longer-term efforts for high-effectiveness/low-ease practices such as benefits management and reporting or charge-back arrangements.
page_or_section: Section 6.2: Exploring how Belgian financial services organisations are implementing IT governance, pp. 5-6

finding_statement: Board-level IT governance mechanisms -- an IT strategy committee at the board of directors and dedicated IT expertise on the board -- are widely promoted in IT governance literature as essential given the board's prime responsibility for governance, but are rated by industry experts as comparatively low in both perceived effectiveness and perceived ease of implementation, and were not adopted by any of the extreme-case organizations studied except one with an atypical, closely-held ownership structure.
mechanism: Making a board of directors more IT-literate or establishing a dedicated board-level IT strategy committee is difficult to achieve in practice (reflected in a near-lowest ease-of-implementation score for board IT expertise), and in typical shareholder-governed organizations, board representatives are primarily concerned with core financial results rather than operational IT issues, making such structures both hard to implement and of limited perceived value in most contexts; the exception was a family-owned organization whose board (composed of family owners rather than external shareholders) operated much closer to daily operations.
operationalisation_hint: Before treating board-level IT governance structures (board IT strategy committee, dedicated board IT expertise) as a necessary readiness condition, assess the organization's ownership and board-involvement model (e.g., closely-held or family-owned versus typical shareholder-governed), since these structures may be neither feasible nor high-value outside of atypical ownership contexts, despite their prominence in IT governance literature and standards (e.g., ITGI, COBIT).
page_or_section: Section 6.2: Exploring how Belgian financial services organisations are implementing IT governance, p. 7

finding_statement: Transformation readiness requires organizational members to collectively value the impending change as needed, important, beneficial, or worthwhile, regardless of whether their individual reasons for valuing it converge.
mechanism: Shared valuation of the change drives change commitment -- the collective resolve to pursue implementation -- independent of the specific (and potentially disparate) reasons members hold for valuing it.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether stakeholders across the organization perceive the transformation as needed/beneficial, not merely whether leadership has communicated a rationale.

finding_statement: Transformation readiness requires a shared, favorable organizational appraisal of whether members know what implementation will take (task demands), whether adequate resources exist (resource availability), and whether the situation currently supports action (situational factors).
mechanism: Change efficacy is a collective judgment of implementation capability, analogous to Bandura's collective efficacy; it is not the same as possessing resources, but the shared belief that available resources and conditions are sufficient to execute the change.
operationalisation_hint: Assess organizational members' shared confidence separately along the three appraisal dimensions (task demands, resources, situational factors) rather than as a single generic confidence score.

finding_statement: Organizational readiness for transformation is not equivalent to possessing financial, material, human, or informational resources; identical resource endowments can yield different implementation effectiveness depending on how members appraise and mobilize them.
mechanism: Structural resources and organizational structure function as inputs into change-efficacy judgments rather than as readiness itself; readiness is the shared psychological state formed from appraising that capacity, not the capacity itself.

finding_statement: The source conceptualizes readiness as a configural, shared team property and links variability in members' readiness perceptions to lower shared readiness. It does not prescribe a specific agreement statistic or deny the relevance of organization-level readiness.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Discussion / "What is organizational readiness for change?"

finding_statement: An organizational culture that embraces innovation, risk-taking, and learning supports transformation readiness, but functions as a distal contextual amplifier rather than a direct readiness component.
mechanism: Culture, along with policies/procedures and past change experience, is theorized to affect readiness indirectly by amplifying or dampening change valence and shaping efficacy appraisals, not by constituting readiness on its own.

finding_statement: The source defines IT-governance structures, processes, and relational mechanisms and proposes an organization-specific mixture of the three categories. It does not establish that one category can never be sufficient in a particular context.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section "IT Governance Structures, Processes and Relational Mechanisms" / Figure 2

finding_statement: Complete IT governance structures and processes in place are not sufficient for effective governance if business and IT stakeholders do not understand each other or fail to collaborate.
mechanism: Two-way communication, active participation, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms (career crossover, cross-training) are what let structurally assigned decision rights actually translate into aligned decisions; without them, structures and processes can exist on paper without functioning in practice.

finding_statement: Organizations can assess IT governance and business/IT alignment readiness along a defined maturity scale (e.g., 0=nonexistent to 5=optimized) across specific criteria, identify a gap between "as-is" and "to-be" positions, and define targeted actions to close it.
mechanism: Maturity models (COBIT, Luftman's alignment maturity, the ITGI governance maturity model) decompose governance capability into scored attributes; a 2002 benchmark survey found average self-assessed maturity for IT strategic planning fluctuating between only 2.0 and 2.5, suggesting realistic target-setting rather than assuming universal optimization.
operationalisation_hint: Score governance/alignment maturity per defined criteria and attributes; set the "to-be" target contingent on industry, size, and strategy context rather than defaulting to the highest level.

finding_statement: Effective IT governance separates board-level strategic oversight (an IT strategy committee that guides and reviews enterprise and IT strategy) from executive-level implementation oversight (an IT steering committee managing IT priorities, costs, and resource allocation), each with different membership and authority.
mechanism: Role clarity between the strategic-oversight body and the operational-execution body prevents both board-level neglect of IT and executive micromanagement without strategic guidance.
operationalisation_hint: Verify that a board-level IT strategy committee and an executive-level IT steering committee both exist and that their mandates do not overlap or leave gaps.
page_or_section: Section "IT Strategy Committee and IT Steering Committee"

finding_statement: Strategic fit and functional integration between business and IT strategy can be operationalized through concrete governance/alignment techniques -- a cascade of balanced scorecards linking IT development, IT operational, IT strategic, and business scorecards; information economics scoring of ROI plus strategic intangibles; and service level agreements.
mechanism: These techniques give the abstract Strategic Alignment Model dimensions (strategic fit, functional integration) measurable, actionable instruments that IT governance bodies can use for prioritization and monitoring.
operationalisation_hint: Adopt one or more of BSC cascade, information economics scoring, or SLA/SLM as the practical mechanism translating SAM into governance decisions.

finding_statement: As with any IT-enabled change, bringing new technology into the organization is not sufficient; digital transformation success depends on accompanying process and operations management changes, which in turn require training people for the unique challenges technology introduces.
mechanism: Technology adoption without corresponding process/operations redesign and workforce training leaves the organizational side of the technological-organizational-social definition of DT unaddressed.

finding_statement: Although practitioner-developed DT maturity models exist (e.g., IDC's), the academic community has not yet converged on a consensual maturity model that can be applied across all sectors of activity to determine an organization's degree of digital transformation.
mechanism: Without a shared, validated maturity/readiness instrument, cross-study and cross-sector comparisons of DT readiness remain difficult, and organizations lack a standardized benchmark analogous to those available in the more mature ITG maturity-model literature.
operationalisation_hint: Note this gap when proposing or selecting a DT-readiness assessment instrument; treat existing practitioner maturity models as unvalidated starting points rather than settled standards.

finding_statement: Digital transformation strategies must jointly coordinate four dimensions -- use of technologies (ambition/role of IT), changes in value creation (deviation from the core business), structural changes (organizational placement of new digital activities), and financial aspects (urgency and ability to finance) -- since misalignment along any one dimension undermines successful rollout.
mechanism: A DT strategy functions as a cross-functional coordinating device precisely because it integrates all four dimensions into one blueprint governing both the transformation process and post-transformation operations, unlike system-centric IT strategy or opportunity-describing digital business strategy.
operationalisation_hint: Assess a firm's current position and target ambition separately along each of the four dimensions (technology use, value creation, structural change, financial aspects) before formulating or evaluating a DT strategy.

finding_statement: A digital transformation strategy is conceptually distinct from an IT strategy (system-centric, infrastructure-focused, limited impact on business-model innovation) and from a digital business strategy (describes desired future business opportunities without guiding how to reach them); it is specifically the blueprint that governs the transformation process itself and operations thereafter.
mechanism: Distinguishing these constructs closes a practice gap in which organizations mistake IT infrastructure roadmaps or business-opportunity descriptions for an actual transformation-governance strategy.
operationalisation_hint: Verify an organization's "digital strategy" artifact actually specifies transformation governance (coordination, prioritization, implementation, reassessment), not just future IT infrastructure or target business opportunities.

finding_statement: The source calls for clearly assigned transformation responsibility, relevant experience, aligned incentives, and preferably continuity of the responsible person. It does not establish a universal single-accountable-owner requirement.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Because digital technology diffusion changes swiftly and creates high uncertainty about a DT strategy's underlying assumptions, transformation-ready organizations define clear procedures and intervals for reassessing both those assumptions and transformational progress, with thresholds that trigger corrective action.
mechanism: Explicit reassessment procedures counteract decision-making biases (e.g., sunk-cost-driven reluctance to course-correct) and preserve management credibility by enabling early corrective action rather than delayed response.
operationalisation_hint: Define reassessment intervals and progress thresholds in advance, before strategy rollout, rather than reactively after problems surface.

finding_statement: Top management support must be sustained from initial planning through execution, and transformation leaders need active stakeholder-engagement skills, because a company-wide DT strategy predictably provokes resistance from different areas of the company.
mechanism: Since DT strategies cut across functional boundaries and affect the entire company, resistance is an expected condition rather than an exception; sustained top-management backing and dedicated stakeholder-engagement skill convert cross-functional scope from a liability into coordinated change.

finding_statement: Transformation-enabling assessment requires separately evaluating the strategic need to transform (clarity and priority of the driving imperative) and the organization's readiness (capability/adaptability to make the changes), since these two dimensions combine to predict outcomes differently: low need predicted failure regardless of readiness; high need with initially low readiness could still succeed if executives invested time in the engagement phase to build buy-in and capability; high need with high readiness sometimes led to over-ambition and only partial success.
mechanism: Positioning each transformation on a need/readiness matrix (an adapted Strategic Options model) before committing resources reveals which lever -- building the case for change vs. building organizational capability to change -- needs the most investment; conflating the two, or assuming high need implies high readiness, was a recurring failure pattern across the case studies.
operationalisation_hint: Score each planned transformation separately on (a) clarity/priority of the strategic imperative and (b) organizational capability/adaptability to execute, using a 2x2 or matrix positioning before finalizing transformation scope.
page_or_section: Chapter 12, Sections 12.3-12.4 ("Strategic Positioning of Business Transformations" and "Transformation Need and Readiness")

finding_statement: Sustained business transformation requires a meta-level orchestration layer that (a) integrates directional disciplines (strategy, value, risk management, which define the case for action) with enablement disciplines (process, IT, organizational change, competence, program management, which deliver the change) and (b) cycles them through four iterative phases -- envision, engage, transform, optimize -- rather than treating transformation as a single linear process or as the sum of independently-run management disciplines.
mechanism: Individual management disciplines each have their own assumptions, terminology, and practitioner communities, which produces fragmentation and disconnected execution when not orchestrated; the meta-management layer supplies the cross-disciplinary linkage, goal-cascading, and feedback loops (treating the whole as a dynamic capability) that let otherwise-siloed disciplines function as one coherent transformation.
operationalisation_hint: Map an organization's transformation initiative against the directional/enablement discipline split and the four-phase lifecycle to check whether a coordinating meta-management layer exists, rather than assuming individually well-run disciplines will self-integrate.
page_or_section: Chapter 1, Section 1.3 (Distinction to Other Frameworks) and Chapter 2 (Meta Management), Sections 2.1-2.2

finding_statement: Solution readiness for IT-enabled business transformation can be assessed by combining an EA-based review of as-is/to-be business and technology architecture with business capability maps (stable functional units linking business and IT architecture) and a maturity assessment of current IT organization, support, and operations, whose gaps define the transformation roadmap.
mechanism: Because business capabilities are more stable than fast-changing business processes, using them (rather than processes) as the unit of readiness assessment gives a durable, EA-linked basis for identifying gaps between current and required capability and for ensuring planned initiatives do not induce IT/business misalignment.
operationalisation_hint: Use business capability maps plus an EA as-is/to-be gap analysis and IT maturity assessment as the concrete readiness-assessment technique before finalizing an IT transformation roadmap.
page_or_section: Chapter 7, Section 7.3 ("Assess and Enable Solution Readiness of the Organization")

finding_statement: Successful architecture-led IT transformation execution depends on five factors: (1) explicitly relating chosen frameworks (e.g., TOGAF, EABOK, ITIL, PMBOK) to the transformation rather than working framework-free; (2) reusing proven patterns, methods, and principles instead of reinventing solutions; (3) governing implementation at an appropriate level of detail rather than over-specifying project-level design decisions centrally; (4) applying the same architecture framework consistently across all levels of detail (capability, segment, solution); and (5) agreeing KPIs (business, technology, application, operational, data, people-related) to measure progress.
mechanism: Each factor addresses a distinct failure mode: framework absence causes ad hoc execution, non-reuse wastes resources and risks quality, over-specification creates unmanageable governance burden, inconsistent frameworks across levels create "translation" losses between organizational levels, and absent KPIs remove the ability to detect deviation from the intended direction.
operationalisation_hint: Audit an IT/architecture-led transformation initiative against all five factors individually; treat missing KPI agreement or inconsistent framework use across levels as leading indicators of execution risk.
page_or_section: Chapter 7, Section 7.7 ("Key Success Factors for Transformational IT Management")

finding_statement: What is empirically observed to matter is not generic executive "commitment" (a vague term) but sustained, continuous personal involvement of a credible leader in the transformation's governance throughout the envision and engage phases, combined with early transfer of change ownership to a coalition of business managers who will deliver or benefit from the changes; dictatorial or autocratic top-down leadership, by contrast, generates resistance.
mechanism: Leadership credibility specifically in the early envision/engage phases determines whether other stakeholders grant buy-in; low personal credibility in three of the case-study failures was directly linked to unsuccessful outcomes (two were later restarted under new leadership), while transferring ownership early to a business-manager coalition built durable change capability rather than dependency on the transformation team.
operationalisation_hint: Assess not merely whether an executive sponsor exists, but whether that sponsor has personal credibility for this specific transformation and sustains visible, continuous governance involvement across the full engage/envision period, and whether ownership is transferred early to a business-manager coalition.
page_or_section: Chapter 12, Section 12.6 ("Lessons Learned in Relation to the Meta Management Key Themes" -- Leadership)

finding_statement: Effective IT governance requires enterprises to explicitly articulate and harmonize six interlocking components: enterprise strategy and organization (which define desirable behaviors), IT governance arrangements (archetypes assigning decision rights), IT organizational structure and mechanisms (committees, processes, communications), and IT metrics/accountabilities tied to business performance goals -- rather than designing governance archetypes in isolation from strategy and organizational structure.
mechanism: Governance arrangements must be harmonized with, and sometimes deliberately transcend, existing organizational structure (as at JPMorgan Chase, where centralized architecture/infrastructure/principles decisions cut across an otherwise decentralized divisional structure to capture cross-business-unit synergies) so that decision rights reinforce rather than fight the enterprise's stated strategic intent.
operationalisation_hint: Map governance arrangements against all six framework components (strategy/organization, archetypes, mechanisms, metrics) to check for harmonization gaps, rather than assessing decision-rights allocation alone.
page_or_section: Chapter 6, "Six Interlocking Components of Effective Governance Design" and Figure 6-1 (JPMorgan Chase case)

finding_statement: Effective IT governance requires assigning clear decision rights across five interrelated decision domains -- IT principles (high-level statements clarifying IT's role, typically 3-7 principles derived directly from business principles), IT architecture (organizing logic for data/application/technical standardization and integration), IT infrastructure strategies, business application needs, and IT investment/prioritization -- because principles decisions establish the direction that the other four decisions must coalesce around, and equivocating on principles limits the efficacy of all downstream decisions.
mechanism: Principles sit atop the decision hierarchy and translate into architecture requirements (standardization/integration road map), which in turn bound infrastructure and application choices; investment decisions marshal resources to convert principles into systems; decisions can flow top-down from principles or bubble up from business application needs, but ultimately investment decisions select and fund the initiatives that embody the principles.
operationalisation_hint: Verify an enterprise can name its own small set (3-7) of clearly articulated IT principles with a traceable line of evidence back to business principles, before assessing governance of the other four decision domains.
page_or_section: Chapter 2, "Five Key IT Decisions: Making IT a Strategic Asset" (Figure 2-1, MetLife and MeadWestvaco examples)

finding_statement: The single strongest predictor of top IT governance performance is the percentage of managers in leadership positions who can accurately describe their enterprise's IT governance: top performers had nearly half of such managers able to do so versus fewer than 30 percent in poor performers, and only 5 percent of all enterprises studied had 80 percent or more of managers able to describe governance.
mechanism: When more managers can accurately describe governance, governance becomes part of the management culture -- people follow, challenge, and improve it; without awareness, people cannot practice governance even if formally designed well.
operationalisation_hint: Survey leadership-level managers on their ability to describe the enterprise's IT governance arrangements as a direct, quantifiable readiness/maturity indicator, benchmarking against the ~30% (poor) vs ~46% (top) vs 80%+ (rare/best-in-class) thresholds from the 256-enterprise CISR study.

finding_statement: Top IT governance performers achieve more direct, differentiated involvement of specific senior leaders in governance -- with empirically estimated relative leverage of CEO (2.1x), COO (1.7x), business unit leader (1.6x), business unit CIO (1.3x), and CFO (1.2x) involvement, all indexed against CIO involvement (1.0x) -- and effective CIO involvement is a necessary but not sufficient condition for effective governance.
mechanism: Different senior roles contribute leverage through different mechanisms: the CEO through occasional high-profile roles (e.g., chairing the investment committee) rather than routine attendance, business unit CIOs through dual reporting relationships that balance business-unit and enterprise priorities and by acting as advocates for enterprisewide governance.
operationalisation_hint: Design differentiated, role-specific involvement roles for the CEO, COO, business unit leaders, business unit CIOs, and CFO rather than treating "executive support" as a single undifferentiated requirement satisfied by CIO leadership alone.
page_or_section: Chapter 5, "What IT Governance Works Best" (leverage list, page ~126)

finding_statement: Top governance performers use federal arrangements for broad-based INPUT to decisions (especially IT principles and business application needs) but rely on more concentrated archetypes (e.g., duopoly) for actually MAKING those decisions; federal input balances corporate and business-unit tradeoffs, while duopoly decision-making is significantly more effective than federal decision-making, which the book associates with slower, more compromised outcomes.
mechanism: Conflating "who provides input" with "who decides" is a common design error: broad federal input avoids the disenchantment and non-transparency risk of narrower duopoly input, but transplanting that same broad-based logic into the actual decision rights (rather than just the input stage) reintroduces the coordination costs and compromise that make federal decision-making comparatively weak.
operationalisation_hint: When designing governance arrangements, specify the input model and the decision-rights model separately for each of the five key IT decisions rather than using one archetype for both.

finding_statement: Enterprise transformation readiness requires the enterprise to explicitly choose one of four operating models -- Diversification (low standardization, low integration), Coordination (low standardization, high integration), Replication (high standardization, low integration), or Unification (high standardization, high integration) -- since this choice, more than strategy statements alone, determines which business process integration and standardization requirements the foundation for execution must satisfy; companies with a foundation supporting a defined operating model reported 17% greater strategic effectiveness plus higher operational efficiency (31%), customer intimacy (33%), product leadership (34%), and strategic agility (29%) than companies without one.
mechanism: The operating model choice is a commitment to a way of doing business that enables rapid implementation of consistent strategic initiatives but will fail to support initiatives inconsistent with its standardization/integration assumptions (e.g., Amazon's distribution/online-interaction capabilities supported adding new product categories, while Barnes & Noble's model was ill-suited to online sales); different organizational levels of the same enterprise (e.g., Johnson & Johnson's divisions) can adopt different operating models to meet different objectives.
operationalisation_hint: Position the enterprise (or each business unit/division) in the standardization x integration quadrant by asking (1) how dependent is one unit's transaction success on other units' data, and (2) how much does the company benefit from units operating identically; treat a shift between quadrants as a transformation, not an incremental change.

finding_statement: Enterprises build and leverage a foundation for execution by progressing through four architecture maturity stages -- Business Silos (local business/functional optimization, no technology standards), Standardized Technology (IT efficiency via technology standardization and centralization), Optimized Core (companywide data/process standardization matched to the chosen operating model), and Business Modularity (reusable, loosely-coupled IT-enabled process components preserving global standards while enabling local difference) -- and skipping stages leads to failure or delayed benefits because each stage has distinct organizational learning requirements that cannot be compressed.
mechanism: Each stage requires organizations to learn a qualitatively different discipline (e.g., moving from Business Silos to Standardized Technology requires business managers to first accept that technology constraints can legitimately override locally-optimal functionality, which only becomes credible once standardization benefits are demonstrated through benchmarking); attempting to reach Optimized Core or Business Modularity without having internalized the prior stage's discipline overloads the organization's capacity for change.
operationalisation_hint: Diagnose the enterprise's current stage (only 12% of studied firms were still in Business Silos, 48% in Standardized Technology) before committing to a transformation roadmap, and sequence the roadmap through the remaining stages in order rather than attempting to jump directly to Business Modularity.
page_or_section: Chapter 4, "Navigate the Stages of Enterprise Architecture Maturity" and Chapter 9, Leadership Principle 5 ("Don't Skip Stages")

finding_statement: When promising strategic opportunities do not leverage the existing foundation for execution, transformation-ready enterprises pursue them as separate, explicitly-budgeted experiments outside the core business (as Schneider National did with logistics, UPS with financial services, and Manheim with online auctions) rather than either forcing them into the foundation or abandoning them.
mechanism: Because non-core-leveraging ventures involve higher risk and slower profitability, treating them as acknowledged experiments -- with distinct budgets, distinct success metrics, and realistic timeframes -- lets the enterprise learn about emerging businesses and new technology capabilities without destabilizing the foundation; successful experiments can eventually "feed the core" foundation.
operationalisation_hint: Establish a separate budget line, success metrics, and timeframe for strategic initiatives identified as not leveraging the current foundation, rather than evaluating them against the same criteria as foundation-leveraging initiatives.
page_or_section: Chapter 9, Leadership Principle 3 ("Feed the Core -- Experiment")

finding_statement: A one-page "core diagram" of the enterprise architecture can function as a compass that managers access to resolve disagreements about next steps in building organizational capabilities; the objective of enterprise architecture is not to specify a particular end state but to serve as a direction-setting blueprint and communication tool for senior managers and business partners.
mechanism: Because companies easily become enamored with the next big project, a simple, stable architecture artifact (as opposed to detailed technical diagrams) keeps attention on incrementally building and then leveraging capabilities rather than repeatedly chasing new opportunities without consolidating benefits from the last one.
operationalisation_hint: Maintain a single-page core diagram as the primary architecture communication artifact for senior managers, reserving detailed technical architecture documentation for lower organizational levels.
page_or_section: Chapter 9, Leadership Principle 4 ("Use Architecture as a Compass and Communication Tool")

finding_statement: Foundation-for-execution transformations require reward structures aligned with enterprisewide (not just local) thinking; State Street's "One State Street" transformation paired a new governance model with a concrete incentive redesign -- business unit executives receiving 50% of bonuses based on business-unit performance and 50% on enterprisewide performance, while all IT professionals received 100% enterprisewide-performance-based incentives.
mechanism: Unaligned incentives can foil a foundation for execution even when governance structures and processes are otherwise well designed, because people rewarded for maximizing local performance will disregard enterprisewide capabilities regardless of formal governance arrangements; explicit incentive redesign is therefore necessary, not merely governance-structure redesign.
operationalisation_hint: Audit whether incentive/bonus structures for business-unit and IT leadership are weighted toward enterprisewide outcomes in proportion to how much enterprisewide standardization/integration the transformation requires.

finding_statement: Beyond internal business-IT alignment needs, transformation-enabling EA adoption is also driven by external regulatory requirements that mandate organizations demonstrate clear insight into and control over their operations and IT -- concrete examples include the US Clinger-Cohen Act (1996), which legally requires every US government agency to maintain an integrated IT architecture under CIO responsibility; the Basel II capital adequacy framework (2004), whose risk-measurement and management requirements for banks are difficult to meet without a sound architectural approach; and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002), whose corporate-accountability and audit requirements depend on IT systems providing clear insight into responsibilities and authorizations.
mechanism: Regulatory frameworks create an external forcing function for EA adoption independent of any internally-recognized business case, because compliance itself becomes infeasible without architectural transparency into processes, systems, and accountabilities -- Basel II, for instance, provides explicit incentives (lower capital requirements) for more comprehensive risk measurement, which in practice requires architectural insight.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's motivation/readiness for an EA-grounded transformation, check for applicable regulatory regimes (financial services, government, publicly-listed) that may make architecture practice a compliance necessity rather than merely a business-value option.

finding_statement: Enterprise architecture is positioned as the "hard" instrument translating mission, vision, and strategy into concrete operational actions, but the book explicitly identifies culture, people, and leadership as an equally or more important "soft" complement without which architecture-driven goal achievement is incomplete.
mechanism: The mission-vision-strategy-goals-actions management pyramid places EA as the mechanism that bridges strategic goals to daily operations, but its authors caution that this "hard" architectural layer must be matched by "soft" cultural and leadership work of equal or higher importance to actually achieve enterprise goals.

finding_statement: AI-based digital transformation readiness should be assessed holistically across four components: current processes (documentation, KPI-based performance measurement, automation-opportunity identification, AI-alignment check), existing systems (identification, functional/technical analysis, data evaluation, vendor evaluation), data landscape (data quality, accessibility, governance), and AI capabilities (existing AI initiatives audit, skills/expertise gap analysis, tools/infrastructure, culture and leadership) -- because assessing any one dimension alone (e.g., only technology infrastructure) misses gaps that block successful AI adoption.
mechanism: Each of the four components addresses a distinct potential failure point: under-documented processes hide automation opportunities and inefficiencies; unassessed legacy systems create hidden integration barriers; poor data quality/accessibility directly undermines AI model reliability; and unassessed AI capabilities (skills, past-initiative lessons, culture) leave organizations unable to execute even when process/system/data readiness is otherwise adequate.
operationalisation_hint: Use the four-component structure as a readiness-assessment checklist before committing to an AI-based transformation roadmap, treating each component's absence or immaturity as a distinct, separately-addressable risk rather than a single generic "AI readiness" score.
page_or_section: Section 2, Figure 2 ("Element of current state assessment"); Section 3, Figure 9

finding_statement: AI initiatives must be continuously (not one-time) aligned along three dimensions -- strategic alignment (AI initiatives tied to organizational strategic objectives), cultural alignment (AI initiatives resonate with organizational values, with explicit attention to ethics, transparency, and employee impact), and operational alignment (AI initiatives integrate smoothly with existing workflows and infrastructure) -- with responsibility shared across business, IT, data, and ethics teams rather than resting solely with IT.
mechanism: Because business strategies, technologies, and market conditions evolve, a one-time alignment check at project launch is insufficient; continuous monitoring and adjustment of AI initiatives against all three alignment dimensions is what prevents technically successful AI deployments from drifting out of strategic or cultural fit over time.
operationalisation_hint: Establish a recurring (not one-time) cross-functional review of AI initiatives against strategic objectives, cultural/ethical values, and operational workflows, with named ownership spanning business, IT, data, and ethics stakeholders.

finding_statement: AI readiness requires a structured skills pipeline: inventorying current employee skills against AI-specific technical requirements (programming, ML algorithms, statistical analysis), conducting a formal skill-gap analysis, developing targeted training/upskilling programs, evaluating the need for external AI expertise or partnerships, and creating career-development paths (mentorship, job rotation, certifications) for employees moving into AI-related roles.
mechanism: Treating skills development as a staged pipeline (inventory -> gap analysis -> training -> external augmentation -> career pathing) rather than a single generic "training" line item makes the skill-building condition actionable and auditable.

finding_statement: AI adoption success is deeply influenced by organizational culture and leadership: a supportive leadership team and a culture valuing openness, collaboration, and innovation significantly boost AI project success, while leadership resistance to change and poor cross-functional collaboration impede it; specific enabling practices include visible leadership buy-in and resource commitment, change-management strategies addressing employee fear of job displacement, a learning culture with ongoing training, a data-driven decision culture, and measuring/celebrating AI-initiative successes.
mechanism: Because AI-induced transformation is inherently a change-management exercise, culture and leadership function as the human/organizational counterpart to the more technical readiness dimensions (systems, data, skills); without them, technically ready organizations still fail to adopt AI successfully.

finding_statement: The source recommends assessing prior and ongoing AI or machine-learning initiatives, including objectives, data use, model-development practices, impact, lessons learned, and organizational effects, to inform subsequent work.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Digital transformation readiness should be understood as progression through four sequential stages: awareness (deciding to initiate DT within a strategic framework), readiness (developing a reference/maturity model revealing DT scope, gaps, and improvement areas, then assessing against it), planning (creating a roadmap by scoring assessment results against organizational goals/priorities), and execution (systematically implementing and sustaining the roadmap).
mechanism: Positioning a maturity-model assessment specifically within the "readiness" stage clarifies that maturity assessment is not itself the goal but a two-step input (reference-model development, then assessment) that only becomes actionable once translated into a scored roadmap in the planning stage.
operationalisation_hint: Map an organization's current DT activities onto the four-stage journey to identify which stage is under-resourced (e.g., an organization jumping to execution without a readiness assessment or planning roadmap).

finding_statement: The authors propose a sector-independent digital maturity model covering six dimensions and 24 sub-dimensions on a five-level scale as a response to gaps identified in their review. The paper presents it as a proposed instrument rather than a universal requirement.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 ("The New Holistic Digital Maturity Model"), Figure 16, Table 6

finding_statement: Digital governance -- including ethics and external-ecosystem management, not just organizational roles/program management/culture -- is a critical component for DT success that existing maturity models systematically under-address: ethics appeared in zero of the reviewed academic or consultancy models despite being included as a sub-dimension in the proposed model.
mechanism: As DT increasingly involves algorithmic decision-making, data use, and external-ecosystem interactions, omitting ethics and ecosystem management from governance assessment leaves an organization structurally unable to detect an entire class of transformation risk that purely structural/cultural governance dimensions do not cover.
operationalisation_hint: When auditing an organization's digital-governance readiness, explicitly check for ethics review processes and ecosystem-interaction management, not just organizational-role clarity and culture-change programs.

finding_statement: Within its examined literature corpus, the review finds limited holistic models and many sector-specific models, and calls for a systematic development approach. It does not establish the absence of every validated holistic or sector-independent model beyond that corpus.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Citing Kurmann and Arpe, the paper identifies top management support, cross-functional collaboration, flatter organizational hierarchies, and intensified people management as crucial success factors for DT implementation.
mechanism: Top management support, cross-functional collaboration, flatter hierarchies, and intensified people management supply the leadership commitment and boundary-spanning coordination needed to turn digital maturity assessment into implemented organizational change.

finding_statement: Digital transformation in manufacturing progresses through four sequential dimensions -- Awareness (external support, organizational culture/structure/strategy, top-management competence, driving the decision to initiate DT), Readiness (organizational structure/culture/leadership/strategy, people/competence, infrastructure investment, i.e. self-assessed preparedness to act), Technology Selection and Relevance (characteristics/selection/integration of digital technologies, infrastructure investment), and Operations (data security, data governance, production-system design, i.e. real-time execution/management once technology is live) -- with eleven critical factors distributed across these stages (several factors, like organizational structure/culture and infrastructure investment, recur across multiple stages).
mechanism: Sequencing the eleven factors into four stages clarifies which factors are decision-triggers (Awareness), which are internal-capability gates (Readiness), which concern technology fit (Technology Selection), and which concern sustained execution (Operations) -- addressing the paper's finding that companies commonly fail by treating DT as an undifferentiated bundle of factors rather than a staged process with different factor-emphases per stage.
operationalisation_hint: Map an organization's current DT effort onto the ARTO stages to identify which stage-appropriate factors are under-addressed (e.g., strong Awareness-stage external pressure but weak Readiness-stage infrastructure investment).
page_or_section: Section "Mapping of 11 critical factors into the ARTO model", Fig. 5; validated in "Results from survey"

finding_statement: Organizations are compelled to initiate DT by external support/pressure factors -- customer demands, competitor quality/technology adoption, industry trends, and regulatory frameworks -- which signal urgency for transformation before any internal readiness work begins.
mechanism: External pressure functions as the awareness-stage trigger distinct from internal readiness capability: an organization can face high external pressure to transform while still lacking the internal structure/culture/leadership needed to act on it, which is precisely the "high need, low readiness" pattern found problematic in case-study evidence elsewhere in the literature.
operationalisation_hint: Audit external pressure sources (customer demand shifts, competitor technology adoption, regulatory requirements) separately from internal readiness capability when diagnosing why a DT initiative has or has not gained organizational traction.

finding_statement: Readiness-stage people/organizational competence requires both leveraging existing workforce abilities and acquiring new skills through targeted training (e.g., VR-based training) and qualification of new employees, alongside team willingness to adopt new technologies and adapt to change.
mechanism: Existing workforce abilities, new skill acquisition, qualification of new employees, targeted education and training, and willingness to adopt change create the competence base that allows employees and managers to participate effectively in digital transformation rather than treating implementation as a purely technical rollout.
page_or_section: Section "Factors related to people and organizational competence"; "Readiness dimension (R)"

finding_statement: Once technology selection is complete and systems are live, sustained DT success in the Operations stage depends on data security (protecting acquired/stored/transmitted data from breaches) and data governance (ensuring data is comprehensively interpreted, securely stored, and flows consistently across the organization for decision-making) -- distinct from and downstream of the readiness-stage organizational factors.
mechanism: DT generates substantially more complex, multi-source data (internal and external) than conventional operations, and this complexity is only manageable if data governance and security practices are established as an operations-stage discipline rather than assumed to follow automatically from earlier readiness or technology-selection work.
operationalisation_hint: Treat data security and data governance as separate, operations-stage audit items even after an organization has passed readiness and technology-selection assessments successfully.
page_or_section: Section "Factors related to data governance"; "Operations dimension (O)"

finding_statement: The cited literature describes financial and expertise constraints for SMEs, while the study's own participant results report company size as less significant for infrastructure investment. The finding should therefore be treated as mixed evidence rather than a general size-contingent barrier.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: For resource-constrained SMEs, transformation-readiness sensing capability can be externally supplied by innovation intermediaries via an "ancillary opportunity spotting capability": intermediaries spot opportunities to develop digital technologies addressing business, environmental, or social challenges of other ecosystem actors, through which SME digital transformation is achieved only indirectly (the transformation opportunity is a by-product of a differently-framed collaboration).
mechanism: Because intermediaries have better ecosystem-wide visibility of actors, technology trends, and opportunities than any single resource-constrained SME, they can identify collaboration opportunities framed around a shared ecosystem challenge (e.g., carbon-neutral solutions) that indirectly pulls SMEs into digital transformation -- a sensing mechanism SMEs could not access alone due to lacking internal R&D and innovation-network access.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an SME's DT sensing capability, check not only internal scanning capacity but also its connectedness to innovation intermediaries capable of ancillary opportunity spotting on its behalf.

finding_statement: For SMEs, seizing capability for digital transformation can be externally supplied via intermediaries' "business model co-creation capability": intermediaries co-create SME business models in direct collaboration with SME stakeholders (customers, suppliers, and even competitors), translating sensed opportunities into resourced action that individual SMEs could not mobilize alone.
mechanism: Intermediaries are well-connected in the ecosystem, experienced in business-model innovation, and able to source complementary actors with relevant resources, which lets them overcome the specific resource barriers SMEs face when trying to seize opportunities identified through ancillary sensing.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether an SME's seizing capability includes access to an intermediary-facilitated business-model co-creation process involving its own customers/suppliers/competitors, not just internal resource-commitment capacity.
page_or_section: Section 4.3 ("Business model co-creation capability") [continues past truncated excerpt; see Table 3 aggregated theme "Integrating resources and building ecosystem collaborations"]

finding_statement: For continued and scaled-up SME digital transformation, intermediaries leverage an "ecosystem revamping capability": altering opportunity and ecosystem structures, bridging inter-ecosystem collaborations, and deploying international best practices to benchmark and restructure the local ecosystem -- moving the locus of transformation capability from the individual organization to the ecosystem level.
mechanism: Because scaling up SME digital transformation requires changes beyond what any single SME or even a single collaboration project can achieve, intermediaries reconfigure the broader ecosystem structure itself (adding members, altering governance mechanisms, connecting to other regional ecosystems) as the mechanism for sustaining and scaling transformation over time.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an SME ecosystem's transformation-sustainability, check for intermediary-led ecosystem-restructuring activity (inter-ecosystem bridging, international benchmarking) in addition to individual-organization transformation capability.
page_or_section: Section on "Ecosystem revamping capability" (aggregated theme: "Revamping ecosystem structure and scaling up digital opportunities"), Table 3

finding_statement: SMEs face internal barriers to digital transformation -- a lack of strategic thinking (driven by focus on short-term benefits) and the expensive, complicated nature of the DT process -- compounded by ecosystem-level barriers: a lack of ability within the ecosystem to spot DT opportunities and identify/assemble relevant competencies, technologies, resources, and actors; a lack of collaboration skills, knowledge, experience, network, and resources; and a lack of mechanisms for scaling up ecosystem collaboration for enhanced SME DT.
mechanism: These barriers compound because they operate at two levels simultaneously: even an SME motivated to transform (having overcome the internal short-termism barrier) still depends on an ecosystem that itself may lack the opportunity-spotting, collaboration, and scaling capabilities needed to support that transformation -- which is precisely the gap that motivates the need for specialized intermediary capabilities.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an SME's DT initiative stalls, separately assess internal strategic-thinking/resource barriers and ecosystem-level opportunity-spotting/collaboration/scaling barriers, since intermediary support addresses the latter but not necessarily the former.
page_or_section: Section 4.1 and Table 3 ("Contextual factors": "Barriers in ecosystem collaboration", "SMEs' internal barriers to digital transformation")

mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.

finding_statement: For SMEs, the sensing phase of digital transformation is operationalized through a formal need assessment -- using tools (e.g., the ApuaDigiin.fi self-assessment tool) or structured processes to understand current business limitations, market circumstances, and objectives -- before committing to a digital transformation strategy, since "one-fits-all" approaches do not match SME-specific needs.
mechanism: A structured need assessment turns sensing from an informal managerial intuition into an explicit diagnostic step: SMEs compare current limitations, market circumstances, business objectives, and improvement needs before selecting a digital transformation strategy.
operationalisation_hint: Use a structured need-assessment tool or process (digital-readiness self-assessment, benchmarking) as the concrete SME-appropriate operationalization of sensing capability, rather than assuming sensing occurs informally.

finding_statement: For SMEs, the seizing phase of digital transformation requires IT-business alignment (ensuring planned technology investment matches actual business needs, preventing mis-investment or over-investment) combined with a research-and-experimentation cycle -- learning, aligning, and innovating iteratively -- until the new digital tool fits the business model.
mechanism: Explicit IT-business alignment checks before committing to technology investment prevent the common SME failure mode of adopting technology that does not match business orientation or service demands, while the research-and-experimentation cycle provides a lower-risk, iterative path to fit that resource-constrained SMEs can sustain.
page_or_section: Section "Learning, digital capability, and alignment"; conceptual-framework "seizing phase" discussion

finding_statement: For resource-constrained SMEs, the transforming phase of digital transformation is best pursued through frugal innovation (small, gradual, resource-appropriate changes using existing internal "atom enablers" rather than large-scale transformation) combined with explicit change management to prepare employees for new business processes (supply chain, production, sales, accounting, customer relationship management).
mechanism: Frugal, incremental innovation is a resource-appropriate substitute for large-scale transformation specifically because SMEs have limited resources; pursuing gradual change while learning about further innovations needed for bigger improvements avoids overextending SME capacity in a single transformation effort.
page_or_section: Section "Transforming phase" discussion (frugal innovation, change management)

finding_statement: Construction-industry digital transformation readiness should be organized across three levels: operational (routine phase-specific activities digitalized via specific technologies, e.g., drones/AI/BIM/IoT/robotics, forming the technological foundation), executive (middle management securing budget and defining policies, standards, and common data infrastructure needed to obtain return from the technology investment), and strategic (top-level vision integration, technology-adoption and resource-allocation decisions, and change-management leadership that defines the organization's digital transformation trajectory).
mechanism: Technology investment at the operational level only pays off if the executive level secures the policies/standards/infrastructure that let it be used properly, and the executive level in turn only functions if the strategic level has committed vision, resources, and change-management leadership -- meaning readiness gaps at any one level (e.g., strong technology adoption without policy/infrastructure support) undermine the digital transformation regardless of investment at other levels.
operationalisation_hint: Assess an organization's DT readiness separately at the operational (technology-in-use), executive (policy/standards/infrastructure), and strategic (vision/resource-allocation/change-leadership) levels rather than treating "digital readiness" as a single undifferentiated construct.
page_or_section: Section 6, "The Digital Transformation Level of Readiness Framework (DTLRF)", Figure 3

finding_statement: Among five factor categories assessed by construction-industry experts, policy and regulation had the highest proportion of factors rated "extremely important" (66.6%), ahead of management (53.3%), technology implementation (37.5%), design (37.5%), and infrastructure (33.3%) -- comprising an internal training structure to upskill personnel, defined technical standards to enhance synergy across efforts, an organizational strategy demonstrating leadership commitment, and incentive programs for internal/external buy-in.
mechanism: Policy and regulation functions as the foundational enabling layer because it establishes the standards, skills, and leadership commitment that technology, design, and infrastructure investments depend on to generate value -- explaining why experts rated it more consistently critical than the technology factors that typically receive the most attention/investment.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing DT readiness investment in construction organizations, treat internal policy/standards/training/incentive development as at least as high a priority as technology procurement, using this study's expert-consensus ranking as a benchmark.
page_or_section: Section 5 ("Results and Interpretation"), policy and regulation discussion

finding_statement: Digital transformation readiness in construction should be assessed separately for each of three project lifecycle phases -- pre-construction (drones, BIM, AI, GIS, VR for design/planning), construction (IoT, robotics, 3D printing, AR/VR for on-site execution), and facility management (BIM/digital-twin integration, IoT/RFID, AI-driven sensing/actuation for asset operation) -- since experts rated construction-phase factors as most consistently "extremely important" (65%), followed by facility management (55%) and pre-construction (46%).
mechanism: Because each phase relies on functionally different technologies and yields different readiness priorities (e.g., stakeholder-engagement/design tools in pre-construction vs. on-site monitoring/safety tools in construction vs. asset-monitoring tools in facility management), a single undifferentiated "construction industry DT readiness" score would obscure which phase is driving or lagging overall organizational readiness.
operationalisation_hint: Score DT readiness separately for pre-construction, construction, and facility-management phases and use the phase-specific technology lists as a checklist, rather than computing one aggregate construction-industry readiness score.
page_or_section: Section 2.2 (phase-specific factor sections) and Section 5, Figure 2

finding_statement: A common data management system for connectivity, storage, and control/monitoring dashboards must span the pre-construction, construction, and facility-management phases as data accumulates across the project lifecycle, since facility-management digitalization cannot occur without appropriate connection infrastructure already established during the construction phase.
mechanism: Because data generated in earlier phases (e.g., BIM models from pre-construction, sensor data from construction) must remain accessible and usable in later phases (facility management), infrastructure that is phase-siloed rather than lifecycle-spanning creates a structural barrier to full digital transformation regardless of how digitally mature any single phase is.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether data infrastructure (storage, connectivity, control dashboards) is designed to persist and remain accessible across all three lifecycle phases, not just within the phase where it originates.

finding_statement: Construction-industry experts rated training structures to upskill and reskill existing human resources, and to close skills gaps concerning new technologies, as a critical component of the policy/regulation factor category necessary for successful digital transformation, alongside government/organizational intervention to define necessary skills and ensure strategic alignment between digital transformation and the workforce.
mechanism: Training structures, upskilling/reskilling programs, and explicit workforce alignment convert technology adoption into usable construction capability by closing skills gaps and preparing personnel for phase-specific digital tools.

finding_statement: Because SMEs typically lack the resources or capabilities to reach high maturity across all organizational processes simultaneously, evaluating maturity separately by dimension (rather than only as a single aggregate organizational score) lets an SME be at different maturity levels in different dimensions simultaneously, enabling it to identify and prioritize the specific dimensions most in need of improvement.
mechanism: A single aggregate maturity score would obscure which specific dimension (e.g., People vs. Digital Technologies) is the binding constraint on overall progress; dimension-level scoring gives SMEs a focused improvement pathway suited to their limited capacity for simultaneous improvement across all areas.
operationalisation_hint: Report and act on maturity scores at both the aggregate organizational level and the individual-dimension level, prioritizing improvement investment in the lowest-scoring dimension(s) rather than spreading effort evenly.

finding_statement: In the assessed Brazilian furniture manufacturer, digital culture, open innovation, employee digital skills, and worker acceptance were among the processes below the Managed-level target. The paper proposes targeted culture, training, and change-management actions for that case.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.

finding_statement: Employee-level transformation readiness follows a temporal causal chain -- past experience with digitalization shapes employee sentiment (stimulus), which shapes cognitive and emotional predispositions toward digital transformation (organism), which in turn determines employees' willingness to participate in DT initiatives (response) -- validated empirically (positive, significant path coefficients) in medium-to-large enterprises in both the US and Vietnam, with no significant cross-country difference.
mechanism: Because a DT initiative itself is too complex, novel, and ambiguous at the outset to function as a direct stimulus employees can evaluate, employees instead rely on their accumulated, fuzzy, gist-based appraisal of prior digitalization experiences as the reference point from which predispositions -- and ultimately willingness to participate -- are formed, even before a formal DT initiative is announced.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing organizational transformation readiness, audit employees' sentiment toward *prior* digitalization efforts (not just attitudes toward the upcoming DT initiative itself), since this prior sentiment is the empirically-demonstrated leading indicator of future participation willingness.
page_or_section: Section 2.3 ("What leads to employee participation") and Section 3 ("Model development"); Fig. 1-2; Results Section 5

finding_statement: Employee sentiment toward digitalization -- the empirically-validated driver of DT predispositions -- decomposes into three psychological-need dimensions grounded in self-determination theory: autonomy (empowerment to act independently plus freedom to innovate/experiment), competence (learning/skill acquisition plus adaptability to navigate uncertainty), and relatedness (communication quality plus cross-functional cooperation) -- each need frustrated or fulfilled by how prior digitalization efforts were experienced.
mechanism: Because these three needs are theorized and empirically supported as universal across employees (not technology- or context-specific), they provide a transferable, measurable readiness-assessment lens: assessing whether past digitalization empowered vs. constrained employees, built vs. stagnated their skills, and connected vs. isolated them predicts future DT participation willingness better than assessing attitudes toward the specific incoming technology.
operationalisation_hint: Operationalize employee-level DT readiness assessment via six sub-dimensions: empowerment, innovation (autonomy); learning, adaptability (competence); communication, cooperation (relatedness) -- scored against employees' experience of prior digitalization efforts specifically, not the pending DT initiative.

finding_statement: The paper critiques accounts that frame participation chiefly as the result of structured interventions, arguing that emotions and prior digitalization experiences also shape willingness to participate. It does not establish that structured interventions only produce surface compliance.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Employee participation in the initial stages of a DT initiative -- before new work practices become routinized -- is disproportionately consequential: early engagement lets employees shape the transformation's direction, fosters ownership that reduces later resistance, and allows organizations to proactively address emerging risks via bottom-up input, whereas after routinization, employees are reduced to executors of fixed procedures with severely restricted opportunity to influence or resist, making early non-participation predictive of sustained disengagement and blame-shifting if the initiative later fails.
mechanism: The dynamics of change are most fluid and open to influence during early phases; once routinized, changes become non-negotiable fixed procedures, which structurally forecloses the window during which participation could have prevented resistance -- meaning organizations that defer employee engagement until implementation or rollout have already lost the highest-leverage opportunity to secure buy-in.
operationalisation_hint: Prioritize securing employee participation (planning input, feedback channels, cross-functional support roles) specifically during the pre-routinization early stage of a DT initiative, treating post-rollout participation efforts as a structurally weaker substitute.
page_or_section: Section 2.2.2 ("Importance of employee participation in the initial stages of digital transformation")

finding_statement: Digital transformation assessment models conflate two distinct constructs that should be measured separately: maturity, which measures how far an organization has progressed in implementing something (e.g., how deployed a CRM platform is), and readiness, which measures whether the behaviors necessary to maximize the results of that implementation are present and consistently practiced (e.g., whether the organization actually uses the CRM to embed customer insights in decision-making) -- a review of 24 existing models found most fail to separate these constructs, defaulting readiness to "being finished" rather than "being ready to adopt change."
mechanism: Because maturity captures deployment status while readiness captures whether an organization has internalized the behaviors needed to extract value from that deployment, a technically mature implementation with low behavioral readiness will fail to generate expected returns -- explaining why organizations with similar technology adoption levels achieve divergent DT outcomes, and why over 70% of DT initiatives reportedly fail to reach expected value despite technology being in place.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's DT status, score maturity (deployment/implementation progress) and readiness (behavioral consistency in leveraging what is deployed) as two separate, non-substitutable metrics rather than a single combined maturity score.
page_or_section: Section "Readiness as a set of behaviors", Table 1

finding_statement: SME digital-transformation readiness should be assessed across five categories -- Business Model (business structure, products/services, innovation), Market (customers, value proposition, go-to-market), Strategy (strategic planning, change management, transformation, organizational strategy, technology), Organization (organizational structure, people, culture, collaboration, leadership), and Processes (process management, monitoring/control, governance) -- decomposed into 20 subcategories, each with literature-derived target behaviors condensed into a single user-friendly "behavior north star" statement that non-expert employees can rate their organization against.
mechanism: Converting literature-derived target behaviors (often technical, bulleted lists) into a single accessible "north star" statement per subcategory makes the assessment usable by general employees (not just management or DT specialists) in resource-constrained SMEs that lack dedicated assessment expertise, directly targeting the "simple enough for any SME to use" design principle.
operationalisation_hint: Use the 20 north-star statements as a lightweight, non-technical readiness questionnaire that any SME employee (not only senior management) can complete, rather than requiring specialist facilitation.
page_or_section: Sections "Categories and subcategories" and "Target behaviors of each subcategory", Tables 3-6

finding_statement: Organizational readiness at the subcategory level should be scored along two independent dimensions -- how frequently a target behavior occurs and how consistently/deliberately it is managed (versus occurring accidentally) -- mapped onto a 1-10 Likert scale that aggregates into four qualitative levels: Immature (behavior absent/no action), Unstructured (behavior sometimes present, evolving), Structured (behavior often present, evolving toward advanced), and Advanced (behavior consistently present, measured, and continuously improved), with the transition from Unstructured to Structured representing the largest single step in the model.
mechanism: Separating frequency from management-consistency lets an assessment distinguish between a behavior that happens by chance (high frequency, low management -- e.g., ad hoc innovation) and one that is deliberately embedded (both dimensions high), which a single-axis maturity scale cannot distinguish; the model treats vertical progress (better management) and horizontal progress (higher frequency) as two independent improvement paths.
operationalisation_hint: Score each of the 20 subcategories on both frequency and management-consistency axes separately, using the resulting four-level color-coded classification (red/orange/yellow/green) to identify whether a subcategory's gap is a frequency problem or a management-consistency problem.
page_or_section: Section "Readiness levels and measuring dimensions", Figs. 3-4
