finding_statement: Because prior DT readiness/maturity models predominantly reflect senior management's view of progress, a readiness assessment should separately capture general employees' perceptions of target behaviors and compare them against senior management's perceptions, since a persistent gap between employee and management perspectives on readiness for change has been shown to play a vital role in whether change is successfully implemented.
mechanism: Senior management may perceive a behavior (e.g., "innovation is embraced") as present because it is stated in strategy documents, while employees who actually execute daily work may perceive its absence in practice; comparing both perspectives surfaces this gap directly rather than relying on a single (management) viewpoint that risks being systematically over-optimistic.
operationalisation_hint: Administer the readiness questionnaire to both general employees and senior management separately, and treat divergence between the two groups' scores on the same subcategory as a specific, actionable readiness gap rather than averaging them into one score.
page_or_section: Introduction and "Proposed readiness assessment model" sections

finding_statement: The longitudinal case documents reconfiguration between centralization and decentralization in digital-transformation governance. It presents this as a contingent pattern in the studied organization, not a universal organizational capability.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Purely top-down, centrally mandated digital transformation strategy is insufficient in multi-business firms; sustained transformation instead depends on ongoing, context-sensitive negotiation between corporate strategic direction and business-unit execution, with business units adapting corporate initiatives to their own operational constraints and customer realities.
mechanism: Business units closer to products and customers face different market conditions, legacy constraints, and profit-margin logics than the corporate level; strategies imposed without accounting for this diversity generate strategic drift, ownership gaps, and resistance (e.g., "not-invented-here" behavior).

finding_statement: Organizations need an explicit capability for pacing, sequencing, and synchronizing digital initiatives with customer and market readiness; deploying digital product features ahead of demonstrated customer readiness results in low activation/uptake even when the technology itself is mature.
mechanism: One business unit achieved near-universal embedded connectivity in its products but observed customer activation rates below 1%, showing that technological deployment and market/customer readiness can be decoupled, undermining the value case for the transformation.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether digital feature rollout is paired with customer segmentation, education, and staged commercialization rather than being driven by technology availability alone.

finding_statement: Embedding digital/connectivity features into existing products is necessary but not sufficient for value capture; monetizing digital innovation requires a separate, harder transformation of the business model (e.g., from one-off product sales to subscription or outcome-based service models), which firms may fail to achieve even after successful technology integration.
mechanism: Existing transactional, profit-margin-driven business logics actively constrain the adoption of new pricing/ownership models (subscription, pay-per-use, outcome-based), so technology integration alone leaves the value-capture problem unresolved.

finding_statement: Beyond formal structural adjustments, sustained transformation depends on localized experimentation (trial-and-error, agile pilots, cross-category steering groups, grassroots cross-unit meetings) that gradually builds new practices, competencies, and collaboration norms even where formal structures lag behind.
mechanism: Formal restructuring alone does not resolve coordination tensions; iterative, path-dependent learning loops at the working level (e.g., minimally-viable-product pilots, informal cross-category meetings) are what actually embed new digital-era routines into day-to-day operation.
operationalisation_hint: Look for evidence of bottom-up practices (pilots, informal cross-unit forums, incrementally shortened development cycles) alongside top-down structural changes, not as a substitute for them.

finding_statement: Digital transformation success is not explained by any single factor but by the joint configuration of leadership vision, digital culture, workforce skills, process/structure redesign, and technological infrastructure, with the effectiveness of this configuration moderated by institutional, industry, organizational, and personal-level contingencies.
mechanism: The same driver, strategy element, or actor can produce different outcomes depending on context (e.g., competitive pressure accelerates transformation in turbulent sectors but only produces incremental change in stable ones; a CDO is effective in flexible governance systems but constrained in rigid hierarchies) -- treating any one element as sufficient on its own misrepresents how transformation actually succeeds.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's transformation-enabling conditions, evaluate the alignment/configuration across leadership, culture, skills, process, and technology jointly, and explicitly note the institutional/industry/organizational/personal contingencies that would moderate their effectiveness, rather than scoring conditions independently.

finding_statement: Organizations formulating a digital transformation strategy follow (or should follow) staged phases: sensing the drivers that make transformation necessary, assessing current digital maturity (via audits, capability analysis, benchmarking, involving both internal and external stakeholders), seizing opportunities by defining vision and strategy, running pilot projects/proof-of-concepts before enterprise-wide rollout, and treating the process as continuous (ongoing KPI evaluation) rather than a one-time initiative.
mechanism: Skipping maturity assessment or piloting increases the risk of misaligned, over-scaled initiatives; treating transformation as a one-time project rather than continuous evaluation risks losing track of whether strategy remains fit for a fast-changing environment.
operationalisation_hint: Check whether an organization's DT strategy process includes an explicit current-state maturity assessment step and a pilot-before-scale step, not just a vision/strategy document.

finding_statement: Beyond appointing a Chief Digital Officer (CDO), organizations benefit from establishing a dedicated cross-functional digital transformation/innovation unit (DTU/DIU), typically led by the CDO, that plans, regulates, and coordinates digitalization across business functions -- distinct in mandate from the traditional IT department, which continues to handle legacy systems, infrastructure, and operational stability.
mechanism: Cross-functional units break down departmental silos and build the dynamic capabilities needed for transformation; conflating this mandate with traditional IT (whose incentives favor operational stability) creates tension between the need for stability and the need for rapid innovation, which some firms resolve via a "bimodal IT" split.
operationalisation_hint: Check for an organizational unit with an explicit cross-functional digitalization coordination mandate, separate from (but coordinated with) core IT operations.

finding_statement: The review presents Chief Digital Officer effectiveness as contingent on unified executive commitment and governance flexibility. It does not directly establish that externally hired CDOs outperform internal promotions.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Barriers such as legacy IT systems, cultural inertia/resistance, workforce skill gaps, and regulatory/compliance complexity do not merely slow transformation -- they actively reshape which strategies are viable and how actor roles must be adjusted, and their intensity is itself moderated by organizational hierarchy, size, and prior change experience (e.g., resistance cascades more strongly in centralized, hierarchical organizations).
mechanism: Because barriers interact with and constrain the feasible strategy/actor configuration rather than being independent negative factors to subtract, transformation planning that treats barriers as a simple checklist to mitigate (rather than as boundary conditions shaping strategy design) will misjudge feasible transformation paths.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness, evaluate whether identified barriers (legacy systems, cultural resistance, skills gaps, regulatory complexity) are being treated as strategy-shaping design constraints, and check whether the organization's hierarchy/size context would amplify or dampen their effect.
page_or_section: Section "Challenges and Barriers of Digital Transformation"; Discussion

finding_statement: Across 47 reviewed studies, institutional readiness (ICT infrastructure, leadership commitment, organizational culture, funding, governance structures) was the most consistently emphasized determinant (present in 38/47 studies, 80.9%) and functions as a mediating mechanism: digital competencies provide capacity, but institutional readiness determines whether that capacity is activated into effective transformation outcomes -- competencies alone were insufficient without it.
mechanism: Institutions with coherent digital strategies and strong leadership achieved sustainable, integrated outcomes, while institutions with weak readiness produced fragmented, short-lived initiatives regardless of the digital competencies present; the COVID-19 period further showed readiness (not raw technology access) determined institutional resilience and continuity.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing transformation potential, treat institutional readiness as a gating/mediating condition to check before crediting digital competency levels as sufficient evidence of transformation capacity.

finding_statement: Investment in digital infrastructure alone does not produce sustainable transformation in the absence of governance coherence and cultural alignment; furthermore, digital transformation policy models transplanted from high-income/Global North contexts into structurally different (e.g., resource-constrained, regulatorily unstable) settings frequently fail, producing implementation gaps rather than the intended outcomes.
mechanism: Regulatory instability, funding limitations, and constrained institutional autonomy in resource-constrained contexts undermine readiness even when infrastructure or policy templates are nominally in place, because those templates assume institutional and governance conditions that do not hold locally.
operationalisation_hint: Assess digital transformation plans for governance coherence, cultural fit, regulatory stability, institutional autonomy, and local resource constraints before assuming infrastructure spending or imported policy templates will translate into public value.

finding_statement: For technologies exhibiting high operational opacity and unpredictable emergent capabilities (e.g., Gen-AI), the organization replaces planned "technology enablement" with continuous Adaptive Sensemaking: an action-first cycle of small-scale experimentation followed by retrospective interpretation to construct a plausible, evolving understanding of the technology's behavior.
mechanism: When a technology's capabilities and internal logic cannot be known in advance, waiting for "predictable convergence" before acting is no longer viable; only iterative probe-and-learn experimentation generates the data needed to understand and exploit the technology's potential.
operationalisation_hint: Applies specifically as a boundary condition: check whether the technology in question exhibits high opacity + emergent (non-linear) capability growth before treating this condition as relevant; for stable/predictable technologies (e.g., standard cloud, ERP), traditional planned-enablement conditions remain more applicable.

finding_statement: Under conditions of extreme technological uncertainty, sustained advantage depends on a higher-order "Dynamic Adaptive Capability" (DAC) -- the organizational capacity to reconfigure its own learning processes -- rather than on possessing specific static resources or even classic Dynamic Capabilities (sensing/seizing/reconfiguring), whose core mechanisms presuppose some baseline predictability that Gen-AI-level uncertainty removes.
mechanism: Classic Dynamic Capabilities theory assumes firms can "sense" signals and "seize" opportunities from an environment that is dynamic but ultimately intelligible; under Foundational Uncertainty there may be no stable signal to sense, so a second-order capability -- learning how to adapt when the nature of change itself is unknowable -- becomes the operative condition.
operationalisation_hint: Distinguish, when assessing an organization's adaptive capability, whether it has built processes for reconfiguring specific resources/routines (classic DC) versus processes for reconfiguring its own learning/discovery processes (DAC) -- the latter is the condition specific to extreme-uncertainty technology contexts.

finding_statement: Organizations operating under Foundational Uncertainty reallocate resources from large-scale, multi-year IT implementation projects toward funding many small, agile, cross-functional experimentation teams, and must redesign financial/strategic control systems (moving away from NPV/stage-gate reviews) to legitimize "learning" itself as a valid, fundable project outcome even without near-term ROI.
mechanism: Traditional capital budgeting processes are designed to select projects with predictable positive returns and are structurally incompatible with a learning-first approach where outcomes are inherently unpredictable; without redesigning these control systems, experimentation initiatives will be starved of legitimate funding.
operationalisation_hint: Check whether an organization's capital allocation process has an explicit funding category for open-ended experimentation/learning, distinct from traditional ROI-gated project appraisal.

finding_statement: Because commoditized AI tools themselves confer little advantage, organizations build Dynamic Adaptive Capability primarily through human-capability investment structured around three pillars: broad AI-literacy education for all employees, psychological safety that reframes intelligent failure as valuable learning, and deliberate human-AI collaboration ("hybrid intelligence") design -- elevating HR/Learning & Development to a strategic role alongside the CTO.
mechanism: If the ultimate source of advantage is the organizational process of adaptation (not the technology itself), then the people and culture that enact that process become the primary locus of competitive advantage, making HR/L&D as critical to transformation as technology leadership.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether digital transformation investment allocates meaningfully to AI literacy programs, explicit failure-tolerance/psychological-safety practices, and human-AI task design, not solely to technology procurement or CTO-led infrastructure.

finding_statement: Large, diversified enterprises do not face a single technological environment but a portfolio of them, and may need to manage stable, predictable technologies (e.g., ERP systems) via traditional rational, plan-driven methods while simultaneously engaging frontier technologies (e.g., Gen-AI) via dynamic, adaptive processes -- requiring an as-yet-unexplored meta-capability for operating under internally conflicting strategic logics, cultures, incentive systems, and capital budgeting processes at once.
mechanism: The cultures, incentives, and budgeting processes suited to rational-mastery transformation are often antithetical to those needed for dynamic-adaptive transformation; applying a single transformation paradigm uniformly across an enterprise's full technology portfolio risks either stifling frontier experimentation or destabilizing stable core operations.
operationalisation_hint: Segment the enterprise technology portfolio by uncertainty/stability and apply different governance, budgeting, incentive, and learning routines to stable core systems versus frontier Gen-AI initiatives.

finding_statement: Organisational benefits from EA depend on the Quality of EA Service Provision -- the extent to which the EA team effectively and efficiently provides IT decision-makers with relevant, timely, high-quality information and advice -- rather than on the mere existence of EA artefacts/documents. This quality construct has three sub-dimensions: EA content quality (what is conveyed), EA communication quality (how it is conveyed), and EA process quality (how it is produced).
mechanism: Teams that treat EA as document production ("ivory tower") fail to be sought out for advice; teams that adopt a service mindset -- becoming trusted advisors proactively embedded in governance and decision processes -- are the ones organisations credit with driving IS decision quality, project delivery, and platform improvements.
operationalisation_hint: Assess EA maturity via service-orientation indicators: whether decision-makers proactively seek out the EA team, whether EA content/communication is tailored to stakeholder needs, and whether the EA team has a clear mandate and efficient internal process -- not merely whether EA artefacts exist.

finding_statement: High-quality EA service improves IS decision-making by (1) creating a transparent, structured decision process that identifies and involves the right stakeholders, (2) providing objective, documented information about the current IS platform and interdependencies to inform decisions, and (3) educating decision-makers on good IT investment practices.
mechanism: Without EA, decision groups rely on unstructured argument among stakeholders with no objective criteria, prolonging decisions and leaving conflicts unresolved; EA principles and documented facts give decision-makers a shared basis for faster, less contested choices.
operationalisation_hint: Check for: a defined stakeholder-identification process for major IT investment decisions, EA principles guiding those decisions (with documented deviations requiring business justification), and an EA team playing an active advisory/educational role in decision forums (e.g., architecture review boards).

finding_statement: High-quality EA service improves IS project delivery by (1) improving project coordination through contextual awareness of interdependencies across the project portfolio (enabling sequencing, avoiding duplicated investment, reducing unanticipated delays) and (2) accelerating individual projects through guiding standards, reusable prototypes, and narrowed solution-selection options at project initiation.
mechanism: Projects run without EA context risk discovering late-stage dependencies ("surprises") that cause overruns; EA-guided standards narrow the design-space early, cutting discovery and evaluation time in the initiation phase specifically.
operationalisation_hint: Look for EA involvement in project-portfolio sequencing/prioritization and for documented standards/reusable components that measurably shorten project initiation phases (e.g., cited 30-60% shortening in one case in the source).

finding_statement: High-quality EA service improves the quality of the organisation's IS platform along four dimensions: alignment of the platform to business needs, platform flexibility (modularity/decoupling enabling reconfiguration), IS resource utilisation (reduced duplication, better reuse), and IS resource complementarity (synergistic, mutually reinforcing IT resource bundles) -- together yielding the largest potential organisational benefits (cost reduction, strategic agility, competitive differentiation via causally ambiguous, hard-to-imitate resource configurations).
mechanism: An organisation-wide view of shared capabilities and interdependencies (rather than project-by-project or business-unit-by-business-unit investment) prevents both under-fit local systems and costly duplication, and lets the organisation deliberately build complementary resource bundles that are difficult for competitors to replicate due to causal ambiguity.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether IT investment decisions are made with an explicit organisation-wide (not just business-unit or project) view of shared capabilities, duplication, and resource complementarity.

finding_statement: EA's causal impact is strongest and most directly measurable on IS decision-making (Mechanism 1), weaker but more tangibly quantifiable on IS project delivery (Mechanism 2), and hardest to isolate causally -- yet potentially most valuable strategically -- on IS platform quality (Mechanism 3), because platform-level benefits depend on the cumulative success of many projects over years plus IT governance, strategic stability, and other confounding factors.
mechanism: Because the mechanism with the clearest, quickest causal link (decision-making) yields relatively modest organisational benefits, while the mechanism with the largest potential organisational benefits (IS platform) has the longest lead time and most confounds, EA teams face a structural difficulty in demonstrating and justifying their value -- project delivery (Mechanism 2) is proposed as the best available middle ground for demonstrating "quick wins" while working toward long-term platform "big wins."
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating EA's contribution to enterprise transformation, do not expect that the mechanism with the clearest evidence (decision-making) is also the one delivering the largest strategic benefit (platform quality); use project-delivery metrics as an intermediate, more tractable proxy for EA value while platform-level benefits accrue over a longer horizon.

finding_statement: Conducting EA is associated with a statistically significant positive increase in business-IT alignment (BITA) maturity across all six Luftman-model dimensions -- communications, competency/value measurement, governance, partnership, scope and architecture, and skills -- with EA-to-BITA path coefficients of 0.51-0.81 (all p<0.01) and an overall EA-to-BITA path coefficient of 0.735.
mechanism: EA provides a structured, evidence-based planning discipline (shared vision, current-state documentation, roadmap) that gives business and IT a common basis for coordinating investment, governance, and communication decisions, which is what the Luftman BITA components measure.
operationalisation_hint: Use before/after (or maturity-delta) comparison on Luftman's six BITA components as a quantifiable proxy for whether an EA initiative is functioning as an alignment-enabling condition.

finding_statement: Among the six BITA dimensions, EA had its largest positive effect on 'scope and architecture' (technical/standardization dimension, delta=1.61, largest path coefficient 0.81) and 'partnership' (delta=1.49), and its smallest effect on 'skills' (human-resource/training dimension, delta=0.58, smallest path coefficient 0.51) -- consistent across business-manager, IT-manager, business-staff, and IT-staff respondent subgroups.
mechanism: EA is fundamentally a planning and standardization activity centered on architecture artefacts and cross-unit coordination, not a training or human-capital-development activity, so its direct effect is concentrated on structural/architectural alignment dimensions rather than workforce skills.
operationalisation_hint: When using EA investment as a lever for BITA improvement, do not expect it to substitute for dedicated skills/training programs; pair EA initiatives with separate human-capital interventions if the skills dimension of alignment is the priority.

finding_statement: Performing EA moved median BITA maturity from levels 1-2 up to levels 3-4 (on Luftman's 5-level CMMI-based scale) but not further, indicating EA by itself cannot bring an organization to the highest alignment maturity levels; the authors explicitly conclude that greater BITA maturity requires the contribution of the other two recognized alignment approaches -- 'relationship' and 'governance' -- in addition to EA ('architecture').
mechanism: BITA maturity models decompose alignment into architecture, governance, and relationship-based mechanisms; EA addresses only the architecture leg, so even a successful EA initiative leaves governance- and relationship-specific gaps unaddressed.
operationalisation_hint: Do not treat a mature EA practice as sufficient evidence of overall business-IT alignment maturity; check specifically for complementary IT governance mechanisms (cf. De Haes & Van Grembergen 2008, corpus_id 1285, batch S7-B001) and relationship/partnership-building practices alongside EA.

finding_statement: In the multi-country study, overall paths from geography, industry, and EA framework choice to business-IT-alignment maturity were near zero and non-significant. Some component-level controls were significant, so robustness should not be claimed for every dimension or framework choice.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Successfully transforming toward a target (data-driven) business model requires developing business and technology capabilities in an integrated, mutually aligned way across all enterprise architecture layers (business model, business processes, people & applications, data & information, infrastructure) matched to a concretely defined target-state archetype -- not simply maximizing maturity in any single layer.
mechanism: Because a target business model requires specific combinations of capabilities across layers (e.g., a "recommendation provider" needs both customer-facing monetization capabilities and predictive-analytics infrastructure), maturity in one layer without corresponding maturity in others leaves the target state unreachable regardless of how advanced the developed layer becomes.
operationalisation_hint: Assess transformation readiness by capability alignment across EA layers relative to a concrete target-state archetype, not by an aggregate or single-layer maturity score.

finding_statement: Two contrasting real-world transformation approaches were observed: a "business first" path (driven by customer demand, starting with strategic vision, value proposition, and new roles at the upper/business layers) which leaves technical/data capabilities (analytics tooling, data quality, machine connectivity rollout) underdeveloped; and a "data first" path (driven by technical affordances and early infrastructure investment, e.g., machine connectivity and data warehousing) which leaves business-side capabilities (monetization/pricing, digital channel management, customer culture) underdeveloped and market realization highly uncertain.
mechanism: Each path is driven by whichever side of the organization initiates the transformation (customer/business demand vs. available technical affordances), and that initiating side naturally develops matching capabilities first while the other side is neglected until it becomes the visible bottleneck blocking further progress toward the target business model.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing a stalled DT/DDBM initiative, check which "side" (business vs. technology) initiated the transformation, since that predicts which capability gaps (technical/data vs. business/monetization) are most likely to be blocking progress.

finding_statement: Management should actively work to minimize the divergence between business-side and technology-side capability maturity during a transformation, rather than allowing one side to advance far ahead of the other, since capability misalignment (in either direction) was found to slow or limit realization of the target business model at both studied manufacturers.
mechanism: Missing "building blocks" of capability on the lagging side (e.g., data analytics competencies on the business-first path, or monetization/channel capabilities on the data-first path) become the binding constraint on transformation progress even when the leading side is highly mature.
operationalisation_hint: Track capability maturity on both business and technology sides in parallel during a DT/DDBM initiative and treat a growing gap between them as an early-warning signal requiring corrective investment, rather than continuing to invest predominantly in the already-stronger side.

finding_statement: Across 47 organizations, the number of architects correlates strongly and linearly with the organization's IT staff size (correlation ~0.96; on average ~4-5% of IT staff, i.e., about one architect per 20-25 IT specialists), but only weakly with total employee headcount (~0.44) or annual revenue (~0.56) -- both popular but poor predictors, given large industry differences in IT spend as a share of revenue.
mechanism: Because EA work volume tracks IT landscape complexity rather than generic organizational size, and IT intensity (IT staff as % of workforce, IT spend as % of revenue) varies by an order of magnitude across industries, sizing EA functions off headcount or revenue systematically misestimates the appropriate number of architects.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking or planning EA function size, use IT staff headcount (target ratio ~1 architect per 20-25 IT staff) as the primary sizing variable rather than total employees or revenue.

finding_statement: As EA functions grow, they require more hierarchical tiers of architecture positions (vertical specialization -- e.g., solution, program, business-area/domain, and corporate tiers in the largest organizations) and more distinct architecture position types at each tier (horizontal specialization -- e.g., separate architects per business area or technology domain), with each individual architect's area of responsibility narrowing accordingly; small EA functions instead rely on one or a few "jack-of-all-trades" architects with fully overlapping responsibilities.
mechanism: A single generalist architect (or a few, with overlapping duties) can cover an entire small organization's architectural needs, but as the volume of necessary architectural work grows with IT size, dividing labor both hierarchically (by scope of planning horizon) and horizontally (by subject area) becomes necessary to keep individual roles tractable.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an EA function, expect low-specialization, single/dual-role structures to be appropriate only for small IT organizations; plan for added hierarchical tiers and specialized subject-area positions as IT staff and architect headcount grow, rather than importing a fixed reference-model structure regardless of scale.

finding_statement: Organizations with a single, non-diversified line of business tend to structure EA functions around traditional EA domains (business, application, data, infrastructure architects serving the whole enterprise), while organizations with diversified business activities structure EA functions around business areas/lines of business instead, with domain architects reserved mainly for purely technical domains (integration, infrastructure, security); more precisely, which EA domains are centralized versus decentralized tracks the organization's operating model (per Ross et al. 2006: diversification/coordination/replication/unification) -- domains tied to processes/applications decentralize under low process standardization, while domains tied to shared data centralize under high data integration.
mechanism: Process standardization and data integration requirements (the two dimensions of operating model) determine which EA domains benefit from being planned globally (by domain architects) versus locally (by business-area architects); imposing one fixed structure regardless of these requirements creates mismatches between architecture team design and actual coordination needs.
operationalisation_hint: Diagnose an organization's operating model (standardization and integration levels) before designing/evaluating its EA function structure, and expect domain-based, business-area-based, and hybrid structures to each be correct for different operating-model profiles rather than treating any one as universally "best practice."

finding_statement: Multinational/geographically distributed organizations tend to have EA functions spatially aligned with their business geography (individual architects or local teams present in major overseas locations), but their core EA teams -- especially those doing enterprise-level, strategic planning -- still concentrate at corporate headquarters, co-located with top-level decision-makers; one studied organization that tried a fully dispersed EA function structure found it problematic and consolidated back toward the head office.
mechanism: EA work is closely linked to strategic business planning, so architects doing enterprise-level (as opposed to purely local solution-level) work benefit from proximity to senior decision-makers and from being able to leverage global technology synergies, while some geographically local architectural decision-making is still needed at major points of presence.
operationalisation_hint: For multinational transformations, expect (and design for) a hub-and-spoke EA structure: strategic/enterprise-level architects centralized near headquarters/senior leadership, with a lighter local architect presence at major regional operations for local decisions.

finding_statement: Across the full range of industry sectors represented in the 47-organization dataset, no industry-specific patterns of EA function structuring were identified -- industry affects other aspects of EA practice (e.g., planning horizon, stakeholder rotation) but not the structural design of the EA function itself, which is instead explained by organizational properties (IT size, business diversification, operating model) that cut across industries.
mechanism: Because the properties that actually determine EA function structure (IT size, diversification, operating model) vary independently of industry classification, treating "industry" as a design factor for EA function structure (as many industry benchmarks implicitly do) conflates a non-causal correlate with the actual causal drivers.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking or justifying an EA function's structure, do not rely on industry-sector comparisons alone; use the organization's own IT size, business diversification, and operating model as the relevant reference points instead.

finding_statement: Successful large-scale data-driven transformation requires a federated governance model: a central governance body (e.g., Data Governance Council) sets shared principles, standards, and cross-domain alignment, while autonomous domain teams retain end-to-end accountability and decision-making for their own data/application products and roadmaps.
mechanism: Pure centralization creates bottlenecks and slows domain-specific responsiveness, while pure decentralization recreates data silos and inconsistency; federating governance lets domains move at their own pace on business-specific needs while a central council still enforces cross-domain interoperability and strategic alignment.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether a transformation initiative has both a central cross-functional governance forum with real decision authority AND named domain-level owners with end-to-end accountability for their own roadmaps -- one without the other is a sign of an unbalanced governance design.
page_or_section: Section 2.2 (DDA Framework Principles: Domain ownership and Federated Governance); Section 3.2.4

finding_statement: Large-scale architectural transformation (e.g., moving to a fully harmonized data-driven architecture) should be broken into one or more deliberate interim phases rather than attempted as a single complete redesign; the number of interim phases needed depends on the size of the change, corporate culture, organizational structure, complexity, and organizational scale.
mechanism: Attempting full immediate harmonization of previously separate architectures/frameworks (e.g., merging data and application domain structures in one step) creates perceived risk and resistance that outweighs the cost-effectiveness of instant full integration; incremental interim states let the organization assimilate change gradually and allow a "step back" to a prior phase if social resistance emerges.
operationalisation_hint: When planning an EA-led transformation, explicitly define one or more interim target architectures/organizational states rather than only a final end-state, and size the number of interim phases to the scale of change and the organization's existing change-readiness.

finding_statement: The critical factor determining whether new data/digital technology investments (e.g., Data Fabric components like knowledge graphs and active metadata) generate value is not the technology itself but the prior establishment of organizational structures (domains, cross-functional teams, operating models) and mindset/cultural readiness; without this foundation, purely technological advancement does not move the organization closer to a data-driven culture.
mechanism: Technology adoption rate -- the actual driver of value realization -- depends on a solid organizational and mindset foundation being established first (or concurrently); deploying advanced technology onto an unprepared organizational structure leaves the technology under-adopted and value unrealized.
operationalisation_hint: Before or alongside investing in advanced data/digital technology, verify that corresponding organizational structures (clear ownership, cross-functional teams, defined operating model) are being established, not just technology procurement.

finding_statement: The case used broad survey and interview input to formulate a data-driven transformation strategy and reports alignment to business needs and stakeholder commitment. It does not demonstrate that response volume itself reduced selection bias.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The case organization's pre-existing culture of agility and cross-functional collaboration facilitated acceptance of the federated/domain-decomposed framework; organizations with more conservative or less mature cultures would likely need more extensive change management to achieve similar commitment. Separately, when different divisions of the same company pursued similar transformations independently with divergent architectural choices (e.g., omitting the domain layer, individual vs. domain-level data-product ownership), this created a need for an overarching global data strategy to prevent new cross-divisional inconsistency/silos.
mechanism: A framework's success is not solely a function of its own design but is conditioned on the receiving organization's prior change-readiness culture; and decentralized, division-by-division architectural decision-making without any enterprise-wide harmonizing strategy recreates the very silo problem the architecture was meant to solve, just at a higher organizational level.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying a federated or domain-based data architecture, assess whether the organization already has cross-functional collaboration capacity, change readiness, and an enterprise-wide data strategy; where divisional initiatives are fragmented, add a global harmonization layer to prevent new silos.

finding_statement: Organizations with no or nascent enterprise architecture (maturity level 0-1) should follow architecture-creation tasks when elaborating strategic actions during IS strategic planning, while organizations with an established architecture (maturity level 2-5) should instead follow architecture-implementation/maintenance tasks -- the appropriate planning process branches explicitly on the organization's assessed architecture maturity level rather than using one uniform planning sequence for all organizations.
mechanism: The tasks needed to progress differ fundamentally depending on whether an architecture must first be created versus already exists and needs implementation or upkeep; applying a maintenance-oriented process to an organization with no architecture (or vice versa) would misallocate effort.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying an EA-driven strategic planning method, explicitly assess architecture maturity level first (per an EACMM-style 0-5 scale) and route the organization to the corresponding creation vs. implementation/maintenance task set rather than a single generic sequence.

finding_statement: In this national government, donor-supported health-sector case, evaluators reported that "objectives of the sponsor were used to override the significance or relevance of the technical submissions" during the architecture-oriented strategic planning process, indicating that external funder priorities can supersede technically/architecturally sound recommendations regardless of the rigor of the EA process used.
mechanism: Donor-funded public-sector transformation initiatives are subject to funding-body priorities and conditions that operate outside the technical/architectural rationale of the EA process itself, so even a well-executed EA-driven strategic planning process cannot guarantee that its technically-grounded outputs will be the ones acted upon.
operationalisation_hint: In donor-funded or externally sponsored public-sector EA planning, explicitly map sponsor incentives and negotiation constraints alongside technical evaluation criteria, because technically preferred architecture options may still be displaced by sponsor priorities.

finding_statement: As organizational maturity increases (tested across 5 levels using the Davenport maturity model), the importance of strategic and organizational-governance-oriented success factors (strategy, business, security, standards/configuration management, human capital management, and environment layers) increases significantly (ANOVA p<0.05, confirmed by Tukey post-hoc grouping), while the importance of technical/foundational factors (data, application, network & infrastructure, and project management layers) remains statistically constant across all maturity levels.
mechanism: Foundational technical capabilities (data quality, application quality, infrastructure, project management discipline) appear to function as a constant baseline requirement regardless of maturity stage, whereas strategic alignment, governance, security, and human-capital conditions become progressively more critical differentiators as an organization advances -- meaning readiness assessments should not apply flat importance weights to all enabling conditions across all maturity stages.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing which enabling conditions to prioritize at a given maturity stage, treat technical/foundational conditions as necessary baseline investments at all stages, but weight strategic, governance, security, and human-capital conditions more heavily as the organization/initiative matures.

finding_statement: Beyond technical capability, data-sharing transformation initiatives (data spaces) require organizations to overcome reluctance to share proprietary data, demonstrate the business value of data sharing, secure sufficiently skilled IT personnel, and absorb the cross-organizational coordination costs of aligning data models, standards, and business processes across multiple autonomous actors.
mechanism: Data-sharing ecosystems involve multiple independent organizations that must reach consensus on both technical and organizational governance capabilities; this consensus-building is costly and slow because it requires balancing competitive concerns (fear of losing advantage by sharing know-how) against collective value creation, and requires a trusted, resourced coordinating body to reach agreement.
operationalisation_hint: Before committing to a data-space/data-sharing initiative, verify: an explicit trust-building governance framework defining roles/responsibilities/decision rights; a demonstrated business case for data-sharing value; availability of skilled personnel; and a designated, resourced governing body with authority to enforce cross-organizational agreements.

finding_statement: Organizations building a data-governance capability for a data-sharing ecosystem can define both an initial and a target architecture state and progressively mature toward it building-block by building-block (e.g., starting with a basic identity-verification solution before migrating to more advanced mechanisms), rather than requiring the full governance system to be implemented at once.
mechanism: Decomposing the data-governance capability into discrete Architecture Building Blocks (principles, organization, roles/responsibilities, metadata, quality, security, lifecycle, monitoring) lets each block mature independently according to the organization's specific maturity level, regulatory constraints, and interoperability requirements, reducing the perceived risk/cost barrier of adopting cross-organizational governance all at once.
operationalisation_hint: Assess governance maturity per building-block (principles, roles, policies, metadata, quality, security, monitoring) separately rather than as a single undifferentiated "governance readiness" score, and sequence investment toward the blocks with the largest maturity gaps.

finding_statement: Enterprises undertaking architecture-led transformation must first establish strategic architecture (vision, target customer segments, product/service portfolio, human-capital strategy, and capacity objectives) before constructing enterprise architecture (business, data, application, technology domains); building EA before SA clarity results in technology investments disconnected from business needs (the "technology-driven trap") and resource waste.
mechanism: Strategic architecture functions as the organization's directional "brain," determining which EA domains and priorities matter (e.g., a venue positioned as a premier concert venue needs different EA priorities than one positioned as a community activity center), while EA feeds back "capability feedback" on technical feasibility and resource constraints, forming a bidirectional strategy-execution loop; skipping the SA step causes IT/system investments to be made without a clear business rationale.
operationalisation_hint: Before committing to EA domain investments, verify that SA elements (customer segments, product/service scope, human-capital strategy, capacity/operations targets) are explicitly defined and stakeholder-validated; treat mismatched SA-EA sequencing as a red flag in transformation readiness assessments.

finding_statement: Large-scale, public-facing transformation (e.g., ESG transformation of a multi-purpose venue operating under a public-private partnership) depends on collaborative engagement of multiple external stakeholders -- government, community, and industry partners -- with government providing institutional support and a favorable policy environment, not merely on internal organizational capability.
mechanism: Government institutional backing and policy environment shape the funding, regulatory permissions, and PPP arrangements within which internal transformation strategies are executed; without this external institutional-support layer, purely internal strategic/architectural readiness is insufficient for large public-facing transformations.
operationalisation_hint: For public-facing ESG or sustainability transformations under PPP or similar institutional arrangements, explicitly assess the policy environment, government backing, and stakeholder-participation mechanisms alongside internal architecture plans, because external institutional support is part of implementation readiness.
page_or_section: Section 6 ("Fifth" key finding); Section 3.2 (PPP case background)

finding_statement: Because legacy information systems continuously accumulate incremental changes (technical debt, ad hoc adaptations, evolving business processes), operational business-IT alignment cannot be assessed once and assumed stable; it requires periodically repeated diagnostic assessment combining quantitative metrics (implementation/representation link counts and rates), qualitative consistency rules (cross-checking functional and data-dimension links), and anti-pattern detection (e.g., pure technical integration, functional silo, monolithic application, multiple functional implementations) to reveal areas of drift.
mechanism: Single-technique assessment (e.g., metrics alone) can mask or mis-signal misalignment -- e.g., a high rate of "unimplemented" business concepts may simply reflect composite/aggregated business processes rather than a true gap -- so triangulating multiple complementary diagnostic lenses reduces false positives/negatives and gives architects actionable, targeted evolution priorities rather than an undifferentiated alignment score.
operationalisation_hint: Assess operational alignment using at least three complementary lenses -- coverage/implementation-rate metrics, cross-layer consistency rules, and anti-pattern catalogs -- and treat single-metric alignment scores as provisional until corroborated by the other lenses; automate detection via scripting where possible (e.g., jArchi over ArchiMate models) to make repeated reassessment practically sustainable.

finding_statement: Organizations achieve IT-business strategic alignment not simply by adopting IT governance (ITG) mechanisms (decision-making structures, formal processes, communication approaches) but only when that adoption translates into genuine organizational commitment to the underlying principles of the ITG framework (e.g., COBIT's five principles: meeting stakeholder needs, end-to-end governance, an integrated evolving framework, a holistic approach, and separating governance from management). Commitment to ITG principles (CCP) fully mediates the relationship between ITG mechanism adoption and strategic alignment -- ITG mechanisms alone do not directly produce alignment.
mechanism: Mechanism adoption can be purely symbolic/instrumental ("following the letter" of governance rules without embracing their spirit/goals), which satisfies structural compliance but does not achieve the values-and-goals-based integration needed for genuine business-IT alignment; only when mechanism adoption is accompanied by felt commitment to the framework's underlying principles does IT become embedded in organizational objectives rather than treated as a separate function.
operationalisation_hint: Assess not only whether ITG mechanisms (steering committees, formal processes, communication channels) are formally in place, but whether staff and leadership demonstrate committed endorsement of the governance framework's stated principles (e.g., via a validated CCP-style instrument); a validated CCP measure is provided in this paper and can be adapted to other principles-based frameworks (ISO/IEC 27001, ITIL, NIST, etc.).

finding_statement: Achieving IT-business strategic alignment requires support for IT from the full top leadership tier -- including the board of directors, not only C-level executives or IT management -- because top leadership support both strengthens organizational commitment to ITG principles and directly improves strategic alignment. ITG that remains a middle-management affair, without board and executive-level involvement, is unlikely to produce strategic alignment.
mechanism: When top leadership actively participates in IT vision and strategy (rather than passively endorsing it), it diffuses awareness of IT-related values, competencies, and governance principles throughout the firm, secures stakeholder buy-in, and helps overcome organizational resistance to IT-enabled change; because boards sit atop the firm's decision-making and governance hierarchy, their direct involvement (not just senior management's) is what confers legitimacy and centralized momentum to governance initiatives.
operationalisation_hint: Measure top leadership support for IT as a construct spanning both board and executive-level participation (not top-management support alone, which is the common but incomplete operationalization in most prior IS research); readiness assessments should specifically check for documented board-level IT engagement, not just CIO/CEO sponsorship.

finding_statement: Contrary to the common assumption that stacking multiple enabling conditions produces compounding benefits, this study found that the interaction between commitment to ITG principles (CCP) and top leadership support has a significant NEGATIVE effect on strategic alignment: the highest alignment outcomes occur either from a balanced-but-not-extreme combination of both, or from high CCP paired with lower top leadership support (or vice versa), rather than from both being simultaneously maximized. Both individual relationships were also found to be curvilinear rather than simply linear.
mechanism: A plausible explanation is a substitutive relationship: heavily formalized, principles-based governance frameworks (like COBIT) may constrain leaders' ability to steer nimbly or lead by intuition, so when both principled commitment AND intense leadership steering are simultaneously very high, they may create friction or redundant/conflicting steering inputs rather than reinforcing one another; leaders lacking deep IT expertise may find highly formalized frameworks and highly assertive personal involvement to be competing rather than complementary steering mechanisms.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating governance-readiness conditions, do not assume leadership support and commitment to formal governance principles can simply be maximized independently; assess whether highly formalized governance and strong top-down steering are complementing each other or generating redundant, conflicting control pressure.

finding_statement: Among the three classic ITG mechanism types (decision-making structures, formal processes, communication approaches), only formal processes and communication approaches were found to positively influence commitment to ITG principles; decision-making structures (e.g., IT steering committees) showed no significant association with principled commitment in this study.
mechanism: Formal processes (continuous monitoring, planning, and capability-development routines) and communication approaches (channels disseminating ITG values and guidelines) directly transmit and reinforce the framework's underlying values across the organization, whereas decision-making structures alone establish authority/roles without necessarily communicating or embedding the values that constitute principled commitment.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an ITG rollout intended to build genuine principled commitment (not just structural compliance), prioritize investment in formal governance processes and communication/dissemination channels; do not assume that establishing decision-making bodies (e.g., steering committees) alone will translate into commitment to governance principles.

finding_statement: Digitally maturing organizations are far more likely than early-stage organizations to organize around cross-functional teams to implement digital business priorities (71% vs. <30%) and to recognize and reward cross-functional collaboration as a core part of culture and operating model (77% vs. 34%); early-stage companies are also far more likely (60%) to report that their traditional hierarchical management structure and decision rights interfere with digital success.
mechanism: Digital initiatives increasingly require multiple functions (product engineering, software, data, customer experience) to work together on the same problem rather than in isolation, so organizations that break down functional silos and reward cross-boundary collaboration can execute digital initiatives that a siloed, hierarchical structure would block or slow.
operationalisation_hint: Assess the percentage of teams organized cross-functionally and whether shared, cross-functional performance metrics/incentives exist, rather than relying on self-reported "we collaborate" claims.

finding_statement: Digitally maturing organizations are far more likely to have cultivated (rather than merely mandated or merely expected) a digital culture that tolerates risk, encourages experimentation, and rewards collaboration -- e.g., 71% of digitally maturing organizations accept risk of failure as a natural part of experimenting, versus 29% of early-stage organizations -- and this culture develops through a virtuous circle in which digital maturity spurs cultural change and cultural change spurs further digital maturity.
mechanism: Early-stage companies tend to drive digital adoption through top-down management mandates, developing-stage companies shift to expecting employee buy-in, while digitally maturing companies deliberately cultivate risk-tolerant, experimentation-friendly culture as an intentional, ongoing practice rather than a one-time directive -- and once such a culture forms, it further accelerates digital initiative adoption, reinforcing itself over time.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing culture readiness, distinguish between three qualitatively different adoption-driving postures (mandating, expecting, cultivating) rather than treating "culture readiness" as a single yes/no attribute.
page_or_section: "Digital Cultures -- Collaborative and Risk-tolerant" section; Figure 8

finding_statement: Organizations become more digitally mature partly by becoming "talent magnets" -- creating environments where employees continuously learn and develop digital skills (going beyond formal training to platforms, communities, and stretch assignments) -- because failing to do so drives measurable attrition: VP-level executives without sufficient digital development opportunities are 15 times more likely to plan to leave within a year than those with such opportunities.
mechanism: The half-life of workplace skills is shrinking, so organizations that rely only on hiring external digital talent (rather than continuously developing internal talent through learning platforms, stretch assignments, and career-growth opportunities) both fail to retain capable existing staff and fail to keep pace with evolving skill requirements; digital talent actively self-selects toward employers offering visible growth opportunities.
operationalisation_hint: Track leadership-level (not just general-staff) attrition risk as a specific readiness indicator tied to digital-development-opportunity provision, since the retention effect is dramatically larger at the VP/leadership level than at staff level in this sample (15x at VP level).
page_or_section: "Invest in Digital Talent: Use It or Lose It" section; Figures 9-10

finding_statement: Digital initiatives are two-to-three times more likely to be reported successful when organizations commit sufficient time, energy, and resources to them (75% success vs. 34% when commitment is insufficient), when organizations provide employees resources/opportunities to thrive digitally (72% vs. 24%), and when leadership has articulated a clear vision for digital business strategy (72% vs. 22%).
mechanism: Digital maturity does not develop accidentally or via a quick fix -- it results from a sustained combination of committed resourcing, employee enablement, and leadership vision-setting; each of these three levers independently and substantially raises the odds of reported initiative success, and organizations lacking any one of them see success rates fall to roughly a quarter to a third of committed peers.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness for a specific digital initiative, check jointly for (a) explicitly committed time/energy/resources (not just a budget line item), (b) employee-facing enablement resources, and (c) an articulated leadership vision -- treat the absence of any one of the three as a red flag rather than assuming resourcing alone is sufficient.
page_or_section: "Do You Have the Will for Digital Transformation?" section; Figure 11

finding_statement: Across three consecutive annual survey waves, having a clear and coherent digital strategy is the single strongest differentiator between digitally maturing and early-stage organizations (80% of maturing organizations report having one, versus 19% of early-stage organizations), and digitally maturing organizations are roughly twice as likely to set strategic planning horizons of five years or more (~30% vs. ~13%). The digital strategy must be integrated with core business strategy and use technology to fundamentally rethink how business is done (76% of maturing organizations vs. 32% of early-stage organizations), rather than being treated as a bolt-on technology initiative.
mechanism: Organizations that treat digital as a separable technology initiative ("talking about digital" or supporting isolated business objectives) rather than integrating it into core business strategy lack a coherent basis for sequencing investment and change over time; a longer strategic time horizon lets organizations plan for structural, cultural, and capability changes that a short-horizon, reactive posture cannot accommodate.
operationalisation_hint: Assess digital-strategy readiness on two joint dimensions -- (a) whether the digital strategy is integrated with/central to overall business strategy (versus a supporting or bolt-on role), and (b) the strategic planning time horizon (multi-year vs. reactive/short-term) -- rather than treating "has a digital strategy" as a single binary check.
page_or_section: "A Digital Lens on Business Strategy" section; Figures 2-4

finding_statement: Synthesizing 125 original dimensions across 22 published digital maturity models, this review identifies 14 recurring common maturity areas: digital culture, technology, operations & processes, digital strategy, organization, digital skills, innovation, customer insight & experience, governance, vision, digital ecosystem, leadership, compliance & security, products & services, and business model. These areas cluster into a "digital foundation" group (technology, digital skills, operations, products & services) and a "transformational capability" group (vision, culture, leadership, governance, innovation, agility).
mechanism: Digital maturity is a holistic, two-sided construct: a strong digital/technological foundation alone does not constitute maturity without the transformational-management capabilities (vision, leadership, culture, governance) needed to leverage that foundation strategically, and vice versa; models that measure only one side systematically misrepresent an organization's true readiness.
operationalisation_hint: When constructing or selecting a digital-transformation readiness instrument, verify that it scores both digital-foundation areas (technology, skills, operations, products/services) and transformational-capability areas (vision, culture, leadership, governance, innovation) rather than only one side.
page_or_section: Table VIII (Most common digital maturity areas); Results section

finding_statement: Domain-specific models (predominantly manufacturing/Industry 4.0) most strongly emphasize "technology," "digital skills," and "operations & processes," and place significantly more weight on "products & services" and "compliance & security," while general (industry-agnostic) models place much more emphasis on "innovation," "customer insight & experience," and especially "digital culture" and other transformational/soft dimensions (leadership, vision, governance). No examined model comprehensively covers both digital-foundation and transformational-management capabilities at once.
mechanism: Domain-specific models are built to reflect the concrete technological realities of a particular industrial context (e.g., Industry 4.0 manufacturing), which biases their dimension set toward technology and operations, whereas general models must abstract away from industry-specific technical detail and therefore lean on more universally applicable "soft" transformational dimensions -- meaning the choice of model type itself introduces a systematic assessment blind spot.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or adapting a maturity-assessment instrument, explicitly check whether it is domain-specific or general in origin, and supplement it with dimensions from the opposite category (technology/operations detail for general models; culture/leadership/governance depth for domain-specific models) to avoid a one-sided readiness picture.
page_or_section: Results section (Figs. 4-5, domain-specific vs. general model comparison); Discussion

finding_statement: The systematic review finds culture in 55% of examined digital maturity models, clusters 25 original attributes into 11 categories, and identifies collaboration, agility/flexibility, and organizational learning as frequently represented attributes.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Although prevailing academic definitions of digital transformation explicitly center on developing new digital business models to create and appropriate value, the "business model" maturity area is addressed by only a small minority of the 22 examined models (e.g., just 2 of the synthesized general models explicitly address it), indicating that most existing maturity assessment practice focuses on exploiting digital technology within existing business models rather than exploring digital business-model innovation.
mechanism: Assessing and improving operational/technological digital capabilities is more tractable and less organizationally threatening than reimagining the business model itself, so maturity-model designers (and the organizations using them) default to measuring the former; this creates a systematic blind spot in which an organization can score highly on most maturity dimensions while never having addressed the business-model-level transformation that academic definitions treat as the defining feature of "digital transformation" (as opposed to mere digitization/digitalization).
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital transformation readiness, explicitly verify that a business-model-innovation dimension is included and is not merely inferred from technology or strategy scores, since this is the dimension most likely to be silently absent from off-the-shelf maturity instruments.
page_or_section: Results and Discussion sections (business model dimension analysis)

finding_statement: Firms build digital sensing capability not only by scanning their own industry and existing partner network but by deliberately searching for and recombining digital solutions already implemented in completely different industries ("technology brokering"), reducing the pressure to invent novel solutions from scratch and lowering the psychological barrier for employees asked to be innovative.
mechanism: Digital innovation does not have to be revolutionary; applying an existing solution from an unrelated industry in a new way is a powerful and more attainable form of sensing than pure invention, but firms have limited natural capacity to search and process knowledge outside their traditional industry boundaries, so this requires a deliberate, dedicated routine (e.g., a consultancy role or cross-industry scanning practice) rather than emerging organically from ordinary business activity.
operationalisation_hint: Establish an explicit routine (internal function or external advisor relationship) tasked with identifying digital solutions from unrelated industries and assessing their applicability, rather than relying solely on within-industry competitive scanning.

finding_statement: A prerequisite sensing capability for digital transformation is internally directed: firms need routines to build an accurate overview of what digital and technical systems already exist within the organization, since lacking this overview is itself an obstacle to transformation -- managers cannot evaluate what new systems or infrastructure are needed, or avoid costly redundant/incompatible builds, without first sensing their own current-state infrastructure.
mechanism: Most digital-sensing capability discussion in the literature is externally oriented (market/competitor/technology scanning), but new digital front-ends or business-model innovations can fail even when well-designed if the firm lacks the underlying infrastructure to support them (e.g., a new digital front-end built for a client that lacked the back-end infrastructure to feed it live data) -- so sensing must also be turned inward before outward-facing digital initiatives can succeed.
operationalisation_hint: Before initiating externally-oriented digital sensing/scanning, conduct an internal audit routine establishing an organization-wide inventory of existing digital/technical systems, their current use, and their fitness for future demands.

finding_statement: A clear, well-communicated digital strategy with defined business objectives is necessary for digital transformation (without it, employees disagree about what capabilities to develop), but because environmental conditions for digitally transforming firms change rapidly, the strategy and its goals must be semi-continuously readjusted -- alternating between exploitation phases (where resources and priorities are fixed/committed, "semistructures") and exploration phases (where flexibility and new options are considered) -- rather than being set once and executed unchanged.
mechanism: Firms face a dilemma between strategic commitment (needed to realize any given strategy and avoid indecision/paralysis) and strategic flexibility (needed because digital environments and technologies change faster than traditional strategic-planning cycles); resolving this via alternating ambidextrous phases lets a firm exploit committed investments while still periodically re-opening the strategy to newly sensed opportunities, rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice between rigidity and constant change.
operationalisation_hint: Structure digital strategy governance around explicit alternating cycles: periods where digital-project priorities and resource commitments are deliberately fixed (exploitation), interspersed with scheduled strategy-review periods where the digital strategy and objectives are reopened for adjustment based on newly sensed opportunities (exploration).

finding_statement: When a digital competence is an essential part of a firm's envisioned digital business model, it should generally be developed internally rather than outsourced, because outsourcing core, high-uncertainty, high-asset-specificity competences creates elevated risk of transactional difficulties and opportunistic behavior by the sourcing partner; outsourcing is more appropriate as a temporary measure in early transformation stages, before the necessity and criticality of a given competence has been determined.
mechanism: Reduced transaction costs favor internalizing competences central to a firm's digital strategy (since high asset specificity and uncertainty otherwise expose the firm to partner opportunism), while competences whose future criticality is not yet clear can reasonably be outsourced provisionally, with the make/outsource decision revisited as the digital strategy and the firm's understanding of its own competence needs matures over time.
operationalisation_hint: Maintain an organization-wide (not siloed per-department) inventory of existing internal competences, and explicitly classify each digital capability need as core-to-strategy (internalize) versus provisional/uncertain (outsource pending further clarity), revisiting the classification as the digital strategy develops.

finding_statement: Strategic focus and intent from senior/executive leadership (including board-level approval) is a necessary contingency for developing digital transformative capabilities, but firms frequently articulate strategic intent for digital transformation that then goes unrealized or is scaled back to minor changes consistent with pre-existing strategic archetypes; this misalignment between stated strategic intent and actually realized strategy is itself an inhibitor of DTC development, distinct from simply lacking strategic intent in the first place.
mechanism: Board-level and senior-management strategic focus provides the resourcing and organizational-priority signal necessary to initiate large-scale digital transformation projects, but organizations may lack the resources, capabilities, or follow-through discipline to convert stated intent into implemented change, so intent alone does not guarantee realized capability development.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness, distinguish between (a) documented/expressed senior-management strategic intent for digital transformation and (b) evidence of actually realized changes consistent with that intent; a gap between the two is itself a diagnostic readiness red flag.

finding_statement: Firms with long histories of success in a particular business model (e.g., license-based software, high-value/low-volume equipment sales) exhibit a "lock-in" effect in which path dependency impedes the development of digital transformative capabilities even when senior managers recognize the urgency of technology disruption and explicitly acknowledge the need to change; this inertia stems from deep organizational, sales-force, and customer-base entrenchment in the prior model, not merely from a lack of awareness or intent.
mechanism: Decades of profitable operation under an established business model create deeply embedded sales, manufacturing, and customer relationships (a specific path) that are difficult to unwind even when managers rationally recognize a superior/necessary alternative (e.g., moving from equipment sales to a cloud/outcome-based model), because switching threatens established, still-profitable revenue streams and requires capabilities the organization has not needed to build.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital transformation readiness in incumbent firms, explicitly test for profitable legacy-model lock-in: examine whether sales incentives, customer expectations, manufacturing logic, or revenue dependence on the existing model are likely to block capability shifts even when leaders acknowledge disruption urgency.

finding_statement: Deeper ecosystem embeddedness through strategic partnerships with competitors and complementors is associated with faster and more sophisticated digital transformative capability development (18 of 20 interviewees identified partnerships as a key enabler), but the realized benefit depends critically on the firm's discipline in strategically managing these partnerships -- firms that limit themselves to a small number of carefully selected, trusted partners (rather than spreading thin across many) report better outcomes than those that do not.
mechanism: No single firm can deliver a complete IIoT/digital solution alone (data collection, cloud transport, analysis, field feedback each may require different specialized partners), so partnerships supply necessary complementary capabilities; but because partners can be simultaneously competitors, poorly managed or overly broad partnership portfolios create competing-interest conflicts and coordination overhead that erode the capability-building benefit partnerships are meant to provide.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing ecosystem-partnership readiness, evaluate not just the number/breadth of partnerships but the presence of a deliberate, limited, and strategically selected partner portfolio with clear governance for managing competing interests.

finding_statement: Faster rates of technology disruption are associated with more aggressive and sophisticated digital transformative capability development, but the same severity of disruption also creates confusion among managers about exactly what capabilities are needed, especially when firms must maintain short-to-medium-term competitiveness without knowing what future market requirements will look like. Moreover, digital transformation itself generates further emerging technologies that fuel additional disruption, creating a continuous, looped change process rather than a discrete transformation event.
mechanism: Technology disruption creates urgency that mobilizes resources and attention, but because disruption is often novel and unprecedented, firms lack established playbooks for responding, so intensifying disruption simultaneously increases both the pressure to act and the uncertainty about which actions will prove correct; because implemented digital transformation itself creates and diffuses new technologies, the disruption that motivated the original transformation is regenerated rather than resolved, meaning firms must treat DTC development as an ongoing capability rather than a one-time project with a defined endpoint.
operationalisation_hint: Frame digital-transformation readiness assessments as recurring/cyclical rather than a one-time gate, and explicitly distinguish "urgency to act" from "clarity about what to do," since high-disruption environments can score high on the former while remaining low on the latter.
page_or_section: Sections 4.1.4.2 (Technology disruption, Proposition 7) and 4.1.4.5 (recurring consequence, Proposition 10)
