finding_statement: Digital seizing (converting sensed opportunities into action) is enabled by two joint capabilities: rapid prototyping (lean, MVP-based, agile product development, increasingly via 3D printing and joint development with partners) and an organization structure explicitly adapted to digital/solution-centric work (moving from product/vertical-based structures to solution-centric teams, sometimes coordinated by a Chief Digital Officer). Core and extended capabilities function like "concentric circles" -- firms must protect and enhance core capabilities while adding extended/complementary capabilities to expand into new digital offerings.
mechanism: Rapid prototyping lets firms absorb the complexity and customization demands of digital/IIoT products economically and test solutions with customers quickly, while solution-centric (rather than product/vertical-centric) organization structures let firms coordinate across previously siloed business units to actually deliver on rapidly prototyped opportunities; without a structural home for solution-centric collaboration, prototyping capability alone cannot be seized upon at scale.
operationalisation_hint: Assess both dimensions jointly: (a) presence of lean/MVP-based rapid prototyping practices and (b) whether organization structure has been explicitly adapted (e.g., solution-centric teams, CDO coordination role) to support cross-business-unit digital initiatives, rather than treating either alone as sufficient.
page_or_section: Sections 4.1.2.2-4.1.2.3 (Rapid prototyping and Organization structure, Propositions 2-3)

finding_statement: Organizational readiness to deploy transformative technologies like AI cannot be captured by a single readiness score; it must be assessed separately across at least four dimensions -- technologies (value-adding potential of the current/future technology portfolio), activities (which organizational activities the technology supports), boundaries (whether organizational boundaries with customers/partners are being reshaped), and goals (whether the technology supports attainment of organizational goals/identity) -- because readiness commonly diverges sharply across these dimensions (e.g., high technology readiness but zero goal-alignment readiness in the illustrated case).
mechanism: Treating "AI readiness" or "digital readiness" as a single undifferentiated score masks exactly where the bottleneck to further transformation lies; in the illustrated case, an organization rated itself highly on current technology capability but scored zero on goal-alignment, revealing that its actual constraint on further digital transformation was not technological capability at all but the absence of any goal-level rationale for deploying the technology further.
operationalisation_hint: Use a structured, multi-dimensional self-assessment instrument (e.g., a 0-4 scored questionnaire completed by a cross-functional management workshop) scoring current AND future/planned capability separately across technologies, activities, boundaries, and goals, and visualize the four scores together (e.g., a radar/scorecard) rather than aggregating into one composite readiness index.

finding_statement: Across the four AI-readiness dimensions, organizations' actual readiness tends to be strongest for technologies and weakest for boundaries and goals, since technology adoption alone is comparatively easy to initiate, whereas rethinking organizational boundaries (with customers, partners, competitors) and organizational goals/identity in light of new technology requires deeper, more contested organizational change that firms are much less prepared to undertake.
mechanism: New technology can often be acquired and deployed in a bounded, contained way (e.g., adding a chatbot function) without disturbing existing organizational boundaries or goals, so technology-dimension readiness develops relatively quickly, whereas boundary and goal changes require renegotiating relationships with external stakeholders and reconsidering the organization's fundamental purpose/identity, both of which face much stronger inertia and ethical/strategic uncertainty (e.g., managers explicitly declining to expand AI use for ethical reasons around customer data).
operationalisation_hint: Readiness assessments should score technology, activity, boundary, and goal dimensions separately, and should expect technology readiness to appear earlier than boundary or goal readiness; low scores on external-boundary redesign or goal reframing should be treated as distinct bottlenecks rather than averaged away by stronger technology scores.
page_or_section: Sections 2.2.3-2.2.4, 3 (Boundaries and Goals dimensions, workshop scores)

finding_statement: Across 284 large Finnish companies (secondary data: annual-report content analysis plus audited financial statements), digital orientation (commitment/openness to digital technology) and digital intensity (breadth of areas digitalized) show no significant direct effect on financial success (net profit or operating profit); their effects on financial performance are realized entirely through digital maturity (systematic, ongoing capability to adapt to digital change), which fully mediates both relationships.
mechanism: Openness/commitment to digital technology and breadth of digital initiatives are necessary inputs, but without the systematic organizational capability to translate them into sustained, coordinated adaptation (digital maturity), they do not convert into financial outcomes; digital maturity is the capability layer that actually captures value from orientation and intensity.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness for financial-performance purposes, do not treat digital orientation (stated commitment) or digital intensity (breadth of digital initiatives) as sufficient readiness indicators on their own; require evidence of digital maturity (systematic, sustained adaptation capability, e.g. per Westerman et al.'s four-level model) before expecting financial returns.

finding_statement: Digital intensity significantly and negatively moderates the relationship between digital orientation and financial success (both net profit and operating profit): the wider the breadth of areas a company digitalizes simultaneously, the weaker the financial return from its digital commitment/orientation.
mechanism: High digital intensity across many operational areas increases the number of engaged actors and organizational complexity, which can jeopardize managerial control over the business even when digital commitment (orientation) is strong; without a correspondingly high level of digital maturity to manage this complexity, spreading digital effort thin across many domains erodes rather than reinforces the financial payoff of digital commitment.
operationalisation_hint: When planning digital transformation scope, deliberately weigh breadth (number of areas digitalized) against organizational capacity to maintain control and coherence; flag high-breadth digital initiatives that are not matched by a correspondingly high digital-maturity level as a financial-performance risk, not an automatic strength.

finding_statement: Across seven organizational-capability themes (Strategy & Ecosystem, Innovation Thinking, DT Technologies, Data, Operations, Organizational Design, DT Leadership), the relative importance of each theme shifts systematically across Teece's sensing, seizing, and transforming mechanisms: Innovation Thinking and DT Technologies capabilities carry the highest relevance during sensing (external scanning, technology/customer-need awareness); Strategy & Ecosystem, Operations, and Data capabilities peak during seizing (partner/network management, internal process improvement, data protection and exploitation); and Organizational Design and DT Leadership capabilities carry the highest relevance during transforming (structural adaptation, culture, incentives).
mechanism: Because organizational capabilities are the concrete, actionable substrate of the abstract sensing/seizing/transforming dynamic-capability mechanisms, and because the relative importance of each of the seven capability themes shifts systematically across the three mechanisms, organizations that try to develop all seven capability themes simultaneously and uniformly misallocate scarce transformation resources; sequencing capability investment to match the currently active mechanism is more resource-efficient than a flat, undifferentiated capability-development agenda.
operationalisation_hint: Use a digital maturity assessment first to identify which of the three mechanism-stages (sensing/seizing/transforming) the organization is currently in, then prioritize capability-development investment in the 2-3 capability themes empirically shown to carry the highest relative relevance for that specific stage, rather than pursuing all seven themes at once.

finding_statement: Quantified relative-relevance analysis shows the transforming mechanism carries by far the highest relevance for DT Leadership capabilities (culture, incentives, mindset, balanced internal/external talent development), while only a small fraction of DT Leadership capabilities is relevant during the initial sensing stage (limited there to promoting experimentation and entrepreneurial aspiration). This suggests intensive culture-transformation investment should be concentrated once an organization has already sensed opportunities and begun seizing resources, rather than necessarily being the very first universal prerequisite.
mechanism: Early-stage sensing primarily requires an open, experimentation-tolerant mindset among a subset of actors, whereas full culture change (incentive redesign, balanced talent recruitment, embedding a customer-oriented and change-embracing mindset organization-wide) is costly and disruptive, and is more efficiently undertaken once the organization has committed to specific opportunities (seizing) and needs to reconfigure structures and routines around them (transforming), rather than attempting a wholesale culture overhaul before any concrete opportunity has been identified.
operationalisation_hint: Stage readiness assessments should not treat culture development as uniformly front-loaded; distinguish early sensing-stage experimentation tolerance from later transforming-stage investments in incentives, talent architecture, and organization-wide mindset change, and expect the heavier capability-development burden to appear after opportunity commitment.

finding_statement: Ambidexterity requires maintaining the operational efficiency of the existing value chain even while pursuing digital exploration; Operations capabilities are explicitly warned to be at risk of being "overlooked" as organizations pursue innovation at the expense of existing business activities, yet the seizing mechanism carries the highest relative relevance for Operations capabilities (leveraging external insight to improve internal processes) and interconnecting operations with other business lines is described as essential specifically for the transforming stage.
mechanism: Existing, profitable business operations fund exploratory digital transformation efforts, so neglecting operational capability development to prioritize innovation can undermine the very resource base that makes exploration sustainable; ambidextrous organizations must therefore treat operational-efficiency capability-building as a parallel, continuous track rather than a lower priority relative to innovation-focused capabilities.
operationalisation_hint: When building a capability-development roadmap for digital transformation, explicitly allocate resources to operational-efficiency capabilities in parallel with innovation/technology capabilities at every stage, rather than assuming operations can be deprioritized until transformation is complete.

finding_statement: Despite this review demonstrating that DT Leadership, Organizational Design, and Strategy & Ecosystem capabilities matter as much as technology-related capabilities at different transformation stages, the broader underlying literature in both the organizational-capabilities stream and the digital-maturity-model stream continues to disproportionately emphasize technological aspects, leaving socio-technical elements (strategy, people, culture) only peripherally considered.
mechanism: Digital transformation research has historically been anchored in an IT/IS disciplinary tradition that defaults to technology-centric framing, so even reviews explicitly aiming for a holistic view (like this one) find that most source literature under-theorizes the socio-technical (people/culture/strategy) side relative to the technical side, requiring deliberate corrective effort (e.g., explicitly incorporating socio-technical-systems theory) to achieve balance.
operationalisation_hint: When using DT capability or maturity frameworks, explicitly audit whether strategy, people, culture, and ecosystem capabilities are being underweighted relative to technology capabilities; treat a technology-heavy profile as a field-level blind-spot risk rather than evidence that socio-technical readiness is unimportant.

finding_statement: Organizations pursuing digital transformation benefit from five specific design-thinking-rooted dynamic capabilities that translate ambiguous technological challenges into human-valued opportunities: (1) extending -- enlarging the shared knowledge base through close collaboration with diverse internal/external stakeholders; (2) debating -- juxtaposing digital/technological and human perspectives via critical questioning to reframe the challenge; (3) cropping -- selecting/retaining only the technological requirements and solution alternatives relevant to actual user needs, rather than being driven purely by data or technical functionality; (4) interpreting -- adopting different perceptual frames (e.g., distinct user archetypes/personas) to uncover new opportunities in the technology; and (5) recombining -- synthesizing technological and human/socio-cultural knowledge into a holistic solution framing.
mechanism: Standard dynamic-capability treatments of digital transformation (sensing/seizing/reconfiguring) are technology- and strategy-centered and risk producing digital solutions that are technically feasible but not meaningful or adopted by end users; design-thinking-rooted capabilities counterbalance this by embedding continuous empathizing, reframing, and synthesis activities throughout the technology-adoption process, ensuring that the opportunities provided by digital technologies result from harmonization with people's lives rather than treating the technology itself as the solution.
operationalisation_hint: When running a digital-transformation initiative, explicitly assign process steps/roles for each of the five capabilities (e.g., structured stakeholder-extension sessions, dedicated debate/critique sessions contrasting technical vs. human framings, criteria-based cropping of requirements against user archetypes, and recombination workshops synthesizing technical and human insights) rather than relying on a generic "user research" phase alone.

finding_statement: In all four cases, the design-thinking dynamic capabilities needed for human-centered digital transformation were built and exercised through a close, iterative collaboration between the transforming organization and an external consulting/design partner, who mediated between technical/business stakeholders and end users; the consulting relationship itself was the vehicle through which extending, debating, cropping, interpreting, and recombining capabilities were enacted.
mechanism: Organizations undergoing digital transformation frequently lack in-house capacity to systematically bridge the gap between business stakeholders' framing of a technological challenge and actual end-user needs; a mediating external partner brings dedicated method (e.g., a Double Diamond discover-define-develop-deliver process) and neutral facilitation that let internal stakeholders debate and reframe the challenge more openly than they might internally, especially where competing internal interests (e.g., IT vs. marketing, senior vs. junior engineers) impede this on their own.
operationalisation_hint: When internal capability for human-centered reframing of a digital-transformation challenge is limited, consider engaging an external design-thinking-oriented consulting partner specifically to mediate between technical/business framings and end-user needs, rather than assuming internal teams can readily build these capabilities unaided.

finding_statement: A TISM-based hierarchical analysis of four SME digital-transformation factors -- Digital Awareness, Digital Strategy and Roadmap, Digital Adoption and Implementation, and Digital Transformation Continuous Improvement -- found all four factors mutually reachable and effectively at the same hierarchical level due to circular feedback relationships (continuous improvement feeds back into awareness; implementation experience feeds back into strategy), rather than forming a strict linear stage sequence.
mechanism: Because implementation reveals new information that must immediately revise strategy, and because continuous-improvement learning reshapes organizational digital awareness, treating digital transformation as a one-time, front-to-back linear project (awareness then strategy then adoption then done) misrepresents its actual dynamics; the cyclical structure lets organizations respond to emerging challenges or opportunities without waiting for a complete transformation cycle to finish.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an SME digital-transformation roadmap, build in explicit feedback loops (e.g., scheduled strategy-revision checkpoints informed by implementation learnings, and awareness-refresh activities informed by continuous-improvement insights) rather than treating awareness-building, strategizing, and implementation as one-off sequential phases.

finding_statement: Strong digital awareness and literacy established early in a transformation directly reduces employee resistance during the later digital-adoption-and-implementation stage, because employees who understand digital transformation's purpose and benefits are less likely to fear job displacement; under-investing in the awareness stage is expected to manifest predictably as resistance problems later, rather than resistance being an independent, unrelated barrier.
mechanism: Employee resistance to digital transformation is frequently driven by fear of job displacement and unfamiliarity rather than by the technology itself; because digital awareness/literacy directly shapes how employees interpret the purpose of adoption efforts, weak awareness-building upstream is expected to compound into stronger resistance downstream, making the two stages causally linked rather than independent barriers to manage separately.
operationalisation_hint: Treat awareness-building as an upstream change-management control: assess whether employees receive early explanation of the transformation's purpose, expected benefits, and role implications, and treat weak digital literacy or weak awareness communication as a predictor of later implementation resistance rather than as a separate downstream surprise.

finding_statement: A rigorous large-sample survey (n=335 managers/leaders, telecom sector) finds dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, transforming) strongly and directly predict digital-transformation success (beta=0.884), but structured change management (based on Kotter's eight-step model: change urgency, visionary coalition, empowerment, sustainability) mediates the large majority of this effect (indirect beta=0.692), meaning dynamic capabilities alone are largely inert for driving DT outcomes unless channeled through a structured change-management process.
mechanism: Dynamic capability theory is explicitly not itself a change-management model; sensing/seizing/transforming capabilities identify and mobilize resources around digital opportunities, but converting that capability into actually implemented, sustained organizational change requires the specific change-management mechanisms of establishing urgency, building a guiding coalition, and institutionalizing the change -- without this structured translation layer, dynamic-capability development does not reliably convert into successful DT outcomes.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness, do not treat dynamic-capability maturity (sensing/seizing/transforming scores) as sufficient on its own; verify that a structured change-management process (explicit change-urgency messaging, a visionary coalition, empowerment mechanisms, and sustainability/institutionalization practices) is in place to translate capability into implemented change.

finding_statement: Among four change-management dimensions tested (change urgency, visionary coalition, empowerment, sustainability), empowerment (removing barriers to change, encouraging short-term wins) was the only one with no significant direct effect on digital transformation success (beta=0.085, not supported), yet it did show a significant mediating effect when channeled through dynamic capabilities (beta=0.133, supported) -- meaning empowerment initiatives detached from actual capability-building are unlikely to drive DT success on their own.
mechanism: Generic empowerment initiatives (removing barriers, celebrating short-term wins) without a substantive basis in organizational capability (timely information flow, resource reconfiguration ability) amount to symbolic gestures that do not translate into DT outcomes; empowerment only becomes effective when it is grounded in real dynamic-capability development that gives employees actual resources, information, and reconfiguration authority to act on.
operationalisation_hint: When designing change-management interventions for digital transformation, do not treat employee empowerment as an independent lever; pair empowerment initiatives explicitly with capability-building efforts (timely information access, resource/authority to reconfigure work) rather than symbolic gestures alone that lack a capability foundation.

finding_statement: SMEs need an organizational-competence hierarchy for digital transformation adapted to their specific constraints (limited resources, limited specialization capability) rather than directly applying digital maturity models designed for large companies (e.g., MIT/Capgemini, McKinsey, Forrester); the proposed model organizes competence at four levels -- resources (physical/human/organizational), capabilities (functional-level ability to exploit resources), competencies (multifunctional integration of capabilities spanning governance, organizational alignment, culture, technology, and employees), and core competencies -- with digital maturity progress as the outcome.
mechanism: Large-firm digital maturity models assume specialization capacity and resource slack that SMEs typically lack, so directly applying them risks setting unattainable or poorly-prioritized capability targets; a hierarchy that explicitly starts from the SME's actual resource base and builds up through functional capabilities before multifunctional competencies gives SME managers a more realistic, sequenced path to digital maturity.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing SME digital-transformation readiness, start from an inventory of actual physical/human/organizational resources rather than benchmarking directly against large-firm maturity-model stage descriptions; build capability-development plans bottom-up (resources to functional capabilities to cross-functional competencies) rather than top-down.

finding_statement: A distinct "information culture" -- the socially shared patterns of behavior, norms and values defining the importance and use of information in an organization, requiring information to flow openly and be relevant/high-quality across all SME employees -- emerged from expert interviews and was added as a new element within the organizational-culture competence dimension, distinct from other culture types (results-oriented, rule-following, relationship-oriented, risk-taking).
mechanism: Because SMEs typically have flatter, less specialized structures than large firms, digital-transformation-relevant information cannot rely on formal specialist channels alone; it must flow openly and be actively valued across the whole workforce for decisions and digital-capability development to be well-informed, making information culture a load-bearing (not merely supporting) element of digital-transformation competence in this context.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether SME employees across all roles (not just IT/management) have open, quality-controlled access to digitalization-relevant information, and whether the organization's culture actively values and rewards sharing such information, as a distinct readiness sub-check separate from general "collaborative culture" measures.

finding_statement: Across a large sample of 400 heterogeneous Italian museums, an organization-wide Digital Readiness Index (DRI) computed as a weighted composite of five dimensions -- people (digital skills), technology (adoption, data analytics, infrastructure), process (front/back office digitization), customer (digital engagement channels), and strategy and investment -- averaged only 0.35/1, with People (0.29) and Process (0.21) scoring as the weakest dimensions, while Technology (0.40), Customer (0.38), and Strategy and Investment (0.38) scored moderately higher.
mechanism: In resource-constrained, historically non-digital organizations, staff digital skills and internal process digitization lag furthest behind because they require deep, sustained investment in human capital and back-office system overhauls, whereas technology adoption and customer-facing digital channels (e.g., social media presence) can be added more incrementally and visibly without requiring the same depth of internal capability change -- meaning readiness gaps concentrate disproportionately in the least visible, hardest-to-fix dimensions.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing organizational digital readiness, compute and report per-dimension scores (not just a single composite index) so that hidden bottlenecks in people/digital-skills and back-office process digitization are not masked by more visible progress in technology adoption or customer-facing channels; benchmark against sector peers per dimension to prioritize investment.

finding_statement: Museum directors flagged that pursuing fully digital service delivery (e.g., fully digital ticketing) risks losing customers who lack digital devices or the ability/willingness to purchase online, particularly older or less digitally engaged visitor segments; complete digitalization removing physical/analogue access points can therefore reduce rather than increase overall customer reach and revenue.
mechanism: Digital-readiness improvement is often implicitly modeled as monotonically beneficial (higher digitalization = better), but in customer-facing service contexts with heterogeneous customer digital-literacy levels, removing non-digital access channels entirely excludes segments who cannot or will not transact digitally, so full digitalization can actively harm the organization's reach and revenue rather than simply representing an unrealized opportunity.
operationalisation_hint: When setting digital-transformation readiness targets for customer-facing processes, explicitly assess the digital-literacy heterogeneity of the served customer base and deliberately retain non-digital access channels where a meaningful segment would otherwise be excluded, rather than treating "fully digital" as an unconditionally desirable end-state.

finding_statement: Despite extensive literatures on "e-readiness" (278 Web of Science articles, ~74% of the combined readiness literature) and "digital readiness" (91 articles, ~24%) as pre-transformation assessment constructs, articles specifically addressing organizational readiness for digital transformation represent only about 2% of the combined literature (7-8 articles identified via systematic PRISMA-based search across 2004-2022), despite digital transformation itself having a vastly larger literature base (5,007 articles) -- revealing a quotable gap between how much is written about "being digital-ready" in general versus specifically "being ready to undertake a transformation."
mechanism: E-readiness and digital readiness research trace back to national/institutional digital-divide assessment (public policy, e-government, e-commerce adoption) and have accumulated decades of measurement tradition, whereas organizational readiness specifically for the more radical, business-model-level change implied by "transformation" is a recent (post-2017), still-nascent research thread that has not yet benefited from the same accumulated conceptual and empirical development.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or evaluating a readiness-assessment instrument for RQ1 purposes, treat off-the-shelf "e-readiness" or general "digital readiness" instruments with caution, since they were developed for a different (broader, less transformation-specific) construct and may not adequately capture the conditions specific to enterprise-scale transformation readiness.

finding_statement: Adapting the CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) framework for organizational digital transformation readiness, this study explicitly adds a "Level 0 (incomplete)" starting point -- where processes are unpredictable, poorly controlled, and management is reactive with inconsistent performance -- below the conventional "Level 1 (initial)" baseline that most existing digital maturity models assume as the starting point, specifically to account for businesses in developing-country contexts that have not yet reached even that baseline.
mechanism: Most published digital maturity models (e.g., standard CMMI-based frameworks) implicitly assume organizations start at "Level 1" with at least an initial, ad hoc approach already in place; but many businesses in developing-economy contexts have not yet reached even this baseline, so readiness models transplanted directly from developed-economy contexts systematically fail to differentiate or represent the actual starting conditions of organizations in less digitally mature economies.
operationalisation_hint: When applying a maturity-based readiness assessment in a developing-economy or otherwise under-digitized context, explicitly include a "no/incomplete process" floor level below the standard "initial" level, rather than assuming all assessed organizations have at least reached a baseline of ad hoc digital practice.

finding_statement: The proposed ODTR framework structures readiness across three interacting levels: the macro-level competitive environment (market and context), the meso-level organization (assessed through the five ODTR dimensions), and the micro-level dimensions themselves (technological resources, business processes, management capability, human capability, corporate culture, which interact without a fixed hierarchy). Critically, the framework is cyclical rather than linear: once digital transformation is achieved, it feeds back to impact both the organization and the competitive environment in which it operates, meaning readiness is not a one-time gate but an input to a recurring loop.
mechanism: Because digital transformation changes an organization's capabilities and market behavior, and because competitors and the broader market simultaneously adapt to the resulting shifts, the competitive environment that originally created pressure for transformation is itself altered by the transformation, which in turn changes the readiness requirements for the organization's next transformation cycle -- so treating "readiness" as a fixed target state to reach once misrepresents the ongoing, environment-reshaping nature of the process.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a readiness-assessment governance artifact, build in a recurring reassessment trigger tied to competitive-environment monitoring (not just internal capability tracking), since a successful transformation changes the environment against which future readiness must be judged.
page_or_section: Section 6 (Figure 4, ODTR framework and Propositions P1-P3)

finding_statement: Across interviews spanning five South African industries, the successful roll-out of digital transformation was found to be driven predominantly by people elements (organisational culture, workforce skills/training, employee well-being); it is critical for organisations to invest in technological infrastructure only once the people elements have been addressed, since people are the drivers of technology implementation rather than a downstream afterthought.
mechanism: Technology investments made before an organisation's workforce has the requisite culture, skills, and psychological readiness to adopt them tend to underperform because the people who must operate and champion the technology are not yet equipped or willing to do so; establishing people-side readiness first ensures that subsequent technology investment lands on fertile ground rather than being undermined by unaddressed cultural or skills gaps.
operationalisation_hint: When sequencing a digital-transformation roadmap, prioritize organisational-culture and workforce-skill/well-being interventions ahead of major technological-infrastructure investment, and treat technology spend as conditional on people-readiness rather than a parallel or preceding track.

finding_statement: Digital transformation initiatives generate identifiable technostress risks for employees -- job security fears from automation (e.g., in mining, where advanced analytics threatens to reduce headcount), techno-invasion as remote-work technologies blur personal/professional boundaries, and techno-insecurity from rapidly evolving skill requirements -- which organisations must actively identify, monitor, and mitigate as a distinct, ongoing risk-management track throughout the transformation rather than treating employee stress as an unavoidable side effect of change.
mechanism: Because digital technologies simultaneously threaten job roles (via automation), blur work/life boundaries (via remote/always-on connectivity), and demand continuously updated skills, employees experience compounding, identifiable stressors that specifically stem from the technology itself (not merely generic "resistance to change"); left unaddressed, technostress degrades employee well-being, trust, and ultimately the adoption success of the transformation, whereas identifying technostressors and monitoring employee strain levels throughout the rollout (not just at the outset) allows targeted interventions.
operationalisation_hint: Establish an ongoing technostress-monitoring track parallel to the technical rollout: identify likely technostressors (overload, invasion, insecurity, complexity) specific to the initiative, evaluate situational factors and design targeted interventions (e.g., structured training, clearer job-security communication, boundary-setting norms for remote work), and monitor employee strain levels continuously, especially during peak transformation activity.

finding_statement: Across a large-sample survey (135 respondents, 44 municipalities) and interview study (24 respondents, 13 municipalities) on municipal digital transformation, sentiment analysis of interview transcripts found negative emotions (fear, frustration, anger) nearly balanced with positive emotions (41% vs. 49%), but qualitative follow-up discussion revealed that most of these negative emotions did not reflect employee resistance to change/technology itself; instead, they reflected dissatisfaction and protest at the organization's failure to act (absence of strategy, structure, or support for digital transformation) -- a fundamentally different diagnosis with different remediation implications.
mechanism: Coding raw sentiment as "negative = resistance to change" without deeper qualitative interpretation risks misdiagnosing the actual barrier; in this study, employees expressing anger or frustration were often protesting the lack of organizational digital-transformation activity (no structure, no strategic plan, no training) rather than opposing change itself -- meaning organizations that interpret negative employee sentiment as resistance-to-technology and respond with change-management/persuasion tactics may be addressing the wrong problem, when the actual fix needed is organizational action (providing structure, strategy, and resources), not overcoming employee reluctance.
operationalisation_hint: When negative employee sentiment toward digital transformation is detected, do not automatically categorize it as "resistance to change"; use follow-up qualitative probing to correctly diagnose whether the barrier is organizational inaction or genuine resistance, since the appropriate remediation differs substantially between the two.

finding_statement: Across a validated six-category, 22-subcategory barrier framework (strategy/governance, process/practice, organization/culture, policy/regulation, people/community, digital/information ecosystem) applied to Canadian municipalities, "absence of data management" was the single most frequently cited barrier subcategory (18% of all 514 coded references, more than double the next-highest subcategory), with the broader Process/Practice/Management category accounting for 29% of all cited barriers -- exceeding Strategy/Governance (9%), Organization/Culture (8%), and Policy/Regulation (7%) combined.
mechanism: In organizations undertaking piecemeal, haphazard digitization (digitizing individual data sets without an overarching data-governance practice), the resulting data remains siloed, unusable for cross-departmental decision-making, and disconnected from asset-lifecycle planning -- so even where individual digitization initiatives exist, the absence of systematic data management (not lack of strategy or culture per se) becomes the single largest practical obstacle to realizing value from digital transformation.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness in asset-heavy, siloed public-sector organizations, prioritize diagnosing data-management practices (data governance, cross-departmental sharing mechanisms, dedicated data teams) as the highest-leverage barrier to address, rather than assuming strategy or culture gaps are the primary bottleneck.

finding_statement: A systematic review of 18 published digital maturity assessment models (from PWC, Deloitte, BCG, government bodies, and academic sources) found that only 5 offered even indirect barrier-evaluation metrics, and none provided questions aimed directly at identifying barriers; the overwhelming majority of maturity models describe where an organization currently sits on a maturity scale without diagnosing what specifically is preventing it from advancing.
mechanism: Maturity models are typically designed around descriptive stage/level frameworks (e.g., "beginner" to "advanced"), which are useful for benchmarking position but do not by themselves reveal the causal obstacles (financial, technical, human, regulatory) responsible for an organization's current position, so organizations using only a maturity score lack actionable diagnostic guidance on where to intervene.
operationalisation_hint: Supplement any digital maturity assessment model with a dedicated barrier-evaluation instrument (e.g., a structured questionnaire scoring specific barrier areas as no/local/enterprise-wide barrier) rather than relying on a maturity score alone to guide intervention priorities.

finding_statement: Validated by manufacturing industry representatives, a barrier taxonomy for high-technology manufacturing digital transformation includes not only common areas (IT infrastructure, existing systems, financial resources, qualified specialists, training, digital policy) but also two less commonly captured areas: "diverse IT maturity of production cooperation participants" (a barrier when key partners/suppliers cannot exchange information in the required digital format) and "insufficient elaboration of secure-access channels/regulatory framework for limited-access information" (a barrier specific to industries handling sensitive, export-controlled, or state-secret information).
mechanism: In defense-adjacent, high-technology, or otherwise regulated manufacturing sectors, digital transformation is constrained not only by internal organizational readiness but by the digital maturity of the broader industrial cooperation network (since production increasingly depends on multi-party digital information exchange) and by legal/security requirements governing how sensitive information may be transferred digitally -- barriers that are largely absent from general-purpose digital maturity frameworks designed for less regulated or single-organization contexts.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital-transformation readiness in regulated, high-technology, or supply-chain-dependent manufacturing contexts, explicitly add barrier-assessment items for (a) the digital-information-exchange maturity of key external cooperation partners and (b) the adequacy of secure/limited-access information-transfer channels and their supporting regulatory documentation.

finding_statement: Across 359 Chinese technology-based SMEs, organizational agility strongly predicts digital capability (beta=0.551, the strongest path in the model), and digital capability has a substantially stronger direct effect on digital innovation performance (beta=0.269) than organizational agility's own direct effect (beta=0.137); digital capability was also confirmed as a significant mediator of the agility-to-transformation relationship (indirect beta=0.148). This indicates agility is a necessary organizational-level precondition, but its practical payoff for transformation success is realized mainly by being converted into digital capability, not through agility's direct effect alone.
mechanism: Organizational agility (rapid responsiveness, adaptability to market/customer change) creates the organizational conditions under which digital capability can be built and exercised, but agility alone -- the ability to react quickly -- does not by itself constitute the capacity to sense, operationalize, and integrate digital technology; digital capability is the more proximate, integrative mechanism that actually converts organizational responsiveness into transformation outcomes, which is why its direct effect on performance outweighs agility's.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing SME digital-transformation readiness, do not treat organizational agility as a sufficient condition on its own; verify that agility is being actively converted into digital capability (sensing, operationalizing, and integrating digital technology) rather than assuming rapid responsiveness alone will produce transformation success.

finding_statement: Contrary to the common literature assumption that top management support is a decisive driver of digital transformation, this study found top management support only partially/weakly moderates both the organizational-agility-to-transformation relationship (beta=0.122, p=0.023) and the digital-capability-to-transformation relationship (beta=0.111, p=0.030) -- both barely above conventional significance thresholds and explicitly described by the authors as "not as significant as previously believed in the literature."
mechanism: In SMEs specifically (as distinct from large enterprises), top management support appears to function mainly as a resourcing and coordinating "guarantee" mechanism -- providing funds, resources, and cross-departmental coordination -- rather than as the primary causal driver of transformation success; because SME organizational agility and digital capability are themselves often embodied directly in a small leadership team, the marginal moderating contribution of separately measured "top management support" is comparatively modest once agility and digital capability are already accounted for.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing SME (as opposed to large-enterprise) digital-transformation readiness, do not over-weight top management support as the primary lever; treat it as a necessary but comparatively modest resourcing/coordination enabler relative to the more consequential organizational-agility and digital-capability conditions.

finding_statement: Across 36 surveyed Italian companies, the "people" and "technology" dimensions scored as the most digitally mature/performing dimensions, while "process" -- the ability of business processes to be repeatably and flexibly executed regardless of who performs them -- was identified as the dimension where digital transformation was hardest to implement, attributed to the inherent rigidity and low replicability of existing production systems.
mechanism: Digital tools can be acquired (technology) and staff can be trained or hired with relevant skills (people) comparatively quickly, but re-engineering established production processes to be standardized, repeatable, and flexible enough to support digital transformation requires restructuring deeply embedded operational routines and physical/organizational workflows, which resist change far more than technology procurement or individual skill-building.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing digital-transformation readiness bottlenecks, do not assume people/culture is always the limiting dimension; explicitly assess process rigidity and replicability as a potentially distinct and harder-to-shift bottleneck, particularly in production/manufacturing-heavy contexts.

finding_statement: Across 36 companies spanning four industrial sectors, zero companies reached the highest "Digital Transformation" readiness level (level 5 of 5); readiness instead clustered at "Not existent" (24.6%), "Basic digital operation" (21.5%), "Advanced digital operation" (30.7%), and "Digital integration" (23.2%). Readiness scaled in a graded, dose-response manner with firm size (small vs. medium vs. large), annual turnover, and the percentage of turnover invested in digital technologies/IT/innovation (companies investing over 5% of turnover scored roughly 3x higher average readiness than those investing less).
mechanism: Achieving full digital transformation requires simultaneous, sustained maturity across people, process, technology, and innovation dimensions, which is disproportionately difficult for smaller or less digitally-invested firms that lack the resource base to advance all four dimensions in parallel; larger firms and those investing a higher share of turnover in digital technologies can sustain broader, more parallel capability development, producing the observed graded relationship between resource commitment/scale and readiness level.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking a firm's digital-transformation readiness, calibrate expectations against firm size and digital-investment intensity (e.g., percentage of turnover) rather than against an absolute "fully transformed" target, since even well-resourced firms in a broad cross-sector sample rarely if ever reach complete transformation.

finding_statement: Rather than pursuing "big-bang" disruption, successful large-scale digital transformation can be decomposed into a repeatable six-step cycle (discover improvement potential, analyse current work, generate ideas, develop/implement, evaluate) applied to small, cross-functional "pain points" identified through regular, mandatory workshops attended by managers from all departments, with each resulting project capped at strict time (e.g., 6-month) and evaluation (feasibility, urgency, strategic value) criteria; visible, fast wins from these small projects build employee morale and management trust, which in turn increases participation in subsequent transformation initiatives.
mechanism: Framing digital transformation as one large, uncertain, resource-intensive program tends to make managers hesitant or resistant, especially in SMEs and even large enterprises facing scope-creep risk; by contrast, decomposing the transformation into small, time-boxed projects that solve problems employees actually experience day-to-day (rather than top-down mandated initiatives) produces fast, visible, and attributable wins, and these visible successes create a self-reinforcing cycle of trust and morale that lowers resistance to the next round of change.
operationalisation_hint: Structure digital-transformation programs as a repeating cycle of short (e.g., 3-6 month), strictly time-boxed projects targeting specific, employee-identified cross-functional pain points -- prioritized by feasibility, urgency, and strategic value -- rather than as a single large multi-year initiative, and use regular mandatory cross-departmental workshops as the mechanism for continuously surfacing new pain points.
page_or_section: Sections 4, 4.3, 5.2 (Digital Kaizen process model; MyFPT and AkaLink cases)

finding_statement: At FPT Software, digital solutions originally built to solve the company's own internal cross-functional pain points (e.g., an employee-engagement app, a skills-inventory platform) were subsequently refined, packaged, and sold to external clients as digital-transformation consultancy services -- a process that transformed the company's own business model and organizational identity from a software-development/IT-outsourcing firm into a digital-transformation service provider, driven both by internal capability-building momentum and external market pressure (intensifying competition, more demanding clients) in the IT-outsourcing market.
mechanism: A large, complex organization that treats its own operational pain points as a "test bed" can generate internally-validated, proven solutions (with demonstrated ROI, adoption, and success metrics) that are directly transferable to external clients facing similar problems; this reverses the usual direction of digital transformation value creation (external offering enables internal improvement) by having internal transformation solutions become the source of a new external value proposition, which in turn requires and reinforces new organizational structures (dedicated client-facing digital-transformation units, evaluation committees).
operationalisation_hint: Use internal pain points as a pilot pipeline for external offerings: capture proven internal solutions, validate adoption and ROI internally first, then package them into client-facing services supported by dedicated commercialization structures and review governance.

finding_statement: At a benchmark central enterprise independently recognized as a first-mover and industry leader in digital transformation (rated overall "digital pioneer" level, 3.24/5), only Infrastructure scored "Excellent" and Top-level Design, Business Process, and Digital Performance scored "Good," while Professional Management (organizational structure, financial management, HR management, R&D digitalization) and Comprehensive Integration both scored only "General" (mediocre) -- the two dimensions explicitly identified by the study as the key factors restricting further digital transformation.
mechanism: Technology infrastructure and top-level strategic commitment are comparatively easier to build and are highly visible to leadership and external benchmarking, so they mature first and fastest even in industry-leading firms; professional management (adapting organizational structure, HR, and financial processes to digital ways of working) and comprehensive integration (breaking down cross-departmental data silos) require deeper, less visible organizational change and therefore lag even when an enterprise is otherwise recognized as an industry digital leader.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking digital-transformation readiness, do not infer that strong scores on infrastructure or leadership commitment imply strong organizational/integration maturity; explicitly assess professional-management and cross-departmental-integration dimensions separately, since these are the most likely residual bottleneck even in otherwise-mature organizations.

finding_statement: At the case enterprise, horizontal integration (business-process integration with upstream/downstream partner enterprises across the value chain) scored "Excellent," while vertical integration (intra-enterprise integration between internal finance/business/R&D/production functions) scored only "General" -- despite both being sub-components of the single "Comprehensive Integration" dimension, they diverged sharply, with external, inter-organizational integration outpacing internal, cross-departmental integration.
mechanism: Because inter-enterprise integration is often driven and standardized by industry-wide platforms, contracts, or shared value-chain protocols (which create external pressure and ready-made integration mechanisms), it can mature faster than intra-enterprise integration, which depends on more difficult, less externally incentivized internal organizational changes (breaking down departmental data silos, unifying financial/R&D/production systems) that lack an equivalent external forcing function.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing "integration" as a digital-transformation readiness condition, measure vertical (intra-organizational, cross-departmental) and horizontal (inter-organizational, value-chain) integration as two separate sub-scores rather than a single composite integration score, since strong performance on one does not imply strong performance on the other.
page_or_section: Sections 5.3, 6.1 (E1 vertical vs. E2 horizontal integration results)

finding_statement: SME e-commerce transformation readiness can be operationalized through three linked dimensions -- Strategy (treating e-commerce as a company-wide strategic priority, not just an add-on channel), Online Sales (personalized, seamless purchase journeys enabled by digital marketing and analytics), and eCustomer Service (post-purchase support via automated tools) -- underpinned by four cross-cutting capabilities: UX, Advanced Analytics, IT Architecture, and IT Delivery & Operation.
mechanism: Treating e-commerce strategically (rather than as an isolated channel project) is what lets the four supporting capabilities be built once and reused across the online-sales and customer-service dimensions, avoiding disconnected, channel-specific IT solutions.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether e-commerce initiatives have an explicit strategic mandate (objectives, resources, defined role in the broader sales/relationship channel mix) before evaluating technology-level capabilities.

finding_statement: Across 13 expert interviews spanning technology, consulting, education, software, and marketing sectors, the most frequently cited barriers to SME e-commerce digital transformation were budget constraints, resistance to change, absence of a clear digital strategy, insufficient technological infrastructure, and difficulty selecting/integrating appropriate technologies -- a consistent barrier cluster across otherwise-diverse SME sub-sectors.
mechanism: These barriers recur because SMEs, unlike large enterprises, typically lack dedicated digital-transformation budgets, in-house technology-selection expertise, and slack resources to absorb the disruption of a change process, so the same handful of constraints surface regardless of the specific SME's sector or initiative.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing SME transformation readiness, check specifically for (1) allocated budget for digital initiatives, (2) an explicit written digital strategy, and (3) a designated resource/advisor for technology selection, since these were the barriers experts raised most consistently.
page_or_section: Table 4 (Key Themes), Digital Preparation and Technological Adoption themes

finding_statement: Among 33+ digital-maturity indicators tested via AHP-DEMATEL for Chinese SMEs, IT system support, organizational process automation, talent/leadership, long-term digital strategy orientation, and customer-value focus rank as the top five causal (driving) factors, while customer customization, rapid R&D, and resource/process efficiency are outcome (result) factors that these causes act through.
mechanism: In DEMATEL causal-effect decomposition, "cause" factors are those whose improvement most influences the rest of the system; ranking IT infrastructure and process automation above generic culture/organization items suggests concrete technology and automation investments are the more immediately actionable levers for resource-constrained SMEs.
operationalisation_hint: When SMEs have limited resources for a full-scope transformation, prioritize IT system support and process automation investments first, since these show the highest centrality/causal weight for driving downstream digital-capability improvements.

finding_statement: Internal cross-functional collaboration has the highest centrality score (degree of interconnectedness with other factors) among all tested SME digital-maturity indicators, ahead of organizational-scientific decision-making, process automation, data-driven decision-making, and IT system support, indicating it functions as the most structurally important "hub" factor linking other digital-capability dimensions together.
mechanism: A factor's centrality in DEMATEL reflects how strongly it is connected (both causing and being caused by) other factors in the system; internal collaboration's top centrality suggests it is the connective tissue letting improvements in strategy, technology, and process dimensions reinforce each other rather than remaining siloed.
operationalisation_hint: Treat internal cross-functional collaboration mechanisms (shared platforms, cross-department routines) as a structural enabler to strengthen early, since weak collaboration may blunt the payoff from investments in other individually-strong dimensions.

finding_statement: A digital maturity model can explicitly incorporate environmental and social sustainability as first-class assessment criteria -- specifically quality management systems, energy management, environmental/social responsibility, and product-recovery/recycling activities -- rather than treating sustainability as a byproduct of digital transformation, addressing a gap the authors identify in prior maturity-model literature.
mechanism: Explicitly scoring sustainability-related practices alongside conventional digital-maturity dimensions lets an organization see whether its digital investments are also being directed toward measurable environmental/social outcomes, rather than assuming digitalization automatically improves sustainability.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or selecting a maturity assessment, add explicit criteria for energy management, quality management systems, and environmental/social responsibility rather than relying on generic "sustainability" as an unmeasured aspiration.

finding_statement: A 7-dimension digital maturity scale achieved good psychometric reliability (Cronbach's alpha mostly >0.8) and validity (KMO 0.83-0.95) via EFA, but was validated only on Turkish manufacturing businesses with small samples (n=50 and n=80), and the authors note the study could not be conducted at a global scale nor across other sectors, so the specific factor structure should not be assumed to generalize beyond this context.
mechanism: Reliability statistics computed on small, single-sector, single-language samples confirm internal consistency within that sample, not cross-context generalizability of the specific latent factor structure; applying the same factor groupings elsewhere without re-validation risks misclassifying items.
operationalisation_hint: Treat the seven top-level dimension names as portable but re-run factor analysis locally before relying on this study's specific sub-factor groupings in a different sector or country.

finding_statement: Organizational readiness for digital transformation should be assessed from both the employee and leadership perspectives, because employees may perceive the organization's foundational readiness (strategy clarity, market awareness, culture) differently than leaders rate it, and this employee-leader gap is itself informative about implementation risk.
mechanism: Leaders assessing their own initiatives risk overestimating clarity and embeddedness of the digital-first culture; polling employees separately and mapping the gap exposes where the leadership's intended strategy has not actually propagated into shared organizational understanding.
operationalisation_hint: Run parallel short questionnaires for employees and for senior leaders on the same set of readiness pillars, and treat the size of the inter-group gap (not just each group's average score) as a risk indicator.

finding_statement: Organizations achieve faster digital innovation when they establish a separate, loosely-coupled fast-speed unit (distinct culture, processes, and structure) to develop lightweight/user-facing digital resources, while leaving stable heavyweight legacy systems to change slowly, connected via boundary resources (APIs).
mechanism: Tight integration between fast- and slow-speed elements reduces overall innovation speed to that of the heavyweight core; loose coupling lets the fast unit iterate independently while still drawing on the core's stable resources.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether transformation initiatives are organizationally and culturally separated (e.g., a spun-off unit or dedicated team) from core legacy operations, and whether integration is achieved via well-defined boundary interfaces rather than tight coupling.
page_or_section: Section 6.1, Nordic Choice/eBerry and DNB/ViPPS cases

finding_statement: Managers must personally understand and champion the two-speed/dynamic-capability logic and be willing to risk developing resources the organization currently lacks (e.g., recruiting external leaders with ecosystem experience) in order to seize fast-innovation opportunities.
mechanism: Top-management understanding of the two-speed logic and willingness to allocate resources/risk (e.g., Østfold Hospital's CEO, Nordic Choice's externally recruited CDO) is the precondition that lets seizing capability translate into an actual fast-innovation unit.
operationalisation_hint: Check whether top management has personally committed to and resourced a specific two-speed configuration, including willingness to recruit external expertise where internal capability gaps exist.

finding_statement: Across 42 reviewed digital maturity models, Technology/IT, operating model/organization, strategy, processes/value chain, customer focus, culture, and human capital were frequently represented. The review presents these patterns as important criteria while noting sector-contingent variation.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Despite dimension-level convergence, no single validated digital maturity model has become the consensual cross-sector standard; models proliferate from academic, consulting, and governmental sources, causing confusion for practitioners, and most models -- whether academic or consultancy-developed -- lack pragmatic empirical validation of their assessment criteria.
mechanism: Absence of a validated, universally accepted instrument means organizations must customize a chosen model to their own context, which is necessary but risks diluting or distorting the model's core assessment logic if over-customized.
operationalisation_hint: When adopting any specific maturity model, favor customization of terminology/weighting over altering the core validated dimension set, and treat model outputs as directional guidance rather than a validated diagnostic score.

finding_statement: Comparing maturity-model dimension frequency across three time windows (2015-2017, 2018-2020, 2021-2023) shows that governance, agility, collaboration, cybersecurity, and monitoring/control criteria have gained visibility in more recently published models relative to earlier ones, even as broad first-generation dimensions like generic "culture" and "leadership" show reduced standalone visibility (often decomposed into finer sub-criteria instead).
mechanism: As organizations accumulate experience with digital transformation, maturity-model authors add finer-grained governance/security/agility criteria to address risks and coordination needs that only become salient once basic technology and strategy dimensions are already addressed by earlier-generation models.
operationalisation_hint: When updating or selecting a maturity model for current use, check whether it includes explicit governance, cybersecurity, and agility/collaboration criteria rather than only the earlier-generation strategy/technology/culture set, since their absence may indicate an outdated instrument.

finding_statement: Across multiple large-sample studies synthesized in this review (e.g., 238 Polish enterprises, 3,146 firms), organizations that prioritized organizational capabilities and cross-functional integration over pure technology investment achieved 15-20% higher resilience scores and were more likely to reach their targeted transformation goals, directly contradicting the traditional technology-first approach to DT.
mechanism: Technology alone does not resolve the organizational complexity (siloed departments, legacy structures, coordination needs) that determines whether digital investments actually translate into improved operations; only firms that embed DT into both daily operations and long-term organizational planning show superior crisis performance.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating DT initiatives, weight organizational-integration readiness (cross-departmental alignment, embedding DT into daily operations and planning) at least as heavily as technology-investment readiness in any readiness assessment.

finding_statement: Firms that pair digital transformation initiatives with strong knowledge-management systems and organizational learning capabilities see DT's impact on organizational resilience amplified by 1.5 to 2 times compared to firms relying on technological sophistication alone, indicating that organizational learning capability -- not technology -- is the primary force-multiplier condition.
mechanism: Knowledge-management systems accelerate cross-departmental learning and knowledge synthesis, letting an organization apply lessons from one DT initiative or disruption to future ones; without this learning capability, technology investments remain isolated wins that do not compound into durable resilience.
operationalisation_hint: Prioritize building organizational knowledge-management and learning-capture mechanisms (post-initiative reviews, cross-departmental knowledge sharing) alongside any digital technology rollout, rather than treating knowledge management as a separate, lower-priority initiative.

finding_statement: The review synthesizes cited evidence that management may overestimate organizational readiness and understate training, adoption-time, and resource requirements. Its table attributes 65% additional-training needs, 18–24-month adoption time, and 40–50% additional investment to separate cited studies.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: A study of 3,146 firms found that only firms making balanced investments in both technology and human-capital development achieved their targeted digital-transformation goals; firms investing heavily in technology without corresponding human-capital investment achieved only about 40% of their targeted outcomes.
mechanism: Technology deployed without matching investment in workforce skills, change management, and talent development lacks the human capacity to actually operate, adapt, or extend the new digital capability, so the technology investment's realized value is capped well below its potential regardless of its technical sophistication.
operationalisation_hint: When allocating a DT budget, require an explicit, tracked allocation to human-capital development (training, talent acquisition, change management) proportional to the technology investment, rather than treating technology spend as the primary or sole budget line.

finding_statement: A comprehensive resilience-through-DT assessment should combine three theoretical lenses that each capture a distinct resilience dimension: the digital maturity model for preparedness and adaptive capacity (data-driven insight, customer-centric cultural readiness), the Industry 4.0 framework for response capability and operational efficiency (IoT/AI/cyber-physical integration), and dynamic capabilities theory for recovery and strategic flexibility (resource sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration) -- using only one lens leaves at least one resilience dimension unassessed.
mechanism: Each framework was independently developed to explain a different slice of organizational response to change (readiness posture, operational-technology integration, and strategic resource reconfiguration respectively); because real disruptions test all three simultaneously, an assessment or roadmap grounded in only one framework will miss the conditions the other two frameworks are best suited to diagnose.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a DT-for-resilience roadmap, deliberately map planned initiatives against all three dimensions (preparedness/adaptive capacity, response capability/efficiency, recovery/strategic flexibility) rather than defaulting to whichever single framework is most familiar to the assessment team.

finding_statement: Across two independently analyzed large-company case studies (insurance, manufacturing), consistent top-management (C-level) leadership that internalizes DT as a pervasive business initiative -- not the existence of a separate, formally documented DT strategy -- was the more decisive success condition; both companies succeeded with only lightly formalized (or entirely informal, "in the head of" a single executive) DT strategies.
mechanism: An explicitly formalized strategy mainly helps pre-digital, less digitally mature organizations check strategic fit and communicate goals broadly; once a credible top-management champion (e.g., a CIO acting as informal CDO) has internalized and consistently communicated the DT direction, the coordinating function of a written strategy document becomes less necessary.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether a credible, consistently-engaged top-management champion exists and is trusted to communicate DT direction, rather than checking only for the existence of a written DT strategy document.
page_or_section: Summary of Findings; Digital Leadership, Strategic Planning, and Strategy Implementation section

finding_statement: DT pervasiveness (ensuring the whole organization, not just IT or a single unit, engages with DT) must be actively coordinated once initiatives multiply, since "too many competing priorities" emerged as a top-five barrier in both case companies; unmanaged pervasiveness therefore risks the same coordination-overload effects associated with rigid planning and organizational silos identified elsewhere in the literature.
mechanism: As pervasiveness increases and DT initiatives are welcomed from all organizational levels (a deliberate enabling design choice), the resulting volume of initiatives creates a new coordination burden that, if not actively screened/prioritized, produces the same silo/coordination-failure symptoms that rigid, centralized organizations already suffer from -- pervasiveness is a double-edged enabler requiring its own governance.
operationalisation_hint: When encouraging pervasive, bottom-up DT initiative generation, pair it with an explicit initiative screening/prioritization mechanism (e.g., a coordinating unit) rather than assuming more initiatives are unconditionally better.

finding_statement: Digital governance (policies, structures, processes, and mechanisms establishing accountability and prioritization for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision, culture, and mindset that inspires innovation, collaboration, and agility) are conceptually distinct enablers of digital maturity, not a single "leadership" construct; without governance, DT efforts lack direction and compatibility with business objectives even if leaders are personally inspiring, while without inspiring leadership, governance structures alone fail to motivate genuine employee participation.
mechanism: Governance supplies the formal coordination and prioritization mechanism (which initiatives get resourced, how risk/compliance is managed), while leadership supplies the motivational and cultural mechanism (why employees should embrace change); an organization strong in one but weak in the other experiences either well-resourced-but-uninspired initiatives or enthusiastic-but-uncoordinated ones.
operationalisation_hint: Assess digital governance (formal policies/accountability for digital initiatives) and digital leadership (vision-communication and culture-building capacity) as two separate readiness dimensions rather than folding them into one "leadership" item.

finding_statement: Organizations progressing toward digital maturity fall into distinct failure/success archetypes depending on whether they are strong in technological capability, leadership/governance capability, both, or neither: "digital enthusiasts" over-invest in every new digital tool but lack governance/coordination and therefore waste resources on non-adaptive, uncoordinated systems; "digital conservatives" have strong governance/leadership discipline but excessive caution prevents them from building powerful technological capabilities; only "digital leaders" excel at both and achieve superior results.
mechanism: Because technology adoption and leadership/governance capability can develop independently of each other, assessing only one (e.g., counting adopted technologies) misses organizations that are technologically active but organizationally incoherent, or vice versa; the two-axis typology exposes which specific combination of strengths and gaps an organization has.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking an organization's digital maturity, plot it on both a technology-capability axis and a leadership/governance-capability axis rather than a single composite score, to correctly diagnose whether the binding constraint is technological or organizational.

finding_statement: Digital transformation readiness assessment should separately score (1) the maturity of management/administrative processes themselves (planned, tracked, standardized, predictable, optimizing) and (2) the maturity of that process's automation/IT support (from paper-based to AI-driven predictive optimization), since a well-managed process can still be unautomated and vice versa.
mechanism: Mixing the two into one score would mask whether the transformation bottleneck is organizational (undefined/ad-hoc processes) or technological (a mature process still executed on paper); scoring both axes separately identifies which lever to pull first.
operationalisation_hint: Score each business (sub-)process on both a CMMI-style process-maturity scale and a parallel automation-readiness scale (0=paper-based to 5=AI-driven optimization), and treat gaps between the two scores as prioritization signals for the transformation roadmap.

finding_statement: The case assesses personnel readiness through digital knowledge/skills and motivation to develop further competencies. It reports that 70% showed high competence, 11% limited manifestation, and 89% endorsed timely technology introduction.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Digital transformation maturity assessment models developed for developed-country contexts are not directly transferable to developing countries because measurable maturity there must also account for a distinct "digital divide" progression (infrastructure access, skills, and outcomes) shaped by socioeconomic and cultural inequality factors (income, education, welfare, culture) not present as binding constraints in developed-economy models.
mechanism: Standard maturity dimensions (organization, technology, strategy, employees, customers, processes, culture) implicitly assume a baseline of infrastructure access and digital literacy that cannot be assumed in developing-country contexts, so an additional digital-divide-stage assessment is needed to correctly locate an organization's actual starting point.
operationalisation_hint: When building or selecting a maturity assessment for a developing-country organization, add explicit digital-divide-stage items (infrastructure access, skills, outcomes) alongside the standard dimensions.

finding_statement: Providing digital maturity assessment as an independently self-administrable, free, web-based dashboard (rather than requiring paid third-party consulting access) removes a resource/access barrier that otherwise prevents resource-constrained organizations, especially in developing countries, from monitoring their DX progress over time.
mechanism: Paid, third-party-dependent assessment tools are financially and logistically inaccessible to many organizations, especially SMEs/public-sector bodies in developing economies, so self-service tooling is itself an enabling condition rather than a neutral implementation detail.
operationalisation_hint: Prefer or design maturity-assessment tooling as low/no-cost and self-administered, allowing repeated re-assessment over time, rather than one-off paid consulting engagements.

finding_statement: Across a pilot test of 5 service-provider companies, the highest overall digital maturity was achieved only when both Digital Capability factors (strategy, competence, customer experience, technology) and Digital Impact factors (business model, smart services, leadership, culture) scored comparably high; companies strong on one dimension but weak on the other did not achieve higher overall maturity, confirming the model's key design principle that capability without impact-leverage (or vice versa) caps maturity.
