mechanism: Digital Capability factors build the technological/organisational foundation, while Digital Impact factors determine whether that foundation is actually leveraged to respond to market/customer demand through new products, services, and business models; a strong foundation without leverage capability produces unused potential, and strong leverage capability without a foundation has nothing to leverage.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing digital maturity, always score both a capability/foundation dimension and an impact/leverage dimension separately, and prioritize the weaker of the two rather than further strengthening whichever dimension is already strong.
page_or_section: Section 3.3 (Digital Service Transformation Maturity Matrix), Section 5.3

finding_statement: In the pilot test of 5 service-provider companies, the "Digital Strategy" factor consistently scored highest among Digital Capability factors, while "Digital Competence" (digital skills, talent, HR-development for digitalization) and "Customer Experience" (simplification of interactions, management of expectations) consistently scored lowest -- indicating these companies feel confident about their digital strategy but lack the competence and customer-experience execution capability to actually deliver on it.
mechanism: A well-articulated digital strategy creates an expectation of execution capability that the organisation's actual digital skills base and customer-facing execution ability do not yet support, so strategy maturity running ahead of competence/execution maturity is a structural mismatch rather than a random variation, likely because strategy formulation requires fewer organisation-wide behavioral changes than building deep talent pipelines or redesigning customer interactions.
operationalisation_hint: When a service organisation reports strong digital-strategy maturity, specifically audit digital-competence/talent and customer-experience execution capability before assuming the strategy will translate into results, since these are the most likely bottlenecks.

finding_statement: In the pilot test, Digital Culture subfactors (innovation, agility, data-driven decisions, collaboration) and "Digital Savvy" of leadership consistently ranked among the lowest-maturity Digital Impact subfactors across all 5 assessed service companies, despite culture being one of the most frequently modeled dimensions (present in over half of the 22 digital maturity models reviewed) and widely recognized in the literature as a critical DT enabler.
mechanism: Culture-related capabilities (agility, collaboration, data-driven decision-making, leadership digital savvy) require sustained behavioral and mindset change across the whole organisation, which is inherently slower to develop than technology deployment or strategy formulation, explaining why culture consistently lags even in companies that have made real progress on more concrete, individually-actionable dimensions.
operationalisation_hint: Treat digital-culture subfactors (innovation, agility, data-driven decisions, collaboration, leadership digital savvy) as long-lead-time investments requiring sustained multi-year effort, and do not expect them to improve at the same pace as technology or strategy-dimension scores.

finding_statement: Experts who pilot-tested the DSTM assessment model explicitly flagged that not all aspects of digital maturity can be accurately assessed by one person, and that employees at higher levels of hierarchy tend to assess digital maturity more optimistically than employees at lower levels, meaning a single-assessor or management-only assessment process risks systematically overstating actual digital maturity.
mechanism: Senior respondents may have more visibility into strategic intent and less exposure to day-to-day execution friction than lower-hierarchy employees, biasing their self-assessment upward relative to the on-the-ground reality that lower-level employees experience directly.
operationalisation_hint: Require digital maturity self-assessments to be completed by an interdisciplinary panel spanning multiple hierarchical levels (not just senior management), and treat single-respondent or management-only assessment scores as likely optimistic upper bounds rather than accurate current-state measures.

finding_statement: A systematic review of 22 existing digital maturity models found that the aspect of developing new digital business models is hardly addressed in almost any of them, and this gap was confirmed empirically in the pilot test, where "Digital Service Business Model" subfactors (framework, ecosystem) scored among the lowest of all Digital Impact factors even in companies that scored well on "Service Engineering & Innovation".
mechanism: Because most existing maturity models were developed with a technology-exploitation lens (assessing how well an organisation deploys and integrates digital tools), they systematically under-instrument the exploration-oriented capability of designing genuinely new digital business models and ecosystems, so organisations relying on these models to guide their DT roadmap will underinvest in business-model innovation relative to technology deployment.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or building a digital maturity assessment, explicitly check whether it includes dedicated business-model and digital-ecosystem-design criteria, since most existing models (and organisations following them) systematically underweight this dimension relative to technology and process dimensions.

finding_statement: A SPICE/ISO-grounded digital maturity self-assessment model was applied independently in a financial-sector case, producing an overall level-three result and dimension-level results without consultant involvement.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: In a financial-sector case study, the Customer dimension scored lowest (2.37) of all seven digital-maturity dimensions -- markedly below Technology (3.80, the highest) -- specifically because customers still depend on employee assistance to use digital services, lack experience using the technology themselves, and show low trust in conducting transactions digitally rather than manually.
mechanism: An organization can achieve strong internal technology maturity (infrastructure, IT security management, application development) while its customer-facing digital maturity lags, because customer trust and self-service capability depend on the customer's own experience and confidence, not on the organization's internal technology investment alone.
operationalisation_hint: When technology-dimension maturity scores substantially exceed customer-dimension scores, prioritize customer-facing digital literacy/trust-building initiatives (guided onboarding, partnership-based ecosystem digitization) over further internal technology investment.

finding_statement: Among Rogers' (2016) six DT-readiness enablers, an expert panel across six Portuguese organisations rated Customer Centricity, Innovation Process, Value Creation, and Organisational Agility as the most impactful for DT readiness, while Competitive Positioning (inter-firm digital-platform collaboration) and Data Management scored notably lower and were considered less of a priority.
mechanism: The four highest-rated enablers all center on internally-controllable, customer- and process-facing capabilities that organisations can develop unilaterally, whereas Competitive Positioning requires trust and collaboration with external, potentially competing parties, and Data Management requires organisation-wide data accessibility that may conflict with data-sensitivity concerns -- both introducing dependencies or risks the four top-rated enablers do not.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing DT-readiness investments with limited resources, favor customer-centricity, innovation-process, value-creation, and organisational-agility initiatives first, and treat inter-firm data/platform collaboration and organisation-wide data accessibility as secondary unless the specific industry context favors them.

finding_statement: Organisations handling sensitive personal or financial data (e.g., banking, insurance) in this study's expert panel gave notably low ratings to sharing ideas/data with competitors and to organisation-wide data accessibility, because data-privacy and compliance obligations must be placed above the general business benefits of broad data sharing and data-driven decision-making that the literature otherwise associates with DT maturity.
mechanism: General DT-readiness frameworks assume data management and cross-organisational data sharing are unconditionally beneficial enablers, but in regulated, data-sensitive industries this assumption breaks down because privacy/compliance risk can outweigh the coordination or innovation benefits that data sharing would otherwise provide.
operationalisation_hint: When applying generic DT-readiness enabler frameworks (e.g., Rogers' six enablers) in data-sensitive/regulated industries, treat data-management and competitive-data-sharing scores as context-contingent rather than assuming higher scores are always better.

finding_statement: A digital transformation program can be structured either top-down (replicating already-proven pilot digital tools across similar processes, starting fast but risking missed problems due to insufficient diagnostic depth) or bottom-up (exhaustively diagnosing all business processes first to identify true pain points, more thorough but significantly delaying the start of transformation); the two approaches are not mutually exclusive and can be run in parallel if kept synchronized.
mechanism: The replication approach treats existing validated tools as the starting point (technology-first), while the process approach treats identified business problems as the starting point (problem-first); each approach's weakness is the other's strength, so combining them lets an organisation start delivering quick wins from replication while a parallel diagnostic effort surfaces problems replication alone would miss.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a DT program roadmap, explicitly decide whether to lead with proven-tool replication (for speed) or full process diagnostics (for thoroughness), or run both in a deliberately synchronized parallel track rather than defaulting to only one.

finding_statement: The cited expert-survey figure reports higher future values for several digital-transformation barrier categories, while the paper predicts that process, investment, and regulatory obstacles will continue to hinder transformation. It does not establish that every barrier will roughly double.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Managers' digital structure readiness (DRR) -- their preparedness and willingness to establish cross-functional teams, support the creation of digital leadership roles, and cultivate risk-tolerant structures -- positively and significantly predicts managers' intention to implement DT (beta=0.269, p<0.01), validated via PLS-SEM on 150 Chinese managers across 11 industries.
mechanism: Managers instrumental in shaping organizational culture, resource alignment, and strategic initiatives translate their personal readiness to build supportive structures directly into a stronger intention to act on DT, because structural readiness defines the conditions under which DT-supporting behaviors become organizationally possible.
operationalisation_hint: Assess individual managers' willingness to design cross-functional teams, support CDO-type roles, and tolerate risk-taking as a distinct readiness indicator, separate from their technology attitudes or strategic knowledge.

finding_statement: Managers' digital technology readiness (DTR) -- their personal propensity to embrace and use new digital technologies, keep up with technological developments, and value data availability -- positively and significantly predicts their intention to implement DT (beta=0.231, p<0.05), the weakest but still significant of the three validated readiness sub-constructs.
mechanism: Managers with high technology readiness are quicker to recognize digitalization benefits and more willing to commit to DT initiatives, but this study's finding that DTR is the weakest predictor (relative to structure and strategy readiness) suggests personal technology enthusiasm alone is the least sufficient driver of implementation intention among the three readiness dimensions.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing manager readiness, do not over-weight personal enthusiasm for technology adoption relative to structural and strategic readiness, since this study found it the weakest (though still significant) predictor of implementation intention.

finding_statement: Managers' digital strategy readiness (DSR) -- their ability to formulate DT goals, allocate resources for digital strategy implementation, and align digital initiatives with organizational strategic goals -- is the strongest of the three validated predictors of managers' intention to implement DT (beta=0.346, p<0.001), ahead of both structural readiness and technology readiness.
mechanism: Managers with high strategic readiness understand the strategic significance of digital technologies for competitive advantage and are proficient at aligning digital initiatives with overarching organizational strategy, which translates into the strongest and most significant driver of their intention to actually implement DT, more so than structural or purely technological readiness.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or developing managers to lead DT initiatives, prioritize assessing and building their strategic-alignment competence (ability to formulate goals, allocate resources, link digital initiatives to business strategy) over generic technology enthusiasm, since this was the strongest validated predictor of implementation intention.

finding_statement: The study positions managerial readiness as an individual-level complement to predominantly organization-level digital-readiness research and notes that hierarchy-level variation remains untested. It does not establish a specific failure scenario for organizations that aggregate readiness.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: A survey of 88 IT experts across six GCC government institutions found no statistically significant relationship between how important a digital transformation maturity factor was rated and the extent to which it was actually implemented (chi-square Asymp. Sig.=0.430 > 0.05, correlation coefficient=0.166, R-squared=0.028), meaning perceived importance explains essentially none of the variation in actual implementation.
mechanism: Recognizing a factor as important does not by itself create the organizational capacity, budget, or institutional will to implement it; in government settings specifically, mission-driven objectives, resource constraints, bureaucratic processes, and competing stakeholder priorities intervene between recognized importance and actual execution in ways that a private-sector, profit-motivated organization may not experience to the same degree.
operationalisation_hint: Do not use stated importance ratings (from surveys, expert panels, or leadership statements) as a proxy for actual implementation progress in government digital transformation assessments; measure implementation directly and independently, and treat large importance-implementation gaps as diagnostic signals requiring investigation into specific institutional barriers.

finding_statement: Government IT experts rated operational flexibility and resilience highly important while reporting difficult application and a large importance-implementation gap. The source does not directly test an explanation based on mandates or bureaucracy.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section VI (Results and Discussions), Section VII (Research Findings and Remarks)

finding_statement: Conventional digital maturity assessment frameworks, mainly constructed by consulting firms for private/commercial organizations, are often unsuitable for government bodies due to fundamental differences in operational mission (value-oriented rather than profit-oriented) and structure; this study built a government-tailored 8-category, 34-factor framework by combining three consulting-firm models, academic literature validation (confirming 25 of 34 factors), and an 88-expert practitioner survey (Cronbach's alpha 0.955) across six GCC countries.
mechanism: Private-sector maturity models are optimized for profit-driven objectives and market competition, while government digital transformation is motivated by service delivery, transparency, and constrained-resource stewardship; applying an unmodified private-sector model risks measuring the wrong success criteria and missing government-specific factors, which only a purpose-built, cross-validated framework can address.
operationalisation_hint: Do not apply commercial/consulting-firm digital maturity models unmodified to public-sector organizations; instead, adapt them through literature validation and practitioner consultation specific to the public-sector mission and operating context before use.

finding_statement: Non-parametric statistical tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U) revealed that scores on the Strategy and Vision criterion varied significantly by job title, with academic/consulting-role respondents scoring it significantly lower than leadership/management respondents, and that technical-role respondents rated Infrastructure maturity significantly lower than leadership respondents did, while age, education, and experience showed no significant effect.
mechanism: Leadership and management roles are positioned to receive and communicate top-down strategic direction (e.g., direct instructions from a minister), giving them a more favorable view of strategy execution, while technical experts working directly with infrastructure daily encounter its limitations first-hand, producing a systematically more critical assessment than leadership's more removed, strategic vantage point.
operationalisation_hint: When surveying digital transformation maturity, disaggregate results by respondent role (leadership vs. technical/operational) rather than averaging across roles, since role-based perception gaps on strategy and infrastructure specifically can mask where real problems lie.

finding_statement: Across a Delphi-informed AHP evaluation by 11 expert participants (consistency ratio below the 0.1 acceptability threshold), Management Commitment received the highest global weight (0.1632) of all 14 critical success factors spanning organizational, people, process, technical, and project-specific dimensions of agile-based digital transformation.
mechanism: Active, sustained leadership engagement that champions agile principles and DT goals provides the strategic alignment and continuous support without which lower-level enablers (team capability, process adaptability, technical infrastructure) cannot translate into sustained transformation outcomes, explaining why experts consistently rank it above all technical and procedural factors.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing resource allocation for an agile DT initiative, ensure sustained, visible management commitment is established and monitored before or alongside investment in technical infrastructure, process redesign, or team-building activities.

finding_statement: Aggregated AHP pairwise comparisons show Organizational factors (34% weight) and People factors (30% weight) together account for 64% of the total importance assigned to five CSF categories, compared to Process (15%), Technical (12%), and Project-specific factors (9%) combined -- indicating that leadership, culture, and team competence outweigh technology and traditional project-management parameters as agile-DT success drivers.
mechanism: Agile-based DT success depends more on the social subsystem (leadership, culture, team capability) than the technical subsystem (tools, technical adaptability) or conventional project constraints (cost, schedule), consistent with socio-technical systems theory's premise that technology alone cannot deliver sustainable transformation value without a supportive social system.
operationalisation_hint: When conducting an agile-DT readiness assessment or allocating a transformation budget, weight organizational and people-related readiness at roughly twice the combined weight of process, technical, and project-management readiness, rather than defaulting to technology-centric investment.

finding_statement: In the Delphi-informed AHP study, project nature, type, schedule, and cost ranked 11th through 14th of 14 critical success factors, and their category received a 0.09 weight. The authors interpret organizational and people enablers as higher priority in their agile-based context.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 4.3, Table 7 (Global ranking of critical success factor)

finding_statement: The 14 validated CSFs map onto three interdependent layers -- an outer Organizational Readiness layer (management commitment, team capability, organizational environment) that conditions an inner Agile Delivery layer (project management process, customer involvement, project manager capability, team environment, digital solution delivery strategy, project definition process, technological adaptability), which in turn conditions an innermost Project Artefacts layer (project nature, type, cost, schedule) -- reflecting how outer structural enablers determine the effectiveness of inner technical and procedural processes.
mechanism: Grounded in socio-technical systems theory, the layered structure formalizes that technology and project-management tools (inner layers) only deliver value when embedded within a supportive social/organizational system (outer layer); attempting to strengthen inner-layer factors without first securing outer-layer readiness will not produce proportional improvements in DT outcomes.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an agile-DT initiative is underperforming despite strong technical execution, check the outer Organizational Readiness layer first (leadership commitment, culture, team capability) before troubleshooting the middle Agile Delivery or inner Project Artefact layers.

finding_statement: Text-mining analysis (cosine similarity of keyword-occurrence vectors, validated by a 1000-iteration permutation test yielding an empirical p-value of 0.000) shows that the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) scale and the Acatech Industry 4.0 Maturity Index (MI) are near-orthogonal (~86-87 degree angle between vectors), confirming that technology maturity and organizational digital maturity are conceptually and statistically independent constructs that must both be assessed, since a highly mature technology can fail in a low-maturity organization and vice versa.
mechanism: Because the two frameworks were developed independently for different purposes (TRL for technology risk assessment originating at NASA; MI for organizational digital-transformation staging), their near-orthogonality is not coincidental but reflects that they measure genuinely separate readiness constructs -- technology push versus organization pull -- neither of which can substitute for the other.
operationalisation_hint: When planning any technology-integration or R&D initiative, score both the technology's TRL and the organization's Acatech MI level separately rather than assuming a high score on one implies readiness on the other.
page_or_section: Section 3 (Method), text-mining analysis and permutation test

finding_statement: A 2D matrix positioning an R&D or digitalization initiative at the intersection of its TRL (1-9) and Acatech MI (1-6) level lets an organization diagnose whether current effort should focus on technology maturation (vertical movement), organizational/data-infrastructure maturation (horizontal movement), or both; minimum thresholds of level 2 on both axes are recommended to avoid deploying advanced solutions into "technological oases surrounded by the desert" (immature environments) or investing in purely theoretical technologies.
mechanism: Restricting planned movement to vertical or horizontal steps (rather than diagonal jumps) forces an organization to address one readiness gap at a time, reducing the risk of overlooking critical technology-validation or organizational-infrastructure steps that a simultaneous two-dimensional leap would skip.
operationalisation_hint: Before greenlighting a digitalization or R&D initiative, plot its current TRL/MI position on the matrix, confirm both axes clear the level-2 minimum threshold, and plan the next step as a single vertical (technology) or horizontal (organizational) move rather than attempting both simultaneously.

finding_statement: In a case study developing a multimodal system to analyze patent sketches and technical drawings, Meta AI's Segment Anything Model (SAM) had a high published TRL (8/9) in natural RGB image contexts but performed at an effective TRL of only about 2 when applied to black-and-white, low-texture technical drawings -- a domain the model was never validated for -- forcing a project reframing from "integrate a pre-trained model" to "develop a new domain-specific approach."
mechanism: Published TRL ratings are context-bound to the domain in which the technology was validated; transplanting a technology into a structurally different application context (different data modality, environment, or use case) invalidates the original TRL rating, and the technology's effective maturity in the new context can be dramatically lower than its nominal rating suggests.
operationalisation_hint: Before assuming a commercially available or published high-TRL technology is plug-and-play ready, explicitly re-assess its TRL specifically within the target application context rather than relying on its TRL rating from the original validation domain.

finding_statement: The authors explicitly acknowledge that while the TRL-MI matrix provides structured guidance for evaluating technological maturity and digital readiness, successful implementation also depends on external organizational factors -- employee engagement, resistance to change, adaptability of existing business processes, and leadership support -- that fall outside the matrix's immediate scope but can significantly influence outcomes.
mechanism: A purely technical/organizational-maturity diagnostic tool cannot capture behavioral and cultural dynamics (resistance, engagement, leadership) that determine whether a technically and organizationally "ready" initiative actually gets implemented successfully, so these soft factors must be tracked as a separate, complementary layer of assessment.
operationalisation_hint: Pair any TRL/MI-based technical-organizational readiness assessment with a separate soft-factor assessment (employee engagement, change resistance, leadership support) rather than assuming technical/organizational maturity scores alone predict implementation success.

finding_statement: Large enterprises commonly undertake preparatory customization and R&D activities as an inherent, resourced part of their operations when adopting Industry 4.0 technologies, but SMEs must shoulder these same propaedeutic activities themselves despite lacking dedicated resources and specialized expertise, compounding their existing constraints of limited financial resources, skill shortages, and fragmented IT infrastructure.
mechanism: Because off-the-shelf Industry 4.0 technologies still require customization and sometimes R&D effort to fit a specific industrial context (per the TRL-context-dependency finding above), and large enterprises can absorb this cost through dedicated R&D functions while SMEs cannot, the same nominal technology-adoption task represents a categorically larger readiness barrier for SMEs than for large enterprises.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing or supporting SME digital transformation readiness, budget explicitly for customization/R&D effort as a distinct SME-specific cost category, and consider public support programs, digital maturity audits, or collaborative innovation ecosystems as compensating mechanisms rather than assuming SMEs can absorb this burden as easily as large enterprises.
page_or_section: Section 2.4 (Addressing the Gaps in Technology Roadmapping)

finding_statement: Digital transformation commitment is strengthened when a single senior "Authorizing Sponsor" is paired with subordinate "Reinforcing Sponsors" at lower organizational ranks, who personally build trust with stakeholders by explaining why they see the change differently and inviting stakeholders to reflect on and voice their own reasoning without fear of judgment.
mechanism: A lone executive sponsor cannot personally reach every stakeholder group, so reinforcing sponsors distributed through the hierarchy extend the sponsorship chain's reach; stakeholders are better persuaded by reasons they discover themselves through trust-based dialogue with a nearby reinforcing sponsor than by directives issued from the top.
operationalisation_hint: When designing DT governance, explicitly assign reinforcing sponsors at each organizational level (not just a single executive sponsor) and equip them to have trust-building, non-judgmental conversations about the change rather than simply relaying top-down messaging.
page_or_section: Sponsorship section, Table I (Delta integration worksheet)

finding_statement: Standard project and agile methodologies (PMBOK, Scrum) engage stakeholders' cognitive processes (planning, adaptive problem-solving) but do not address the emotional uncertainty people feel when facing change; explicitly understanding and communicating from each stakeholder's individual Frame of Reference (FOR) -- their existing beliefs, concerns, and reasoning -- rather than arguing facts, is what converts resistance into engagement.
mechanism: People react to change with both cognitive and emotional responses; when a Change Agent listens to and reflects a stakeholder's FOR back to them without judgment, the stakeholder feels understood and shifts from defending a position to exploring their own thoughts and motives, which reduces resistance more effectively than presenting additional facts or logical arguments.
operationalisation_hint: Before or alongside standard requirements-gathering and sprint-planning activities, have a designated change agent map each stakeholder group's frame of reference (concerns, incentives, prior experience with similar changes) and tailor communication content and channel to that frame rather than using one uniform message.
page_or_section: Communication section, Table I (Delta integration worksheet)

finding_statement: Across three case organizations (factory automation, local government, utility services), EA information consistently refines from coarse-grained strategic content (vision, drivers, desired results produced by the sensing capability) to tactical content (solution ideas, portfolios, gap analyses produced by the mobilizing capability) to fine-grained operational content (directives and guidelines that enable the transforming capability to actually reconfigure resources) -- with explicit feedback loops connecting all three levels back to strategy.
mechanism: Because sensing, mobilizing, and transforming are sequentially dependent dynamic sub-capabilities, the EA information each produces must progressively increase in granularity and specificity to be usable by the next capability; a strategic-level input (e.g., a vision statement) cannot directly drive operational transformation without being refined through the intermediate mobilizing stage into concrete solution ideas and resource-mobilization plans.
operationalisation_hint: When designing EA governance for digital transformation, explicitly design the information hand-off from strategic (sensing) to tactical (mobilizing) to operational (transforming) artifacts as a deliberate refinement pipeline with feedback loops, rather than assuming strategic documents alone will inform operational execution.

finding_statement: In two of three case organizations, core cultural values (e.g., a local government's stated commitment to "openness and transparency") were found to actively shape how vision-derived desired results were elaborated and pursued, demonstrating that values function as a live interpretive filter on strategic sensing -- yet in the same organization, the CIO explicitly questioned whether the published vision was authentic guidance or "just meant as window dressing to make us look better," while a factory-automation strategy manager treated the mission/vision as a genuine and consistently invoked starting point for all change initiatives.
mechanism: Vision statements only function as effective sensing-capability inputs when stakeholders perceive them as authentic and operative rather than as marketing artifacts; core values appear to be a more consistently trusted and operative guide across organizations than formally documented vision statements, suggesting values may be a more reliable EA-information input than vision documents in organizations where vision credibility is in question.
operationalisation_hint: When using EA vision/mission artifacts to drive digital transformation sensing, first verify (e.g., via stakeholder interviews) whether the vision is perceived internally as authentic strategic guidance or as symbolic messaging, and supplement or substitute it with documented core organizational values where vision credibility is low.
page_or_section: Section IV.A (EA information driving the sensing capability)

finding_statement: Organizational digital-transformation readiness can be operationalized as four capability dimensions -- Technology Capability, Organizational Capability, Strategic Capability, and Ecosystem Capability -- assessed continuously through a closed feedback loop (data perception, capability assessment, decision recommendation, execution feedback) rather than as a one-time static snapshot, with dimension weights recommended to vary by industry context (e.g., technology capability weighted higher in manufacturing, digital culture/agile structure weighted higher in financial services).
mechanism: Mapping the three dynamic-capability sub-processes (sensing, seizing, transforming) onto a continuous data-to-decision-to-feedback pipeline, rather than a periodic survey-based assessment, is intended to let a readiness assessment track capability drift as the environment changes, though this paper's own claims about the superiority of its specific dynamic-weighting algorithm rest on largely synthetic data and should not be relied upon.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a digital-transformation capability assessment, consider structuring it around four generalizable dimensions (technology, organization, strategy, ecosystem) evaluated on a recurring/continuous basis rather than only at a single point in time, and expect dimension weightings to be industry-context-dependent rather than universal.

finding_statement: A single illustrative three-year manufacturing-enterprise transformation trajectory showed technology capability investment concentrated in year 0-1, organizational change concentrated in year 1-2, and strategic/ecosystem alignment concentrated in year 2-3, with strategic capability starting as the most lagging dimension but achieving the largest relative improvement in the later stage.
mechanism: If organizations tend to invest in visible technology infrastructure first because it is the most immediately actionable lever, while strategic and ecosystem capabilities require organizational maturity and experience gained from the earlier technology/organizational-change phases before they can be meaningfully developed, this would explain a natural (rather than merely coincidental) sequencing pattern.
operationalisation_hint: Treat this specific three-phase sequencing (technology, then organization, then strategy/ecosystem) as a single illustrative case pattern rather than a validated prescriptive roadmap, and verify against additional independent case evidence before using it to plan a multi-year transformation roadmap.

finding_statement: A concept-centric analysis of all 36 IT capabilities and 315 sub-elements (Capability Building Blocks) in the IT Capability Maturity Framework (IT-CMF) identified seven recurring Foundational Capability Building Blocks -- Governance, Resourcing, Roles/Responsibilities/Accountabilities, Skills and Competence Development, Culture, Stakeholder Management, and Communication -- that appear across the large majority of the 36 distinct IT capability domains.
mechanism: Because these seven elements recur so consistently across otherwise-distinct capability domains (from risk management to enterprise architecture to innovation management), maturing them has a multiplying effect across the entire IT capability portfolio, letting organizations focus a capability-improvement program on a manageable number of generically-applicable areas instead of independently maturing all 36 domain-specific capabilities.
operationalisation_hint: When planning an IT/digital capability improvement program, prioritize maturing the seven foundational building blocks (governance, resourcing, roles/accountabilities, skills, culture, stakeholder management, communication) as cross-cutting investments rather than treating each of the 36+ specific IT capability domains as requiring independent improvement effort.

finding_statement: Traditional funding models do not effectively support digital service delivery, and literature shows a shift toward dynamic financial management practices leveraging pay-for-use or service-based cost models instead of fixed budget allocations, alongside the need for a stable operational backbone (for efficiency/scalability) and a separate digital services platform (for agility/rapid innovation).
mechanism: Fixed, upfront budget-allocation models assume predictable, stable resource consumption, but digital services scale elastically and unpredictably, so financing them with traditional funding models either starves fast-growing digital initiatives of needed resources or over-commits budget to services whose usage does not materialize as planned.
operationalisation_hint: When resourcing digital transformation initiatives, adopt pay-for-use or service-based cost models for digital platforms and services rather than fixed annual budget allocations, while maintaining traditional budgeting for the stable operational backbone.

finding_statement: Digital transformation is characterized by new or expanded job roles (chief digital officers, data analysts, data scientists, security/risk managers, compliance specialists) that must be filled despite digital talent demand rapidly outpacing supply, driving organizations toward inventive talent-acquisition approaches such as external communities of expertise, social network referrals, expertise-location software, internal venture funds, and crowdsourcing new digital business ideas.
mechanism: Because conventional recruiting channels cannot fill the volume and specificity of digital-role demand fast enough, organizations that rely solely on traditional hiring pipelines will experience a structural roles/accountabilities gap that undermines transformation execution regardless of how well governance or strategy are designed.
operationalisation_hint: When planning a digital transformation's organizational design, explicitly budget for and pursue non-traditional talent-acquisition channels (expert communities, referral networks, internal venture funds, crowdsourcing) for newly required digital roles, rather than relying solely on conventional recruiting.

finding_statement: Securing stakeholder support and "psychological ownership" of digital initiatives depends critically on trust-building, since trust enhances multi-stakeholder cooperation and buy-in and helps alleviate problems caused by stakeholders pursuing alternative agendas; this goes beyond simply identifying stakeholders and communicating with them.
mechanism: Stakeholder importance is a function of power, legitimacy, and urgency, meaning different stakeholders require different engagement approaches; without deliberately cultivated trust and a sense of ownership (not just information), stakeholders with competing agendas can undermine a digital initiative even when nominally "engaged" through standard communication channels.
operationalisation_hint: When managing stakeholders in a digital transformation, design engagement activities specifically to build trust and a felt sense of ownership (e.g., visible sponsorship, empowering stakeholder involvement in decisions, responding demonstrably to feedback) rather than treating stakeholder management as equivalent to a communication/information-sharing plan.

finding_statement: Beyond establishing a formal communication plan and channels, effectively managing bi-directional information exchange (listening and responding to stakeholder feedback) demonstrates respect and increases trust, while informal conversations between digital-transformation leaders and other stakeholders promote collegiality, bonding, rapport, and a shared understanding of the project vision.
mechanism: A one-way, top-down communication plan (however well-designed) only transmits information; it is the act of listening and visibly responding to feedback, plus informal relationship-building outside formal channels, that signals respect and builds the trust needed for stakeholders to remain committed through a long transformation process.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a digital transformation communication strategy, budget explicit time and mechanisms for two-way feedback loops and informal relationship-building conversations, not just scheduled formal updates (emails, reports, briefings).

finding_statement: Across 33 interviews spanning multiple industries and hierarchy levels, the decision to structurally separate versus integrate a digital initiative is best driven by two joint criteria: (1) whether the activity is exploratory (radical, future-oriented, high-risk) or exploitative (incremental, efficiency-focused, using existing products/processes) and (2) how close the activity is to the core business; distant exploration should be separated (e.g., in an innovation hub, think tank, or spun-off unit), while exploitation close to the core should be integrated, with exploration close to the core admitting either option depending on additional risk factors.
mechanism: Distant exploration needs freedom, dedicated budget, and different processes/culture that a core organization's follow-up-oriented, efficiency-focused culture would suppress, whereas exploitation requires deep process/product/customer knowledge that only exists within the core organization, so applying the wrong structural choice in either direction either stifles innovation or produces solutions disconnected from real business needs.
operationalisation_hint: Before deciding whether to structurally separate a digital initiative, explicitly classify it on two axes -- exploration vs. exploitation, and closeness to the core business -- and use the resulting quadrant (not intuition or a blanket "digital vs. non-digital" split) to decide on separation, integration, or a hybrid approach with safeguards.

finding_statement: Separating all digital activities from the core business as a blanket strategy (e.g., to build a digital mentality via M&A or internal startup culture) creates a risk that the digital unit is favored over the core business -- perceived as receiving investment, new office spaces, and prestige while the core business is "asked for more EBIT" -- generating a sense of injustice, and can leave the core organization permanently "in the non-digital world" because knowledge about new technologies and digital mindsets never transfers back.
mechanism: Blanket separation conflates exploration (which genuinely benefits from separation) with exploitation (which needs integration), so activities that should have been integrated get isolated instead, cutting off the knowledge-transfer and cultural-diffusion channels the core business needs to digitize its own processes, while simultaneously creating a two-tier status system between "favored" digital staff and "legacy" core staff.
operationalisation_hint: Before separating all digital activity into a dedicated unit, explicitly distinguish which of those activities are exploration (appropriate for separation) versus exploitation (which should remain integrated or closely linked), and establish deliberate knowledge-transfer mechanisms back to the core business regardless of the chosen structure.
page_or_section: Results section (Organizational separation: Digital/Core business), Discussion

finding_statement: The digital maturity grade of an incumbent company acts as a trigger point for rethinking organizational separation decisions: early in a digital transformation, separating digital activities helps generate a startup culture and build digital literacy that does not yet exist internally, but as the company matures and grows closer to the core business, the pull for digital improvements in the core business increases, becoming a trigger to dissolve or integrate the previously separate digital hub.
mechanism: Early separation solves a bootstrapping problem (lack of internal digital knowledge/culture), but that same separation becomes counterproductive once digital capability has matured, because continued separation at that stage blocks exactly the core-business integration and efficiency gains the company set out to capture -- meaning the optimal organizational structure is not fixed but should be re-evaluated as maturity increases.
operationalisation_hint: Treat organizational separation/integration decisions as time-bound, not permanent: schedule periodic re-assessment of digital maturity grade specifically as a trigger to revisit whether a previously separated digital unit should now be integrated into the core business.

finding_statement: Employees shifting temporarily between a digital innovation lab and the core business (e.g., one day per week) enables mutual learning: core-business employees bring process/product/customer knowledge into exploration activities and improve the transferability of resulting innovations back into exploitation, while digital-hub employees transfer digital skills and work methods back to the core business -- mitigating the risks of missing know-how (from over-separation) and diminished digital activity in the core (from under-integration), provided leaders maintain a stable core team for process continuity.
mechanism: Full-time separation loses core-business knowledge transfer, while full integration loses the freedom/speed benefits of a dedicated exploration space; a flexible, limited-time rotation structure captures both benefits simultaneously by having the same individuals carry knowledge across the boundary rather than requiring the organizational boundary itself to dissolve.
operationalisation_hint: When structural separation is chosen for digital exploration, add a temporal-ambidexterity mechanism (e.g., scheduled rotations, one-day-a-week arrangements) so that core-business employees gain exposure to the innovation hub and hub employees stay connected to core-business needs, rather than leaving the two groups permanently isolated from one another.

finding_statement: Applying a socio-technical-systems lens (People, Structure, Task, Technology) to why Digital Maturity Models fail to support digital transformation steering, an exploratory interview study found that issues extend well beyond the DMM's own design (complexity, inflexibility, context-fit): missing stakeholder inclusion beyond the steering committee, absent leadership involvement, lack of strategic-goal linkage, insufficient governance anchoring of DMM outputs into the transformation process, and inadequate workflow/iteration integration all independently degrade or eliminate DMM value, even when the model itself is well-designed.
mechanism: A DMM is a socio-technical artifact whose value depends on the surrounding organizational system (people, structure, task processes), not just the technical artifact itself, so organizations that select or build a well-designed DMM but neglect stakeholder engagement, governance anchoring, or iterative re-application will still see the model abandoned or underutilized regardless of its technical quality.
operationalisation_hint: When adopting any digital maturity model as an operationalization/assessment tool, budget explicit attention (beyond model selection or design) to stakeholder inclusion across all affected groups, leadership visible buy-in, governance structures for translating DMM outputs into transformation actions, and a defined iteration/update cadence -- treating these as prerequisites for value, not optional extras.

finding_statement: Organizations typically approach strategic topics by first defining their strategy and then identifying the capabilities needed to achieve it, but DMMs frequently reverse this sequence by prescribing the capabilities required to meet a predefined (often peer-group-derived) target maturity state that the organization cannot easily adjust -- creating a structural mismatch between the organization's own strategy-formulation logic and the DMM's built-in logic that was identified as a specific barrier to DMM adoption.
mechanism: Because DMMs are usually built from generic industry best-practice or peer-group benchmarks rather than an individual organization's specific strategic goals, applying a DMM's prescribed capability targets can feel like being handed someone else's destination rather than a tool for reaching one's own, undermining buy-in and usage even when the model's content is otherwise sound.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying a DMM as a steering tool, explicitly reconcile its prescribed target-state capabilities with the organization's own strategy-first goal-setting process, and be prepared to adapt or reinterpret DMM benchmarks rather than treating them as a substitute for organization-specific goal derivation.
page_or_section: Section 4 (Structure component: strategic alignment and governance)

finding_statement: A two-round Delphi study (53 experts, Kendall's W=0.51) demonstrates that digital transformation readiness is better captured as a configurational pattern of how strategic attention is allocated across seven interdependent domains (Competition, Customer, Data, Innovation, Regulation, Technology, Value) than as an additive/compensatory composite score, because in interdependent systems underdevelopment in one domain constrains the effectiveness of investments in others -- meaning strength in one domain cannot substitute for weakness in another, contrary to the compensatory logic implicit in most maturity models and composite readiness indices.
mechanism: Additive/compensatory scoring assumes domains are independent contributors to an overall score, but complementarity theory shows that the marginal return on investment in one domain depends on the development level of related domains, so an organization can appear "digitally mature" in aggregate while having a critical, unaddressed imbalance that a compensatory score would mask entirely.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or interpreting any digital transformation readiness/maturity assessment, avoid producing a single aggregated score; instead, report and interpret domain-level scores as a distribution/profile, explicitly flagging domains that are low relative to their structural importance rather than allowing high scores elsewhere to offset them.

finding_statement: Across a 53-expert Delphi panel, Customer (26.99% weight) and Value (22.43% weight) domains together account for nearly half of total strategic-attention weight in digital transformation, followed by Data (13.98%) and Innovation (13.91%), with Technology (11.08%) forming a secondary layer, while Regulation (6.42%) and Competition (5.20%) receive the lowest weights -- a stable pattern confirmed across two Delphi rounds with minimal variation (average rank change ~0.05).
mechanism: Experts consistently prioritize domains with direct, near-term value-creation impact (customer engagement, business-model value capture) over domains addressing external constraints (regulation) or positioning (competition), likely because the former are more directly actionable and within organizational control, while the latter are perceived as boundary conditions rather than primary transformation levers.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing digital transformation investment under resource constraints, expect and validate that customer-engagement and value-creation initiatives will typically be favored over regulatory-compliance or competitive-positioning initiatives, and treat significant deviation from this pattern (e.g., disproportionate regulation focus) as worth investigating for context-specific justification.

finding_statement: Although Regulation and Competition receive the lowest Strategic Focus Index weights among seven transformation domains, the study explicitly cautions that low weight does not indicate dispensability: these domains define boundary conditions and competitive constraints that shape the effectiveness of other domains, so their exclusion or complete neglect can undermine the coherence of transformation efforts even though they warrant comparatively less concentrated strategic attention.
mechanism: Because domains are interdependent, a domain's low relative priority reflects its role as an enabling/constraining boundary condition rather than a primary value-creation lever; removing attention to it entirely (rather than proportionally reducing it) risks removing a necessary condition for the higher-priority domains to function, which a simple ranked-priority list could obscure.
operationalisation_hint: When using any domain-prioritization framework to allocate digital transformation resources, retain a baseline minimum investment in low-weighted but structurally necessary domains (e.g., regulatory compliance, competitive monitoring) rather than deprioritizing them to zero, even when they rank last in strategic-attention weight.

finding_statement: Comparing Technology & IT versus Manufacturing & Consumer expert subgroups, the Strategic Focus Index profiles showed systematic, not uniform, variation: Technology & IT contexts assigned substantially greater priority to Technology (+6.99 percentage points) and Innovation domains, while Manufacturing & Consumer contexts assigned greater priority to Regulation (+4.47pp), Data (+3.25pp), and Value/Customer domains -- demonstrating that industry context reshapes which domains warrant the greatest strategic emphasis.
mechanism: Different industries face different structural constraints and opportunity profiles (e.g., technology-sector firms compete primarily on infrastructure/innovation speed, while manufacturing/consumer firms operate under heavier regulatory and execution-alignment requirements), so the same seven-domain structure produces meaningfully different optimal prioritization configurations depending on sector.
operationalisation_hint: When applying any cross-domain digital-transformation prioritization framework, benchmark an organization's domain-emphasis profile against same-industry peers rather than a generic cross-industry average, since a "balanced" profile in one industry context may represent significant misalignment in another.

finding_statement: The Strategic Focus Index's diagnostic logic requires jointly considering both the size of a domain's prioritization gap (relative to its expected/ideal emphasis) and its structural importance (its interdependency with other domains) when deciding where to reallocate strategic attention; a domain with a moderate gap but high systemic importance may warrant higher-priority corrective action than a domain with a larger gap but lower overall structural influence.
mechanism: Because domains are interdependent rather than independently contributing to outcomes, ranking correction priorities by gap size alone would misallocate attention to easily-identified but low-impact gaps while leaving high-impact structural bottlenecks (moderate gap, high interdependency) unaddressed.
operationalisation_hint: When translating a domain-level readiness/prioritization assessment into an action plan, score each underemphasized domain on both gap size and structural/interdependency importance, and prioritize corrective investment in the domains that rank high on both dimensions rather than defaulting to a simple largest-gap-first sequencing.

finding_statement: Across 16 expert interviews, organizational agility for digital transformation was described in two distinct, non-overlapping ways: (1) a "liquid organisation" path that dissolves classical departments and functions in favor of project-oriented, competency-based grouping with leaders acting as moderators rather than supervisors, and (2) a stable, hierarchical organisation that retains its classical organisational chart but layers in new agility-enabling roles (e.g., data scientist, community manager, digital consultant) to inject quick-response capability without restructuring.
mechanism: Both paths achieve the same underlying goal -- faster response to market opportunities and changing circumstances -- through different mechanisms: the liquid path removes structural friction by eliminating departmental boundaries entirely, while the role-injection path adds specialized quick-response capacity into an otherwise unchanged structure, meaning organizations do not have to choose between "agile" and "traditional" as a binary but can select the path matching their risk tolerance for restructuring.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing or designing organizational agility for digital transformation, do not assume agility requires abandoning hierarchy; consider whether a targeted new-roles approach within the existing structure could achieve comparable responsiveness with lower disruption than a full liquid-organization redesign.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 (New structural requirements: Agility of organisational structure)

finding_statement: Interviewees' understanding of "culture of change" as a digital-transformation structural requirement split into two distinct modes: a disruptive mode emphasizing radical rethinking and reorientation, abandoning old structures to find new ways of operating, and an evolutionary mode characterized simply by tolerating mistakes and treating them as improvement opportunities (e.g., accepting that "five projects fail") without any other fundamental changes.
mechanism: Treating "culture of change" as a single undifferentiated construct risks organizations pursuing failure-tolerance initiatives (the evolutionary mode) while believing they have achieved the deeper structural reorientation the disruptive mode requires, or vice versa attempting radical reorientation without first establishing the failure-tolerant conditions that make experimentation psychologically safe.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's "culture of change" readiness, explicitly distinguish whether the goal is evolutionary failure-tolerance (a necessary but lower-intensity precondition) or disruptive structural reorientation (a more intensive, less common transformation), since these require different interventions and should not be conflated in a single culture-readiness score.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 (New structural requirements: Culture of change)

finding_statement: The systematic review reports 30 process-oriented frameworks (73%), seven structure-oriented frameworks (17%), and four behavior-oriented frameworks (10%). It does not compare their empirical validation rates.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Of 65 quality-screened agile EA studies, the dominant research contributions were frameworks/methods (27 studies) and models (20 studies), while only one study each contributed a tool or a set of guidelines; only 5 of 65 studies used quantitative methods (mostly surveys), with the overwhelming majority (53 studies) qualitative (mostly case studies and literature reviews) -- indicating that despite growing framework proliferation, agile EA's quantifiable business-value impact remains largely unestablished.
mechanism: Conceptual frameworks are comparatively easy to publish because they require only a proposed design plus an illustrative case study, whereas demonstrating quantified business value requires longitudinal data collection, control-group comparison, or large-N surveys that the field has not yet invested in, meaning organizations adopting agile EA today are relying on frameworks whose claimed benefits are largely asserted rather than measured.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating whether to adopt a specific agile EA framework, treat its claimed benefits (speed, leanness, flexibility, learning) as plausible but empirically under-validated, and consider that internal pilot measurement of business-value outcomes will likely be necessary since the published literature rarely provides quantified validation to rely on.
page_or_section: Section III.B (Research Question 2, Types of research contributions), Table VII-VIII

finding_statement: The review identifies framework-specific limitations and unresolved empirical gaps for leading agile EA frameworks. These limitations should be treated as framework-specific cautions rather than a single broad comparative claim about generalizability.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section III.C.3, discussion of Gill/Masuda/Daoudi frameworks

finding_statement: Despite organizations increasingly adopting agile EA frameworks (e.g., AIDAF) in the context of digital transformation, the readiness of an organization to adopt agile EA has rarely been discussed in the reviewed literature, even though a specific "agility index" concept -- examining an organization's agile-EA readiness from the perspectives of motivators, enablers, and blockers -- has been proposed as a necessary but largely unapplied assessment dimension.
mechanism: Adopting an agile EA framework without first assessing organizational readiness (what motivates the change, what capabilities enable it, and what specific blockers exist) risks applying a framework mismatched to the organization's actual starting conditions, since the reviewed frameworks (Gill, AIDAF, Daoudi) each proceed directly from framework application to case-study evaluation without a preceding readiness assessment step.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying any agile EA framework, conduct an explicit readiness assessment covering motivators (why the organization wants agile EA), enablers (what capabilities/resources support it), and blockers (what specific organizational factors would impede it), rather than assuming framework applicability based only on the framework's general appeal.
page_or_section: Section III.C.3, citing Kaddoumi et al.'s agility index concept

finding_statement: Based on gaps identified across 65 reviewed studies, future agile EA maturity models and readiness-assessment tools should incorporate governance, organizational culture, leadership, and organization-wide understanding of agile principles as core evaluation dimensions -- an integrated readiness-assessment approach that does not yet exist in the current agile EA literature, which instead concentrates almost entirely on process/workflow frameworks.
mechanism: Existing agile EA frameworks concentrate on the technical/process mechanics of applying agile methods to EA development, but successful adoption also depends on governance structures that authorize and sustain the practice, a culture receptive to iterative/collaborative ways of working, leadership that champions the shift, and consistent understanding of agile concepts across organizational layers -- none of which current process-oriented frameworks explicitly assess.
operationalisation_hint: When building or selecting an agile EA readiness/maturity assessment tool, deliberately include governance, culture, leadership, and cross-level agile-principle understanding as explicit evaluation dimensions, since this combination does not yet exist in a validated instrument in the published literature and would need to be assembled from complementary sources.

finding_statement: Leadership commitment functions as a catalytic trigger that shifts organizations from resource exploitation toward capability reconfiguration, but its enabling effect is contingent and double-edged: transparent, sustained communication builds shared direction, while unclear execution or autocratic follow-through simultaneously generates momentum and erodes trust, and middle managers are structurally caught between strategic loyalty and operational stability.
mechanism: Leadership vision inscribes a shared direction that lowers coordination costs across a fragmented organization, but because leadership commitment alone does not resolve the stability-vs-change tension, its net effect on readiness depends on whether execution follow-through (clear instructions, consistent middle-management support) accompanies the vision.
operationalisation_hint: Assess not only whether leadership expresses commitment/vision but whether execution mechanisms (clear instruction cascades, middle-manager change-agent support, transparent communication cadence) accompany it.

finding_statement: Organizations that build surge capacity -- the ability to rapidly mobilize, redeploy, and scale resources -- during periods of relative operational stability are better positioned to absorb sudden environmental shocks (e.g., COVID-19, regulatory change, competitive disruption) without compromising service delivery or losing transformation momentum.
mechanism: Surge capacity is not built reactively during a crisis; it is accumulated in advance through resource slack and redeployable capabilities during stable periods, so that when disruption hits, the organization can compress decision cycles and reallocate resources rapidly instead of being paralyzed by the shock (illustrated by low-cost carriers' sub-30-minute turnaround capability).
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether the organization maintains redeployable resource slack and rapid-reallocation routines during non-crisis periods, not only its crisis-response playbooks.

finding_statement: IT infrastructure, human capital, and resource-management systems that resolve pre-existing inefficiencies during DT simultaneously introduce new dependencies, coordination burdens, and single points of failure, so that DT resources do not reduce organizational complexity but redistribute it, requiring ongoing managerial attention rather than one-time investment.
mechanism: As systems grow more integrated and complex (e.g., ERP overhauls, centralized knowledge platforms), failures become harder to diagnose and more disruptive, and skill-building initiatives that close technical gaps simultaneously open new generational/cultural divides -- so every resource investment that increases capability also increases the surface area for fragility.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing resource adequacy for DT readiness, evaluate not only whether resources exist but what new dependencies, failure points, or coordination burdens each resource investment creates.

finding_statement: Employee resistance to digital transformation should be interpreted as a signal of unaddressed capability gaps rather than as simple opposition to change; participatory, collaborative cultural-readiness approaches (internal testing, feedback gathering before launch) build confidence but can also slow decision-making momentum, so cultural readiness is not a purely positive lever but its own tension to manage.
mechanism: Organizations that treat resistance as diagnostic information (what skill, information, or trust is missing) rather than as a disciplinary problem can convert it into targeted capability investment; but the same collaborative mechanisms that surface this information (broad internal testing, consensus-seeking) inherently slow the pace of implementation.
operationalisation_hint: Track resistance patterns as a diagnostic signal (which employees, which tasks) rather than only as an adoption-rate metric to suppress.

finding_statement: Digital transformation readiness should be understood not as the static presence of enabling conditions (leadership commitment, cultural readiness, external pressure) but as the capacity of these conditions to catalytically trigger a shift from resource exploitation to capability reconfiguration when activated -- organizations with similar resource endowments can experience divergent transformation trajectories depending on whether enabling conditions actually activate this shift.
mechanism: Enabling factors do not resolve organizational tensions when present; they function as catalysts that force organizations to question existing value-creation logic and identity claims, and their catalytic effect (rather than their mere presence) is what differentiates transformation trajectories across otherwise similarly-resourced organizations.
operationalisation_hint: Assess readiness by asking whether enabling conditions have historically triggered actual capability-reconfiguration episodes in the organization, not merely whether they are nominally present (e.g., a documented DT strategy, a culture survey score).

finding_statement: In the 43-company assessment, Ecosystem Exploitation and Employee Structure Modification had lower average maturity than several technology and innovation dimensions. Results vary across the reported company-size and sector segments.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 3.1, Maturity Level of the Dimensions

finding_statement: The 'Employee Structure Modification' dimension (incorporating new roles, redefining positions, offboarding misaligned employees) is the single lowest-maturity dimension in large enterprises specifically (mean 1.667/4, with 46.67% at level 2 or below), while SMEs show comparatively higher and more agile structural adaptation on the same dimension -- indicating that organizational size moderates this enabler in the opposite direction from what resource-based intuition would suggest.
mechanism: Large enterprises face greater structural inertia (established role hierarchies, larger workforces requiring renegotiation) that slows employee-structure adaptation, whereas smaller, less formalized SMEs can reconfigure roles and responsibilities with comparatively less friction despite having fewer resources overall.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing this enabler, benchmark large-enterprise structural adaptability against SME peers rather than assuming larger firms have an advantage due to greater resources.
page_or_section: Section 3.1, Maturity Level of the Dimensions

finding_statement: The 'Transformation Management' dimension (follow-up/adjustment of strategy, performance-capacity management, pacing the transformation, data-driven decision-making) shows notably low maturity especially in SMEs (one-third at level 1) despite comparatively stronger 'Transformation Planning' maturity -- indicating a systemic execution gap between strategic intent and the adaptive-governance capability needed to seize and pace transformation in practice.
mechanism: Planning capability (defining strategy, roadmaps, objectives) can be developed through one-off strategic exercises, whereas transformation management requires sustained, iterative capacity to monitor, adjust, and pace execution over time -- a capability that develops more slowly and is more resource-intensive to sustain, particularly for SMEs with limited dedicated management bandwidth.
operationalisation_hint: Assess transformation-management (execution/adjustment) maturity separately from transformation-planning maturity, since strong planning scores do not predict strong execution-pacing capability.

finding_statement: Capability-based maturity assessment instruments that decompose abstract dynamic-capability constructs (sensing, seizing, transforming) into concrete, measurable microfoundation items (23 items across 5 thematic areas in this study) provide more granular and actionable readiness diagnostics than maturity models that focus primarily on technology adoption or that are constrained to a single industry sector.
mechanism: Because DC microfoundations (e.g., 'digital opportunity scanning,' 'employee structure modification') are each independently measurable and tied to specific organizational routines, gaps become locatable and actionable at the routine level, rather than being obscured within a single aggregate technology-adoption or industry-specific score.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or selecting a maturity assessment instrument for RQ1 purposes, prefer instruments that decompose capabilities into routine-level microfoundation items over single-score or technology-only indices.

finding_statement: Leadership competence and attitude is one of the most mature enabler dimensions across the sample (32.56% of companies at the highest maturity level), empirically reinforcing leadership as a foundational DT enabler; leadership, financial resources, human capital, and technological infrastructure function jointly as a threshold-level 'supporters and enablers' layer that appears to reach adequate maturity before higher-order transformation capabilities (ecosystem exploitation, structural redesign) do.
mechanism: Because supporter/enabler-layer capabilities (leadership, financial resources, human capital, infrastructure) are foundational inputs rather than transformation activities themselves, they can be built up independently and tend to mature earlier, creating the necessary but not sufficient base on which higher-order transforming capabilities are subsequently built.
operationalisation_hint: Verify enabler-layer maturity (leadership, financial resources, human capital, infrastructure) as a precondition check before assessing higher-order transformation-capability maturity.

finding_statement: SME digital maturity is consistently asymmetric: cultural/strategic and customer-facing dimensions (Digital Culture & Skills 61%, Customer Experience 50%, Digital Strategy & Leadership 42%) score markedly higher than analytical and technical dimensions (Data & Analytics 23%, Infrastructure & Cybersecurity 20%, Industry 4.0 & Advanced Technologies 24%), and these technical gaps co-occur with reported skill shortages, financial constraints, and investment-return uncertainty.
mechanism: Cultural and strategic readiness (leadership commitment, openness to change) can be built through low-cost internal effort, whereas data-analytics, cybersecurity, and advanced-technology capability require capital investment and specialized skills that resource-constrained SMEs systematically underinvest in, producing a durable, structural (not incidental) maturity gap between soft and technical dimensions.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing SME transformation readiness, expect and specifically probe technical/analytical dimensions (data, cybersecurity, advanced tech) as the binding constraint even where cultural/strategic dimensions score well.

finding_statement: Digital maturity assessment tools for SMEs should move beyond diagnostic scoring ('where are we') to generate rule-based, threshold-triggered strategic, organizational, and technological recommendations ('what to do next') for each below-target dimension, since most existing maturity models stop at measurement and leave SMEs without actionable prioritization guidance.
mechanism: A rule-based mapping between maturity thresholds and predefined action categories (strategic, organizational, technological) converts an assessment instrument from a purely diagnostic model into an adaptive decision-support system, which pilot users (87% of respondents) confirmed supported their decision-making more than diagnostic scoring alone would.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or selecting a maturity-assessment instrument for RQ1 purposes, prefer instruments with an explicit threshold-to-action recommendation layer over diagnostic-only scoring tools.
