finding_statement: Digital transformation initiatives that are designed from scratch for a specific organization -- mocking up new human/machine-agent roles, responsibilities, and decision-making frames before specifying technical requirements -- may deliver more tailored, better-fitting solutions than the common practice of adapting pre-tested digital transformation 'cases' copied from other organizations via a generic hypothesis-to-proof-of-concept-to-MVP pipeline.
mechanism: Case-copying practice treats digital transformation as an IT project (pick an alternative, adapt it), which risks importing solutions misaligned with a specific organization's processes and stakeholders; a dedicated design stage that first defines new roles, responsibilities, and interaction scenarios before technical specification aims to produce solutions tailored to the receiving organization rather than generic transplants.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating a proposed digital-transformation approach, check whether solutions were custom-designed around the organization's own process/role scenarios versus adapted wholesale from another organization's 'case.'
page_or_section: Section 4, Authors vision of design role in digital transformation process

finding_statement: Across 15 major digital maturity models (147 total variables, mapped onto the six Archimate 3.0 EA layers), none covers all six layers: 14 of 15 models address the Strategy and Business layers and most address Application, but only 6 of 15 partially address the Technology layer, and none addresses the Physical or Implementation-and-Migration layers at all -- creating a systematic assessment blind spot in precisely the technical/implementation layers that originate and support digitization.
mechanism: Maturity-model developers have concentrated on business-side dimensions (strategy, culture, customer experience) because these are more universally applicable and easier to survey across organizations, leaving the more implementation-specific and heterogeneous technical layers (infrastructure, migration) systematically under-modeled despite digitization being technologically driven.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or composing a digital maturity assessment instrument, explicitly check which EA layers it covers and supplement with a technology/infrastructure-layer-specific instrument if the chosen model stops at Strategy/Business/Application.

finding_statement: Because no single existing digital maturity model provides full-stack coverage across all EA layers, organizations and researchers should select or combine maturity models based on which specific architectural layer(s) (Strategy, Business, Application, Technology, Physical, Implementation and Migration) are most relevant to the transformation initiative being assessed, rather than assuming any single popular model (e.g., MIT/Capgemini, IBM) provides a complete picture.
mechanism: Since different models were built with different layer emphases (e.g., Kiron et al. 2016 covers Strategy only; TM Forum and IBM models cover four layers), composing an assessment from multiple layer-complementary models closes coverage gaps that any single model would leave.
operationalisation_hint: Before adopting a digital-maturity assessment tool for RQ1 purposes, cross-check its layer coverage against Table 2 of this paper (or an equivalent layer-mapping) and supplement gaps rather than treating one model as sufficient.

finding_statement: Organizations that maintain continuous data lineage between project-execution-phase systems (design, construction) and operations-phase systems (maintenance, monitoring) via an EA-based common data environment reduce information loss at the project-to-operations handover point, compared to siloed or tool-centric management where project-phase data rarely reaches operational systems.
mechanism: A shared digital-twin/common-data-environment layer lets operations managers access as-built project data directly, so predictive-maintenance and operational decisions are informed by real construction/design data rather than re-estimated or reconstructed information.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing architecture-led transformation readiness, check whether a mechanism exists for project-phase data to flow into operational systems, not only whether EA artifacts exist for each phase independently.

finding_statement: Digital maturity in engineering/infrastructure enterprises does not follow from adopting individual digital tools (BIM, IoT) in isolation; it requires reorganizing management logic itself to link project-phase data continuously with operational decision-making, reinforcing the broader finding that technology adoption alone is insufficient without organizational restructuring.
mechanism: Isolated tool adoption (e.g., BIM without a corresponding operational-data pipeline) leaves the underlying siloed management logic unchanged, so digital tools fail to compound into transformation-level maturity without a structural change to how project and operations management are integrated.
operationalisation_hint: Do not equate individual digital-tool adoption with organizational digital-transformation maturity; verify whether management logic/process integration has also changed.

finding_statement: Traditional EA practice -- rooted in IT, using a waterfall development approach, organized around organizational/integration/software/infrastructure layers, and targeting IT-architect audiences -- is structurally mismatched with digital-transformation requirements for business-focus, agile/iterative development, strategic and business-model-layer integration, and ecosystem/platform-oriented value creation; this mismatch is a key reason EA remains largely unused and poorly understood in SME digital-transformation practice.
mechanism: Because EA and business-transformation disciplines originate in different fields with different languages, description techniques, and target audiences, EA's IT-rooted vocabulary and detailed-upfront-planning approach create a genuine translation gap with the customer-integrated, fast-iterating, ecosystem-spanning practices digital transformation demands, rather than EA simply being underused due to lack of awareness.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing whether EA can support a specific digital-transformation initiative, check whether the EA approach in use has been adapted toward business-focus, agility, and ecosystem/platform layers, rather than assuming a traditional/IT-focused EA practice will transfer directly.
page_or_section: Section 4, Criticism on Enterprise Architectures; Table 1

finding_statement: SME digital-transformation planning can be operationalized as a macro cycle (defining and incrementally refining the whole-enterprise architecture, from an unconstrained 'ideal architecture' toward a legacy-constrained 'real architecture') paired with a micro cycle (implementing and testing individual capsuled 'user stories' drawn from an architecture backlog, analogous to a Scrum product backlog), allowing agile, incremental EA development instead of upfront, complete architecture specification.
mechanism: Deriving an unconstrained ideal architecture first (without legacy or resource restrictions) and only then reconciling it against the real, legacy-constrained architecture prevents premature anchoring on existing systems, while decomposing the gap into independently-runnable, prioritized user stories (the architecture backlog) lets small SME teams make incremental progress without needing to complete a full upfront architecture before starting implementation.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an SME-appropriate EA planning method, structure it as a macro (whole-enterprise, incrementally-detailed) and micro (individual-capability, sprint-based) cycle pair rather than a single upfront architecture specification.
page_or_section: Section 5, Approach for Digital Transformation in SMEs; Figure 3

finding_statement: Organizations with higher EA practice maturity (measured via DyAMM across 17 focus areas) have significantly higher-quality IT investment decision outcomes (achieving intended results, on time, on budget, stakeholder-satisfactory) than organizations with lower EA maturity (top-quartile mean EAM 2.00 vs. bottom-quartile mean 0.53, t=-3.89, df=49.34, p<.001), and top-quartile organizations have a longer-established EA tradition (9.4 vs. 5.5 years).
mechanism: A more mature EA practice systematically produces the artifacts and insights (see related conditions) that decision-makers need to evaluate IT investments against strategy, risk, and interdependencies, so EA maturity operates as a upstream, measurable precondition for downstream decision quality rather than a symbolic or compliance-only capability.
operationalisation_hint: Use a validated EA-maturity instrument (e.g., DyAMM) as a leading indicator of an organization's capacity for high-quality IT investment decisions, not only as an EA-function health metric.
page_or_section: Section 5.1, Comparison EA maturity; Proposition P1

finding_statement: Organizations with high-quality IT investment decision outcomes use significantly more diagnostic (e.g., heat maps) and actionable (e.g., roadmaps, policies) EA artifacts in preparing IT investment decisions than low-quality-outcome organizations (e.g., 82.4% of top-quartile cases use roadmaps vs. 34.4% of bottom-quartile cases; chi-square significant for roadmaps, policies, heat maps, future-state architectures, standards, landscape diagrams, project-start architectures, business-capability models, guidelines, and solution outlines), whereas purely 'enabling' artifacts (current-state architectures, principles) show no significant difference between groups.
mechanism: Enabling artifacts (current/future-state architecture documentation) are necessary groundwork for gap analysis but have little standalone decision-support value; diagnostic artifacts translate that groundwork into visible gaps (heat maps) and actionable artifacts translate gaps into committed plans (roadmaps), so it is specifically the diagnostic-plus-actionable artifact layer, not artifact production volume in general, that drives decision quality.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating an EA practice's contribution to transformation-related decisions, count diagnostic and actionable artifact usage specifically, not total EA-artifact output or the mere existence of current/future-state architectures.
page_or_section: Section 5.2, Comparison EA artifacts and insights; Table 12; Proposition P2

finding_statement: EA provides significantly more strategic-type insights (fit with business strategy, relationship with future IT investments, risks of IT investment) in the preparation of IT investment decisions in high-quality-outcome organizations than in low-quality-outcome organizations (e.g., fit with business strategy used by 70.6% of top-quartile vs. 28.1% of bottom-quartile cases), while more tactical insights (feasibility, solution alternatives, consequences for current state) show no significant difference between groups.
mechanism: Strategic insights connect an individual IT investment to the bigger picture (long-term objectives, portfolio interdependencies, risk exposure), which is precisely the kind of judgment decision-makers cannot derive from project-level technical analysis alone, so EA's distinctive value-add in decision quality comes from supplying this bigger-picture framing rather than from tactical project details decision-makers could obtain elsewhere.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA's contribution to a specific investment decision, verify whether strategic-fit, future-investment-relationship, and risk insights were actually supplied, not only whether some EA insight was consulted.

finding_statement: Among all 17 EA-maturity focus areas measured, 'Relationship to the as-is state' (analyzing and connecting current and future architecture) shows the single largest maturity gap between top- and bottom-quartile organizations (79.5% of top-quartile cases at the highest measured level vs. 15.6% of bottom-quartile cases), and this maturity dimension is a statistically supported precondition for producing the diagnostic/actionable artifacts that drive investment-decision quality (Proposition P4).
mechanism: Without a mature capability to connect current and future states (a rigorous as-is/to-be gap analysis), organizations cannot produce credible heat maps or roadmaps, because both artifact types are fundamentally representations of that gap; as-is-state maturity therefore functions as a gating capability that other artifact-production capabilities depend on, rather than one equally-weighted maturity dimension among many.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an organization's EA practice fails to produce useful diagnostic/actionable artifacts, check as-is/to-be gap-analysis maturity first as the most likely binding constraint.

finding_statement: EA-specific maturity in 'Commitment and motivation' (business/IT management support, resourcing, strategic acknowledgment of architecture) and 'Interaction and collaboration' (stakeholder involvement, shared ownership) each statistically predict the percentage of strategic insights that EA delivers in IT investment decision preparation (Propositions P5, P6), giving a specific mechanistic pathway from leadership/collaboration maturity to downstream decision-quality outcomes via the EA function.
mechanism: Senior management commitment provides the EA function with time, budget, and legitimacy to engage in strategic (not just operational) analysis, while cross-stakeholder collaboration surfaces the business context EA needs to generate strategic (rather than merely technical) insights -- so these two enablers operate specifically through the EA function's capacity to produce strategic insight, not merely as generic organizational virtues.
operationalisation_hint: When strengthening an EA function's contribution to transformation decisions, prioritize commitment/motivation and interaction/collaboration maturity specifically as levers for increasing strategic-insight delivery.

finding_statement: A federated enterprise/platform architecture -- combining shared single-source-of-truth registries (e.g., facility and provider registries), common interoperability standards (e.g., SNOMED, ICD-10/11, HL7/FHIR), and modular 'plug-and-play' components with standardized interfaces -- allows a large, decentralized network of semi-autonomous organizational units (e.g., different states/regions with differing local needs) to scale digital transformation and exchange information without each unit needing bespoke, one-off integration, and without changes cascading uncontrollably through the whole system.
mechanism: Because each participating unit adheres to shared standards and consumes/produces data through common registries and interfaces rather than building bespoke point-to-point integrations, individual components (e.g., a clinical decision-support module) can be upgraded, added, or customized locally (e.g., one state adopting different protocols) without requiring redesign of the whole system.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness for scaling a transformation initiative across decentralized organizational units, check for shared registries/interoperability standards and modular interface design, not merely for the presence of a a central IT system.
page_or_section: Section, Enterprise architecture: a platform thinking approach; Plug-and-play model

finding_statement: Distributed data architectures that functionally separate the transactional datastore layer (routine operational read/write) from the distributed analytics/processing layer (reporting, dashboards) become architecturally necessary once transaction volume crosses a capacity threshold; a system built with a unified transactional/analytical data architecture that worked adequately up to a given user volume can degrade in application performance once volume grows further, requiring separation of the two layers to restore performance without impacting transaction users.
mechanism: Concrete evidence: the Digital LifeCare platform's unified data architecture worked up to 10 million beneficiaries but began to degrade in application performance as volume increased to 15 million; separating the transactional datastore from the distributed analytics/processing layer resolved this, after which the platform scaled to 100 million beneficiaries with capacity for 500 million.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing architecture readiness for a transformation initiative expected to scale substantially, verify whether transactional and analytical data-processing layers are architecturally separated, especially before volume approaches an order of magnitude beyond current levels.
page_or_section: Section, Distributed data and processing architecture as a pathway to scale

finding_statement: The study of 18 healthcare organizations in 11 Asia-Pacific countries identifies lack of EA knowledge, limited leadership involvement, and communication gaps as barriers to EA adoption in that context.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Discussion, paragraph on leadership and communication

finding_statement: Among 18 healthcare organizations (mostly Ministries of Health) evaluating or adopting EA, interoperability/standardisation (20.3% of goal mentions) and governance (17.7%) were cited as primary EA-adoption goals far more frequently than cost reduction (11.4%), contrasting with earlier EA-adoption studies (mostly of private organizations) where cost reduction and transparency were emphasized more heavily.
mechanism: In public healthcare organizations facing severe interoperability problems (fragmented vertical health programmes, siloed systems) as their most visible and urgent pain point, EA adoption is framed primarily as a mechanism for safety/quality of care through interoperability rather than as a cost-cutting exercise, suggesting that the goals organizations attach to EA adoption are shaped by sector-specific pain points rather than being uniform across public and private contexts.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an EA-adoption business case, elicit the specific adoption goals relevant to the sector/context in question rather than assuming cost reduction is the default primary driver.

finding_statement: Across three large-scale agile transformations, the cases describe reduced attention to enterprise architecture during transformation and later renewed attention to enterprise-level architecture. The pattern is reported as case-based rather than a general sequence.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section IV.B.3, Attention Paid to EA; Section V, Discussion

finding_statement: Before undertaking a large-scale agile transformation, organizations should explicitly assess and redefine EA roles and processes for agile fit (rather than assume they transfer unchanged or should be eliminated), introduce new cross-team integrator/lead-architect roles that work hands-on with agile teams while maintaining enterprise-wide architectural vision, and establish regular cross-team coordination checkpoints (e.g., quarterly business reviews) to balance team autonomy with top-down architectural guidance.
mechanism: All three case organizations that gave agile teams too much autonomy and too little top-down direction experienced misalignment and coordination failures; adding integrator roles and regular cross-team planning checkpoints let architects quickly identify inter-team dependencies and route them to structured discussion points, which measurably improved communication and dependency management across all three cases.
operationalisation_hint: When designing governance for a large-scale agile-plus-EA transformation, budget for (a) an ex-ante EA role/process redesign step, (b) dedicated integrator/lead-architect roles, and (c) recurring cross-team coordination checkpoints, rather than assuming self-organizing teams alone will produce enterprise-level coherence.
page_or_section: Section V, Discussion; Section VI, Conclusion

finding_statement: Dynamic enterprise architecture capabilities (EA-sensing, EA-mobilizing, EA-transforming) have no significant direct effect on organizational benefits (beta=0.06, t=1.12, not significant); their entire effect on organizational benefits (competitive advantage, process agility, increased customer value) is fully mediated through business-IT alignment (beta=0.468, then 0.312 to benefits) and process innovation (beta=0.335, then 0.332 to benefits), confirmed via bootstrapped mediation analysis on a validated PLS-SEM model (n=299).
mechanism: EA capabilities do not translate into firm-level benefits by themselves; they must first produce an intermediate capability state (better business-IT alignment or higher process innovation), and only that intermediate state generates measurable organizational benefit, meaning organizations expecting quick, direct returns from EA-capability investment will not observe them until the mediating capabilities are also built.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating whether EA-capability investment is paying off, measure business-IT alignment and process innovation as intermediate outcomes rather than expecting a direct, immediate link between EA capability and financial/competitive benefits.

finding_statement: EA deployment practices -- the deliberate, methodical use of EA principles and approaches for strategic deployment of IT/business resources, rather than the mere existence of EA artifacts -- explain 45% of the variance in dynamic enterprise architecture capabilities (beta=0.668, t=17.96, p<0.0001), and EA deployment practices themselves show no significant direct effect on business-IT alignment, process innovation, or organizational benefits once dynamic EA capabilities are accounted for.
mechanism: Deployment practices function as the resource-level antecedent from which capabilities are built (per the resource-based view/dynamic-capabilities-view distinction between resources and capabilities); practicing EA methodically builds the firm's capacity to sense, mobilize, and transform using EA, but the practices themselves have no direct payoff independent of the capability they build.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA maturity for RQ1 purposes, measure EA deployment practice intensity as a leading indicator of future dynamic EA capability, not as a benefit driver in its own right.

finding_statement: The study reports that dynamic enterprise-architecture capabilities explain 22% of the variance in business-IT alignment. It shows a partial association and does not test which complementary governance or relationship mechanisms explain the remaining variance.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Dynamic enterprise architecture capability can be validly and reliably operationalized as a second-order dynamic-capabilities-view construct composed of three empirically distinct first-order capabilities -- EA-sensing (identifying business/IT opportunities and threats via EA), EA-mobilizing (evaluating, prioritizing, and resourcing potential solutions via EA), and EA-transforming (reconfiguring business processes/technology landscape via EA) -- each measured with 5-6 validated Likert items (all loadings >0.77, AVE >0.68).
mechanism: Grounding EA-based capability explicitly in Teece's sensing/seizing/transforming dynamic-capabilities logic, rather than treating 'EA capability' as an undifferentiated construct, allows researchers and practitioners to diagnose which specific sub-capability (opportunity-sensing, resource-mobilizing, or process-transforming) is underdeveloped in a given organization.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA-based transformation readiness, use the three-part sensing/mobilizing/transforming decomposition rather than a single undifferentiated 'EA capability maturity' score.

finding_statement: Dynamic enterprise architecture capabilities have a significant positive effect on firms' process innovation (beta=0.335, t=6.62, p<0.0001), which in turn significantly affects organizational benefits (beta=0.332, t=5.85); this process-innovation pathway operates as a mediating channel independent of, and in addition to, the business-IT-alignment pathway.
mechanism: EA-based sensing/mobilizing/transforming capabilities help firms spot, prioritize, and resource new IS/IT and process opportunities (e.g., cloud, IoT, AI adoption in key processes), so EA's contribution to organizational benefits operates through two parallel, non-redundant intermediate capabilities (alignment and innovation) rather than a single pathway.
operationalisation_hint: When modeling how EA contributes to transformation outcomes, account for both an alignment-improvement pathway and a process-innovation pathway as distinct, additive mechanisms rather than treating 'EA benefit' as a single undifferentiated effect.

finding_statement: When a transformation initiative spans multiple independent organizations (a collaborative network or virtual enterprise) rather than a single enterprise, traditional single-enterprise EA frameworks are insufficient; an explicit data-exchange/data-space layer is needed to bridge underlying technology infrastructure and higher-level business/value-creation layers across organizational boundaries, providing a shared overview of available data, ownership, and access conditions that no single participating organization possesses alone.
mechanism: Traditional EA methodologies assume a single enterprise with complete overview of its own data and ICT systems; when value creation instead depends on data and services distributed across independent organizations, no single organization's EA can provide the needed overview, so a dedicated cross-organizational data-layer construct becomes necessary to make data discoverable, negotiable (ownership/access conditions), and usable across the collaborative network.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing architecture readiness for a multi-organization or ecosystem-spanning transformation initiative, check for an explicit cross-organizational data-discovery/access layer, not just each participant's individual EA.

finding_statement: Across 110 organizations, EA implementation -- system changes actively carried out through the EAM function itself (e.g., non-business-driven infrastructure consolidation, shared technical services, reusable application services) -- is a necessary condition for the presence of technical IT capabilities (fsQCA consistency 0.913, exceeding the 0.9 necessity threshold) but is not a necessary condition for strategic IT alignment (consistency 0.894, below threshold), indicating that technical IT flexibility specifically requires active EAM-driven implementation, whereas alignment can be reached through other configurations without it.
mechanism: Technical IT flexibility (modularity, connectivity, compatibility) depends on shared infrastructural components and reusable services actually being built and maintained, which only active EA implementation work produces; strategic alignment, by contrast, can be achieved through planning, programming, or stakeholder-participation activities that do not require the EAM function itself to execute system changes.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing weak technical IT capabilities (poor modularity/connectivity/compatibility), check specifically whether the EAM function is executing non-business-driven implementation projects, since this is the one EAM component found necessary for this outcome.

finding_statement: EA documentation (architectural descriptions of dependencies, meta-models, repositories) is present in some empirically important sufficient configurations for technical IT capabilities and strategic IT alignment, but is shown as irrelevant ('does not matter' whether present or absent) in other equally sufficient configurations, and is even absent in some valid configurations -- reinforcing that architecture documentation alone, without active implementation, programming, and stakeholder engagement, does not reliably or uniquely produce capability or alignment benefits.
mechanism: Because fsQCA configurations require documentation only in some, not all, sufficient paths to the outcome, documentation is neither necessary nor a core condition for either outcome; the paper's authors explicitly note that only a limited subset of prescribed architectural artifacts are typically deemed useful in practice, suggesting extensive documentation processes can produce artifacts irrelevant to actual capability or alignment gains.
operationalisation_hint: Do not treat the completeness or currency of EA documentation as a proxy for EAM maturity or benefit realization; assess implementation, programming, and stakeholder-participation activity levels directly instead.

finding_statement: Organizational size (large, >250 employees, vs. SME) is part of the core sufficient conditions for strategic IT alignment -- specifically the pairs EA-programming*large-organization and EA-planning*large-organization -- but organizational size does not appear as a core condition for technical IT capabilities, indicating that large organizations specifically benefit from investing in target-architecture planning and standards/rules development (EA programming) to achieve business-IT alignment, while technical capability gains are not similarly size-contingent.
mechanism: Large organizations have more complex IT landscapes and larger stakeholder groups to coordinate, so the standardization and long-term roadmap functions of EA planning and programming become the specific mechanism through which size translates into alignment; SMEs achieving alignment likely rely on other, less formalized coordination mechanisms not captured by these EAM components.
operationalisation_hint: When recommending EAM investment priorities, differentiate by organizational size: large organizations pursuing strategic IT alignment should prioritize EA planning and programming; this size-contingency does not apply when the goal is technical IT capability.

finding_statement: The fsQCA analysis identified five distinct sufficient configurations of EAM components (documentation, planning, programming, implementation, communication and support, governance, stakeholder participation) for each of the two outcomes (technical IT capabilities and strategic IT alignment), confirming that there is no single 'one-size-fits-all' EAM approach -- different organizations can reach the same capability outcome through different combinations of present, absent, or 'doesn't matter' EAM components.
mechanism: Because EAM components interact in configurational (non-linear) rather than strictly additive ways, an organization missing one component (e.g., EA governance) can still reach the outcome if other components (e.g., EA implementation and programming) are strongly present, so readiness assessments based on scoring each EAM component independently and summing them would misrepresent which organizations are actually positioned to achieve the outcome.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EAM-driven transformation readiness, use configurational (combination-based) diagnostics rather than an additive checklist of individually-scored EAM components.

finding_statement: EA governance (formal review/approval processes, compliance tracking, sanctioning of standard violations) is present in the empirically most relevant sufficient configurations for both technical IT capabilities and strategic IT alignment, but is also shown as irrelevant ('does not matter' whether present or absent) in other equally valid, empirically relevant configurations for both outcomes -- indicating governance is one viable lever among several rather than a universally necessary condition, consistent with existing findings that governance mechanisms are only one of several IT-governance-practice categories that jointly (not individually) predict alignment performance.
mechanism: Because centralized governance mechanisms (review/approval, compliance sanctioning) are harder to implement in decentralized or ecosystem-embedded organizations, some organizations achieve the same alignment/capability outcomes through strong implementation and programming activity instead of formal governance, suggesting governance's contribution is substitutable within a broader configurational logic rather than independently required.
operationalisation_hint: When designing EA governance mechanisms, treat formal review/compliance processes as one substitutable lever within a broader configuration, not as a universally required gatekeeping step.
page_or_section: Section 6.1.1, EA documentation and governance discussion

finding_statement: When a business-model transformation requires an enterprise to take responsibility for resources/products across their entire lifecycle and across multiple external organizations (suppliers, customers, reclamation partners) rather than within a single linear value chain, standard EA frameworks (with five generic layers) must be extended with additional dimensions for materiality (ecological resource properties), ownership (judicial/ethical/practical responsibility), cross-organizational relationships, and lifecycle documentation (quality, age, location of resources) to remain fit for purpose.
mechanism: Traditional EA layers (strategy, business, application, data/technology) are designed to describe a single enterprise's internal structure; they have no native construct for tracking a resource's state and ownership as it crosses multiple organizational boundaries over an extended lifecycle, so a transformation requiring exactly this (e.g., circular economy, extended producer responsibility, product-as-a-service models) needs purpose-built additional EA dimensions rather than reusing the standard layer set unmodified.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA readiness for a transformation that extends enterprise responsibility across organizational boundaries and product lifecycles, check for explicit ownership, materiality, and cross-organizational traceability constructs in the architecture, not just the standard business/application/technology layers.
page_or_section: Section 2.3, Identifying EA Requirements; Section 5, CEEAF

finding_statement: A three-step, iteratively-refined capability-modeling method -- (1) identify entities important to the organization (customers, suppliers, products, processes), (2) convert each entity into a named capability by adding 'management' (e.g., 'supplier management'), (3) identify the constituent actions/verbs needed to exploit each capability -- provides a practical, repeatable entry point for architects to map current organizational capabilities against a target business-model transformation, with iterative refinement (merging, creating umbrella capabilities) continuing until the marginal benefit of further refinement flattens.
mechanism: Starting from concrete, already-identified organizational entities rather than an abstract capability taxonomy gives architects a low-ambiguity starting point; converting entities into named capabilities and then decomposing each into constituent actions makes the resulting capability model both business-legible (named after real organizational entities) and technically actionable (broken into implementable actions).
operationalisation_hint: When building a capability model to support an architecture-led transformation initiative, use the entity -> capability -> constituent-action decomposition method as a lightweight starting technique before more elaborate capability frameworks.

finding_statement: Augmenting an EA modeling notation (ArchiMate) with a dedicated business-motivation modeling framework (the Business Motivation Model, structured as a hierarchy of mission -> strategic orientation/drivers -> goals -> objectives) creates a technique for tracing IT/business-system capabilities (e.g., business analytics, supply-chain automation) forward to the specific strategic objectives and orientations they enable, addressing a documented limitation of prior EA-alignment models that only show unidirectional traceability from business strategy down to IT.
mechanism: Because most EA-alignment approaches only model the top-down decomposition of strategy into IT requirements, they cannot show how an existing or planned IT capability (e.g., an ERP module) contributes back up to specific strategic drivers (aggressiveness, proactiveness, etc.); explicitly layering a motivation hierarchy on top of the technology/application/business layers of an EA notation closes this gap.
operationalisation_hint: When modeling architecture-led transformation readiness, check whether the EA/strategy model supports bidirectional traceability (capability-to-strategy as well as strategy-to-capability), not only top-down decomposition.
page_or_section: Section 3.4, Linking the Business Layer to the Motivation Layer

finding_statement: Extending the Strategic Alignment Model (business strategy, business infrastructure/processes, IT strategy, IT infrastructure/processes) with TOGAF-derived technology/application/business/motivation layers provides a proposition-level mechanism (e.g., 'ES-enabled optimized processes enables Campaign Management, which enables Product Promotion, which enables Market Penetration') for tracing specific IT capabilities forward to the strategic goals and orientations they support -- addressing the same unidirectional-traceability limitation identified in prior EA-alignment literature.
mechanism: By explicitly inserting an intermediate 'Business Layer' between IT infrastructure/processes and business strategy, and defining item-by-item propositions linking specific application-layer capabilities to specific business-layer capabilities to specific motivation-layer objectives, the model provides a granular, testable (in principle) chain of enablement rather than an abstract claim that 'IT supports strategy.'
operationalisation_hint: When modeling architecture-led transformation readiness, look for an explicit intermediate capability layer connecting granular IT capabilities to specific strategic objectives, rather than a direct, unmediated IT-to-strategy link.
page_or_section: Section 3, Towards a New Model; Propositions PA/PB

finding_statement: The paper argues that the Zachman Framework is an explanatory theory and ontology that supports holistic understanding but does not provide a detailed implementation process or prescriptive method. It discusses broader EA criticism and misunderstanding without testing a direct outcome effect.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 4, The ZFEA as IS Theory; Section 5, Conclusion

finding_statement: Across three distinct decade-long strategic episodes at a major international bank (2008 financial crisis and merger integration; 2012-2016 core-IT modernization; 2016-2018 digital-technology-company strategic pivot), the effective EAM control-mechanism portfolio shifted from predominantly formal, top-down modes (input and behavioural control: architectural task forces, mandated blueprints, management oversight) during the crisis/scarcity episode, toward increasingly informal, relational modes (clan control, self-control: networking activities, voluntary team engagement, joint architectural discussions) during the later stability-and-innovation-focused episodes -- with each shift explicitly triggered by a major strategic realignment.
mechanism: Formal control mechanisms (resource allocation, behaviour monitoring, output tracking) can be established quickly and produce nearly immediate effects, which is valuable when resources are scarce, environmental uncertainty is high, and a clear target exists (e.g., merger integration under financial-crisis pressure); informal control mechanisms (shared norms, intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement) take longer to build effects but are better suited to situations with less resource pressure and more emphasis on innovation, exploration, and buy-in, where clear a priori targets and detailed roadmaps are not yet available.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or diagnosing an EA governance approach, first characterize the current situational context (crisis/scarcity vs. stability/innovation-focus) and select the emphasis of the control-mechanism portfolio (formal vs. informal) accordingly, rather than applying one EAM governance style uniformly regardless of context.
page_or_section: Section 4, Episodes I-III; Section 5, Discussion; Table 2

finding_statement: Formal EA control mechanisms are faster to implement and produce more immediate, visible impact, but informal control mechanisms -- even though slower to take effect -- produce more durable, long-term appreciation and legitimacy for the EAM function within the organization; consequently, even in scarcity/crisis situations well-suited to formal control emphasis, deliberately positioning EAM as a source of stability and safety (an informal-control-adjacent stance) measurably increased organizational appreciation of EAM over time compared to relying on formal control alone.
mechanism: Because formal control (mandated blueprints, oversight, reporting) can be perceived as an unwelcome external restriction that generates only compliance rather than buy-in, while informal control (shared norms, voluntary engagement) builds genuine organizational commitment but requires sustained relationship-building effort, an EAM function that relies solely on whichever mode is situationally optimal in the short term risks under-investing in the mode (informal) that produces durable legitimacy -- explaining why organizations can have long-standing, formally mature EAM functions that still fail to generate perceived value.
operationalisation_hint: Even when situational analysis favors emphasizing formal control mechanisms (e.g., during a crisis), deliberately invest some effort in informal-control-building activities (positioning EAM as a stabilizing, trustworthy function) to build durable long-term legitimacy rather than relying on formal control's short-term compliance alone.

finding_statement: Enterprise architecture quality can be validly and reliably decomposed into seven statistically distinct attributes -- quality of EA products and services, alignment and integrity, scalability, reusability, reliability, maintainability and portability, and security -- each confirmed via exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis (all factor loadings >0.4, Cronbach's alpha >0.7, AVE >0.5) and each explaining substantial variance in overall EA quality (R-squared ranging from 0.47 to 0.74 across the seven attributes).
mechanism: Because the seven attributes emerged from rigorous factor analysis (not a priori theoretical assertion) on 168 expert responses and each shows strong discriminant and convergent validity, this decomposition provides an empirically defensible (not merely conceptually plausible) basis for structuring an EA quality assessment instrument, rather than treating 'EA quality' as a single undifferentiated construct.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an EA quality assessment instrument for RQ1 purposes, structure it around these seven validated attributes and their associated indicators rather than a generic or single-dimension quality score.

finding_statement: Among the seven validated EA quality attributes, 'quality of EA products and services' ranks first in expert-weighted importance (TOPSIS closeness coefficient 0.71) followed by alignment and integrity (0.66), while 'security' ranks last (0.14) -- indicating that, contrary to a common assumption that security is a top EA priority, EA experts weight the usefulness and correctness of EA deliverables (documentation, models, guidance) and business-IT alignment substantially higher than security when judging overall EA quality.
mechanism: EA quality, as judged by practicing enterprise architects, is primarily about whether EA deliverables are useful, correct, and aligned with business strategy -- the core value-delivery function of EA -- rather than about the presence of security controls, which may be perceived as a baseline expectation or as belonging more properly to IT security/risk functions than to the EA function's own quality assessment.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing EA improvement investments, weight product/service usefulness and business-IT alignment more heavily than security-specific EA attributes, consistent with expert-derived importance rankings rather than assumed priorities.

finding_statement: Among all 30 validated EA quality indicators, the single highest-ranked by expert-weighted importance (TOPSIS closeness coefficient 0.81) is 'EA process is top-down, business strategic-driven, and future-oriented,' followed closely by 'EA processes and EA outcomes are in line with business objectives' (0.73) -- indicating that the process characteristic of being strategically driven and forward-looking outranks all specific product, technical, or infrastructure indicators in determining perceived EA quality.
mechanism: Because the top two indicators both concern the EA *process*'s orientation toward business strategy and the future (rather than technical correctness or product completeness), this suggests that EA quality is fundamentally judged by whether the EA function operates as a forward-looking, strategically-integrated capability rather than by the technical sophistication of its artifacts -- a process-orientation-over-artifact-quality finding.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an EA practice is perceived as low-quality, check first whether the EA process itself is top-down/business-strategic/future-oriented before investigating specific technical or product-level deficiencies.

finding_statement: Existing EA evaluation models are disproportionately narrow in layer coverage: despite EA being associated with four layers (business, information, application, and infrastructure), the great majority of existing EA evaluation/quality models are built at the application and information layers, with only a small minority addressing business and infrastructure layers -- and evaluation methods, metrics, and models are more established at the software-architecture level than at the full enterprise-architecture level.
mechanism: Because EA evaluation research has historically borrowed heavily from software-architecture quality frameworks (e.g., ISO 9126), which were designed to assess technical systems rather than business/organizational structures, existing EA evaluation models inherit a technical/application-layer bias that leaves the business and infrastructure layers comparatively under-assessed despite being equally constitutive of EA.
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or composing an EA quality/maturity assessment instrument, explicitly verify coverage of the business and infrastructure layers, not only application and information layers, since most existing instruments are skewed toward the latter.
page_or_section: Section 1.1, Motivation; Section 2.2, Software architecture analysis

finding_statement: Enterprise architecture management (EAM), despite its intended purpose of providing a holistic business-IT view, has in practice emerged as an IT stand-alone approach separated from business domains with a documented lack of integration between IT organizations and senior management, and traditional highly-formalized EA processes lack the ability to configure capabilities with the dynamics required to exploit Industry 4.0-driven business model innovation potential -- necessitating more dynamic, mission-oriented EA standards (e.g., RAMI 4.0, Unified Architecture Framework) instead of static process-driven approaches.
mechanism: Highly formalized EAM processes optimize for reusability and smooth deployment of a relatively stable target architecture, which conflicts with the need for continuous, rapid reconfiguration of capabilities as digital-technology-driven business opportunities emerge and dissolve, so EAM's traditional emphasis on formalized, IT-siloed process compliance actively works against the flexible, business-integrated capability configuration Industry 4.0 transformation requires.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating whether an EAM practice supports Industry 4.0/digital-transformation goals, check whether it operates as an integrated business-IT capability-configuration function or as a formalized, IT-siloed compliance process.

finding_statement: When scored against criteria specific to multi-agency, legally-distinct organizational contexts (cross-organization collaboration, shared-services promotion, legislation/mandate-based governance, top-down cascading across independent units), widely-used single-enterprise EA frameworks (ZFEA, TOGAF) score poorly (40/100 and 50/100 respectively in this study's weighted validation exercise) specifically on cross-organization collaboration and shared-services criteria (0 of 10-15 available points each), while scoring adequately on criteria assuming a single, unified decision-making entity.
mechanism: Standard EA frameworks were designed assuming a single enterprise with unified strategic decision-making authority; when the transformation scope instead spans multiple legally distinct, only loosely coordinated organizational units (e.g., government agencies, but by extension holding companies, franchises, or consortia), these frameworks have no native mechanism for mandating cross-unit collaboration or shared services, since compliance in such multi-unit settings typically requires an external mandate (legislation or equivalent binding governance) that generic EA frameworks do not natively provide.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA framework fit for a transformation spanning multiple legally distinct organizational units, explicitly check for cross-organization collaboration and shared-services mandating mechanisms, since generic single-enterprise frameworks are unlikely to natively provide them.
page_or_section: Section 2.2 and 3.1, Validation Exercise Capability comparison; Tables 6-7

finding_statement: The article discusses economic development, regulation, and cultural context in its research scope and literature framing. The cited sections do not establish an empirically tested moderation relationship between EA maturity and digital-transformation success.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 1.5, Scope of the Research; Section 2.4, Cultural Differences in EA Implementation

finding_statement: Across 17 large corporations, only 1 fully adopted a named EA framework/methodology horizontally (2 more applied one only within limited departments), yet 8 of the 17 organizations still scored 'high' capability on enterprise-architecture-best-practice (EABP) criteria -- achieving this through strong strategic practices (clear, well-communicated strategy), effective governance (resource provision plus KPI-based monitoring), and horizontal (enterprise-wide, not siloed) information systems, rather than through formal EA framework/methodology adoption.
mechanism: Because the EABP capability matrix scores strategic, governance, business-process, and information-system practices independently of whether a named EA framework label is applied, organizations can achieve most of the practical benefit associated with EA (cohesive strategy execution, resource-tracking, avoidance of departmental silos) via disciplined strategic and governance practice alone, indicating that formal framework adoption is one route to EA-capability but not a strictly necessary one.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA readiness, evaluate underlying EABP practices (strategic clarity, governance monitoring, horizontal information systems) directly rather than using 'has the organization adopted an EA framework' as a proxy for readiness.

finding_statement: In organizations scoring 'high' on EA-best-practice capability, governance boards performed two distinct, jointly necessary functions: (1) support -- provisioning needed resources and formulating enabling regulations/policies, and (2) monitoring -- using KPIs mapped to strategic objectives to track progress toward strategy fulfillment; organizations lacking either function (e.g., support without KPI monitoring, or vice versa) scored lower.
mechanism: Support alone (resources, policy) without outcome monitoring risks resource allocation that is not verifiably linked to strategic progress, while monitoring alone without resource support cannot remove the barriers that monitoring reveals; the combination of both functions in the same governance body is what let high-scoring organizations both diagnose and act on EABP gaps.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing governance-board effectiveness for EA readiness, verify both functions are present: resource/policy support AND KPI-based strategic-progress monitoring, not just one.

finding_statement: Even among the most EA-best-practice-capable organizations in this study's sample, formal EA framework adoption (e.g., TOGAF) was typically implemented only vertically -- within a limited number of departments or embedded in a specific ERP system (e.g., SAP) rather than applied horizontally across the whole enterprise -- meaning the framework's theoretical enterprise-wide scope was not realized in practice even in relatively mature organizations.
mechanism: Because implementing an EA framework horizontally requires coordinating change across every department's existing processes and systems simultaneously, organizations default to piloting or embedding the framework within whichever department or system (often the ERP-supported ones) is easiest to reach, leaving other departments outside its scope even when the organization is otherwise EA-capable.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing claimed EA framework adoption, verify the actual organizational scope (horizontal/enterprise-wide vs. vertical/departmental) rather than accepting framework adoption as a binary yes/no.

finding_statement: Organizations scoring 'high' on EA-best-practice capability distinguished themselves from 'average'-scoring organizations not by having a strategy (both groups did) but by how thoroughly that strategy was communicated: high-scoring organizations ensured employees at all levels were aware of strategic plans and how their work contributed to them, while average-scoring organizations often had a publicly stated strategy that lacked detailed goals or structured communication mechanisms (e.g., balanced scorecards) reaching all employee levels.
mechanism: A strategy that exists only as a public statement (website, annual report) without being actively translated into detailed goals and objectives that individual employees can connect to their own work fails to align dispersed organizational effort even though it technically satisfies 'having a strategy,' explaining why strategy communication depth, not strategy existence, is the actual differentiator.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing strategic-clarity readiness for EA/transformation initiatives, verify depth and reach of strategy communication (detailed goals connected to individual roles, structured tools like scorecards) rather than merely confirming a strategy document exists.
page_or_section: Section 4.1, discussion of 'high' vs. 'average' organizations; Table 6, item 3

finding_statement: In organizations scoring 'low' on EA-best-practice capability (illustrated by two health-sector organizations in this study), senior management specialized in a substantive professional domain (e.g., medicine) but lacking organizational-technology and business-management training was associated with weak strategic direction and governance, since these same senior managers were responsible for setting strategy and governance but lacked the background to do so effectively for EA purposes.
mechanism: When an organization's leadership pipeline selects for deep domain/professional expertise (e.g., clinical excellence in healthcare) rather than general management or technology literacy, the resulting senior management may be well-qualified for the organization's core professional mission but under-equipped to drive the strategic-clarity and governance practices that EA capability depends on.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA readiness in professionally/technically specialized sectors (e.g., healthcare, engineering, legal), separately evaluate senior leadership's organizational-technology/business-management literacy rather than assuming domain expertise implies EA-relevant governance capability.

finding_statement: A validated 5-factor model -- governance, top management commitment, technology and infrastructure, EA team capability, and communication -- jointly explains 63% of the variance in EA implementation success (quality, timeliness, and budget adherence), with all five factors showing statistically significant positive relationships with success (p<0.05) in a survey of 86 EA practitioners.
mechanism: Because all five factors remain significant predictors simultaneously (not just individually correlated) after controlling for multicollinearity, EA implementation success is better modeled as the joint product of governance, sponsorship, technical readiness, team competence, and communication than as attributable to any single 'magic bullet' factor.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA implementation readiness, evaluate all five factors together (governance, sponsorship, technical readiness, team capability, communication) rather than focusing on just one, since the validated model shows they jointly, not individually, explain most of the variance in success.

finding_statement: Among five validated critical success factors for EA implementation, governance is the single strongest predictor of EA implementation success (beta=0.292, the highest standardized coefficient among all five factors), operationalized specifically as a documented governance structure, clearly defined and documented roles/responsibilities/authorization, active monitoring of the transition-plan structure and strategy, and the use of proper architectural frameworks/methodologies/processes.
mechanism: Governance provides the consistency and timeliness mechanisms (monitoring, documented roles, transition-plan oversight) that convert other favorable conditions (sponsorship, technical readiness, team skill) into an actually completed, on-time, on-budget EA implementation, which is why it outweighs the other four factors in predictive strength despite all five being individually significant.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing limited EA-implementation-readiness improvement effort, prioritize governance structure/roles documentation and transition-plan monitoring first, since it is empirically the strongest single predictor of implementation success among validated CSFs.

finding_statement: Top management commitment is the second-strongest validated predictor of EA implementation success (beta=0.241), operationalized specifically as full management participation in all EA project steps with decision-making influence, ensuring project objectives are well-suited to enterprise needs, utilizing change management within the EA project, and selecting appropriate team members -- a more granular, actionable definition than generic 'executive sponsorship.'
mechanism: Top management commitment functions through concrete, observable actions (participating in project steps, applying change management, selecting the right team) rather than as an abstract sentiment, which is why it can be operationalized and measured as a significant predictor rather than treated as an unmeasurable soft factor.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing executive-support readiness for EA implementation, check for the specific behaviors (full participation in project steps, change-management application, team-selection involvement) rather than a general 'leadership is supportive' impression.

finding_statement: An EA modeling notation (ArchiMate) can serve as a common translation layer mapping elements of informal, business-stakeholder-facing project-planning canvases (e.g., ML canvas, AI canvas) onto elements of a formal business-IT alignment model (business goals, processes, applications, technology), enabling changes discovered during business-stakeholder discussions (e.g., available training-data volume) to be propagated consistently into the formal architecture representation, and vice versa, illustrated through a real bank ML project where a data-availability insight surfaced in canvas discussions was successfully propagated into the formal alignment model.
mechanism: Because business stakeholders in AI/ML initiatives typically engage with informal, accessible planning artifacts (canvases) rather than formal EA models directly, an explicit element-to-element mapping between the two notations lets insights and changes surfaced in accessible business discussions be captured consistently in the rigorous architecture representation needed for cross-project consistency, rather than the two artifact types drifting out of sync.
operationalisation_hint: When governing AI/ML-driven transformation initiatives, establish an explicit mapping between business-facing planning canvases and the formal EA/business-IT-alignment model used for the initiative, rather than treating the two as independent, unsynchronized artifacts.

finding_statement: Comparing obstacles identified across 9 Iranian governmental organizations against 20 independent prior EA-obstacle studies conducted in Finland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, the United States, and South Africa, across both government and private sectors, three obstacles were most frequently and consistently cited across nearly all prior studies: lack of communication and collaboration, lack of management support, and inability to establish a common understanding of EA -- indicating these are near-universal EA development obstacles rather than context- or country-specific ones.
mechanism: Because these three obstacles recur independently across studies conducted in very different political, economic, and organizational contexts (unlike the country-specific obstacles this same study also identified, such as political sanctions), they likely reflect fundamental, generic properties of EA-development projects (cross-stakeholder complexity, tacit knowledge, change-averse incentives) rather than context-contingent factors.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA-development readiness in any context, prioritize evaluating communication/collaboration mechanisms, management-support depth, and common-understanding-building efforts, since these are the most consistently validated obstacles across countries and sectors.
page_or_section: Section V, Discussion; Table 2 comparison with 20 prior studies

finding_statement: A priority framework derived from 18 identified EA-development obstacles organizes them into concentric layers of criticality: (1) top-management commitment (most critical -- constant management change, lack of management knowledge/support, budget provision) must be addressed first, since without it the project is likely to fail entirely; (2) infrastructure and organizational-strategy preparation (communication/collaboration mechanisms, outdated organizational statutes, change-management tools, unclear strategy, structural deficiencies) should be addressed second; (3) personnel engagement (common understanding, personnel knowledge, change resistance, motivation) should be addressed third; external obstacles (EA-consultant quality, political/regulatory issues) are managed in parallel as a separate category largely outside direct organizational control.
mechanism: Because top-management commitment determines whether budget, continuity, and organizational priority are available at all, addressing infrastructure or personnel-level obstacles before securing management commitment risks wasted effort on a project that management may not sustain; conversely, addressing personnel engagement before infrastructure/strategy clarity is established risks generating enthusiasm for a project whose direction is not yet coherent.
operationalisation_hint: When planning an EA-development readiness intervention, sequence remediation efforts as: (1) secure top-management commitment, (2) establish infrastructure/strategic clarity, (3) build personnel engagement, while separately and continuously managing external (regulatory/consultant) obstacles.
page_or_section: Section IV.B, Analyzing the identified obstacles; Fig 1

finding_statement: Enterprise architecture initiatives spanning multiple organizations (extended enterprise architecture, EEA) are jointly influenced by six analytically distinct factors: precision (how precisely stakeholders, strategy, and mutual obligations are defined), imbalance (power asymmetry between partner organizations, e.g., customers typically holding more power than suppliers), heterogeneity (organizational and technological differences between stakeholders, sometimes requiring standards adoption), transformation (the need for artifact-translation mechanisms between differing stakeholder architectures), temporality (the relationship's lifecycle, duration, and synchronization requirements, illustrated by relationships lasting from months to 20+ years), and maturity (operational stability and continuous-improvement capability once the EEA reaches a steady state) -- illustrated through a real case of a European fashion trading company managing distinct EEA relationships with online retailers, department stores, and tax authorities.
mechanism: Because a single-enterprise EA framework implicitly assumes one authoritative strategy-setting entity, extending EA across organizational boundaries introduces six qualitatively new sources of friction (imprecise mutual obligations, asymmetric power, heterogeneous legacy systems, translation needs between differing architectures, divergent relationship lifecycles, and varying operational maturity across partners) that a single-enterprise EA framework has no native mechanism to address, explaining why generic EA frameworks extended informally to multi-organization contexts frequently underperform.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA readiness for a transformation initiative that spans multiple organizations, explicitly evaluate all six factors (precision, imbalance, heterogeneity, transformation, temporality, maturity) rather than assuming single-enterprise EA practices transfer directly to the multi-organization context.

finding_statement: Despite the term 'extended enterprise architecture' implying a neutral, shared architecture across partner organizations, most EEA literature and the illustrated case both indicate that EEA initiatives are coherent primarily from a single lead organization's perspective (the entity defining the strategic objective for the collaboration), since a joint strategic objective genuinely shared and co-owned by legally and organizationally independent enterprises rarely exists in practice -- what appears to be a joint EEA is more often one organization's EA extended to encompass its view of partner interactions.
mechanism: Because strategy formulation authority resides within each individual legally distinct organization, a truly shared, jointly-owned strategic objective across organizational boundaries is structurally difficult to establish and sustain; what functions in practice is usually one organization (often the more powerful party in the relationship) defining the architecture and relationship terms, with partner organizations accommodating rather than co-authoring it.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness for a cross-organizational architecture-led transformation initiative, identify the de facto lead organization and evaluate the initiative from that organization's perspective, rather than assuming a symmetric, jointly-governed architecture exists between equal partners.
page_or_section: Section 4.1, Critical Case Study Discussion; Section 5, Conclusions

finding_statement: Across a systematic review of 59 papers on EA-PM integration, the most developed and frequently cited mechanism connecting project management to enterprise architecture is project-EA conformance -- verifying that new or changed project artifacts, relationships, and processes remain aligned with a pre-existing EA (exemplified by Foorthuis et al.'s multi-year research stream and Project Conformance Framework, cited across many of the reviewed papers) -- rather than EA being built anew from each project or PBO design being addressed independently.
mechanism: Because most organizations already possess some form of EA before undertaking new projects, the practical integration challenge is predominantly one of verifying and maintaining conformance of new project outputs to that existing architecture (via artifact review, portfolio-level dependency checks) rather than co-designing EA and PM from scratch, which is why conformance-checking mechanisms dominate the literature over alternative integration approaches.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing project-EA integration readiness, check whether a conformance-verification mechanism exists (reviewing new project artifacts against the existing EA) rather than assuming EA and project planning are integrated by default.

finding_statement: Across this systematic review of 59 papers, the tension between EA (providing long-term consistency) and Agile project management (providing flexibility) is repeatedly identified as a recurring, unresolved challenge, with authors explicitly noting that these two disciplines' core benefits (consistency vs. flexibility) can directly oppose each other and calling for a 'proper mix' of the two rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.
mechanism: EA is designed to establish and maintain long-term structural consistency across the enterprise, while Agile project management is designed to enable rapid, iterative adaptation to changing requirements; when both are applied to the same initiative, the consistency-seeking and flexibility-seeking mechanisms structurally pull in opposite directions unless a deliberate reconciliation approach (e.g., lightweight architecture checkpoints within agile sprints) is designed.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness for combining EA governance with agile project delivery, verify that a deliberate reconciliation mechanism exists (not just co-existence by default), since the tension between the two is well-documented and unresolved by default in most reviewed literature.

finding_statement: Despite an extensive systematic review, no article was found that explicitly and substantively applies EA to project-based organizations (PBOs -- organizations that derive income primarily from client projects) as a design object; existing EA-PM research is concentrated overwhelmingly (45 of 59 articles) on internal projects developed within a parent organization for internal objectives, with only 14 of 59 addressing external-client project delivery (predominantly in the architecture/engineering/construction industry).
mechanism: EA research has historically developed within an internal-IT-transformation paradigm (aligning a single organization's own strategy, business, and technology), so its methods and frameworks implicitly assume the organization is the ultimate beneficiary of the projects being aligned; this assumption does not transfer cleanly to PBOs, where the client (external to the parent organization) is the beneficiary, leaving a genuine, unaddressed methodological gap for organizations whose business model is client-project delivery.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA-readiness for organizations whose core business is delivering projects to external clients (PBOs, e.g., engineering/construction/consulting firms), do not assume existing EA-PM literature and tools transfer directly, since they were developed almost entirely for internal-project contexts.
page_or_section: Section 3.5.4; Section 4, Discussion, response to RQ2

finding_statement: Among the five EA layers analyzed in this review (strategy, business, application, technology, all-layers), the business layer is by far the most frequently addressed in EA-PM literature (31 of 59 articles) -- covering strategy alignment, project governance, and general PM-practice alignment with the business as a whole -- while the application and technology layers, though also significant (21 and 15 articles respectively), are specifically and narrowly linked to automating PM activities via project management information systems (PMIS), project control, and project quality rather than to broader business alignment.
mechanism: Because the core challenge researchers have prioritized is aligning projects and PM practices with organizational strategy and governance (a business-layer concern), the application/technology layers receive attention mainly instrumentally -- as the automation substrate for executing already-aligned PM activities -- rather than as an independent architectural concern in their own right within the EA-PM literature.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA-PM integration readiness, expect (and specifically probe for) stronger existing alignment at the strategy/governance layer than at the technical PMIS/automation layer, since the literature and, by extension, common practice concentrate effort there.

finding_statement: Enterprise architecture (EA) and project portfolio management (PPM) address complementary but distinct scopes -- EA determines technical goals and constraints (IT requirements, legacy/platform/interoperability limitations) scoped to IT projects, while PPM determines organizational goals and constraints (budget, resources, capacity, business-change initiatives) scoped to all strategic change initiatives across the enterprise -- and a systematic literature review found that most prior strategic-alignment models include one of these two functions but omit the other, indicating that EA-PPM connectivity is chronically underestimated in both theory and practice.
mechanism: Because EA lacks the organizational/business-portfolio view needed to capture business-IT relations at the whole-enterprise level, and PPM lacks the technical perspective needed to implement IT strategies, decision-making conducted within either function's silo alone (without deliberately exchanging technical and organizational analyses) will systematically miss either technical feasibility constraints or organizational resource/priority constraints.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing IT-project or transformation-initiative readiness, verify that EA's technical-goal analysis and PPM's organizational-goal analysis are both being conducted and are being explicitly exchanged, not merely that one or the other function exists.
page_or_section: Literature Review section; Table 1, Scope and focus of EA and PPM

finding_statement: Roadmapping -- a joint planning technique combining EA's technology/architecture schedule (e.g., life-cycle-driven system replacements) with PPM's organizational schedule (e.g., geographic expansions, acquisitions) into a single master plan that harmonizes priorities and places projects on a shared timeline -- is proposed as the concrete technique for reconciling EA and PPM plans that would otherwise remain in separate, unsynchronized schedules.
mechanism: Because EA and PPM each maintain their own schedule containing elements the other does not track (EA: system life-cycle replacements; PPM: non-IT organizational changes), producing a single joint roadmap forces explicit identification of interdependencies and gaps between the two schedules that would otherwise go unnoticed until they caused project conflicts or resource contention.
operationalisation_hint: When operationalizing EA-PPM alignment for a transformation initiative, establish a joint, periodically-reviewed roadmap combining both functions' schedules rather than maintaining them as separate planning artifacts.
page_or_section: Section, Roadmapping as the Technique for IT Project Alignment

finding_statement: When a business-function or application change creates a misalignment between EA's business and application layers, the organization has an explicit mechanism (a resource-allocation policy, potentially algorithmic) for selecting among adding, replacing, updating, or disposing of applications to restore alignment within budget, rather than reacting ad hoc to each misalignment event.
mechanism: Misalignment following organizational or IT change is treated as a normal, recurring "critical incident" in EA evolution rather than an exception; an explicit resource-allocation intervention (grounded in EA documentation of application relationships/costs) lets the organization re-optimize its application portfolio systematically each time such an incident occurs, improving the governance-criteria maturity of its BITA.
operationalisation_hint: Maintain EA documentation of application interdependencies and costs current enough to support a periodic (not purely reactive) application-portfolio re-optimization exercise whenever business functions, applications, or data change.

finding_statement: Even where an organization has a working dynamic resource-allocation mechanism for realigning EA after change, that mechanism is only as accurate as the shared domain knowledge and mutual understanding between business and IT roles that feeds its inputs (e.g., which applications support which business functions, and how well); the paper explicitly ranks shared-knowledge-building above resource-allocation tooling in priority.
