mechanism: Accurate estimation of applications' supporting values for business functions depends on business and IT roles sharing enough domain knowledge to agree on those values; without that shared understanding, a resource-allocation algorithm optimizes against inaccurate inputs regardless of its own sophistication.
operationalisation_hint: Before investing in resource-allocation/optimization tooling for EA realignment, first establish routine mechanisms (joint workshops, shared documentation) for business-IT domain-knowledge sharing that the tooling will depend on.

finding_statement: Prior to a technology-driven transformation (illustrated via cloud adoption/"cloudification"), the organization has a well-defined business architecture and explicit policies/principles governing solution selection, design, and the transition program, produced through an EA-based, life-cycle-oriented analysis of the mutual influences among all entities and artefacts involved (not limited to a narrow business-IT-alignment view).
mechanism: A holistic EA view spanning technology, processes, human organization, legal/financial/contractual relationships and their life cycles lets management identify prerequisites and pitfalls (interoperability, security, vendor lock-in, cost escalation) before committing to a specific transformation, converting an otherwise ad hoc technology adoption into an assessed, staged undertaking.
operationalisation_hint: Before adopting a new technology platform (e.g., cloud), require documented business architecture, explicit selection/design policies, and a staged transition roadmap as gating artifacts rather than proceeding directly to vendor selection.

finding_statement: Because a cloud platform, the business, and its environment all continue to evolve after initial adoption, the organization must treat the resulting EA solution as requiring ongoing maintenance and growing in-house architecture competency, rather than as a completed, one-off transformation project.
mechanism: Cloud services and the surrounding business context are "moving targets" that change during and after the transformation project; an organization that treats cloudification as a single completed exercise will see its EA-based alignment decay as the platform and business needs shift.
operationalisation_hint: Track architecture-competency headcount/training and schedule periodic re-assessment of the cloudification solution against evolving business needs and vendor offerings, rather than a single go-live sign-off.

finding_statement: Even where EA frameworks (TOGAF, RAMI4.0, IIRA) are formally adopted, the organization lacks a common vocabulary and stable communication channels between business and IT professionals, which remains a serious obstacle to designing and implementing balanced architectural solutions under digital transformation.
mechanism: Without shared terminology and stable business-IT communication, individually optimized architecture components fail to compose into an aligned whole, since alignment requires an integrated approach that only a common language and communication practice can support.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether business and IT stakeholders can describe EA artifacts and decisions using a shared vocabulary, and whether communication channels between them are stable rather than ad hoc.

finding_statement: Sustained organizational transformation is achieved when a central governance pattern orchestrates Technology Management, Innovation Management, and Digital Transformation as interacting components (rather than managing each as an independent, siloed discipline), with strategic objectives and KPIs cascaded from a shared strategic triad down to each component.
mechanism: A governance-centered orchestration layer radiates a common regulatory framework, policies, and monitoring roles to all components; because the components generate constant interaction and feedback, the organization is kept in continuous evolution rather than settling into disconnected, independently-run management processes.
operationalisation_hint: Establish a single governance function responsible for cascading strategic objectives/KPIs into Technology Management, Innovation Management, and Digital Transformation plans, and for monitoring their interaction rather than evaluating each in isolation.

finding_statement: The organization performs a preliminary assessment of its current maturity level across Technology Management, Digital Transformation, and Innovation Management, compares it to a desired future state, and uses the resulting gap plus organization-specific factors (size, sector, public/private status, structure) to tailor its implementation plan and select relevant KPIs.
mechanism: A generic implementation plan applied uniformly across organizations of different size/sector fails to reflect their differing baseline maturity and risk profile; an explicit current-vs-future gap assessment, combined with contextual factors, produces a tripartite (technology/innovation/DT) plan fitted to that specific organization.
operationalisation_hint: Score current maturity separately for Technology Management, Innovation Management, and Digital Transformation; define the target state for each; use the three gaps (not a single composite score) to prioritize implementation actions and select KPIs.

finding_statement: The framework identifies multilevel communication and shared domain knowledge as long-term principles for business-IT alignment. It links insufficient all-level communication to an incomplete shared understanding and difficulty communicating strategic plans.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The organization treats business-IT misalignment as a normal, recurring feature of a complex adaptive system rather than a one-time design failure, and maintains a four-part cycle -- EA design (rational, top-down BITA design via an EA framework such as DoDAF), misalignment sensing (detecting deviations between intended and realized business/IT strategies), misalignment governance (short-term correction via root-cause analysis and adaptive mechanisms), and misalignment prevention (long-term principles such as modular design, sufficient upfront complexity, and quickened learning loops) -- to keep sustaining alignment as the environment changes.
mechanism: Because organizations are complex adaptive systems where symptom-only correction produces short-term improvement followed by long-term performance degradation, treating EA design as the rational top-down component and coevolutionary sensing/governance/prevention as the emergent bottom-up component lets the organization reconcile top-down control with bottom-up adaptation across both short-term and long-term time horizons.
operationalisation_hint: Establish an explicit misalignment-sensing step (comparing intended vs. realized business and IT strategies) as a routine part of EA management, distinct from and prior to any governance/correction action.

finding_statement: Senior/top management provides sustained, visible support and involvement in the EA program (approving deliverables, granting EA "power and visibility" to guide strategic initiatives), while a formal communication plan and stakeholder-management plan ensure business and IT stakeholders share information and avoid the silo/stove-piped style that EA is meant to replace.
mechanism: Without management support, EA lacks the visibility and authority to influence strategic initiatives, and EA teams must actively maintain that support by demonstrating value and quick wins; without formal communication/collaboration mechanisms, business units cannot reach shared goals or a common understanding, so the information collected is unreliable and resulting EA artifacts fail to depict the true organizational picture.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether the EA program has documented senior-management approval authority over deliverables and a formal, maintained communication/stakeholder-management plan, not merely nominal executive sponsorship.

finding_statement: EA investment is converted into quality EA assets only to the degree the organization has continuous (not fixed-term project) funding, EA team capability, a tailored EA framework/tools/meta-model, a business-driven (not IT-driven) EA vision, and established EA governance; those assets then produce EA benefits only if properly represented, communicated to stakeholders, and integrated with existing organizational practices (project management, IT operations, service delivery); and those benefits translate into improved organizational performance only if external business/market conditions are also favorable -- often realized incrementally through multiple "cycles of EA" rather than a single completed project.
mechanism: Because EA investment is a necessary but not sufficient condition at every stage, an organization can fund EA generously and still fail to realize business value if any single gating factor (funding continuity, team capability, framework fit, vision orientation, governance, appropriate use, or external conditions) is missing; project-based, fixed-term EA funding in particular is identified as actively hindering effective EA development.
operationalisation_hint: Structure EA funding as an ongoing operating budget line (not a fixed-term project budget), and track EA progress as a series of benefit-focused cycles (e.g., "reduce costs" then "improve agility") rather than a single go-live milestone.

finding_statement: Organizational readiness to adopt and establish EA practice is assessed across four elements validated by expert consensus: Catalyst Enabler (EA vision, culture, change management, resources, governance), People (stakeholder support, competency/skills, management commitment), Process (business motivation/purpose, communication, policy and rules), and Technology (EA repository, tools, security) -- comprising 14 factors and 45 items in total.
mechanism: A single-dimension or narrowly-scoped readiness checklist (e.g., prior MPS assessments covering only 4 or 9 factors) fails to capture the holistic people/process/technology/catalyst view that EA scholars recommend; consolidating factors from systematic review and expert interviews into 4 elements, then validating them through 3 rounds of Delphi consensus (IQR 0-1, median 4-5 on all 45 items), produces a comprehensive and expert-endorsed readiness taxonomy.
operationalisation_hint: Before EA establishment, score readiness separately against all four elements (Catalyst Enabler, People, Process, Technology) rather than a single composite index, to identify which specific element is the binding constraint.

finding_statement: Management commitment (direct, active involvement, not merely nominal endorsement) is agreed by all 13 Delphi experts to be an important readiness factor, but is explicitly characterized as necessary without being sufficient on its own for EA readiness -- it must be accompanied by the other readiness elements (process, technology, catalyst enablers).
mechanism: Passive or symbolic management "buy-in" does not translate into readiness; only direct and active management involvement (e.g., engaging with EA governance, allocating resources) functions as a genuine enabler, which is why this factor alone cannot guarantee readiness even when present.
operationalisation_hint: Distinguish, in readiness assessments, between documented active management involvement (meetings attended, resources allocated, decisions made) versus mere stated support.

finding_statement: The organization defines EA roles (e.g., Enterprise Architecture Manager) with an explicit, structured linkage between tasks, responsibilities, required skills, and skill proficiency levels, rather than relying on a generic role label or an incomplete skills framework, so that recruiting, skill development, and internal capability-gap planning can be done consistently.
mechanism: Generic or inconsistent EA role labels (documented via job-market evidence and the incompleteness of TOGAF's own Architecture Skills Framework, which describes only 1 of 9 roles in detail and assigns undifferentiated skill levels across all roles) make it difficult for HR and hiring managers to evaluate candidates consistently or for organizations to identify internal skill gaps and plan training.
operationalisation_hint: Extend a generic EA skills framework (e.g., TOGAF's Architecture Skills Framework) with a detailed, external skills taxonomy (e.g., SFIA) mapped role-by-role, and generate a standard role fact sheet (skills, skill levels, tasks, responsibilities) for each EA role before recruiting or internal capability planning.

finding_statement: Digital-transformation leadership succeeds only when housed in a mission-driven organizational entity with genuine cross-government political backing and cultural values of collaboration/transparency (illustrated by Australia's Digital Transformation Agency), rather than embedded within a traditional, control-oriented central agency (Canada's Treasury Board Secretariat) whose core mandate (financial planning, resource allocation, spending accountability) structurally conflicts with an innovation/collaboration mission.
mechanism: A central agency personifying traditional public administration's managerial-control ethos lacks the capacity to foster the intra-organizational collaboration digital transformation requires, so digital-transformation units placed inside it (e.g., Canada's Canadian Digital Service within Treasury Board) are structurally undermined regardless of the individual talent or intentions of the people staffing them.
operationalisation_hint: Assess whether a digital-transformation unit reports into a control/compliance-oriented central function (finance, audit, traditional CIO) versus a separately-chartered entity with its own political/executive sponsorship and innovation-oriented mandate.

finding_statement: The organization evaluates digital/technical staff performance against specified deliverables and outcomes rather than hours logged or physical office attendance, enabling the locational and scheduling flexibility needed to recruit and retain specialized digital talent (e.g., AI, cybersecurity) who could otherwise command higher private-sector salaries.
mechanism: Reverting to in-person, hours-logged accountability after a period of flexible/hybrid work directly undermines recruitment and retention in specialized digital fields where private-sector compensation already exceeds public-sector pay; outcome-based accountability substitutes for compensation competitiveness by preserving the flexibility that is itself a valued attribute for this talent pool.
operationalisation_hint: Define and track deliverable/outcome-based performance metrics for specialized digital roles as an explicit alternative to location- or hours-based monitoring before mandating in-person attendance.

finding_statement: The organization (or federated network of agencies) establishes an adaptive architecture pipeline with five stages -- vision and scope, discover, implement, govern, and adapt -- that connects an overarching strategic direction to a centralized architecture guidance library and an end-to-end investment oversight/governance framework, with a feedback loop from real-world operations back into both the architecture guidance and future investment decisions.
mechanism: Making digital/ICT investment decisions in isolation, without a whole-of-ecosystem adaptive architecture and investment approach, produces redundancies, inefficiencies, inconsistencies, lack of interoperability, and suboptimal use of shared funds; an explicit pipeline connecting strategy to architecture guidance to investment governance to operations (with feedback flowing back upstream) prevents individual actors from making counter-productive isolated decisions.
operationalisation_hint: Before approving a digital/ICT investment in a federated or multi-unit organization, verify it has passed through explicit vision/scope, discover (gap analysis against a shared architecture library), and investment-governance stages, with a defined feedback mechanism from operations back to the architecture library.

finding_statement: A shared, publicly/internally accessible architecture guidance library (specifying domains, capabilities, policies, standards, and designs) is used in close integration with an end-to-end investment oversight process (strategic planning, prioritisation, contestability, assurance, sourcing, operations) so that individual business units or agencies assess whether a proposed digital/ICT initiative "fits in" with what already exists, fills a genuine gap, or duplicates an existing capability before investment approval.
mechanism: Without shared guardrails, individual units default to siloed architecture decisions and inconsistent investments because each unit lacks visibility into what other units have already built or planned; a jointly maintained guidance library cross-referenced against every stage of the investment lifecycle gives every unit the same reference point for reuse and consistency decisions.
operationalisation_hint: Require every proposed digital/ICT investment to be checked against a shared architecture guidance library (for reuse/duplication) before it proceeds through investment governance stages (prioritisation, contestability, assurance).

finding_statement: The organization extends TOGAF ADM's Architecture Vision and Business Architecture phases with an explicit business-strategy model -- SWOT analysis grounded in Resource-Based View and Porter's Five Forces to determine business strategy, followed by mapping that strategy into a Balanced Scorecard strategy map (financial, customer, internal-process, learning-and-growth perspectives) and then into business functions/processes -- rather than relying on TOGAF's native (comparatively IT-focused) business architecture guidance alone.
mechanism: TOGAF is repeatedly noted in the literature as focusing more on IT development and lacking detail on business-and-IT strategic alignment; inserting a structured business-strategy-determination step (SWOT/RBV/Porter) and an explicit strategy-to-BSC-perspective-to-business-function mapping before proceeding to information-system and application architecture closes that gap and makes the resulting alignment measurable.
operationalisation_hint: Before or during the TOGAF ADM Architecture Vision and Business Architecture phases, conduct a formal SWOT-based business-strategy determination and map resulting strategic objectives into a Balanced Scorecard strategy map linked explicitly to business functions/processes.

finding_statement: The organization designs and maintains its Enterprise Architecture using explicit, validated design principles across four dimensions: Objective (align architecture to stakeholder/citizen needs), Stage (consistency within each architecture layer, compatibility of specifications across layers, and dynamicity that allows the architecture to be adjusted as things change), Scope (vertical and horizontal alignment spanning organizational domains/silos), and Mechanism (explicit modelling of all concepts involved in the alignment to enable traceability and alignment analysis).
mechanism: Because complex, multi-domain organizations are challenged by silo-based service delivery, a single alignment principle (e.g., "align business and IT") is insufficient; decomposing alignment into layer-internal consistency, cross-layer compatibility, over-time dynamicity, cross-domain vertical/horizontal scope, and an explicit modelling mechanism gives architects a checklist of distinct, individually actionable design considerations rather than one vague mandate.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or auditing an EA specification, evaluate it separately against each of the four principle dimensions (objective, stage, scope, mechanism) rather than a single holistic "is it aligned?" judgment.

finding_statement: Beyond aligning within a single functional silo, the organization enables alignment both vertically (across levels of abstraction, e.g., strategy to architecture to solution design) and horizontally (across domains operating at the same level of abstraction, e.g., energy, mobility, and tourism service domains), since digital transformation initiatives increasingly require design and delivery of services driven by integration across domains rather than within isolated silos.
mechanism: Domain-siloed EA practice (e.g., a smart-city energy department architecting independently of mobility or tourism departments) reproduces the fragmentation that digital/ecosystem-oriented transformation is meant to overcome; explicitly designing for both vertical (abstraction-level) and horizontal (domain-level) relationships lets an operating model drive innovation and collaboration across domains.
operationalisation_hint: When scoping an EA alignment initiative, explicitly map both vertical relationships (strategy-to-implementation refinements) and horizontal relationships (cross-domain dependencies at the same abstraction level) rather than scoping to a single department or domain.

finding_statement: When prioritizing which digital-transformation technologies to adopt to strengthen EA practice, Big Data and Cloud Computing (over IoT, AI, and Cyber-Physical Systems) exert the greatest positive combined influence across TOGAF's 21 architecture principles, especially those governing data (Data is an Asset, Information Management is Everybody's Business, Common Vocabulary and Data Definitions, Data Security) and infrastructure/application flexibility (Common Use Applications, Technology Independence, Ease-of-Use, Control Technical Diversity).
mechanism: Cloud Computing eliminates the need for complete in-house software/hardware infrastructure, directly strengthening principles about application commonality, technology independence, and ease-of-use; Big Data initiatives directly touch principles governing data management and (per surveyed companies) operational efficiency and non-strategic direction, explaining why these two technologies dominate the influence ranking over AI and CPS in this analysis.
operationalisation_hint: When sequencing DT-technology adoption to improve EA maturity, prioritize Cloud Computing and Big Data initiatives first if the goal is to strengthen data-governance and infrastructure-flexibility architecture principles specifically.

finding_statement: The organization draws on a repository of Enterprise Architecture Patterns -- reusable, Archimate-modelled solutions to problems that recur across many organizations (e.g., cloud service adoption patterns, sustainability-characteristic patterns) -- selecting and combining a guiding pattern (e.g., a Business Model + operational-model pattern) with supporting patterns across the ADM's Preliminary, Vision, Business, Application, and Technology phases, rather than designing each EA specification from scratch.
mechanism: Because many transformation challenges (including sustainability-driven ones) are common across organizations, treating each EA specification as a bespoke, from-scratch design wastes effort that could be avoided by reusing patterns already validated elsewhere; a documented pattern-combination methodology (parallel, associative, layer-supporting, aggregation, and decomposition relationships between patterns) lets architects assemble a specification faster and with a shared vocabulary for communicating it to stakeholders.
operationalisation_hint: Before starting a new EA specification project, search an EA-pattern repository for a guiding pattern matching the organization's target business model, and iteratively select supporting patterns for each ADM phase (business, application, technology) rather than designing each layer from a blank slate.

finding_statement: To make an organization's sustainability commitments (e.g., avoiding slave labour in supply chains, reducing emissions, using bio-materials) explicit and actionable in EA artifacts, the organization represents them using the Motivation layer of the modelling language (goals, drivers, constraints) rather than trying to force them into standard Business/Application/Technology layer concepts, which have no native construct for environmental or social cost.
mechanism: Standard enterprise-modelling languages (e.g., Archimate) were not designed with environmental/social externalities in mind, so sustainability characteristics like waste reduction or ethical sourcing do not map cleanly onto any existing Business, Application, or Technology layer concept; the Motivation layer's goal/driver/constraint concepts are the only available construct expressive enough to capture these requirements without extending the language itself.
operationalisation_hint: When specifying a sustainability-driven transformation objective in an EA model, encode it as a Motivation-layer goal, driver, or constraint attached to the relevant Business/Application elements, rather than omitting it or attempting to express it as a Business-layer cost attribute alone.

finding_statement: The organization applies Portfolio Decision Analysis (PDA) -- treating business functions as decision goals and candidate applications (legacy and new) as discrete alternatives with costs, values, budget constraints, and synergy discounts -- to select a cost-efficient application portfolio that supports business functions within the EA design process, rather than allocating IT resources through subjective, ad hoc decision-making.
mechanism: Because applications in the information system architecture are often redundant and complex due to legacy accumulation, and EA design otherwise allocates resources subjectively, formalizing the business-function-to-application alignment as a portfolio selection problem (with explicit costs, values, budgets, and synergy relationships) yields multiple cost-efficient portfolios from which a final selection can be made using decision rules (maximum rule, minimum-regret rule, core index).
operationalisation_hint: Model the alignment between business functions and candidate applications as a PDA problem with explicit cost/value/budget/synergy parameters before making IT resource-allocation decisions in the EA design process, rather than deciding case-by-case.

finding_statement: The organization's EA practice is understood (and can be evaluated) as contributing to alignment through five distinct stages -- Alignment Scoping (deciding which components/relations, across domain, abstraction level, and timeline, are in scope), Alignment Embodiment (representing them with a given intensity, medium, and repository), Alignment Augmentation (computing/analyzing the represented relations), Alignment Realization (activating the models so human/technical actors learn and act on them), and Alignment Maintenance (periodically evaluating and re-cycling the models) -- rather than assuming that simply producing EA artifacts automatically achieves alignment.
mechanism: Alignment is a continuous process, not a static deliverable; EA models only influence organizational reality to the extent they are actively used ("activated") by human or technical actors, so an EA practice that invests heavily in scoping and representing relations (Embodiment) but never activates the models (Realization) or revisits them (Maintenance) will fail to produce real alignment even with high-quality artifacts.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an EA practice is not delivering alignment benefits, assess each of the five stages (Scoping, Embodiment, Augmentation, Realization, Maintenance) separately rather than treating "EA quality" as a single undifferentiated variable.

finding_statement: The organization calibrates how much Alignment Insight and Recommendation (AIR) capability to build -- how broad the scoping, how intense/formal the representation, how much computation/augmentation -- to what is cost-effective for its specific alignment goals and ROI pressures, and treats alignment maintenance (periodic evaluation and re-cycling of EA models) as a permanent, recurring activity rather than a one-time deliverable.
mechanism: Because AIR capability has a cost proportional to its scope, intensity, and computational sophistication, and because the organizational environment keeps changing (partly as a side effect of actors learning and acting on AIR itself), over-investing in comprehensive, highly formal EA models produces diminishing returns relative to a "just enough, continuously maintained" approach.
operationalisation_hint: When scoping an EA alignment initiative, explicitly size the investment (domain breadth, representation formality, computation sophistication) to the specific alignment goal at hand, and budget for recurring maintenance cycles rather than a single build phase.

finding_statement: The organization maintains an explicit Law Architecture -- a holistic, multidimensional representation of legal policies and their derived legal rules, and their relationships to business capabilities, processes, organization units, data concepts, information systems, and technology -- developed through a dedicated Law-Architecture-Development-Method (LADM) and integrated into the existing EA framework (e.g., inserted into TOGAF ADM immediately after Architecture Vision and before Business Architecture), rather than treating law compliance as an implicit, ad hoc concern addressed only by legal experts working separately from technical architects.
mechanism: Administrative/regulatory laws are typically written in natural-language text that non-legal technical architects cannot reliably interpret, while legal experts lack the enterprise-model knowledge to specify compliant IT systems; explicitly modeling legal policies and rules as first-class architecture artifacts (with matrices linking them to capabilities, processes, data concepts, and technology) closes this bidirectional knowledge gap and produces traceable compliance requirements rather than one-off manual interpretation.
operationalisation_hint: Before or during Business Architecture design in a regulated domain, run a structured legal-policy-mapping and legal-rule-mapping exercise (top-down article-by-article or goal-oriented) and maintain explicit matrices linking each legal policy/rule to the business capability, process, data concept, IS component, or technology requirement it governs.

finding_statement: The organization staffs a Law Architect role (an IT professional knowledgeable enough in administrative law and the public/regulated domain to analyze laws and extract compliance requirements) working directly alongside Legal Counsel (a qualified legal professional responsible for validating extracted policies and rules), rather than routing compliance analysis through either technical architects or legal staff working in isolation.
mechanism: Effective regulatory compliance requires both a good knowledge of the enterprise model (held by architects) and a good knowledge of the applicable law (held by legal experts); without a boundary role combining or bridging both types of knowledge, compliance requirements extracted by one side alone are prone to misinterpretation or incompleteness.
operationalisation_hint: Assign or contract a dedicated Law Architect role for regulatory-compliance-heavy EA initiatives, with a formal review/validation loop through Legal Counsel before compliance requirements are handed to Business/IS/Technology architecture phases.

finding_statement: The organization restructures its EA around fine-grained, loosely-coupled Packaged Business Capabilities (PBCs) -- each with its own dedicated data source and independent development/test/deployment lifecycle -- orchestrated via cloud-native technologies (Kubernetes, micro-frontends) and organized around cross-functional teams aligned to business functions rather than technical specialization, in place of monolithic or even microservices architectures that still suffer data-isolation and coordination overhead.
mechanism: Loose coupling and independent data ownership per PBC lets individual business teams develop, test, and deploy their module without redeploying or destabilizing the rest of the system, directly reducing downtime risk and shortening the cycle from feature conception to production; assigning cross-functional teams full lifecycle ownership of a PBC (design through maintenance) further removes the coordination overhead that pure technical-specialization team structures create.
operationalisation_hint: When restructuring EA for agility, decompose the business into fine-grained Packaged Business Capabilities with dedicated data sources, assign each to a cross-functional (not technically-siloed) team with full lifecycle ownership, and adopt a shared cloud-native orchestration layer (e.g., Kubernetes) rather than allowing ad hoc per-team infrastructure choices.

finding_statement: Beyond the technical modular design, the organization invests in structured governance (a centralized API/interface registry, shared design standards, ongoing integration checkpoints across distributed teams) and change management (developer training for the steeper systems-thinking/integration skill set the modular paradigm demands), and tailors the adoption strategy to organizational scale -- phased integration for large enterprises with legacy complexity, incremental modularization starting from specific business functions for resource-constrained SMEs.
mechanism: Without a centralized registry and shared standards, multiple distributed teams independently implement redundant logic, producing conflicting behaviors and integration delays even though each team's individual module is technically sound; and because the modular paradigm demands a steeper learning curve (systems thinking, integration skills) than traditional architectures, technical readiness alone is insufficient without matching organizational alignment and change-management investment.
operationalisation_hint: Before scaling composable-architecture adoption across multiple teams, establish a centralized interface/API registry and shared design standards, and assess/invest in developer systems-thinking and integration skills as an explicit change-management workstream, not an afterthought.
page_or_section: Sections VIII.B, VIII.E (Applicability Across Enterprise Scales, Limitations)

finding_statement: The organization explicitly develops and maintains an organization-specific coherence framework spanning a level of purpose (mission, vision, core values, goals, strategy) and a level of design (roughly 9-11 organization-specific coherence perspectives such as Finance, Customer, Processes, Governance, each with core concepts, guiding statements, core models, and explicit cross-perspective relationships), rather than relying on traditional Business-IT-alignment thinking or project/programme management (budget, resources, deadlines) alone to coordinate transformation.
mechanism: Project and programme management traditionally guard "on time and within budget" but not structural coherence across an enterprise's strategy, capabilities, and portfolio; without explicit governance of the ~20 cross-perspective relationships (roughly twice the number of perspectives) that connect an enterprise's guiding statements, individual projects optimize locally and coherence degrades even when each project succeeds on its own terms -- and coherence has been shown to correlate positively with enterprise performance (Leinwand & Mainardi).
operationalisation_hint: Before undertaking a strategic-level enterprise transformation, explicitly identify the organization's coherence perspectives (typically 9-11 for a 1000+ employee enterprise) and their guiding statements (typically 200-400, split ~10-25% principles / 30-45% policy statements / 30-45% objectives), and map the ~20 cross-perspective relationships that must remain mutually consistent.

finding_statement: Before applying a coherence-governance method, the organization verifies it meets specific applicability preconditions: a few hundred+ employees with a relatively high degree of division of labour, a sufficiently democratic (non-autocratic) leadership style, already fairly mature management/governance processes, and that the specific enterprise issue at hand has a significantly long time horizon, a significantly high investment level, and an expected impact spanning a broad range of business segments.
mechanism: Coherence-governance methods require broad stakeholder engagement, cross-perspective negotiation, and sustained senior-management involvement; applying such a method to an immature organization, an autocratic leadership context, or a narrow/low-stakes issue wastes the substantial coordination effort (on average 7.5 person-months for a first iteration) the method demands without a commensurate payoff, since the method is not claimed to be universally applicable.
operationalisation_hint: Before committing to a coherence-governance initiative, explicitly test the three suitability questions (long time horizon? high investment? broad cross-segment impact?) alongside the three organizational-maturity preconditions (scale/division-of-labour, leadership style, governance maturity), and decline or postpone if the answers are negative.

finding_statement: Because a coherence-governance method was developed and validated predominantly within Dutch government agencies and other large, well-established organizations with a relatively democratic and consensus-based decision-making culture, its applicability to organizations with different cultural profiles (e.g., more autocratic, less consensus-oriented, non-Dutch, smaller/less mature) remains unverified and should be treated as an open question rather than assumed.
mechanism: A method's design choices (workshop-based, consensus-driven confrontation of guiding statements across perspective owners) implicitly assume a certain organizational culture is present to make those design choices work; if that cultural precondition does not hold in a different context, the method may fail even when the organization otherwise meets the formal maturity/scale preconditions.
operationalisation_hint: When considering an enterprise-coherence-governance method developed in one cultural/organizational-type context (e.g., Dutch government-heavy consensus culture), explicitly assess whether the target organization's decision-making culture matches that context before assuming direct portability.

finding_statement: When communication and collaboration problems emerge in an EA project (e.g., an under-resourced EA team, insufficient domain-expert involvement, or unclear stakeholder commitment), management addresses them by reallocating resources -- adding architects, domain experts, external consultants, or even merging/expanding the project -- and/or by changing working practices (e.g., surveys to check whether architecture artifacts are understandable, inviting non-EA experts such as a lawyer onto the EA team), which measurably improves EA artifact quality, understandability, and interoperability.
mechanism: EA teams that are too small or lack domain expertise cannot adequately engage stakeholders or produce artifacts stakeholders find understandable and usable; visibly reallocating resources (more people, money, or technology) or changing how the team works signals management commitment and directly increases the team's capacity for the communication-intensive work EA requires, in turn improving artifact quality and downstream interoperability.
operationalisation_hint: When an EA project shows early signs of communication/collaboration breakdown (single-person EA team, stakeholder complaints about incomprehensible artifacts), treat this as a resourcing/practice problem to be corrected immediately rather than an inherent, unavoidable project risk.

finding_statement: The organization treats communication and collaboration explicitly in EA project risk management (identifying insufficient team expertise, unclear stakeholder communication, and missing communication plans as named risks with mitigation plans) and defines an explicit "communication and collaboration" architecture principle in the architecture definition document -- with a statement, rationale, and implications -- rather than leaving communication/collaboration as an implicit, generic assumption.
mechanism: Because EA work is often funded and managed as a "project" despite architects experiencing it as a continuous process, communication/collaboration risks are easily neglected in project planning; explicitly naming them as risks (per standard risk management practice) and as a formal architecture principle with stated rationale and implications gives them the same governance weight as other EA principles (e.g., TOGAF-style technical principles), which none of the three studied projects had done despite acknowledging the need.
operationalisation_hint: Add an explicit communication-and-collaboration architecture principle (with statement, rationale, implications) to the architecture definition document, and list communication/collaboration gaps as named risks with mitigation owners in the EA project risk register.

finding_statement: Rather than pursuing composable enterprise architecture as a massive, enterprise-wide rationalization and consolidation initiative, the organization implements it evolutionarily as part of the regular delivery of individual business initiatives -- using a pre-existing "good enough" Business Capability Map and Holistic Value Delivery value stream as reference artifacts, and applying a 6-step method (understand business drivers, understand holistic scope of the initiative, understand current situation, understand enterprise-level reuse needs, design as API-first/Headless PBC per MACH principles, implement and consolidate) to each initiative as it arises.
mechanism: A full enterprise-wide composable rearchitecting effort requires huge upfront investment and would hinder regular business operations and delivery of new business changes; embedding composability principles into the existing initiative-delivery process instead lets an organization incrementally reduce redundancy and increase reusability (business capability by business capability) without pausing business-as-usual delivery, at a fraction of the cost and disruption.
operationalisation_hint: Before scoping any new business initiative, check it against the existing Business Capability Map and Holistic Value Delivery value stream to identify reuse/consolidation opportunities and enterprise-level dependencies, rather than treating each initiative as an isolated IT delivery task.

finding_statement: When a technically "ideal" composable solution (e.g., a new independent microservice built per MACH principles) is estimated to cost more and take longer than the business need allows, the organization makes an explicit joint business-IT trade-off decision to instead adjust an existing (even legacy monolith) solution to meet the same business-IT-aligned, acquiring/PSP-agnostic objectives via a more modular, API-exposed design -- rather than insisting on the architecturally purest option regardless of cost/schedule.
mechanism: An external team with microservice/cloud expertise but no experience with the company's existing systems produced a cost/timeframe estimate for the "ideal" MACH solution that was rejected as too high-cost and too slow for a pre-sales-critical initiative; choosing instead to extend the existing legacy "PSP 1" monolith (whose internal team already had marketplace-API experience) achieved the same business-IT-aligned, agnostic front-end objective at acceptable cost and speed, confirming that cost-effective composable outcomes can also be achieved via modular monoliths, not only via full microservice rearchitecting.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating architecture options for a time- and cost-constrained business initiative, explicitly compare a "textbook ideal" rearchitecting option against a modular-monolith or incremental-extension option using the same business-alignment criteria (API-exposed, agnostic front-end), rather than defaulting to the theoretically purest technical solution.

finding_statement: Business-IT alignment through EA is best developed via five sequential stages: identifying vision/mission/goals, SWOT-based strategy analysis, Balanced-Scorecard-based strategy mapping, BPMN-based business process modeling, and IS/IT determination -- with the review finding that papers lacking an explicit strategy-analysis step or a strategy map cannot determine or measure organizational performance from their resulting alignment.
mechanism: Reviewing 25 papers empirically classified by which of the five stages they cover shows a consistent pattern: omitting strategy analysis produces inconsistent business strategy that undermines downstream business-process/IS-IT alignment, and omitting a strategy map removes the only mechanism for measuring organizational performance against the alignment achieved -- meaning the five stages are not equally optional, and dropping the strategy-analysis or strategy-map stages carries specific, identifiable costs.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating an existing BITA-through-EA effort, check specifically for the presence of a strategy-analysis step (e.g., SWOT) and a strategy map (e.g., BSC/KPIs) -- their absence is diagnostic of an inability to determine business strategy consistency or measure resulting organizational performance, respectively.

finding_statement: The organization operationalizes its enterprise IT architecture as a Design Structure Matrix (capturing direct dependencies among business groups, applications, schemas, servers, and databases), computes its transitive closure to classify components into Core (mutually interdependent, high coupling), Peripheral, Shared, and Control groups, and uses Core-membership -- rather than simple direct-dependency counts -- as the primary predictor of how costly a given software component will be to change.
mechanism: Regression analysis on 77 applications at a large pharmaceutical firm found Core membership (capturing indirect/cyclic coupling) to be a highly significant predictor of change cost (p=0.005, explaining 26% of variance) and the single most powerful, parsimonious predictor -- once Core membership is accounted for, direct coupling counts and closeness-centrality-within-Core add no further explanatory power -- because it is the potential for changes to propagate through indirect chains of dependency, not just immediate neighbors, that drives the cost and difficulty of modification.
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing which software components to isolate/refactor for improved modifiability, classify components via transitive closure of the full dependency matrix (Core vs. Peripheral) rather than by counting only their direct dependencies, since Core membership is the stronger, more parsimonious cost-of-change predictor.

finding_statement: The organization invests in collecting dependency data on its enterprise IT architecture through a combination of methods -- IT Service Owner surveys/interviews, automated server and network traffic scanning tools, and manual aggregation -- rather than relying solely on existing architecture documentation or high-level conceptual models, because many actual dependencies between components are unknown to or overlooked by the people formally responsible for those systems.
mechanism: At the study firm, automated scanning tools discovered many dependency links that had been overlooked by or were entirely unknown to the IT Service Owners responsible for those systems, demonstrating that the theoretical/documented system architecture can deviate substantially from the actual architecture in operational use -- meaning any EA analysis based only on documentation (as with TOGAF's idealized planning matrices) risks being systematically wrong about the very dependency structure it purports to describe.
operationalisation_hint: Before relying on documented EA matrices (e.g., TOGAF's Application Interaction Matrix) for architecture decisions, cross-validate them against automated dependency-discovery tools (server/network traffic scanning) rather than assuming the documentation reflects the architecture actually in use.

finding_statement: The organization complements its formalized EA model (ArchiMate business/application/technology layers) with business process mining applied to event logs from the actual IT systems in use (e.g., SAP S/4 HANA), so that EA compliance principles such as "a system is supporting and aligned with business processes and avoids functional redundancy" are assessed via quantitative deviation analysis of real operational data rather than the qualitative, subjective judgment of the architect or system owner alone.
mechanism: Prior EA maturity/compliance assessments (e.g., heat maps scoring "P/M/L/F" per principle) relied on the architect's or solution owner's subjective estimation; applying process mining to event logs reveals actual process variants and deviations (e.g., multiple undocumented variants of an engineering-change-request process), giving enterprise architects concrete, quantitative evidence to replace or supplement subjective compliance scores and to lead better-informed discussions with stakeholders.
operationalisation_hint: For EA principles framed as compliance/alignment checks (e.g., "system X avoids functional redundancy with process Y"), set up a process-mining case against the system's event logs before finalizing a qualitative maturity score, prioritizing processes most critical to downstream data quality/traceability.

finding_statement: The organization treats EA modeling (formalizing business processes, applications, and infrastructure in one repository) and EA evaluation (via process mining and maturity scorecards) as a permanent, cyclical 8-step process -- design, evaluate, decide, design solution, validate conformance, implement, review, re-model -- rather than a one-time architecture documentation exercise, specifically because engineering/PLM domains combine a need for IT-architecture stability with a need for high flexibility in domain-specific authoring tools, which continuously threatens to drift the as-documented EA away from actual practice.
mechanism: Cross-functional, multidisciplinary engineering domains require variety and flexibility in domain-specific tools (CAx, design automation) that business units adopt for their own efficiency, without necessarily complying with company-wide EA standards, causing downstream data-quality issues; and the emergence of mixed on-premise/cloud PLM solutions further complicates governance -- so the EA model must be continuously revalidated against actual operational data (via process mining) rather than assumed accurate once documented.
operationalisation_hint: In engineering/PLM contexts where business units frequently adopt their own domain-specific authoring tools, schedule recurring EA-model-vs-operational-data reconciliation cycles (steps 1-2 and 7-8 of the continuous improvement method) rather than a single upfront EA documentation effort.

finding_statement: The organization manages EA artifact-enabled value creation by jointly attending to three interacting factor groups: EA practice assimilation (the diversity, breadth, and depth of EA use across the organization), EA practice success factors (awareness/benefits acknowledgment, sufficient artifact quality/availability, architect knowledge/skill, correct organizational anchoring, and stakeholder commitment/engagement), and EA practice inhibitors -- rather than treating any one group (e.g., just "getting artifacts adopted") in isolation.
mechanism: Prior EA-value research has examined assimilation, success factors, and inhibitors as separate research conversations; because these three groups interact (e.g., an inhibitor like business-IT governance mismatch can simultaneously suppress assimilation breadth and undermine a success factor like stakeholder commitment), managing them jointly rather than separately gives a more complete, actionable account of how EA artifacts translate into realized organizational value.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing an underperforming EA practice, assess all three factor groups together (current assimilation diversity/breadth/depth, presence/absence of the five success factors, and presence/absence of the seven inhibitors) rather than addressing only the most visible symptom.

finding_statement: The organization proactively screens for seven documented EA-practice inhibitors before or during EA value-realization efforts: (1) business-IT governance mismatch (e.g., centralized IT vs. decentralized business, hierarchical stratification blocking architect access to senior executives); (2) lack of common terminology/communication skills between architects and business; (3) cultural resistance (e.g., EA perceived as legislatively mandated rather than genuinely valuable, business leaders reluctant to negotiate with architects); (4) financial/budget-transparency factors; (5) insufficient business/IT leadership sponsorship; (6) organizational instability (frequent leadership rotation, constant organizational flux); and (7) a troublesome EA history/reputation that demotivates EA staff and stakeholders alike.
mechanism: Each inhibitor independently degrades a specific mechanism EA value depends on: governance mismatch blocks strategic engagement; poor terminology prevents mutual understanding; cultural resistance and instability undermine the sustained stakeholder relationships EA requires; funding opacity and weak sponsorship remove the resources and authority needed to enforce EA compliance -- so screening for all seven, rather than assuming EA failure has one root cause, is necessary for accurate diagnosis.
operationalisation_hint: Before launching or troubleshooting an EA initiative, explicitly check for each of the seven inhibitor categories rather than assuming EA underperformance stems from a single generic cause like "lack of buy-in."

finding_statement: EA practice success specifically requires stakeholder commitment and engagement -- divided into strategic engagement (a self-evident partnership between enterprise architects and senior business leaders at the organization-wide planning level) and tactical engagement (close cooperation between architects and change-initiative stakeholders at the implementation level) -- underpinned by a sufficient level of mutual trust, correct organizational anchoring/positioning of the EA function, and formal governance mandate with senior-leadership support to enforce compliance with EA standards.
mechanism: Without strategic engagement, business leaders do not discuss future plans with architects and architects lack visibility into strategic direction; without tactical engagement, change-initiative teams resist EA-imposed restrictions; and without a formal mandate backed by senior leadership, architects cannot enforce compliance with established standards/principles regardless of their technical quality.
operationalisation_hint: Distinguish and separately cultivate strategic engagement (architect-to-senior-leadership partnership) from tactical engagement (architect-to-implementation-team cooperation) rather than treating "stakeholder engagement" as a single undifferentiated relationship to manage.

finding_statement: The review distinguishes pre-decision EA value as improvement opportunities for decision-making from post-decision EA value as longer-term value enabled by EA, and highlights the interdependence of the two phases.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.

finding_statement: The organization classifies its EA artifacts by type -- considerations (general-direction principles), standards (technical reference models for new initiatives), visions (long-term future-state agreements like reference architectures), landscapes (as-is views like context diagrams), outlines (business-leader-understandable conceptual designs of proposed initiatives), and designs (developer-actionable detailed solution architectures) -- to clarify which artifact type is appropriate for which decision-making purpose.
mechanism: Different EA value mechanisms map to different artifact types (e.g., "landscape" artifacts support complexity control and compliance assessment, while "outline" artifacts support stakeholder communication and change-initiative prioritization); without this classification, organizations conflate different artifact purposes and misjudge what a given artifact can or cannot support.
operationalisation_hint: When creating or requesting an EA artifact, first identify which of the six artifact types is needed for the decision at hand (e.g., a "vision" for long-term agreement vs. a "design" for developer implementation) rather than producing a generic, undifferentiated "architecture document."

finding_statement: The organization models each candidate strategic initiative using a hybrid i*/ArchiMate metamodel (soft goals refined into hard goals, mapped via weighted influence relationships to business and information-system layer services) and computes impact and weighted-impact metrics via matrix multiplication (chaining strategy-to-business and business-to-IS relationship matrices) before deciding whether to implement, partially implement, delay, or replace a given initiative.
mechanism: Without proactive, quantified impact assessment, organizations undertake adaptation projects for which they are not ready, leading to ad-hoc components/relationships that are difficult to maintain and align, project abandonment, and wasted effort; computing per-hard-goal weighted impact on each EA layer lets management compare initiatives objectively and identify which specific hard goals drive the most disruptive changes before committing budget.
operationalisation_hint: For each candidate strategic initiative (hard goal), compute its weighted impact on the business layer and IS layer using the organization's EA model before approving implementation, and use the comparison across hard goals to decide sequencing (implement first, delay, or drop).

finding_statement: The organization calculates, for each EA layer affected by a strategic initiative, the average weight per intra-relation (sum of intra-relation weights divided by the number of intra-relations) as a distinct metric from raw impact, using a high average weight as a signal that changes to that layer's components are tightly interdependent and must be executed simultaneously rather than incrementally, raising the alignment risk of the change.
mechanism: A layer can have many affected elements (high impact) but low interdependency (safe to change incrementally), or fewer affected elements but high interdependency (risky, requires simultaneous coordinated change); conflating these two dimensions into a single "impact" score would hide this important distinction between change volume and change coordination risk.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing a strategic initiative's readiness for implementation, report both impact (how many elements/relations are affected) and average intra-relation weight (how tightly those elements depend on each other) as separate readiness indicators.
page_or_section: Section "Evaluation of the Impact of a Strategic Initiative"

finding_statement: The organization applies a "holistic initiative footprinting" methodology -- using a Business Capability Model and Value Streams as a shared business-IT reference, combined with heatmapping (colour-coding affected/dependent capabilities and systems) and storytelling (gradually revealing business and IT dependencies to stakeholders) -- to scope a strategic initiative's true end-to-end dependencies, cost, timeline, and scope before finalizing the business case, rather than relying on a business case built without IT insight.
mechanism: Business cases built without systematic IT-dependency discovery routinely underestimate scope, cost, and timeline because they miss integration dependencies (e.g., with adjacent business capabilities), dependencies on separately-running initiatives, and pre-existing process debt that must be resolved before digitalization -- all of which the footprinting methodology's gradual capability/system decomposition is specifically designed to surface early.
operationalisation_hint: Before finalizing a business case for a digital initiative, walk the affected value-stream steps through progressively deeper heatmapped decomposition (value stream -> business capabilities -> supporting IT systems -> system capability gap analysis) with business and IT stakeholders together, rather than estimating cost/timeline from the business side alone.
page_or_section: Sections 5, 6 (Holistic Initiative Footprinting Methodology, Case Study)

finding_statement: The organization extends the standard three-layer EAM model (business, application, technology) with two additional layers to plan Industry 4.0 transformations: an Operational Layer (production processes, I4.0 components, and sensors, modeled at an abstract/type level rather than instance level, connected to all three standard layers) and an External Interface Layer (partner systems and customers directly involved in production, enabling horizontal integration) -- because the growing similarity between production machines and IT applications (shared security/update/release-management requirements) makes it impossible to cleanly separate operational technology (OT) from business IT within the traditional three layers.
mechanism: As OT and IT converge (production machines increasingly resemble IT applications in their management requirements), traditional EA layers cannot represent the interdependencies enterprise architects need for I4.0 impact analysis (e.g., which business capability depends on which production sensor); adding an Operational Layer as a bridge -- modeled abstractly by type rather than by instance to keep it tractable for architects -- lets the operational department maintain detailed OT models separately while still connecting them to the EA for holistic planning.
operationalisation_hint: When planning an Industry 4.0 transformation, explicitly model an Operational Layer (production processes/I4.0 components/sensors, at the type level) connected to business, application, and technology layers, plus an External Interface Layer capturing partner/customer touchpoints in the production process.

mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.

finding_statement: The organization designs its Enterprise Architecture with explicit resilience measures -- the ability to identify and assess vulnerabilities of enterprise resources in the integrated architecture, prepare for disruptions, adapt to new/changing circumstances, and restore full capability after an unexpected disruption -- as a distinct condition from (but hypothesized to be positively influenced by) general EA maturity and digital transformation maturity.
mechanism: Traditional EA maturity models assess process/practice sophistication but not specifically the organization's capacity to anticipate, absorb, and recover from disruptions (e.g., pandemic-driven supply/demand shocks); explicitly designing "resilience by design" into EA artifacts (a paradigm borrowed from civil engineering post-Hurricane-Sandy) is hypothesized to be a distinguishable, EA-maturity-dependent capability rather than an automatic byproduct of EA maturity.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing organizational readiness for disruption, evaluate EA resilience as a separate dimension from EA maturity, using resilience-specific attributes (diversity, redundancy, adaptability, flexibility, agility, vulnerability-to-risk, responsiveness) rather than assuming general EA maturity implies resilience.

finding_statement: The organization's EA resilience strategies are catalogued and applied according to which of three temporal phases they address: Readiness (preparation before a disturbance, e.g., creating a disruption-management culture, forecasting and risk assessment), Responsiveness (actions during a disruption, e.g., acceptance of consequences, revision of systems, postponement of decision-making), and Recovery (actions after a disruption, e.g., collaboration with stakeholders, knowledge management, sense-making).
mechanism: Different resilience actions are appropriate at different points in a disruption's lifecycle; forecasting/risk-assessment activities (Readiness) address a fundamentally different need than mid-crisis system revision (Responsiveness) or post-crisis sense-making (Recovery), so cataloguing strategies by temporal phase lets an organization identify gaps in its resilience posture across the full disruption lifecycle rather than only preparing for one phase.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA resilience preparedness, inventory which of the 33 known resilience strategies (per Ramezani & Camarinha-Matos' classification) the organization currently applies in each of the three phases (Readiness/Responsiveness/Recovery), and treat phases with no strategies as priority gaps.

finding_statement: The organization treats Alignment and Communication as the two central, interconnected EA-effectiveness constructs that mediate the effect of the other four constructs (Governance, Scope, Top Leadership Commitment, Skilled Teams/Training/Education) -- e.g., top leadership commitment must be communicated to be effective, governance requires communicated roles/responsibilities, and skilled teams need communication skills to translate business requirements into EA -- rather than treating all six constructs as independent, equally-weighted factors.
mechanism: A synthesis of five independent EA-effectiveness measurement approaches found that Alignment and Communication were the three common elements shared across all of them (alongside Scope), and an 11-expert Delphi-style validation confirmed direct or indirect relationships flowing from these two constructs to the other four -- meaning interventions that improve communication or alignment have leveraged, multiplicative effects on the other constructs, rather than each construct needing separate, independent improvement.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing low EA effectiveness, prioritize improving Alignment and Communication first, since the synthesis model shows these two constructs mediate (are prerequisite to) governance, scope clarity, leadership commitment translating into action, and skilled-team effectiveness.

finding_statement: The organization defines EA project scope by producing four specific artifacts: as-is documentation showing the current architecture status, an IT strategy, a target ("to-be") architecture, and a plan for reaching the to-be architecture from the as-is state -- with the scope documentation also stating the anticipated benefits of the EA effort -- rather than leaving "scope" as an informal, undocumented understanding.
mechanism: Without explicit as-is/to-be/transition-plan documentation, an EA effort lacks a defined boundary and cannot be evaluated for completeness or progress; scoping is identified across multiple independent CSF frameworks (Bricknall et al., Ylimäki, Wan et al.) as a recurring, distinct success factor precisely because organizations frequently start EA modeling before defining these boundary artifacts.
operationalisation_hint: Before beginning EA modeling work, produce and get sign-off on four scope artifacts: as-is documentation, IT strategy statement, to-be target architecture, and a transition plan between them.

finding_statement: The organization deliberately balances its "absorptive capacity" (the ability to recognize the value of new external information, assimilate it, and apply it commercially) against the cost of scanning and analyzing every captured signal, rather than attempting to absorb and act on all detected trends -- explicitly avoiding "blind imitation" of competitors and instead finding its own equilibrium between resources, investments, risks, and the internal/external knowledge enablers it monitors.
mechanism: In a VUCA (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous) environment, knowledge has a quick time-to-obsolescence, and scanning/analyzing every captured data point can be highly expensive without certain payoff; treating sensing as a continuous listening process rather than an "absorb everything" mandate lets the organization increase context/self-awareness while still being selective about which signals warrant an architecture response.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a sensing capability, define explicit filtering/prioritization criteria (e.g., ranking by threat to current portfolio, as in the illustrative case) rather than instrumenting maximal data collection without a corresponding assessment/triage step.

finding_statement: A federated (multi-business-unit/multi-segment) organization establishes segment-level EA staff units (each supporting its own segment while coordinating with the parent enterprise and sibling segments), a small set of cross-segment governance boards (an EA Blueprint Board for methodology/standards, an EAM Board & Strategy Council for strategic direction, and an EA Portfolio Board for project/investment prioritization, each capped at ~7 members), and a defined role hierarchy (Enterprise Manager, EA Sponsor, EA Governor, EA Portfolio Manager, EA Subject Manager, EA Solution Architect, EA Designer, EA Analyst, EA Method Specialist, EA Repository Administrator) -- rather than relying on informal, ad hoc coordination between autonomous business units.
mechanism: Federated enterprises face inter-dependencies between business units (shared resources like HR/finance, reused sub-products between units) that cannot be coordinated through hierarchy alone when units are peers (horizontal, same-level relationships) rather than parent-child (vertical, hierarchical); explicit boards provide the venue for negotiated, non-hierarchical coordination while segment-level EA staff units provide the local capacity to actually implement agreed standards, with a capped board size (≤7) preventing the ineffectiveness of oversized decision-making bodies.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing EA governance for a multi-business-unit conglomerate, distinguish vertical coordination (parent-segment, resolved via hierarchical boards/directives) from horizontal coordination (peer-segment, resolved via negotiated interfaces supported by each segment's EA staff unit) and staff a Portfolio Manager role to coordinate cross-cutting project/resource dependencies.

finding_statement: The organization establishes and maintains fewer than 30 EA principles per governance area, including at minimum: (1) EA pursues value creation evident in every deliverable; (2) stakeholders are identified before any EA artifact is designed; (3) every EA artifact has a clearly stated maturity level; (4) every EA artifact is self-contained; (5) every design follows Service-Oriented-Architecture principles with clearly defined interfaces; (6) standards, reference designs, and glossaries are used extensively; (7) every EA artifact has an identified owner; (8) artifacts follow proper modeling/visualization guidelines; (9) a culture of digital information transfer is established; and (10) a culture welcoming innovation and improvement suggestions is established.
mechanism: Without an explicit, bounded principle set (kept under ~30 per area to remain usable), federated EA governance risks either paralysis (too many competing rules) or inconsistency (no shared rules at all); documenting each principle with ID/Name/Statement/Rationale/Implication (per standard EA-principle practice) and capping the set size keeps the principles both comprehensive and practically enforceable.
operationalisation_hint: Draft EA governance principles using the ID/Statement/Rationale/Implication format, cap each governance area at under 30 principles, and explicitly include ownership (principle 7) and stakeholder-identification (principle 2) as non-negotiable baseline principles.

finding_statement: A federated organization replaces a standard centralized EA Architecture Board (TOGAF's recommended 4-5 top-management members) with a three-tier structure -- subunit-populated Networks (one per core business area, aggregating proposals and voicing subunit needs), a democratically-elected Steering Committee (drawn from Network representatives, prioritizing proposals), and a Board (populated by business-manager representatives from all subunits, making final accept/decline decisions) -- so that architecture governance decisions retain legitimacy across autonomous, voluntarily-associated subunits rather than being imposed top-down.
mechanism: TOGAF's Architecture Board assumes a centralized, hierarchical mandate that a federated organization's (semi-)autonomous subunits will not accept, since no single party holds authority to control adherence across voluntarily-associated peers; embedding subunit representatives at every governance tier (Network -> Steering Committee -> Board) increases "anchoring" -- the felt ownership and buy-in of subunits toward proposals -- which the case organization found necessary to secure voluntary purchase/adoption of jointly-developed IT/business solutions.
operationalisation_hint: In a federated (multi-autonomous-unit) organization, replace or extend a small, centrally-appointed Architecture Board with a tiered structure: business-area Networks feeding a representative-elected Steering Committee feeding a cross-subunit Board, ensuring every governance decision traces back to subunit-nominated representatives.

finding_statement: When adopting TOGAF (or a similar centralized-by-default EA framework) in a non-centralized organizational structure, the organization must explicitly recognize and compensate for two specific gaps: (1) the Requirements Management phase gives no guidance on how to collect and prioritize requirements emerging from multiple autonomous sources (only that prioritization should follow "the architecture vision," which itself presumes a single, agreed vision); and (2) the Architecture Board concept presumes a small (4-5 member), top-management-mandated group able to enforce compliance, which has no counterpart in an organization where authority is legitimately distributed.
mechanism: Frameworks such as TOGAF were originally developed assuming centralized IT/management, so their governance and requirements-management guidance implicitly requires a single locus of decision authority; applying them unmodified to federated or decentralized organizations reproduces governance and decision-making irregularities rather than resolving them, because there genuinely is no party empowered to play the assumed centralized role.
operationalisation_hint: Before adopting a mainstream EA framework (TOGAF, FEA, etc.) in a federated or decentralized organization, explicitly audit the framework's governance and requirements-management guidance for hidden centralization assumptions, and design a compensating multi-party governance mechanism rather than assuming the framework's default guidance will transfer.

finding_statement: The organization extends its Enterprise Architecture meta-model (built on ArchiMate) with product-centric concepts -- Offering (products/services combined for value creation), Ecosystem (an offering or group of offerings plus their key actors), Touchpoint (customer interaction channels, pre/purchase/post-purchase), Experience (the actor's subjective response to an interaction), Concern (an actor's problem/need), and Technology Area (a domain of IT-intensive methods/solutions) -- so that smart, connected products (which combine physical, "smart," and connectivity components) are represented within the same EA alongside traditional enterprise-IT elements, rather than being modeled in a separate, disconnected product-development silo.
mechanism: As physical products increasingly embed software, sensors, and connectivity ("product-IT"), traditional EA models (which capture only enterprise-IT: business/data/application/technology layers) miss the substantial IT content now residing inside the product itself, causing duplicated architecture effort and missed integration opportunities (e.g., shared encryption/logging services needed by both product software and enterprise software); explicitly extending the EA meta-model with product-facing concepts closes this representational gap so both product-IT and enterprise-IT can be jointly planned and aligned.
operationalisation_hint: When a product line is undergoing (or has undergone) digitization/connectivity additions, extend the EA meta-model to explicitly include Offering/Ecosystem/Touchpoint/Experience/Concern/Technology-Area concepts, and use the three method components (ecosystem-of-offerings mapping, customer-journey mapping, data-driven-business-options mapping) during Business Architecture development (TOGAF ADM phases B/C) to surface product-IT integration needs early.

finding_statement: The organization differentiates its IT governance and delivery model by mode: Mode 1 (enterprise-IT: accounting, finance, HR) is governed for stability, efficiency, and low cost using traditional EAM practices, while Mode 2 (product-IT: embedded/connected product software) is governed for fast turnaround, frequent updates, and high business involvement using DevOps-style teams -- with the enterprise architecture method explicitly required to remain applicable across both coexisting modes rather than assuming a single delivery cadence.
mechanism: Established enterprises (unlike digitally-native startups with a "clean slate") carry years of legacy technology, governance, and financing structures on the enterprise-IT side, while product-IT demands rapid, frequent, business-driven iteration to remain competitive; without an explicit bimodal governance split (and a method that can operate across both), the slower enterprise-IT governance model tends to be applied to product-IT by default, throttling the innovation speed the product side needs.
operationalisation_hint: When planning digital transformation of a physical-product business, classify system/architecture components as Mode 1 (enterprise-IT, stability-governed) or Mode 2 (product-IT, agility-governed) early, and assign differentiated governance cadences (e.g., DevOps teams for Mode 2) rather than applying uniform enterprise-IT governance to both.
