finding_statement: The organization derives a business-capability inventory for a defined transformation scope (here, Smart Factory operations within a Digital Factory Twin initiative) via a Structured Literature Review, then structures the resulting capabilities hierarchically into top-level groups (Smart Assets, Smart Working, Smart Manufacturing, Smart Supply Chain, Smart Products) with each group bounded to a minimum of two and maximum of five sub-capabilities for clarity, and validates the map's stability by requiring that no changes occur to the top two hierarchy levels after a case-study review with an industry partner.
mechanism: Ad hoc or purely case-derived capability lists risk being idiosyncratic to one organization's context and unstable as new capabilities are discovered; grounding the initial map in a broad literature synthesis (1,383 sources here) before case validation, combined with an explicit stability criterion (no top-two-level changes post-validation), produces a capability map robust enough to serve as a shared reference across multiple organizations rather than a one-off artifact.
operationalisation_hint: When scoping a digital-twin or Industry 4.0 transformation initiative, first derive a candidate capability list via structured literature review, group it hierarchically (2-5 sub-capabilities per group) by van Riel's generic capability-map method, then validate stability against a real case before treating the top-level structure as fixed.
page_or_section: Sections 3-4 (Research Design, Proposed SF Capability Map)

finding_statement: The organization works through a five-step procedure to operationalize a capability map for a transformation initiative: (1) define strategic objectives for the initiative; (2) identify requisite capabilities from the capability map/repository; (3) assess each identified capability's strategic relevance (business impact, alignment, feasibility); (4) conduct a fit-gap analysis distinguishing capabilities that are missing entirely from capabilities that exist but need maturity enhancement; and (5) plan capability realization as a roadmap with milestones informing resource allocation and prioritization.
mechanism: Without a defined procedure connecting strategic objectives to a capability roadmap, capability maps risk being descriptive reference documents that are never operationalized into actual investment decisions; the fit-gap step in particular is necessary because "missing capability" and "immature existing capability" require different remediation actions (build vs. enhance), and conflating them leads to misallocated transformation investment.
operationalisation_hint: When using a capability map (Industry-4.0-specific or general-purpose) to plan a transformation initiative, run the five-step procedure explicitly, keeping the fit-gap analysis's two perspectives (missing vs. immature capabilities) as separate roadmap workstreams.

finding_statement: A data architecture assigns data ownership and production responsibility to decentralized, domain-oriented teams (each domain independently produces and publishes its own data products, accompanied by a data contract, to a shared Data Product Catalog) while a Federated Governance layer defines and enforces enterprise-wide, non-negotiable standards -- access/compliance/privacy/exchange policies, interoperability (technical and semantic) requirements, and documentation policy -- that all domains must follow regardless of their operational autonomy, with a Self-Serve Data Platform providing the shared infrastructure (storage, query engines, access control, ETL) domains use to implement these standards themselves.
mechanism: Fully centralized, monolithic data architectures create bottlenecks (central teams cannot keep pace with all domains' data needs, causing low domain-specific knowledge and long lead times), while fully decentralized data ownership without any shared governance risks incompatible standards, data duplication, and siloed, non-interoperable data products; federating governance (shared, enforceable policies) while decentralizing production (domain-owned data products) captures the scalability benefit of decentralization without sacrificing enterprise-wide consistency and security.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a data architecture for a large, multi-domain organization, model three explicit ArchiMate layers -- Domain-Driven Data-as-Product, Self-Serve Data Platform, Federated Governance -- and ensure the governance layer's policies (access, compliance, privacy, exchange, interoperability, documentation) are enforced identically across all domains regardless of each domain's operational autonomy.
page_or_section: Sections 4.2-4.4 (Domain-Driven Data as a Product, Self-Serve Data Platform, Federated Governance)

finding_statement: An organization selects its data mesh implementation from a spectrum of archetypes rather than assuming full decentralization is always the goal: a fine-grained fully-federated mesh (maximum domain autonomy and specialization, but capability duplication/cost/complexity risk), a fully-governed mesh (a central data-distribution layer improving compliance at the cost of flexibility), a hybrid federated mesh (middle ground, simplified management with some overhead), and value-chain-aligned/coarse-grained meshes (suited to complex supply chains or post-merger organizations with larger, less granular domain boundaries).
mechanism: No single data mesh archetype solves all organizational data challenges; an organization's appropriate degree of federation depends on factors such as its number and boundary-clarity of business domains, its M&A history, and its supply-chain complexity, so treating "data mesh" as a single fixed target architecture (rather than a spectrum to select from) risks over- or under-decentralizing relative to organizational needs.
operationalisation_hint: Before committing to a data mesh implementation, explicitly assess organizational factors (domain boundary clarity, M&A/supply-chain complexity, data literacy/technical-expertise levels) against the four archetypes to select the appropriate degree of federation rather than defaulting to the most decentralized (fully-federated) form.

finding_statement: The organization structures its EA-driven transformation process explicitly through Choo's three-mode Knowing Cycle: sense-making (bracketing raw organizational/environmental data via interviews/workshops, interpreting it to produce the current-state/baseline architecture and an architecture vision), knowledge creation (converting stakeholder-shared tacit knowledge into explicit architectural artifacts stored in an EA repository, modeling the target/to-be architecture), and decision-making (using the created knowledge to identify, develop, and select transformation initiatives that close the gap between baseline and target architecture) -- rather than treating architecture development as a purely technical modeling exercise disconnected from organizational knowledge processes.
mechanism: EA artifacts (models, repositories) are themselves a form of organizational knowledge, and the process of producing them mirrors the general organizational knowing cycle (making sense of a changing environment, creating new knowledge to address it, deciding how to act); making this connection explicit lets architects deliberately manage the sense-making step (contextualizing stakeholder input) as a precondition for knowledge creation, rather than treating architecture documentation as a standalone deliverable.
operationalisation_hint: When running an EA-driven transformation, explicitly stage the work as sense-making (interviews/workshops to build the current-state model and architecture vision) -> knowledge creation (converting stakeholder tacit knowledge into target-architecture artifacts in a managed repository) -> decision-making (deriving and selecting prioritized transformation initiatives from the baseline-target gap).
page_or_section: Sections 2(d), 4(d) (Transformation and the Organizational Context; Implications for the business transformation framework)

finding_statement: Enterprise architects treat business process re-engineering -- evaluating and drastically redesigning business operations for improvement -- as the primary practical mechanism through which EA delivers business transformation, with process evaluation forming part of the current-state architecture assessment whose findings become recommendations for future-state transformation initiatives.
mechanism: Nearly unanimous agreement (all but one of 22 surveyed South African enterprise architects) that EA enables business transformation specifically through process re-engineering suggests this is not an isolated theoretical claim but a broadly shared practitioner belief across a national sample, reinforcing process redesign as the operational bridge between an EA's baseline/target architecture models and actual organizational change.
operationalisation_hint: When using EA to support business transformation, prioritize identifying and re-engineering business processes flagged during the current-state assessment as the primary lever for realizing the transformation, rather than treating process change as a secondary outcome of architecture/technology change.

finding_statement: An organization adopting a new architectural/technology paradigm (here, microservices) assesses and advances its readiness along two distinct dimensions in tandem -- technical maturity (API design, service discovery, authentication, performance monitoring, orchestration sophistication) and organizational maturity (talent/hiring, licensing/monetization model, management buy-in, business-model realignment) -- since observed organizations rarely show a high level of maturity on one dimension while remaining low on the other, and full paradigm benefits require both to progress together.
mechanism: Technical implementation of a new architectural style (e.g., building working microservices) is necessarily visible and easy to observe, biasing organizational attention and investment toward the technical dimension; but the paradigm's business value (agility, new revenue models, faster time-to-market) depends equally on organizational changes (talent, licensing, business-model shift) that are less visible and easier to neglect, so tracking only technical maturity produces a false sense of overall transformation readiness.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing readiness to adopt a new architectural/technology paradigm, score both a technical-maturity dimension and an organizational-maturity dimension (each on the same level scale) rather than a single combined or technical-only score, and treat a large gap between the two dimensions as a specific risk flag.
page_or_section: Sections 3.1-3.3 (Maturity Levels, Maturity Dimensions, Technical/Organizational Maturity Dimension)

finding_statement: The illustration contrasts a technically driven microservices transformation that neglected financial and operational impacts with a manager- and finance-backed transformation that evolved faster. It reports an unresolved integration and earning-model issue in the first company.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 4 (Illustration on two organizations, Company A vs. Company B)

finding_statement: The organization treats EA artifacts (e.g., solution overviews, landscape diagrams, architecture assessments) as instruments of knowledge conservation that explicate otherwise-tacit organizational knowledge, and recognizes that this knowledge conservation, improved communication, and improved insight form a cyclic, mutually-reinforcing "EA value fundament" -- each of the three reinforces the other two -- which in turn precedes and enables improved decision-making, and improved decision-making is what ultimately drives improved organizational performance (agility, lower cost of change, etc.), rather than treating EA artifact creation as valuable in itself.
mechanism: Across 29 interviews at 4 case firms, interviewees consistently described a causal chain rather than a flat list of independent benefits: artifacts make tacit knowledge explicit ("that is not self-evident," per Delta's CIO), explicit knowledge enables communication ("it's about the conversation and conviction," per Gamma's business owner), and only informed, well-communicated decisions translate into measurable organizational-performance gains -- meaning organizations that document EA artifacts without cultivating the communication/insight cycle around them fail to realize the downstream performance benefit.
operationalisation_hint: When justifying investment in EA artifact creation, frame the value case around the causal chain (knowledge conservation -> communication/insight -> decision quality -> organizational performance) rather than listing EA artifacts or values as independent deliverables; prioritize pairing artifact creation with deliberate communication practices (workshops, walkthroughs) rather than "throwing artifacts over the fence."
page_or_section: Sections 4.1-4.2, Fig. 1 (EA Artifacts and EA Value; EA Artifacts and Organizational Performance)

finding_statement: The organization should expect that EA artifact names, boundaries, and exact content will differ substantially across firms and even across prior research studies (e.g., what one firm calls a "high-level design" another calls a "solution overview"; what one study treats as a single artifact, interviewees at another firm say already contains sub-artifacts), and should not assume a universal, standardized EA-artifact taxonomy exists to adopt off-the-shelf.
mechanism: Comparing this study's 17 identified artifacts against prior EA-artifact research (e.g., Kotusev's separate solution overview/landscape diagram/context diagram categories, which several interviewees said overlap in practice) reveals persistent disagreement on artifact boundaries and definitions across both practice and the academic literature, an immaturity trait the authors explicitly attribute to the EA discipline rather than to any single firm's idiosyncrasy.
operationalisation_hint: When introducing EA artifacts into an organization, adapt artifact names/boundaries to local practice and terminology rather than importing a fixed external taxonomy unchanged, and expect genuine artifact-boundary disagreement even among experienced practitioners.

finding_statement: The organization extends TOGAF's standard Business Architecture (Phase B) deliverables with an explicit "Sensing" routine (environmental scanning, stakeholder interviews, assumption validation) at the outset of each planning cycle, a "Mobilizing" capability (engaging stakeholders enterprise-wide to build support and reallocate resources, replacing the generic "seizing" construct per Van de Wetering's EA-specific refinement), and a "Transforming" step (recombining processes/assets), plus a dedicated "Process Matrix" artifact that captures version history, decision rationales, and governance checkpoints for lifecycle management -- rather than treating Business Process Architecture as a static, one-time blueprint exercise.
mechanism: TOGAF's ADM Phase B provides only high-level guidance on process catalogs and value-stream maps without prescribing how to embed ongoing, iterative reconfiguration in response to environmental change, causing architects to adapt or skip process-reconfiguration steps inconsistently across organizations (per Kotusev's and the same authors' own prior case findings); explicitly mapping each ADM step to a sensing/mobilizing/transforming micro-foundation, and adding version/lifecycle governance via a Process Matrix, closes this gap so BPA artifacts function as living routines rather than one-off documentation.
operationalisation_hint: When developing a Business Process Architecture under TOGAF, add an explicit environmental-sensing step before defining baseline/target process architecture, treat stakeholder mobilization as a distinct capability-building activity (not merely "seizing opportunities"), and introduce a Process Matrix artifact to track process versions, decision rationales, and governance checkpoints across the process lifecycle.
page_or_section: Sections 2, 4 (Related Work; Functional Requirements and Artifact Development)

finding_statement: The organization interleaves "Mobilizing" and "Transforming" sub-phases within each major TOGAF ADM stage, so that a gap analysis (baseline vs. target business architecture) immediately triggers a design sprint and a stakeholder validation workshop rather than proceeding linearly through the ADM once; strategic objectives, capability maps, and process flows are continuously revisited and refined as each cycle completes, and workshops with business owners are held to validate architecture outputs at each iteration.
mechanism: Static, linear BPA execution (define baseline -> define target -> plan migration, done once) cannot keep pace with turbulent environments where new environmental cues (from the sensing step) invalidate prior assumptions mid-cycle; embedding a feedback loop that loops back from gap analysis to reassessment institutionalizes the "transforming" (continuous renewal) aspect of dynamic capabilities directly into the architecture method rather than leaving it to ad hoc re-planning.
operationalisation_hint: When executing TOGAF ADM Phase B in a volatile environment, explicitly schedule a design-sprint-and-validation-workshop loop triggered by each gap analysis, rather than treating gap analysis as a single milestone followed by linear migration planning.
page_or_section: Section 5.1 (Changes from Literature Review to Final BPA Development Method)

finding_statement: The organization decomposes its business architecture into modules (What: modularization, KPIs, strengths; Who: customers; How: business model) and works through five concrete steps -- (1) decompose business processes into modules, (2) quantify each module via KPIs, (3) identify module strengths from the KPI data, (4) identify the most valuable customer segment for those strengths, (5) sense/seize/transform to develop a new business exploiting that strength -- so that non-technical executives (who understand overall business architecture but often lack digital-era experience) can follow a concrete, step-by-step process rather than relying on the abstract, unspecified "iterative cycle" Teece's dynamic-capabilities theory describes without a reproducible model.
mechanism: Teece's dynamic-capabilities theory asserts the necessity of an iterative sensing-seizing-transforming cycle but (per the paper's own review of Teece and Kikuzawa) does not provide a specific, reproducible model for executing it; decomposing the business into quantifiable modules gives executives concrete artifacts (KPIs, strength profiles) to reason about and discuss, translating an abstract capability-theory prescription into a walkable procedure that bridges the digital-literacy gap between technically inexperienced senior management and DX initiatives.
operationalisation_hint: When guiding management through a digital-transformation understanding process, break the business into modules with the F&WM What/Who/How dimensions, quantify each module's current performance via KPIs before attempting any DX intervention, and use the resulting strength/weakness profile to identify which customer segments and business-model changes to pursue next.
page_or_section: Sections 4-5 (Proposal for unrolling the DC iteration cycle; Application of the DC cycle unrolling framework)

finding_statement: The organization discovers strengths it was not previously aware it possessed by quantifying decomposed business modules via KPIs -- in the case company, modularizing the production division into technical capability, production system, and factory utilization revealed that technical capability held steady even as production-system/factory utilization declined with falling house orders, surfacing "technical capability" as an unrecognized strength the company had never considered offering externally.
mechanism: Without module-level KPI quantification, a capability embedded inside an existing product line (e.g., technical capability used only internally to produce parts) remains invisible as a standalone asset because it is never measured or discussed independently of the product it currently serves; decomposing and quantifying at the module level exposes such latent strengths as candidates for new business models targeting new customer segments.
operationalisation_hint: When exploring new business opportunities during digital transformation, quantify business modules independently via KPIs even where they currently serve only internal/existing products, since module-level (rather than product-level) measurement is what surfaces strengths that can be redeployed toward new markets.

finding_statement: The organization designs its Enterprise Information System so that each business process (defined purely by its input and output data) maps directly to one application component and one or more highly-cohesive technology-layer "commands" connected only through data objects (Unix-pipe-style), producing a microservice/loosely-coupled architecture in which business-process analysis and design are simultaneously data-and-application design -- rather than designing business processes, applications, and technology as separate, loosely-synchronized layers.
mechanism: Because each command/component has a single, sophisticated function processing only input/output data, dependencies between components are minimized, letting the organization refactor (re-develop) individual parts of the EIS without cascading changes through the rest of the system; the real-case company achieved measurable multi-year re-development at lower cost specifically because the architecture's loose coupling meant that a single business-process change corresponded to a bounded application-component change rather than a system-wide rewrite.
operationalisation_hint: When designing an EIS intended for frequent Agile/Lean-style refactoring, define business processes strictly by their input/output data, map each process 1:1 to an application component built from small, single-function IO-based commands, and connect components only through data objects rather than shared middleware or direct calls.

finding_statement: Before implementing an IO-data-driven architecture, the organization first identifies and eliminates business processes that do not create business value or that overlap with other processes (per the Data Driven Process Design Method), and in the real case, hears "weak signals" directly from front-line employees together with company leadership to decide whether a given activity constitutes waste before optimizing the remaining process for the target architecture.
mechanism: An IO-data-based architecture directly mirrors whatever business processes are fed into it (each process becomes an application component), so redundant or non-value-creating processes carried into the architecture become redundant, costly application components that persist indefinitely; front-line-employee-sourced signal collection combined with leadership review is the mechanism the case company used to filter which processes deserved architectural investment.
operationalisation_hint: Before mapping business processes to architecture components, run a process-value review (soliciting front-line employee input alongside leadership judgment) to eliminate non-value-creating or overlapping processes, so the resulting architecture does not encode organizational waste as permanent application structure.

finding_statement: The organization governs emerging, decentralization-enabling technologies (such as Low-Code Development Platforms) by deliberately assembling a portfolio of paired strategy clusters -- e.g., formal application registration + informal community "show and tell" sessions; formal risk-tiered guardrails + informal co-design with citizen developers; formal RACI role definitions + informal architect-to-developer mentoring -- rather than choosing either strict centralized top-down control (which citizen developers experience as bureaucratic, eroding the agility that motivated LCDP adoption) or unstructured decentralized enablement (which produces uncontrolled application proliferation, architectural drift, and security exposure).
mechanism: Across three organizations in different regulated sectors (finance, healthcare, manufacturing), purely centralized governance consistently suppressed the innovation/agility benefit that justified adopting decentralized development platforms in the first place, while purely informal/decentralized governance consistently produced shadow-IT-like proliferation, technical debt, and security exposure; pairing formal instruments (which supply clarity, traceability, and safeguards) with informal practices (which cultivate capability, legitimacy, and shared ownership) is what let all three organizations sustain both architectural coherence and development speed simultaneously.
operationalisation_hint: When governing any decentralization-enabling technology (low-code platforms, citizen development, or by extension AI-assisted/agentic development), design governance as an explicit portfolio combining at least one formal instrument (registration, risk tiers, RACI) with at least one informal enabling practice (community sessions, co-design, mentoring) for each governance challenge identified, rather than defaulting to either pure top-down control or pure laissez-faire enablement.
page_or_section: Findings section (Strategies; Discussion and conclusion, "A conceptual model of balanced governance")

finding_statement: The organization requires mandatory registration of every citizen-developed application with a minimal documentation set (ownership, data classification, dependencies), conducts periodic audits and scheduled portfolio reviews to retire duplicate/obsolete applications, and complements these formal instruments with informal practices such as lightweight documentation templates and community "show and tell" sessions where teams present what they built -- producing "information symmetry": a shared, accurate, current picture of the application landscape held jointly by architects, governance boards, and citizen developers.
mechanism: Decentralized, citizen-led application development is invisible to central EA/IT by default (applications emerge outside established governance boundaries), and this invisibility -- not citizen development itself -- is the proximate cause of architectural drift, technical debt, and duplicated effort; making the landscape visible via registration and hygiene practices is a prerequisite that "completes the loop" enabling other governance mechanisms (proportionate guardrails, secure-by-default pipelines) to function, since none of them can operate correctly against an undocumented, unknown application inventory.
operationalisation_hint: When decentralized/citizen development platforms are introduced, mandate lightweight but non-negotiable application registration (owner, data sensitivity, dependencies) from day one, schedule periodic portfolio reviews to retire redundant applications, and pair these formal requirements with informal show-and-tell/community practices that make documentation a shared norm rather than a compliance burden.
page_or_section: Findings section (Visibility and portfolio hygiene; Mechanisms)

finding_statement: The organization designs governance guardrails (standards, review gates, exception procedures) to be transparent (rationale for each rule explicitly communicated), proportionate (control depth scaled to risk, not uniformly strict), and co-designed with citizen developers and business stakeholders through participatory forums and a Center of Excellence that provides rapid, supportive advisory rather than only enforcement -- because when developers perceive governance as arbitrary or purely restrictive, they bypass rules or engage in only superficial compliance, whereas participatory, explained governance is experienced as legitimate and is followed voluntarily.
mechanism: Multiple case interviewees explicitly described a shift from viewing governance as "unnecessary bureaucracy" (leading to bypassed rules) to viewing it as legitimate, collaboratively-developed guidance once they were included in standards discussions (e.g., HealthComp drawing nurse managers and administrative coordinators into governance forums); perceived legitimacy is the mechanism that converts a governance mandate from an imposed cost into a voluntarily-adopted practice, directly reducing the shadow-IT and non-compliance behaviors that erode architectural coherence.
operationalisation_hint: When rolling out governance guardrails for decentralized development, explain the rationale behind each rule (not just the rule itself), scale control depth to actual risk rather than applying uniform maximum scrutiny, and establish a participatory forum (e.g., a Center of Excellence) where citizen developers co-own the standards backlog rather than only receiving it.
page_or_section: Findings section (Governance frameworks and pragmatic guardrails; Center of Excellence and participatory governance; Mechanisms)

finding_statement: The organization codifies responsibility-accountability (RACI-style) mappings across the full lifecycle of decentralized development (from ideation through retirement), explicitly redefining the role of EA/IT staff from centralized gatekeepers/controllers toward supportive guides who mentor and collaborate with citizen developers -- in one case structurally separating an "enabling" function (platform, tooling, standards, reusable building blocks) from a "delivery" function (actual application development) -- so that ownership is unambiguous both on paper and in day-to-day practice.
mechanism: When decision rights are not explicitly codified, citizen developers gain de facto production capability without corresponding accountability, generating persistent "who owns this now" conflicts between IT, business units, and developers that stall decisions and require repeated escalation to resolve; explicitly redefining and separating the enabling role (owned by EA/IT) from the delivery role (owned by developer teams) resolves this ambiguity structurally rather than relying on ad hoc case-by-case negotiation.
operationalisation_hint: When decentralizing development authority to business units or citizen developers, formally separate the "enabling" function (platform/tooling/standards ownership, retained by EA/IT) from the "delivery" function (application development ownership, devolved to business-facing teams), and document a RACI-style decision-rights map spanning the full application lifecycle rather than leaving ownership boundaries implicit.
page_or_section: Findings section (Role redefinition and alignment of decision rights; Mechanisms)

finding_statement: The organization classifies each decentrally-developed application into a risk tier (e.g., prototype, departmental solution, enterprise-critical application) and scales the depth of governance controls accordingly -- lightweight checklists and automated tests for low-risk prototypes, multi-party security/architecture review for enterprise-critical changes -- with periodic recalibration of tier assignments based on incidents and usage signals, rather than applying either uniformly strict or uniformly lax controls across the entire application portfolio.
mechanism: Applying maximum governance scrutiny to every citizen-developed application (including trivial departmental workflow replacements) creates unnecessary friction that erodes the agility benefit of decentralized development, while applying uniformly light governance to all applications (including those handling sensitive data or supporting critical operations) creates unmanaged risk exposure; explicitly tiering by risk lets the organization preserve speed for the majority of low-stakes applications while concentrating scarce governance attention on the minority that actually warrants it.
operationalisation_hint: When governing a growing portfolio of decentrally-developed applications, define at least three risk tiers (e.g., prototype, departmental, enterprise-critical) with explicit, proportionate control requirements per tier, and schedule periodic tier-reassignment reviews triggered by incidents or usage-pattern changes.
page_or_section: Findings section (Balanced portfolio and risk-tiering; Mechanisms)

finding_statement: Before rolling out a large-scale, multi-stakeholder IT-enabled system (e.g., a national health insurance information system spanning public and private providers), the organization/government conducts a systematic readiness assessment of the technological environment -- surveying which facilities operate on paper-based vs. electronic records, which IT solutions are already deployed, and where infrastructure gaps exist -- rather than proceeding to implementation without first identifying these gaps.
mechanism: The analysis found no readiness assessment had been conducted before the South African NHI pilot, and the resulting disjointed, non-compatible IT solutions across public/private healthcare facilities directly caused the interoperability and connectivity failures (poor connectivity, hardware problems, data duplication) documented in the pilot's evaluation reports; a prior readiness assessment would have surfaced these incompatibilities before rollout rather than after failure.
operationalisation_hint: Before implementing a multi-stakeholder IT-enabled system spanning organizationally-independent providers, conduct a formal technological readiness assessment (current state of paper vs. electronic records, existing IT solutions and their compatibility) and use its findings to inform architecture design, rather than proceeding directly to implementation.

finding_statement: The organization selects and designs IT solutions specifically for their capacity "to adapt, support, and enable organizational practices and change" (flexibility), so that as new stakeholder types, service categories, or requirements are added to a decentralized multi-stakeholder system over time, existing solutions can accommodate the additions without breaking interoperability with already-integrated systems.
mechanism: A geographically-dispersed system with multiple independent, non-uniformly-mature stakeholders (as in a national health system spanning public/private providers across different regions) will continuously enroll new participants and requirements over time; without flexible (adaptable) IT solutions, each addition risks either being rejected for incompatibility or requiring costly, disruptive re-integration of the entire existing solution set.
operationalisation_hint: When designing IT solutions for a decentralized, multi-stakeholder system expected to grow or evolve its participant base over time, evaluate candidate solutions explicitly for adaptability/extensibility rather than for feature-completeness alone, since accommodating future stakeholder/requirement additions without breaking existing integrations is the primary risk factor identified.

finding_statement: A multi-actor urban mobility ecosystem (spanning municipal, metropolitan, and national regulatory bodies alongside private operators and technology suppliers) establishes an explicit inter-institutional coordination mechanism -- e.g., a dedicated business-layer component formalizing joint oversight between fragmented municipal and metropolitan competencies -- so that new automated/shared mobility services can be deployed without being blocked by unresolved authority overlaps between government levels.
mechanism: Expert interviewees explicitly identified fragmented governance (unclear regulatory authority split between municipal, regional, and national bodies, with liability for incidents undefined) as the central barrier to deploying Shared Autonomous Vehicles in Lisbon, echoing the same finding across international comparison cities (Singapore, Stockholm); explicitly modeling an "Inter-institutional Coordination" component in the business layer of the reference architecture directly responds to this fragmentation rather than leaving it as an external, unaddressed policy problem.
operationalisation_hint: When designing a reference architecture for a multi-actor public/private service ecosystem (mobility, or by extension any service crossing multiple government levels and private operators), include an explicit inter-institutional coordination component in the business layer that formalizes joint oversight, rather than assuming existing regulatory bodies will self-coordinate.
page_or_section: Sections 4.1, 6.2 (Reference Model as Foundation; Governance, Interoperability and Organisational Implications)

finding_statement: The organization designs the application layer of a new automated-service architecture to include explicit trust-building components -- safety dashboards, in-app emergency/panic-button interfaces, remote human-monitoring/intervention services, and transparent incident-reporting mechanisms -- rather than treating user trust as an outcome to be achieved solely through marketing or after-the-fact communication.
mechanism: End-user interviews revealed persistent safety anxieties specific to the absence of a human driver (especially at night or in isolated situations) and explicit demands for visible safety features (cameras, emergency buttons, real-time monitoring) before users would consider adoption; embedding these features architecturally (as first-class application-layer components, not add-ons) directly targets the adoption barrier identified as most decisive by end-users, ahead of price or convenience concerns.
operationalisation_hint: When architecting a new automated or AI-driven public-facing service, include specific application-layer components for safety monitoring, emergency intervention, and transparent incident reporting from the initial design stage, treating them as adoption-enabling infrastructure rather than optional enhancements added after user concerns surface.
page_or_section: Sections 4.3, 6.2 (Overview of the Model -- Application Layer; Qualitative Evaluation Findings)

finding_statement: The ten-expert study observes practitioners bypassing or supplementing formal EA frameworks with lightweight architectural principles in AI integration. Its broader 'EA Paradox' claims are framed as theory and testable propositions, not established general evidence.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The organization prioritizes AI integration efforts at the Business layer (reconfiguring ecosystem actors, roles, and strategic decision-making) and Data layer (cross-organizational data pipelines, data-driven decision-making) of its Enterprise Architecture, treating Application-layer and Technology-layer AI investments as necessary enabling infrastructure rather than the primary source of strategic AI value.
mechanism: Across a 10-expert Likert-matrix survey (4 EA layers x 3 Innovation-Ecosystem dimensions), Business-layer intersections (actors, processes) and Data-layer processes received the highest strategic-importance ratings (means of 5.0-5.5 on a 1-6 scale), while Application and Technology layers scored consistently lower (3.8-4.6); qualitative interviews explained this pattern by describing the Business and Data layers as "translational zones" where AI bridges human expertise and machine intelligence to reshape decision-making and actor collaboration, whereas Technology-layer infrastructure was perceived by digital-native firms as a commodity (though manufacturing-sector experts viewed it as a higher-risk bottleneck, indicating sector-dependent variation).
operationalisation_hint: When prioritizing AI-EA integration investment, direct initial effort toward Business-layer decision-making/actor-collaboration processes and Data-layer pipeline/governance infrastructure before Application- or Technology-layer investments, while expecting more disagreement on Technology-layer priority in asset-heavy (e.g., manufacturing) sectors versus digital-native sectors.
page_or_section: Section 4.1 (Quantitative assessment: prioritizing AI's strategic focus); Section 4.3

finding_statement: The organization maps its AI-governance challenges onto a 4x3 matrix crossing EA's vertical layers (Business, Application, Data, Technology) against an Innovation Ecosystem's horizontal dimensions (Actors, Resources, Processes), using the resulting 12 named interfaces (e.g., "ecosystem strategy alignment" at Business-Actors, "data sovereignty and ethical governance" at Data-Actors, "interoperability standards" at Technology-Processes) as boundary objects to identify specifically where AI initiatives are failing to align with ecosystem-level objectives, rather than treating "AI governance" as a single undifferentiated concern.
mechanism: The authors demonstrate that specific socio-technical failures map cleanly onto specific matrix cells -- e.g., isolated AI pilots failing due to missing grounding in the "automated compliance and co-creation" (Application-Processes) interface, or sensitive-data leakage into public AI assistants representing a breakdown at the "data sovereignty and ethical governance" (Data-Actors) and "data sharing agreements and APIs" (Data-Resources) interfaces -- showing that the matrix has diagnostic power beyond being a visualization device.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing why an AI initiative is failing to deliver ecosystem-level value, locate the failure on the EA-layer x IE-dimension matrix (which vertical layer, which horizontal dimension) before prescribing a generic "more governance" response, since the appropriate fix (compliance workflow vs. data-sharing agreement vs. interoperability standard) differs by matrix cell.

finding_statement: The organization treats environmental/energy-efficiency practices for its own AI infrastructure (optimizing code for energy efficiency, selecting renewable-powered data centers, monitoring the carbon cost of model training) as a mandatory precondition of any AI-driven sustainability initiative, rather than assuming that AI's efficiency gains elsewhere in the ecosystem automatically produce a net-positive sustainability outcome.
mechanism: Experts with circular-economy backgrounds explicitly warned of a "rebound effect" in which the environmental cost of training and running large AI models can exceed the efficiency gains the AI enables elsewhere (e.g., in logistics optimization or supply-chain transparency), meaning organizations pursuing AI for sustainability without also managing AI's own computational footprint risk a net negative or neutral sustainability outcome despite reporting local efficiency wins.
operationalisation_hint: Before launching an AI-for-sustainability initiative, require a Green-AI baseline (energy-efficient code, renewable-powered compute, carbon-cost monitoring of model training/inference) as a governance gate, and evaluate the initiative's net sustainability impact (efficiency gains minus AI's own computational footprint) rather than reporting only the downstream efficiency gains.
page_or_section: Section 4.2 (Theme 1: AI's evolving role as a catalyst for sustainable innovation); Section 5 (EA Paradox sustainability tension)

finding_statement: The organization develops its Business Capability Map (BCM) as a business-focused (not IT-reference) artifact, starting from a generic reusable template and existing internal/consultancy materials rather than from scratch, modeling first only the core ~20% of capabilities that deliver the most business value ("good enough and fast, not exhaustive"), and then iteratively enriching and validating it through real initiatives with domain experts -- rather than attempting exhaustive, abstract, upfront capability modeling that can take years to complete.
mechanism: The literature (Van Riel & Poels, Kotusev & Alwadain, cited in this paper) documents that BCMs are widely recognized as valuable EA artifacts but remain rarely used systematically in practice because most guidance is either proprietary/consultancy-driven (limiting transparency) or academically conceptual/normative (offering limited practical insight); adopting a "good enough," pragmatic-first, iteratively-enriched approach (grounded in organizational sensemaking theory, valuing plausibility over precision) avoids the years-long, stalled full-BCM-construction failure mode that abstract methodologies risk in large organizations.
operationalisation_hint: When building a BCM for strategic alignment, start from a generic template adapted to organizational language, model only the highest-value ~20% of capabilities first, use verb-avoiding noun naming with stable capability identifiers and hierarchical numbering, and treat the BCM as a living artifact enriched through real initiative engagement rather than a one-time deliverable -- following the 16 guiding principles the authors distilled from literature and practice (business-focus, template-start, leverage-existing-versions, pragmatic-value-focus, test-and-refine, established-terminology, pragmatism-over-taxonomy, learn-as-you-go, hierarchical-but-ontological structure, organization-agnostic design, capability uniqueness, noun-naming, structured numbering, stable identifiers, value-stream validation, and non-process-based structuring).
page_or_section: Section III (Methodology); Section IV.A.1 (BCM Development Guidance, 16 principles)

finding_statement: The organization maintains an End-to-End (E2E) Value Stream artifact -- a small number of high-level, customer-visible steps (e.g., sales, onboarding, service delivery, support, invoicing) that collectively deliver value to the customer, each mapped to the underlying business capabilities that enable it -- and uses this artifact as a checklist during early initiative scoping (well before formal IT engagement) to surface critical cross-functional dependencies and support early scope/cost estimation, deliberately excluding internal-only activities not visible to the customer.
mechanism: A prior "E2E Value Chain" artifact that included internal (non-customer-facing) activities like clearing or risk/fraud processing proved too extensive and lacked capability integration, reducing its usefulness for quick initiative scoping; restricting the value stream to a small number of customer-visible steps and pairing each with its enabling capabilities lets project managers identify dependencies and estimate scope early, without waiting for detailed IT architecture documentation to be produced.
operationalisation_hint: When scoping a new cross-functional initiative, first identify which of the organization's customer-facing E2E Value Stream steps the initiative touches, cross-reference each touched step against its enabling business capabilities (from the BCM) to surface dependencies, and use this checklist for early cost/scope estimation before engaging IT in detailed design.
page_or_section: Section IV.A.3 (Value Stream Mapping Guidelines); Section III (E2E Value Stream figures)

finding_statement: The 28-study synthesis describes a socio-technical relationship among change management, enterprise architecture, and governance in South African public-sector digital transformation. It does not establish that all three are jointly necessary in every public-sector setting.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Abstract; Literature Review (Change Management Capabilities; Enterprise Architecture, Integration, and Service Quality; Governance, Coordination, and Pathways to Scalable Reform); Theoretical Framework

finding_statement: Even where change-management, enterprise-architecture, and governance conditions are otherwise favorable at a national or departmental level, the public-sector organization must separately address uneven digital infrastructure (connectivity, hardware) and digital-skills distribution across rural, peri-urban, and urban service points, since reforms designed and piloted in well-resourced urban contexts do not automatically scale to under-resourced local governments and municipalities.
mechanism: Multiple reviewed studies documented that rural and peri-urban municipalities faced limited connectivity and lower digital literacy that blunted digital-inclusion efforts even when national digital strategy, EA standards, and governance frameworks were in place; this geographic/resource disparity was identified as a distinct barrier requiring hybrid workshops, mobile-based micro-training, and human-assisted service channels rather than being resolved automatically by national-level policy or architecture investments.
operationalisation_hint: Before scaling a nationally-designed digital-transformation reform to all municipalities/regions, assess local infrastructure and digital-literacy baselines separately from the national EA/governance rollout, and provision hybrid (human-assisted, mobile, or low-bandwidth) channels specifically for under-resourced areas rather than assuming uniform digital readiness.
page_or_section: Literature Review (Governance, Coordination, and Pathways to Scalable Reform); Recommendations

finding_statement: The organization evaluates its EA's dynamism not as a single "flexibility" score but as an aggregated result across four intersecting axes -- five dimensions (Flexibility/Adaptability, Modularity, Expressiveness, Extensibility, Durability/Prediction), a six-step process (Monitor, Compare, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Update Knowledge Base), ArchiMate architectural layers (Business, Application, Technology, Motivation, etc.), and eight metric categories (Structural, Process, Performance, Quality, Alignment, Capacity, Governance, Adoption) -- using the Goal-Question-Metric method to derive concrete, goal-linked metrics for each axis intersection rather than a single composite adaptability rating.
mechanism: Single-score or maturity-stage EA evaluation approaches (e.g., simple maturity models) mask which specific combination of dimension, process-step, layer, and metric-category is actually underperforming; a four-axis GQM structure lets an organization pinpoint, for example, that its Expressiveness dimension specifically lags at the process-alignment metric within the Business layer, producing a targeted rather than generic improvement recommendation.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing EA dynamism/adaptability, avoid single composite maturity scores and instead define goals per dimension (flexibility, modularity, expressiveness, extensibility, durability, prediction), derive GQM-style questions and metrics for each dimension across the six-step dynamic-EA process and relevant architecture layers, and aggregate only after granular measurement to preserve diagnostic detail.

finding_statement: The organization tracks its EA dynamism dimensions independently (e.g., in the illustrative case: Flexibility=80, Modularity=75, Expressiveness=70, Extensibility=85, Prediction=90, Durability=95 but with a lower Update-Frequency sub-score of 65) rather than assuming uniform maturity across all dimensions, using a radar/spider-chart visualization to make uneven dimension profiles immediately visible to stakeholders.
mechanism: An organization can simultaneously show strong technological extensibility/prediction capability while lagging specifically in process-alignment (Expressiveness) or knowledge-base update frequency (part of Durability), because these dimensions depend on different organizational mechanisms (technology integration capacity vs. business-process documentation discipline vs. review cadence); a uniform or averaged score would mask exactly which mechanism needs attention.
operationalisation_hint: When diagnosing EA adaptability gaps, report dimension-level scores individually (e.g., via radar chart) rather than only a single aggregated dynamism score, and prioritize improvement action on the specific lowest-scoring dimension/sub-metric (e.g., low process-alignment or low update-frequency) rather than uniformly across all dimensions.
page_or_section: Section (Results and Discussion; Fig. 6 Radar Graph)

finding_statement: The organization builds technological readiness -- advanced IT infrastructure supporting emerging technologies, employees with sufficient technical expertise in AI/IoT/Blockchain, digital systems compatible with new technologies, and active investment in digital-readiness upgrades -- as a distinct precondition before attempting to integrate AI, IoT, and Blockchain into its enterprise architecture, rather than assuming integration capability can be built independently of infrastructure/skills maturity.
mechanism: Across 312 valid survey responses from EA/IT professionals, technological readiness showed a significant positive effect on integration capability (beta=0.46, p<0.001); firms with robust infrastructure, compatible systems, and skilled employees were empirically more able to establish the interoperable data architectures, standardized APIs, and governance protocols needed for AI/IoT/Blockchain to interact seamlessly within the enterprise architecture.
operationalisation_hint: Before launching AI/IoT/Blockchain integration initiatives, assess and invest in the four readiness sub-dimensions (infrastructure robustness, system compatibility, employee technical proficiency, ongoing digital-readiness investment) as a prerequisite, since these were empirically found to significantly predict subsequent integration-capability development.
page_or_section: Section 4 (Results and discussion, H1); Table 1 (Technological readiness construct)

finding_statement: The organization treats integration capability (the ability to synchronize new AI/IoT/Blockchain technologies with legacy systems, applications, and data flows across departments) as the operative mechanism that converts technological readiness into realized organizational value (efficiency, innovation, competitive differentiation) -- readiness alone does not produce value without this integration step -- and separately ensures top management actively sponsors integration efforts (resource allocation, cross-departmental coordination, signaling strategic priority), since this leadership support was found to amplify how strongly readiness translates into integration capability.
mechanism: The survey found a significant mediation effect (technological readiness -> integration capability -> value creation, indirect effect beta=0.21-0.23, p<0.001) and a significant moderation effect of top management support on the readiness-integration relationship (beta=0.17, p<0.001), empirically confirming that firms with high readiness but weak integration mechanisms or weak leadership sponsorship fail to realize anticipated technology benefits, consistent with dynamic-capabilities theory's emphasis on resource orchestration over mere resource possession.
operationalisation_hint: When planning AI/IoT/Blockchain adoption, explicitly build integration-capability mechanisms (standardized APIs, governance protocols, modular system design, cross-functional coordination) as the conversion step between readiness and value, and secure active top-management sponsorship (resource commitment, cross-functional legitimacy) specifically to strengthen how effectively readiness translates into integration capability -- not merely as generic "leadership buy-in."
page_or_section: Section 4 (Results and discussion, H2-H4); Table 3 (SEM results)

finding_statement: The organization maintains synchronization between its strategic-motivational model (BMM: vision, mission, goals, strategies, tactics) and its operational-process model (BPMN: business processes, activities, events) by routing transformations through an intermediate intentional goal model (i*: actors, goals, softgoals, tasks, dependencies), using a classified set of transformation heuristics (e.g., BMM Strategy <-> i* Objective/hard-goal; i* Task <-> BPMN Activity; i* Goal <-> BPMN End Event) with explicit human-judgment checkpoints where automatic mapping is ambiguous, rather than attempting direct, ad hoc BMM-to-BPMN correspondence.
mechanism: Organizations naturally lose strategy-operations synchrony over time as market dynamics and internal process evolution diverge from originally-defined motivational statements; because BMM (motivation) and BPMN (operations) have no natural direct correspondence, routing transformations through the intentional i* layer -- which explicitly represents actor goals and dependencies -- provides a principled bridge that reduces the natural abstraction gap and makes the alignment process repeatable and generalizable rather than one-off and ad hoc.
operationalisation_hint: When strategy and operational process models drift apart over time, use an intentional/goal-model layer (i* or equivalent) as an explicit intermediate representation, applying classified heuristics to transform BMM motivational elements into goal-model elements and goal-model elements into BPMN process elements, flagging transformation steps that require human judgment (e.g., distinguishing AND/OR decomposition, aligning directives to softgoals) rather than assuming full automation is possible.

finding_statement: The organization maintains two concrete support artifacts alongside its strategy-operations alignment process: a symmetric construct-mapping matrix (recording which BMM/i*/BPMN element types correspond to each other, independent of search direction) and a sequential alignment log (recording each specific transformation operation -- add, update, delete -- performed on model instances, with reference numbers linking related operations across models), so that alignment decisions remain traceable and auditable rather than existing only as tacit analyst knowledge.
mechanism: Without explicit, persisted traceability artifacts, strategic-operational alignment work performed by an analyst (which relies heavily on subjective human judgment for ambiguous mappings) becomes effectively irreproducible and unauditable as models grow beyond small/moderate size, especially without dedicated tool support; a standing matrix plus a chronological operation log lets subsequent analysts or tools reconstruct why and how a given operational element was derived from a given strategic element.
operationalisation_hint: When performing bidirectional strategy-operations model alignment, maintain a persistent construct-mapping matrix (element-type correspondences) and a sequential alignment log (specific instance-level operations with cross-references) as artifacts separate from the models themselves, rather than relying on the analyst's memory or one-off scripts.
page_or_section: Section "Support artifacts in the alignment," Figures 1-2

finding_statement: The organization models its business and application architecture layers in a standard notation (ArchiMate) and explicitly establishes two distinct types of inter-layer links between them: implementation links (a business-layer functional concept, e.g., a business process, is implemented by an application-layer functional concept, e.g., an application function) and representation links (a business-layer data concept, e.g., a business object, is represented by an application-layer data concept, e.g., a data object) -- rather than relying on informal, undocumented correspondence between the two layers.
mechanism: Without explicit, typed inter-layer links, software architects lack a structured "cartography" connecting business processes to the application components that realize them, making it impossible to systematically detect alignment problems (e.g., business functions with no corresponding application support, or legacy application functions no longer tied to any current business process); defining implementation (functional) and representation (data) links as first-class, tool-representable relationships (specialized from ArchiMate's Association relationship) creates the structural foundation needed for automated alignment analysis.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing Business-IT alignment analysis capability, explicitly model business and application layers in a standard EA notation (ArchiMate or equivalent) and define two link types -- functional implementation links and data representation links -- connecting them, using tool support (e.g., Archi with jArchi scripting) to make the resulting cartography machine-queryable rather than only visually inspectable.

finding_statement: The organization computes specific, targeted metrics on its business-application link cartography -- e.g., the rate of business functional concepts with zero implementation links (unimplemented functions), the rate of application functional concepts not implementing any business function (dead/orphaned code candidates), and identification of application functions implementing more than one business function (monolith-application risk) -- rather than relying on a single aggregate "alignment score" that would obscure which specific structural problem is present.
mechanism: In the real SoftSlate case, 41.6% of business processes were initially flagged as "unimplemented" by the raw metric, but manual inspection revealed this partly reflected composite/parent business processes correctly implemented only through their sub-processes rather than genuine misalignment -- demonstrating that targeted, interpretable metrics (rather than a single opaque score) let domain experts distinguish genuine anti-patterns (the "Pure technical integration" and "Monolith application" BITA anti-patterns identified in prior work by Gouigoux & Tamzalit) from false positives requiring contextual judgment.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating Business-IT alignment quality, compute separate, named metrics for each known anti-pattern (unimplemented business functions, non-implementing application functions, over-implemented/monolith functions) rather than a single composite alignment percentage, and pair automated metric computation with human review of flagged items before concluding a genuine misalignment exists.
page_or_section: Section 5 (Evaluating the Alignment); Section 7.3 (Evaluating the Alignment, SoftSlate results)

finding_statement: The organization extracts relevant, reusable subsets ("slices") of its large Enterprise Architecture Repository for developing new EA artifacts by combining an automated graph-traversal search algorithm (which quickly and reliably retrieves all components directly related to a starting component via a given relation type) with a manual screening step (where a human analyst judges correlation validity and consistency of each candidate result) -- applied recursively until no further relevant components are found -- rather than attempting either pure manual browsing (infeasible at scale) or pure automatic scripting (unable to handle ambiguous, human-oriented model semantics).
mechanism: In the validation case study, the organization needed to check only 18 of 701 total relations (2.6%) to construct a valid 4-component slice for a new roadmap artifact, but manual-only search across all 71 views would have been infeasible to do exhaustively and reliably, while pure automatic search could not resolve ambiguous cases (e.g., missing view associations, unnamed components, inconsistent relation semantics across Realization vs. Aggregation types) that require human judgment about model quality and relevance.
operationalisation_hint: When developing a new EA artifact from an existing large repository, define a slicing criterion (starting component + view + relation type of interest), run automated graph traversal to retrieve directly-related candidates, manually screen each candidate for correlation validity and data-quality consistency, and recurse on validated results until no new relevant components emerge -- rather than manually browsing the full repository or relying on one-time automated scripts alone.
page_or_section: Section 4 (A Method for EA Model Slicing); Section 5 (Evaluation, ArchiSurance case study)

finding_statement: The organization expects and specifically checks for data-quality inconsistencies in its EA repository -- missing component attributes (e.g., unnamed components), inconsistent or duplicated use of similar relation types for similar purposes, and orphaned/dangling model elements resulting from unregulated prior edits (e.g., models deleted from views but not from the underlying repository) -- treating these as a normal, expected characteristic of human-maintained EA repositories rather than a rare exception, and builds manual validation steps into any reuse workflow accordingly.
mechanism: Unlike source code (which is executed by computers and therefore must be formally correct), EA models are typically created by and for humans with varying levels of expertise and rarely enforced discipline, so inconsistency issues accumulate naturally over the repository's lifetime; treating manual/flexible validation as a first-class step (rather than an afterthought) is what let the case-study analysts correctly ignore several inconsistent/orphaned relations rather than propagating errors into the new artifact.
operationalisation_hint: When designing any EA-repository reuse or automation workflow, budget explicitly for manual data-quality validation (checking for missing attributes, inconsistent relation semantics, orphaned elements) as a standard step, rather than assuming the repository is as internally consistent as formally-verified software artifacts.

finding_statement: The organization redefines its enterprise/solution/domain architects' primary function from directly authoring design artifacts (diagrams, documentation, code) to curating, validating, and contextualizing GenAI-generated outputs -- requiring new competencies (prompt engineering, GenAI model evaluation, professional oversight/judgment of AI suggestions) that complement rather than replace foundational architectural skills (technical expertise, stakeholder communication, strategic thinking, governance oversight).
mechanism: Across 33 systematically reviewed studies, GenAI consistently and reliably accelerates artifact generation (code, diagrams, documentation) and supports design ideation/trade-off exploration, freeing architects from lower-value creation tasks; but because GenAI outputs are probabilistic, opaque ("black box"), and prone to hallucination, someone must validate outputs before implementation -- shifting the architect's value-add from artifact creation to artifact validation, contextualization against enterprise objectives, and collaborative decision-making with AI as a tool rather than a replacement.
operationalisation_hint: When integrating GenAI into architecture practice, explicitly redefine architect role expectations and performance criteria around curation/validation competencies (prompt engineering, model-output evaluation, professional oversight) rather than assuming existing artifact-creation-centric role definitions remain unchanged, and invest in training that builds these new competencies alongside (not instead of) traditional architectural skills.
page_or_section: Section 4.3 (Evolving Role, Tasks, and Required Skills); Section 5 (Discussion)

finding_statement: The organization assesses its readiness to integrate GenAI into architecture practice across four distinct domains rather than a single generic "AI readiness" measure: (1) infrastructure and skilled personnel (technical capacity, GenAI literacy among staff), (2) data governance maturity (data quality, stewardship, privacy controls), (3) legal and system compatibility (regulatory compliance such as GDPR, technical interoperability with existing systems), and (4) strategic alignment (coherence between GenAI deployment plans and overarching business strategy).
mechanism: The reviewed studies found that absent sufficient investment in upskilling (prompt engineering, GenAI evaluation, responsible-AI-use training), organizations struggle to realize productivity gains regardless of technical GenAI capability, and organizations with greater awareness of agile principles tend to support more adaptive architecture practices that create more favorable conditions for GenAI integration -- indicating readiness is multi-dimensional and that strength in one domain (e.g., infrastructure) does not compensate for weakness in another (e.g., data governance or strategic alignment).
operationalisation_hint: When assessing organizational readiness for GenAI-enabled architecture practice, evaluate all four domains separately (infrastructure/skills, data governance, legal/system compatibility, strategic alignment) rather than a single composite readiness score, and prioritize remediation of the weakest domain rather than assuming overall technical capability is sufficient.

finding_statement: The organization adopts a dynamic, evolving AI-governance framework -- staged from "Initial" to "Optimizing" maturity levels, characterized by increasingly defined responsibilities, continuous monitoring, established safeguards, embedded fairness/transparency/accountability principles, and audit trails for sensitive-data handling -- rather than a static, one-time governance policy, recognizing that GenAI model performance and applicable regulation both continue to evolve.
mechanism: Reviewed studies found that organizations with formalized AI policies, ethical oversight, and traceability mechanisms integrate GenAI into architecture workflows more effectively, while underdeveloped governance frameworks lead to accountability gaps that undermine trust in AI-generated outputs, particularly for high-stakes architectural decisions; a staged maturity model (rather than a binary has-governance/does-not) lets organizations track and communicate incremental governance progress as both GenAI capability and regulatory expectations shift.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing AI governance for architecture practice, define a maturity progression (e.g., Initial through Optimizing) with explicit criteria for each stage (responsibility definitions, monitoring mechanisms, safeguards, audit trails), and revisit/upgrade the governance framework as GenAI capabilities and regulations evolve rather than treating an initial policy as permanent.

finding_statement: The organization treats GenAI outputs as requiring mandatory human validation before implementation in architectural work, because GenAI systems function as "black boxes" whose internal reasoning is inaccessible (undermining governance traceability), frequently produce contextually incorrect but plausible-sounding outputs ("hallucinations") leading to rework, and have limited context windows that reduce their effectiveness for large-scale enterprise-wide modeling that requires embedded domain knowledge beyond what fits in a single prompt.
mechanism: Multiple reviewed studies documented that GenAI's probabilistic nature means outputs are neither guaranteed to be optimal nor contextually precise, and that limited context windows specifically reduce effectiveness in large-scale enterprise contexts compared to smaller, bounded design tasks -- meaning organizations that deploy GenAI for end-to-end architectural reasoning without human validation checkpoints risk both governance failures (untraceable reasoning) and quality failures (undetected hallucinated content).
operationalisation_hint: When applying GenAI to architectural tasks, scope its use to bounded, human-validated sub-tasks (artifact drafting, design-alternative generation, knowledge retrieval) rather than fully-automated end-to-end enterprise-scale reasoning, and require explicit human sign-off before GenAI-suggested changes are implemented, particularly for governance-relevant or large-scope decisions.
page_or_section: Section 4.1 (Opportunities and Challenges of GenAI for Architects); Table 5

finding_statement: The organization deliberately allocates specific tasks between human architects and GenAI tools (rather than defaulting to maximal AI delegation) and invests in continuous training on GenAI risks and best practices, because excessive dependence on GenAI outputs was found to weaken architects' ability to recognize systemic trade-offs and perform nuanced risk assessments, and a related behavioral risk ("social loafing") causes individuals to reduce their own analytical effort when AI assistance is available.
mechanism: Reviewed studies identified a steep learning curve for mastering GenAI tools combined with a documented tendency toward social loafing (reduced individual effort when AI assistance is present) as behavioral barriers distinct from technical GenAI limitations; without deliberate task-allocation design and ongoing training investment, these behavioral dynamics erode exactly the critical-thinking capacity that human oversight of AI outputs depends on, creating a compounding risk.
operationalisation_hint: When deploying GenAI tools for architects, explicitly define which tasks remain human-only (nuanced trade-off/risk assessment, final validation) versus AI-assisted, and pair GenAI rollout with ongoing training that reinforces (rather than atrophies) architects' independent analytical judgment.
page_or_section: Section 4.1 (Opportunities and Challenges); Section 4.4 (Factors Influencing GenAI Adoption Trajectory)

finding_statement: The organization establishes EAM as a federated "Governance EAM" model -- a central EAM department that formulates EA strategy and enterprise-wide standards, complemented by a decentralized network of embedded architects operating within business domains -- rather than a fully centralized model (all architects consolidated into one function led by a Chief Enterprise Architect) or a fully virtual/decentralized model (no central EAM organization, only a loose community of architects).
mechanism: Across 13 semi-structured expert interviews, the federated Governance EAM model scored highest specifically because it retains proximity to business-domain stakeholders through embedded architects (avoiding the "ivory tower syndrome" that lowered the centralized model's organizational-penetration score) while still providing the clear top-management mandate and authority that experts identified as necessary for EAM to fulfill its governance responsibilities (a criterion on which fully decentralized/virtual models scored lowest).
operationalisation_hint: When selecting an organizational EAM implementation model, favor a federated structure combining a central EAM department (for strategy/standards/mandate) with embedded architects placed within business domains (for proximity/penetration), rather than choosing between full centralization and full decentralization as a binary choice.

finding_statement: The organization uses a structured "fitting matrix" artifact -- crossing seven collaboratively-defined success criteria (organizational penetration/reach, top-management mandate, visibility/lighthouse character, suitability for EAM work, ability to function as an architecture guild, adaptability/scalability, effort/risk for change) against candidate EAM approaches (Virtual, Central Operative, Governance, Supportive), each further subdivided by C-suite anchoring role (CIO/COO/CEO) -- with Likert-scale-derived numerical scoring, to select the EAM implementation option best fitted to its specific organizational context, rather than adopting a generic "best practice" EAM model uncritically.
mechanism: The literature explicitly documents an absence of established methodologies or practical guidance for context-specific EAM implementation decisions (unlike abstract organizational blueprints such as EAM archetypes), so a transparent, criterion-based scoring matrix lets an organization make its EAM-model choice traceable and comparable across options rather than relying on unstructured expert opinion alone.
operationalisation_hint: When deciding how to organizationally implement EAM, define success criteria collaboratively with internal experts (not adopted wholesale from literature), score each candidate EAM approach/anchoring-role combination against these criteria using a consistent scale (e.g., Likert-derived), and select based on the resulting comparative scores rather than defaulting to whichever model is most commonly discussed in EAM literature.

finding_statement: The organization establishes institutional articulation -- two or more departments/units working together to formulate a shared set of aims, objectives, boundaries, and deliverables for EA -- as an explicit precondition for EA practice, ensuring enterprise architects possess (or actively build, through cross-functional engagement) a holistic understanding of business processes, information artefacts, and IT solutions, rather than allowing EA practice to remain siloed within an expert function disconnected from business context.
mechanism: Applying Structuration Theory, the analysis found that many enterprise architects are technical experts who lack a holistic view of the organization, making institutional articulation (the alignment between business and IT units on EA's boundaries and deliverables) challenging and static rather than evolving and recursive as Giddens' theory would prescribe; without this articulation, EA's intended role in solving business-IT challenges is undermined by a persistent structural gap between what architects understand and what the organization actually needs.
operationalisation_hint: Before or during EA practice rollout, establish explicit, recurring cross-departmental articulation mechanisms (joint objective-setting between business and IT units, not just one-off scoping) so that EA boundaries and deliverables are actively negotiated and updated rather than fixed once and left static.

finding_statement: The organization recognizes that EA practice, by its disciplined and highly specialized nature, tends toward excessive rigidity -- rules and regulations strictly applied to manage resources, with enterprise architects sometimes failing to adapt fast enough to continuously evolving business needs -- and deliberately builds in mechanisms to counteract this rigidity (e.g., through Instantiation practices that create new context-specific attributes) rather than assuming strict rule compliance alone guarantees EA success.
