mechanism: The analysis (drawing on Kotusev and Giddens) found that many organizations fail with EA specifically because of its excessive rigidness, not despite following its rules -- structure exists only as it is instantiated in action, so a purely rule-bound EA practice that does not allow for contextual reinterpretation and adaptation (instantiation) becomes a source of failure rather than success, even when formally compliant.
operationalisation_hint: When designing EA governance rules and standards, explicitly build in instantiation/adaptation mechanisms (documented exceptions, contextual reinterpretation processes) rather than treating rule compliance alone as sufficient for EA practice success, since rigidity itself has been identified as a distinct failure factor.

finding_statement: The organization expresses interoperability and governance rules as machine-readable integration profiles (each specifying actors, transactions, use cases, and grouping/dependency rules between profiles) rather than as separate, human-readable policy documents disconnected from the technical architecture, so that compliance with governance requirements can be automatically or semi-automatically verified against the architecture itself rather than through manual audit alone.
mechanism: Static compliance checking alone (verifying a system meets a standard at one point in time) does not manage the ongoing lifecycle of evolving standards, leading to "standard lock-in" as stakeholders adopt updates at different paces; embedding governance rules directly into the same machine-readable specification that defines the system's interoperable building blocks means that as profiles evolve (via structured Change Proposals preserving backward compatibility), compliance verification evolves with them automatically rather than requiring separate, manually-maintained governance documentation.
operationalisation_hint: When designing governance for a multi-stakeholder, multi-vendor standards ecosystem, express governance/compliance rules as part of the same machine-readable architectural specification used to define system interoperability (e.g., integration profiles with explicit actors/transactions/dependencies), rather than maintaining governance policy as a separate, loosely-coupled document.
page_or_section: Section 2 (Methodology, IHE Technical Framework and Process); Section 6 (Conclusions)

finding_statement: The organization requires that candidate solution architectures be validated at structured, supervised conformance-testing events ("Connectathons") where implementations must successfully interoperate with at least three independent vendor implementations before being published as an accepted "Integration Statement" usable in procurement and system design, rather than accepting self-declared or single-vendor-tested conformance claims.
mechanism: Governance rules that exist only on paper (or even in machine-readable specifications) risk diverging from actual multi-vendor implementation behavior unless there is a concrete verification mechanism; requiring interoperability against a minimum of three independent vendors at a structured testing event operationalizes the governance rules into observable, falsifiable outcomes, closing the loop between specification and real-world deployment and directly fostering vendor-neutrality.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing an interoperability governance regime for a multi-vendor ecosystem, require conformance validation events with a minimum multi-vendor threshold (e.g., three independent implementations) before publishing any implementation as compliant, and use test-assertion-derived (not just self-reported) evidence of that validation.

mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The organization documents, as an explicit design decision (not an oversight), which architectural notation elements are deliberately excluded from a cross-functional viewpoint and why (e.g., Application Function, Application Interaction, Technology Interface, Node, Device -- all justified as "of interest only to the IT audience of this viewpoint") -- producing a viewpoint specification that names both what is included and, with rationale, what is intentionally left out.
mechanism: Without an explicit exclusion rationale, viewpoint designers risk either over-including elements (recreating the "excessively broad" problem the custom viewpoint was meant to solve) or arbitrarily excluding elements without a principled basis that could be revisited as team needs evolve; documenting the justification per excluded element (as in this paper's Table 1) creates a traceable design record that can be audited or adjusted later.
operationalisation_hint: When specifying a custom architectural viewpoint, produce and retain an explicit table of excluded notation elements with a one-line rationale each (e.g., "of interest only to the IT/business audience"), not just a list of included elements, so that scope decisions remain traceable and revisable.

finding_statement: The organization decomposes its digital transformation strategy through four sequenced governance dimensions -- strategy decoding (breaking macro-strategy into specific technical indicators and architectural requirements via a strategy-business-IT mapping), process reconstruction (standardized cross-sector process re-engineering with automated decision mechanisms), data governance (a unified data asset system), and technology adaptation (a technology-radar mechanism for dynamically integrating emerging technologies) -- rather than pursuing digital-technology adoption without an explicit strategy-to-execution decomposition path.
mechanism: Energy-sector organizations face fragmented business processes and slow decision cycles that a purely technology-driven digital transformation does not resolve on its own; sequencing strategy decoding before process reconstruction, data governance, and technology adaptation ensures that specific digital initiatives (e.g., intelligent scheduling, virtual power plants) are traceable back to macro-strategic goals (e.g., "dual-carbon target") through an explicit mapping, rather than being adopted as disconnected point technologies.
operationalisation_hint: When planning digital transformation in a large, multi-business-unit organization, first decode macro-strategy into specific architectural requirements via an explicit strategy-business-IT mapping, then sequence process reconstruction, data governance, and technology adaptation as dependent follow-on stages rather than pursuing them independently or in parallel without a shared strategic anchor.
page_or_section: Section 3 (The Enterprise Architecture Design with FDR); Section 4.2 (Application of FDR-EA)

finding_statement: The organization establishes a three-tier data asset catalogue (group-level, business-level, and equipment-level) and achieves real-time fusion of data from multiple sources (via technologies such as data lakes and stream computing) as its data-governance mechanism, rather than allowing each business unit or equipment domain to maintain isolated, non-interoperable data stores.
mechanism: Heterogeneous systems and decentralized data architecture across business domains (e.g., clean energy, hydropower, energy storage) were found to impede cross-business-unit synergy and intelligent scheduling; structuring the data asset catalogue into explicit tiers (rather than a flat or ad hoc structure) combined with real-time fusion technology directly targets the "data silos" identified as the core bottleneck constraining smart-system construction.
operationalisation_hint: When addressing data-silo problems in a multi-business-unit digital transformation, define an explicit multi-tier data asset catalogue (e.g., group/business/equipment levels) and invest in real-time, multi-source data fusion infrastructure (data lakes, stream computing) rather than attempting point-to-point data integration between individual systems.
page_or_section: Section 3 (Data governance Rule); Section 4.1 (Challenges in Digital Transformation)

finding_statement: The systematic review distinguishes covert Shadow IT from overt Business-managed IT. When an instance becomes transparent, it can be categorized and assigned continuation, decommissioning, and governance-responsibility decisions; some risks can therefore be better mitigated.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The organization allocates governance responsibility for each categorized, overt Business-managed IT instance along an explicit spectrum -- full governance transfer to the IT organization (for high-criticality, high-security-risk, or maintenance-burdensome instances), co-governance split by task (IT organization providing platform/risk-management/implementation-support while the business unit defines requirements and designs the application), or full governance retention by the business unit (for limited-scope instances or those requiring business-specific skills to run) -- rather than applying one uniform governance policy to all business-unit-led IT instances regardless of their individual risk profile.
mechanism: The reviewed literature identifies instance criticality, functional/strategic scope, and required skill type as the key factors determining which governance allocation is appropriate; a uniform policy (e.g., "all business-unit IT must be centrally governed" or "all business-unit IT is autonomous") either wastes IT-organization capacity on low-risk instances or leaves genuinely critical instances under-governed, whereas categorization-then-allocation lets governance effort scale with actual risk.
operationalisation_hint: After identifying and categorizing a business-unit-led IT instance (by criticality, functional scope, and required skill type), explicitly decide its governance allocation on the IT-organization-to-business-unit spectrum (full IT governance / co-governance / full BU governance) rather than defaulting to a single organization-wide policy for all such instances.

finding_statement: The organization treats gaps in business-IT alignment -- specifically, insufficient IT-organization understanding of business needs, insufficient communication, inadequate user training, and excessive process formalization (heavy documentation even for small pilot projects) -- as the primary root cause to address when Shadow IT or Business-managed IT proliferates, rather than treating the proliferation itself as the problem to suppress through restriction alone.
mechanism: Across the reviewed literature, "IT organization and BU non-alignment" was the joint most-cited causing factor (41% of literature items, tied with IT system shortcomings), consistently linked to low trust between business units and the IT organization built up over time from detrimental prior experiences; this indicates that Shadow IT/Business-managed IT is frequently a symptom of an underlying alignment failure rather than a primary organizational pathology in itself.
operationalisation_hint: When observing high rates of Shadow IT or Business-managed IT, first diagnose whether IT-organization-and-business-unit misalignment (communication gaps, unmet needs, excessive process formalization) is the underlying driver before implementing restrictive policies, since addressing the alignment root cause (per this review's GG3 "IT systems gap resolution" recommendation) may reduce the phenomenon more effectively than prohibition alone.

finding_statement: The organization implements technical monitoring and identification mechanisms -- IT architecture assessments, help-desk request evaluation, employee surveys, and scanning of installed software on end-user devices -- specifically to surface covert Shadow IT instances and render them overt (thereby reclassifying them as Business-managed IT), recognizing that this identification step is the necessary precondition before any instance categorization or governance-allocation decision can be made.
mechanism: Because Shadow IT is covert by definition, an organization structurally cannot categorize or allocate governance to instances it does not know exist; deploying monitoring/identification mechanisms (even though these can be bypassed by employees and are imperfect) is what "completes the loop" from unknown covert risk to known, governable instance -- without this step, all of the more granular instance-governance approaches (IG1-IG5) remain inapplicable.
operationalisation_hint: Before attempting to apply any instance-level Business-managed-IT governance framework, first invest in monitoring/identification mechanisms (architecture assessments, help-desk analysis, employee surveys, device software scans) to surface covert Shadow IT instances, since these mechanisms are the structural prerequisite for the rest of the governance process rather than an optional add-on.

finding_statement: The organization implements a co-governance model for continued Business-managed IT instances in which the IT organization provides shared infrastructure/data/application-layer platforms, manages security/privacy risk assessments, and offers continuous implementation support (project management, vendor management, service management expertise) -- while the business unit retains ownership of defining requirements and designing/developing the application itself -- rather than either fully centralizing or fully devolving the instance.
mechanism: This split-responsibility (task-based) co-governance model was found to be the fastest-growing research theme in the reviewed literature (a 35-percentage-point increase in coverage between the pre-2016 and post-2016 periods for the "IT organization & BU instance co-governance" theme specifically), reflecting practitioner recognition that business units possess domain-specific requirements knowledge the IT organization lacks, while the IT organization possesses platform/security/project-management expertise the business unit lacks -- neither party alone can safely and effectively govern the instance.
operationalisation_hint: For Business-managed IT instances warranting shared governance, explicitly split responsibilities along task lines: assign the IT organization to platform provisioning, risk/security management, and implementation support, while the business unit retains requirements-definition and application-design ownership -- rather than negotiating an undifferentiated "shared responsibility" without clear task boundaries.

finding_statement: Linking a strategic-level NFR-tree decomposition of business/IT objectives to a management-level i* Strategic Rationale Diagram of stakeholder and user goals lets an organization evaluate -- before committing development resources -- how a candidate technology adoption (a "strategic opportunity") will contribute to strategic objectives, stakeholder goals, and end-user needs simultaneously, via traceable contribution links rather than ad hoc/generic roadmaps.
mechanism: Demonstrated via the StratAMoDrIGo framework (NFR tree for strategic value + i* SRD for stakeholder/user value, joined by explicit traceability, Section 5.3/Fig. 4) applied to two Covid-19-driven IT adoptions at a Belgian hospital; external DT expert (10+ years experience) confirmed the approach filled a gap versus the organization's prior ad hoc/generic-roadmap practice.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating a candidate technology adoption under time pressure, build a lightweight NFR-style decomposition of the strategic objectives it should serve, and a companion actor/goal model of affected stakeholders and users, explicitly linking objectives to stakeholder goals and end-user features so the adoption decision can be reasoned about (and reconfigured) before implementation rather than assessed only in hindsight.
page_or_section: Sections 4-5.3 (Ontology, Model-based value representation), Section 7 (case study), pp. 561-573, 845-853

finding_statement: A baseline organizational digital maturity (mastery of current IT infrastructure, clarity of strategy, and knowledge of stakeholders) must be reached before an organization can meaningfully pursue agility at the strategic level; strategic agility is not attainable purely through tooling/frameworks without this contextual maturity.
mechanism: Raised by the external digital-transformation expert consulted for framework validation, who explicitly stated that "before being agile at all organizational levels, especially at a higher one, a digital maturity needs to be reached" and characterized StratAMoDrIGo as a way of building toward that maturity rather than a substitute for it.
operationalisation_hint: Before rolling out strategic-agility tooling or governance frameworks, assess whether the organization has the baseline prerequisites (documented/understood IT infrastructure, clear strategic objectives, mapped stakeholders) that the expert identifies as necessary; treat a framework like StratAMoDrIGo as a maturity-building mechanism, not a shortcut around missing fundamentals.

finding_statement: Structural governance bodies (e.g. IT steering committees) cannot make effective decisions without mature supporting processes (e.g. portfolio management); relational mechanisms (training, awareness campaigns, informal business/IT meetings) receive the most attention during initial ITG implementation and become progressively less critical once ITG is embedded in day-to-day operations.
mechanism: Synthesized from a comparative review of ITG literature (Van Grembergen & De Haes 2004b; Weill & Ross 2004a and 30+ other sources) cataloguing 20+ structure, 20+ process, and 15+ relational mechanisms (Tables 4-6) and noting their interdependency and lifecycle-dependent salience.
operationalisation_hint: Sequence governance rollout: stand up relational mechanisms (training, awareness, informal business/IT contact) first to build shared understanding, then formalize structures (steering committees, architecture boards) only once supporting processes (portfolio management, exception handling) are mature enough to make them effective; expect relational-mechanism intensity to taper as governance becomes routine.

finding_statement: What strategically works for one enterprise does not necessarily work for another, even within the same industry; SME contexts (different economic, cultural, managerial environment; decision-making concentrated in one person; low IS-project volume limiting organizational learning) require ITG models purpose-built for that context rather than narrowed-down large-enterprise frameworks -- explaining persistently low ITG/framework adoption rates in SMEs (e.g. only 16% of SE-European enterprises surveyed had implemented any best-practice framework, only 3% COBIT).
mechanism: Argued via synthesis of contingency-factor literature (Devos et al. 2009, 2012; Rusu & Gianluigi 2017) combined with adoption-rate survey evidence (Kolar & Groznik 2017; Winniford et al. 2009; Debreceny & Gray 2013).
operationalisation_hint: Before adopting or recommending an ITG/EA governance framework, explicitly assess organizational contingency factors (size, industry, maturity, structure, culture, strategy) and adapt/scale the framework accordingly rather than applying a generic or merely-narrowed large-enterprise model; treat low framework-adoption rates in SMEs as a symptom of this contextual mismatch rather than a training/awareness gap alone.
page_or_section: Section 3.4 (Contingency Factors) and Discussion, pp. 299-302, Table 7

finding_statement: Cross-case coding of 9 companies at varying DevOps maturity showed that the two factors predominantly shaping how organizations design their risk-mitigation and control processes are (a) risk appetite -- willingness to accept consequences of common failures such as a faulty deployment, and (b) DevOps/team maturity -- extent of independent operation and process automation. Mapping these two factors onto a 2x2 matrix yields four validated situational strategies (continuous delivery; continuous deployment; experimental learning; agile teams responsible for dev & ops), each pairing a different preventive/detective control mix and degree of team autonomy.
mechanism: Derived via axial/selective coding of the 17 interviews across 9 companies, then formalized as the "DevOps risk management matrix" and independently validated (with only minor axis-label adjustments) by 4 industry experts plus a 6-respondent survey of field-study participants.
operationalisation_hint: When designing or auditing governance for a decentralized, high-autonomy delivery team (not only DevOps, but any team with merged development/operational decision rights), first jointly assess its risk appetite and its process/team maturity, then select a control strategy (ranging from heavier manual preventive approval to fully automated detective-control-based autonomy) matched to that quadrant rather than applying one fixed control regime organization-wide.

finding_statement: Across the 9 companies and confirmed independently by an IT-audit/IT-risk expert, soft governance mechanisms (communication, psychological safety to "speak up" about mistakes, team responsibility/ownership, a culture of continuous improvement) are a prerequisite for the effectiveness of all other (hard, automated) controls in high-autonomy delivery teams -- one expert stated soft controls were "the most important controls" because the others "would only be effective if the soft controls were."
mechanism: Consistent theme across 17 interviews (change control, security, and monitoring sections all surfaced soft-governance dependencies) and corroborated by 2 of 4 independent validation experts, one of whom explicitly ranked soft controls above hard/automated controls in importance for DevOps-style teams.
operationalisation_hint: Before or alongside investing in automated technical controls (pipeline gates, monitoring, automated testing) for a decentralized delivery team, establish the soft-governance foundation first: explicit team responsibility, blame-free escalation of mistakes, and continuous cross-team communication -- treat automation investment without this foundation as likely ineffective regardless of technical sophistication.

finding_statement: Prior literature on DevOps risk management assumes progressive full automation of preventive IT controls; the empirical field study found this assumption does not hold in practice -- most of the 9 companies studied were not ready to (or did not intend to) fully automate their controls, either due to being mid-transition or due to a deliberately low risk appetite, and instead operate durable hybrid manual/automated control environments.
mechanism: Contrast between the multivocal literature-review findings (Section 4, mostly grey-literature "idealized" automated-control recommendations) and the empirical coding results from 17 interviews across 9 companies (Section 5), explicitly framed by the authors as a novel contribution correcting the literature's implicit assumption.
operationalisation_hint: When benchmarking an organization's IT-control maturity against DevOps/agile governance literature, do not treat partial automation or continued reliance on manual controls as an immature or transitional failure state by default -- for organizations with lower risk appetite or certain regulatory contexts, a stable hybrid control environment may be the appropriate end-state, not a waypoint toward full automation.

finding_statement: Across the companies studied, security, risk and compliance departments increasingly took on advisory roles (providing training, being consulted on demand, conducting periodic audits) rather than pre-deployment gatekeeping, with the responsibility for correct day-to-day execution of security/compliance practices shifting to the DevOps team itself -- a structural governance redesign distinct from simply adding automation.
mechanism: Cross-case pattern identified in interview coding (Sections 5.2.3-5.2.4) and explicitly named as an implication in the discussion (Section 8.1): "a shift of responsibility from what is traditionally considered to be the second line of defense towards the DevOps teams."
operationalisation_hint: When decentralizing delivery authority to autonomous teams, explicitly redefine the mandate of central security/risk/compliance functions from approval gates to advisory/audit support, and correspondingly build the compliance/security literacy and accountability of the team itself -- rather than assuming decentralization alone will substitute for governance oversight.

finding_statement: Companies with mature, highly automated deployment pipelines preserved separation-of-duties objectives -- despite DevOps teams holding both development and operations responsibility -- through automated substitutes: mandatory two-developer/peer approval before code enters the pipeline, fully automated production deployment so that no individual can deploy without passing automated controls, and temporary/timed-password access to production granted on request rather than standing access.
mechanism: Consistent finding across change-control and access-management interview sections (5.2.1-5.2.2): e.g. one company gave developers no standing production access at all, requiring two-developer approval before code entered the (fully automated) deployment pipeline; other companies used timed-password temporary access as an intermediate solution.
operationalisation_hint: When auditors or governance designers raise separation-of-duties concerns about merged development/operations teams, evaluate whether automated-pipeline substitutes (mandatory multi-person code review, fully automated deployment with no manual override path, temporary rather than standing production access) achieve the same control objective before insisting on traditional organizational role-separation, which may not be feasible in a DevOps-style team structure.
page_or_section: Section 5.2.2 (Identity and access management & Separation of duties), pp. 484-506

finding_statement: Eight of thirty literature-derived strategic-level ITG mechanisms were independently confirmed by at least 4 of 5 strategic-level interviewees as situational rather than permanently important: integration of governance and IT organizational structure (needed at ITG start-up, fade after roles are set); financial reporting & control and project reporting & benefits management (only become relevant once the enterprise is raising ITG maturity and has the prerequisite process maturity in place); digital transformation and outsourcing management (contingent on external factors -- market verification, regulation); knowledge management on ITG (relevant both at start-up and during maturity-raising); IT audit committee (situational for some roles).
mechanism: Semi-structured interviews (Yin case-study protocol) with 5 strategic-level roles in one insurance enterprise, each asked which of 30 literature-derived mechanisms they considered important, whether importance changed over time, and why; a mechanism was classified situational if named as such by 4 of 5 roles.
operationalisation_hint: Before assessing an organization's ITG mechanism set against a generic checklist, first determine which lifecycle stage it is in (start-up vs. maturity-raising) and which external conditions apply (regulatory pressure, market pace); do not expect mechanisms like project reporting/benefits management or digital-transformation governance to matter equally at every stage -- treat their absence early on as expected, not as a gap.
page_or_section: Section 3.2 (Universal and Situational ITG Mechanisms) and Section 4 (Discussion), pp. 863-880, 990-1010

finding_statement: Eight mechanisms were confirmed by at least 4 of 5 strategic-level interviewees as universally, permanently important regardless of ITG maturity stage: strategic ITG committee (described as the "umbrella" mechanism underpinning the whole ITG); business/IT alignment, IT risk management and resource management (process mechanisms); and partnership rewards & incentives, shared understanding of business/IT objectives, executive/senior management leading by example, and IT leadership (relational mechanisms).
mechanism: Same 5-interview strategic-level case study as above; universal mechanisms were those interviewees described as important "from the very beginning of the ITG and...important all the time since the ITG was implemented," with relational mechanisms explicitly described as forming the basis that enables formal structures and processes to function.
operationalisation_hint: Treat this 8-mechanism set (strategic ITG committee, business/IT alignment, IT risk management, resource management, partnership rewards & incentives, shared understanding of business/IT objectives, executive good example, IT leadership) as a non-negotiable governance baseline to establish regardless of an organization's size, maturity, or sector, before layering in situational mechanisms as conditions warrant.
page_or_section: Section 3.2 (Universal and Situational ITG Mechanisms), pp. 925-958

finding_statement: Across all 9 universities studied, moving IT-project prioritization and governance from being an IT-department-internal decision to a formal process owned by the senior Governing Board produced a consistent, independently-corroborated "before/after" mentality shift (Table 5): from "the IT Service decides which projects are developed" to "the board decides," from no public planning to public annual planning, and from only the IT Vice-Manager being involved to the entire Board of Directors being involved in IT projects as transversal, strategic matters.
mechanism: Qualitative double-interview study (written questionnaire plus individual interview) with strategic-to-operational actors (chancellors down to IT service directors) across 9 public universities that had implemented the SITPP model, cross-referenced against the ISO/IEC 38500 Good Governance principles (Table 6: Responsibility, Strategy, Acquisition, Performance, Compliance, Human factor, Transparency, Participation, Accountability, Reuse of information).
operationalisation_hint: To raise an organization's IT/Good-Governance maturity, do not treat IT project selection as an IT-department operational task -- formally route strategic IT-project prioritization through the senior governing body itself (board, executive committee), require published/public prioritization criteria and rankings, and require senior members beyond the CIO/IT lead to take ownership of IT-project decisions in their own domains.

finding_statement: Across the universities studied, a dedicated IT Project Portfolio Office (PPO) role/structure -- advising promoters and requesters on strategic framing, evaluating and ranking project proposals for the governing board, and monitoring/reporting execution back to both the CIO and the board -- was identified as playing "a major role in the success of the strategic project portfolio, acting as a catalyst."
mechanism: Cross-case qualitative interview analysis (Section 4.2, Table 1-2) identifying PPO as one of a small set of essential roles/structures (alongside Requester, Promoter, Project Manager, Governing Board, CIO, IT Service) required for the SITPP model to function, explicitly recommended as a minimum a physical office plus a designated director.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing formal strategic IT-portfolio governance, create (or designate) an explicit Project Portfolio Office function -- even if staffed by a single person -- responsible for translating between senior-governance strategic criteria and IT-management execution realities, rather than expecting the CIO or governing board alone to bridge that gap.

finding_statement: Across nearly all 9 case universities, a single CIO's (or equivalent top IT manager's) sustained leadership and persuasion -- acting as the cohesive link between the governing board and IT management, and securing the Chancellor/CEO's and governance team's involvement from the very start of implementation -- was identified by interviewees as the single most decisive factor in the model's successful adoption.
mechanism: Cross-case qualitative interview finding (Section 7.1): "a highly relevant fact obtained from the interviews is that in practically all cases, it was the CIO's convincing and […]"
operationalisation_hint: When introducing formal strategic IT-governance structures, invest deliberately in a single accountable champion (CIO or equivalent) who can broker between senior leadership and IT management, and secure top-executive (CEO/Chancellor-level) sponsorship from the outset rather than after initial rollout.

finding_statement: Despite universally positive outcomes, interviewees across the 9 universities consistently named three recurring negative aspects/risks: (1) it is "essential and very difficult" to convince top management to take on strategic IT-project decision-making; (2) IT service staff show resistance due to an apparent loss of decision-making power; (3) implementation is costly in effort and time (agreeing criteria, defining processes, training personnel, and above all achieving cultural change).
mechanism: Cross-case qualitative interview synthesis (Section 7.1, "negative aspects" summary), corroborating a consistent pattern across otherwise-successful implementations.
operationalisation_hint: When planning a rollout of formal strategic IT-governance/portfolio structures, budget explicitly for a sustained change-management effort (senior-management persuasion, IT-staff change resistance, criteria/process design, training) rather than treating the governance redesign as a low-cost policy or documentation exercise.
