finding_statement: A systematic literature review of 34 papers on ITG maturity published since 2012 found 13 using COBIT alone, 5 combining COBIT with other frameworks, and only 5 (relatively) new ITG maturity models altogether -- of which only the MIG model addressed specific soft-governance focus areas in detail; COBIT 5.0 addresses the social/soft dimension only holistically via generic "enablers," not through operationalized, assessable focus areas.
mechanism: Systematic literature review (Scopus, 2012-spring 2018, manual relevance screening) of ITG maturity model literature, cross-tabulating each of the 34 included papers against the ITG maturity model or framework it used (Table 1 in the source).
operationalisation_hint: When selecting or designing an ITG maturity assessment for an organization, do not assume that adopting a mainstream framework (COBIT, ITIL, etc.) will surface soft-governance (behavioral, cultural, relational) maturity in an actionable way -- verify explicitly whether the chosen framework operationalizes soft governance into assessable focus areas, or supplement it with a dedicated soft-governance instrument.
page_or_section: Section 3.1 (Result of the systematic literature review), Table 1, pp. 320-373

finding_statement: Senior management and IT specialists chronically miscommunicate because they use fundamentally different tools -- business model design tools (e.g. Business Model Canvas) versus IT governance frameworks (e.g. COBIT) -- with no shared translation layer; mapping Business Model Canvas building blocks to COBIT 5 enabling processes produces a list of business imperatives that function simultaneously as business objectives and as IT-department objectives, giving both sides a common reference point.
mechanism: Systematic literature review (108 sources) converting Business Model Canvas building blocks into 29 candidate business imperatives, then mapping each against COBIT 5's enabling processes and governance practices to identify which imperatives are achieved when COBIT 5 is effectively implemented.
operationalisation_hint: When senior management and IT specialists are misaligned on priorities, do not rely on either side's native tool alone (Business Model Canvas or COBIT) as the shared artifact -- instead, jointly select the 5-7 entity-specific business imperatives most relevant from a comprehensive literature-derived list, translate each into concrete operational measures, and only then determine the technology-architecture implications, rather than starting technology-architecture design directly from either a business-model or a governance-framework document.
page_or_section: Findings and Practical implication for management sections, Figure 2-3, pp. 566-582, 834-899

finding_statement: Basic business assumptions are expected of every entity regardless of industry and are adequately governed by basic IT solutions/internal controls, but this baseline governance does not achieve business-IT alignment; alignment specifically requires identifying the small number (recommended 5-7) of business imperatives unique to an entity's competitive context and designing the technology architecture explicitly to support those, not the generic baseline.
mechanism: Conceptual distinction developed from the literature review and Boshoff (2014)'s prior unpublished work, contrasting "basic business assumptions" against "business imperatives" as two categorically different levels of business objective that require different levels of IT governance response.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating whether an organization has achieved business-IT strategic alignment, do not accept "we have standard IT controls in place for compliance and operations" as sufficient evidence -- specifically probe whether the organization has identified its handful of unique, competitive-advantage-driving business imperatives and can show its technology architecture was deliberately designed to support them.
page_or_section: Concepts underlying this research section, pp. 361-395

finding_statement: Across the case studies (detailed for Case 1, a Dutch national-government body, in Table 5), soft-governance focus areas showed large before/after changes once discussed in interview (e.g. Participation: 10 participants at level A pre-interview dropping to 2 post-interview, with 5 moving to level B and 3 to level C; Understanding & trust: 10 at level A pre-interview dropping to 6), whereas hard-governance focus areas like IT decision-making showed minimal change (9 vs. 8 at level A). Where changes occurred, they were always toward a higher maturity level, never lower.
mechanism: Third-cycle MIG assessment instrument (self-report Likert-scale statements per focus area/maturity level) administered to participants, followed by semi-structured interviews discussing and, where warranted, correcting the self-assessed results; before/after comparison tabulated per focus area across all 10 organizations.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing ITG (or any governance) maturity via self-report instruments, treat soft-governance/behavioral results as provisional until validated through structured follow-up interviews -- hard-governance/structural self-assessments can be trusted with less follow-up verification, but soft-governance self-assessments routinely under- or over-state maturity until participants receive clarification on what each level actually means.

finding_statement: Participants overwhelmingly agreed with their own self-assessed results for "Culture" and "Informal organization" with little to no need for interview-based correction (e.g. 9-10 of 10 participants agreeing per culture dimension in Case 1, Table 6) -- markedly more stable than the soft-governance maturity-level results discussed above -- attributed by the authors to the culture questionnaire being an already-validated instrument (OCAI) rather than a newly-designed one.
mechanism: Comparison of participant agreement rates between the OCAI-based culture/informal-organization questionnaire (Questionnaire 2-3) and the newly-designed maturity-level statements (Questionnaire 1) across the same 10 case studies.
operationalisation_hint: When constructing a new organizational-assessment instrument, prefer incorporating existing, already-validated psychometric instruments (e.g. OCAI for culture) for any dimension where one exists, rather than authoring new assessment statements from scratch -- new statements are demonstrably more prone to participant misinterpretation and require interview-based correction to be trustworthy.

finding_statement: Across all 10 case studies, participants and students rated "the MIG instrument combined with interviews" as more useful for practice (scores of 4.9-5.2 on a 6-point Likert scale) than "the MIG instrument" alone (scores of 3.9-4.7) -- a consistent, substantial gap replicated across both organization-side participants (cases 1-2) and student-led assessments (cases 3-10).
mechanism: Post-assessment evaluation questionnaire (6-point Likert scale, evaluation template adapted from an existing expert-review-of-maturity-models template) administered after each of the 10 case studies, comparing instrument-alone vs. instrument-plus-interview usefulness ratings.
operationalisation_hint: When deploying any self-report organizational-maturity instrument in practice, budget for a structured interview/discussion phase as a required complement, not an optional add-on -- the evidence indicates the interview phase, not the instrument itself, is what participants credit with making results usable in their own organization.
page_or_section: Section 4.2/5.3 (Evaluation of the results), Tables 5/9, pp. 795-825

finding_statement: Despite three design cycles of targeted improvement (introducing a six-point Likert scale, adding a departmental/corporate dual perspective, expanding documentation), the top suggested improvement after the third cycle remained "equivocal, unclear or excessively black and white statements/questions," and participants explicitly noted that "without the interview, the participant might misinterpret questions" -- an issue that documentation improvements alone did not fully resolve.
mechanism: Cross-cycle comparison of participant/student-suggested improvements (Table 3, cycle 2; Table 7-8, cycle 3) showing persistent semantic-clarity issues despite iterative design responses.
operationalisation_hint: Before adopting any published governance-maturity assessment instrument wholesale, plan for at least one local pilot cycle with structured interviews to surface organization-specific misinterpretations of the instrument's statements, rather than assuming a literature-validated instrument will be immediately reliable as a pure self-service survey.
page_or_section: Sections 4.1-5.2 (Evaluation of the second/third cycle), Tables 3, 7-8, pp. 503-534, 726-791

finding_statement: The same five governance subsystems (S1 operational IT services, S2 coordination/standards, S3 operational control, S3* audit, S4 environmental-intelligence/future-scanning, S5 policy/normative governance) are designed once at the whole-organization level and then recur identically in structure at each nested recursion level (e.g. re-applied to the "internet banking" sub-unit within the disaster data center project), giving a single governance methodology that scales fractally rather than requiring bespoke governance design at each organizational layer.
mechanism: Customization of Espejo, Bowling & Hoverstadt's VIPLAN methodology for IT governance specifically, demonstrated via systematic action research (Checkland & Holwell FMA framework) in designing a disaster data center for a major Iranian bank, involving a 30-person expert team.
operationalisation_hint: When designing IT governance for a large, multi-layered organization (enterprise down to individual service/project level), consider applying the same recursive 5-subsystem governance template (operations, coordination, operational control, audit, environmental scanning, policy) at each layer rather than designing bespoke governance structures per layer -- this VSM-based approach may reduce governance-design effort in highly nested organizations.
page_or_section: Findings and Results section, Table 1/3, Figs. 6-16, pp. 311-780

finding_statement: A dedicated environmental-scanning/intelligence governance subsystem (VSM System 4) -- explicitly tasked with tracking emergent technology trends, monitoring competitor/market moves, and defining forward-looking strategic plans -- is identified as the specific structural mechanism responsible for achieving dynamic (adaptive) alignment between business strategy and IT value as conditions change, distinguishing "viable" governance from static governance models that lack any equivalent function.
mechanism: Structural design decision within the customized VIPLAN/VSM methodology (Table 1, System 4 row), instantiated in the case as a research-and-development team of data-center experts tasked with tracking future data-center and banking-technology trends.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing whether an organization's IT governance structure supports adaptive/dynamic business-IT alignment (not just static compliance), check specifically for a dedicated, resourced environmental-scanning/intelligence function (distinct from operational management) responsible for sensing external technology and market shifts and translating them into governance-level strategic plans.
page_or_section: Table 1 (System 4 row) and Step 6 System 4 design description, pp. 503-513, 774-779

finding_statement: The MIG model operationalizes ITG maturity across nine focus areas spanning three domains -- Hard (functions & roles, formal networks, IT decision-making, planning, monitoring, each assessed via CMM-style levels), Soft (continuous improvement, leadership, participation, understanding & trust, each using a distinct existing maturity model), and Context (culture via Quinn's Competing Values Framework, informal organization, sector) -- because most existing ITG research and maturity models cover only the hard, process/structure side.
mechanism: Focus Area Maturity Model (FAMM) design methodology combining literature-derived maturity models per focus area (e.g. Bessant et al. for continuous improvement, Collins for leadership, Reich & Benbasat for understanding and trust) into a single instrument, built using Hevner's three design-science cycles (Relevance, Design, Rigor).
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's IT governance maturity, do not rely on frameworks that only cover structure/process (e.g. most COBIT-based assessments); explicitly assess soft/behavioral focus areas (leadership, participation, trust, continuous improvement) using dimension-appropriate instruments, and separately capture situational context (culture, informal organization, sector) rather than treating it as a residual "relational mechanisms" catch-all.

finding_statement: After testing and rejecting three established alternatives for measuring informal organization (Cobb's informal-influence variables, Galbraith's seven types of lateral relations, Mintzberg's sociogram -- all found too laborious to implement and unable to reach practitioner consensus during model design), the authors found a simple solution: reusing the same nine focus areas from the hard/soft maturity model, with two formal/informal-contrast statements per focus area (e.g. "Decision-making on IT investments and projects is formally organized").
mechanism: Iterative design-science choice made during first-cycle instrument construction, documented as a specific research contribution to the underlying MIG model.
operationalisation_hint: When an ITG (or broader governance) maturity instrument needs to capture the gap between formal/documented practice and actual informal practice, consider reusing the instrument's own existing dimension structure (asking a formal-vs-informal contrast per dimension) instead of importing a separate, more complex social-structure framework that may prove too laborious to apply consistently.
page_or_section: Section 4.2 (Choices necessary for the implementation), pp. 277-296

finding_statement: A structural element (e.g. a "standard office") explicitly responsible for steering and monitoring standard usage -- rather than leaving standardization oversight diffuse across roles -- controls key standardization aspects (cost-benefit, diffusion, adoption) and reveals critical non-compliance areas needing action.
mechanism: Organizational Control Theory's Measurement construct applied to ICITS; validated across 7 experts from 6 organizations (purpose/relevancy Avg 4.71/5, applicability/adequacy Avg 4.71/5, testable-proposition ratings 4.29-4.43/5); experts from large organizations independently confirmed already using dedicated standard offices and described it as reducing management complexity.
operationalisation_hint: When an organization's IT footprint grows complex enough that standards proliferate (multiple technology, data, and process standards), establish an explicit organizational unit or role accountable for steering and monitoring standard usage and compliance -- rather than treating standardization oversight as an informal, diffuse responsibility.

finding_statement: Managing standards as passing through defined phases -- initiation/approval, introduction with benefit communication, use with monitoring and audits, and discontinuation/replacement -- prevents standards from being treated as one-off documents and establishes standardization as a continuous, planned process responsive to changing environmental conditions.
mechanism: Grounded in Organizational Control Theory's Planning and External Environment constructs; unanimously endorsed across all 7 confirmatory-round experts (purpose/relevancy Avg 5.0/5, applicability/adequacy Avg 4.71/5, testable-proposition Avg 4.71/5, SD 0.49) despite most experts not having a formally-named lifecycle in their own organization -- they described equivalent informal patterns or ITIL/ISO-based practices instead.
operationalisation_hint: When establishing governance for IT (or other organizational) standards, explicitly define and communicate a lifecycle (creation, rollout, active use/monitoring, retirement/replacement) rather than treating standard creation as a terminal event -- this supports resource planning and keeps standardization visibly "alive" as an ongoing management responsibility.

finding_statement: Non-compliance with IT standards is fundamentally a goal-misalignment problem: employees follow standards more reliably when adherence (or non-adherence) has visible personal consequences (positive sanctions/rewards for compliance; negative sanctions -- high individual cost -- for deviance), rather than relying on policy documentation alone.
mechanism: Grounded in Organizational Control Theory's Evaluation-Reward construct and management-by-objectives (MBO) literature; confirmed by 6 of 7 experts (one abstained for lack of MBO experience) with Avg 4.33/5 applicability and testable-proposition ratings of 4.00-4.17/5 -- notably lower and more variable than other design principles, with one expert expressing explicit doubt about incentive-based compliance mechanisms.
operationalisation_hint: When designing governance for IT (or other) standards in an organization with persistent non-compliance, do not rely solely on documentation and monitoring -- explicitly define and communicate incentives (or costs of non-compliance) tied to individual performance objectives, while recognizing this mechanism has more mixed practitioner buy-in than purely structural/informational mechanisms.

finding_statement: Passive, on-demand communication (users having to seek out manuals or ask for information) was identified as a major cause of insufficient standard-related knowledge; actively pushing information (via email, brochures, workshops, meetings) before or during rollout counteracts faulty user behavior and resistance stemming from information gaps.
mechanism: Grounded in Organizational Control Theory's Organizational Culture construct and open-communication-culture literature; this was the most strongly and unanimously validated design principle across all 7 experts from 6 organizations (purpose/relevancy Avg 5.0/5, SD 0; applicability/adequacy Avg 4.71/5; all three testable propositions rated 4.57-4.71/5) -- though experts cautioned that information overload (flooding users with irrelevant detail) can itself increase resistance.
operationalisation_hint: When rolling out a new governance standard or artifact, proactively push concise, benefit-focused communication to all affected users through established channels (not just technical documentation) -- but calibrate volume carefully, since excessive or irrelevant information communicated this way can itself increase user resistance.

finding_statement: The authors explicitly restrict their design theory's scope to organizations of medium-to-large size and medium-to-high IT/IS complexity, reasoning that smaller organizations have lower division of labor (making dedicated standardization roles impractical) and that certain challenges (e.g. architectural transparency) are far less pressing with simpler architectures; the theory presupposes a baseline of EAM, project-management, and governance maturity already in place.
mechanism: Explicit boundary-condition statement in the design theory's "Purpose and Scope" specification (a required component of IS design theories per Gregor & Jones' anatomy), grounded in the reasoning that division-of-labor and architectural-transparency needs scale with organizational size/complexity.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying this ICITS design theory (or extracting lessons from it for broader governance conditions), verify the target organization has the baseline maturity assumed here (working PM, EAM, governance framework) -- for smaller or IT-management-immature organizations, treat these design principles as aspirational targets to grow into rather than an immediately applicable governance blueprint.

finding_statement: The systematic review proposes configurations linking structural governance, risk/compliance, and IT-information mechanisms. Its narrative synthesis presents interdependence as a pattern; it does not establish universal performance comparisons for every isolated governance cluster.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
page_or_section: Section 4.4 (Synergistic Governance Mechanism Model), Section 5 (Discussion), pp. 1188-1407

finding_statement: The systematic review identifies concentrated family, foreign, and managerial ownership as recurring negative or non-uniform conditions in financial-governance-performance relationships. The heterogeneous synthesis does not establish cross-country consistency or a digital-investment interaction.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: IT-enabled dynamic capabilities (agility, innovation-mediation processes) combined with business/IT strategic-alignment mechanisms (COBIT-based frameworks, board-level IT expertise, CIO/CTO structures) are consistently and positively associated with institutional/corporate performance outcomes (firm value, innovation investment, operational efficiency, strategic IT use) across the reviewed studies, more consistently than IT governance's direct association with financial-performance metrics specifically.
mechanism: Synthesis of the "Alignment & Strategic Integration" and "Dynamic Capability" SGMM clusters across the reviewed studies (e.g. Vejseli et al. 2022 on agile/general ITG models improving performance via alignment; Ilmudeen 2022 on IT-enabled dynamic capabilities improving performance/agility; Al Romaihi et al. 2023 on board IT knowledge strengthening corporate-governance-performance links).
operationalisation_hint: When pursuing digital/architecture-led transformation, prioritize building the alignment infrastructure (board-level IT expertise, ITG frameworks like COBIT, formal business-IT alignment structures) as the mechanism through which IT-enabled dynamic capabilities translate into measurable institutional performance gains, rather than expecting IT capability investment alone to produce performance without an explicit alignment layer.

finding_statement: Of the reviewed studies, 26 examine corporate governance -> corporate performance and 13 examine corporate governance -> financial performance, but only 8 examine IT governance -> corporate performance and just 3 examine IT governance -> financial performance -- meaning claims about IT governance's direct financial-performance effects rest on a very small evidence base and should be treated cautiously rather than generalized.
mechanism: Quantitative breakdown of the 46 included studies by governance-type x performance-dimension category (Table 2), explicitly reported by the authors as a limitation on the strength of inferences about the IT-governance-financial-performance relationship specifically.
operationalisation_hint: When citing or building on claims that "IT governance improves financial performance," check whether the underlying evidence is drawn from the (currently very thin, ~3-study) direct IT-governance-to-financial-performance literature or from the much larger corporate-governance or IT-governance-to-corporate-performance literatures -- and treat direct financial-performance claims about IT governance specifically as provisional pending more research.

finding_statement: The review notes that CEO duality often weakens or neutralizes formal-governance effects across included studies. Heterogeneity prevents a near-universal or structural-causality conclusion.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: Across the surveyed sample, system trust (SYT) showed the strongest and most significant path to ITG effectiveness of any relationship in the model (t=13.334, p<0.001), with the overall ITG construct explained at R square=0.813 by the full model -- indicating that stakeholders' trust that the IT system is efficient, effective, flexible, and resiliently supported by key stakeholders functions as the critical mediating condition converting good information/system/service quality into governance effectiveness, more so than quality perceptions acting directly.
mechanism: PLS-SEM structural model (23 hypotheses, bootstrapping analysis) fit to survey responses (five-point Likert) from 300 teachers/staff/management across Indonesian high schools, following the De Haes/Van Grembergen ITG mechanism framework as the base theoretical reference.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing whether an IT governance mechanism is functioning, do not rely solely on information/system/service-quality metrics -- explicitly measure stakeholder trust in the IT system itself (perceived efficiency, effectiveness, flexibility, resilience/support), since this appears to be the more proximate driver of realized governance effectiveness.
page_or_section: Section III.D (Bootstrapping Analysis) and III.E (Discussion), Table XVII, pp. 622-679

finding_statement: Of 23 hypothesized paths, 5 were statistically non-significant, concentrated in the discomfort (DSC) and insecurity (INS) readiness constructs' relationships to information quality and system trust (e.g. DSC->QOI, DSC->QSY, DSC->SYT, INS->QOI, INS->SYT all non-significant) -- while the positive-affect constructs (hopefulness, breakthrough/innovativeness) showed consistent significant effects, suggesting that in this context, reducing user discomfort/insecurity mattered less for governance outcomes than fostering positive engagement with IT.
mechanism: PLS-SEM bootstrapping results (t-statistics against the 1.96 critical value at alpha=0.05) across the 23-hypothesis path model, discussed by the authors with proposed contextual explanations (e.g. users not encountering actual security issues, differing interpretations of system-quality terminology).
operationalisation_hint: When designing interventions to improve stakeholder readiness for an IT governance initiative, do not assume that addressing user discomfort/security anxiety is the priority lever -- in this (education-sector) evidence, building positive attitudes and perceived benefit had more consistent effects than reducing negative affect; verify which readiness dimension actually predicts outcomes in the target context before investing.

finding_statement: Platform-process tension (the platform must be versatile enough for complex organizational processes yet promote scalable standard functionality); platform-people tension (citizen-developer autonomy vs. technical safeguards); and process-people tension (domain-expert autonomy to improve their own workflows vs. cross-unit consistency, compliance, and interoperability) are three empirically distinguishable tension types, each requiring its own paired flexibility/standardisation guideline rather than a single governance lever.
mechanism: Cross-case thematic analysis of 57 interviews (IT professionals, citizen developers, managers, platform experts) across SoftCo and TechCo, organized around the three canonical LCNC elements (platform, process, people) identified in prior literature.
operationalisation_hint: When designing governance for decentralized/citizen-driven technology development (LCNC or analogous business-unit-led initiatives), explicitly diagnose which of the three tension types (platform-process, platform-people, process-people) is at stake for a given initiative before selecting a governance response -- a single generic "more/less control" policy will not fit all three.

finding_statement: A dedicated, cross-functional Center of Excellence -- combining technical and non-technical stakeholders (platform/solution/enterprise architects, developers, SCRUM masters, customer-success managers, testing/release staff) plus internal and external experts -- acting as a non-directive central coordinating and advisory body (not a command-and-control gatekeeper) is identified as the key governance structure enabling both citizen-developer autonomy and organization-wide scalability of decentralized development initiatives.
mechanism: Cross-case comparison showing SoftCo's 250-person Center of Excellence (more LCNC-mature) providing "portfolio guidance" and best-practice recommendations to Lines-of-Business without directly controlling their scope/planning/delivery, versus TechCo's comparatively less centralized coordination at an earlier maturity stage.
operationalisation_hint: When scaling decentralized/citizen-led technology development across business units, establish a cross-functional Center of Excellence staffed with both technical and business-facing roles (plus external platform-vendor expertise where available) as an advisory/coordinating hub -- not a gatekeeping approval body -- to reconcile local autonomy with organization-wide scalability and best-practice consistency.

finding_statement: Organizations actively shape the evolution of their LCNC platform (via idea portals, user communities, and -- at higher maturity -- formal vendor "design partnerships" with preview access to unreleased features) to close gaps between platform capability and organizational process needs, while periodically reverting custom-built solutions back to newly-available vendor-native functionality ("back to baseline") to preserve long-term maintainability and upgrade compatibility.
mechanism: Documented across both case organizations, with SoftCo (higher maturity, longer platform tenure) exhibiting a more advanced design-partnership relationship with ServiceNow than TechCo; explicit "back-to-baseline" practice described by a SoftCo solution architect as a deliberate, ongoing architectural discipline.
operationalisation_hint: When a standardized platform's built-in capabilities fall short of organizational process needs, treat vendor engagement (feature-request channels, design partnerships) as a governance lever for gaining necessary flexibility without permanent custom-code debt -- and institute a recurring practice of reassessing and reverting custom developments to platform-native equivalents as the vendor's feature set matures.

finding_statement: Citizen (non-technical) developers require stronger guardrails (controlled sandbox/test/production environment separation, mandatory use of out-of-the-box features) to prevent technical debt and data risk, whereas technically-trained LCNC users can be granted more customization latitude; similarly, low-risk/individual-use-case automation (e.g. routine email tasks) tolerates more experimentation and local variation, while mission-critical or cross-functional processes (e.g. enterprise-wide ITSM/ticketing) require harmonized logic, data models, and workflows for interoperability and compliance.
mechanism: Derived from contrastive analysis of guideline implementation differences between SoftCo and TechCo (Section 6.2-6.3), explicitly framed by the authors as practical organizational implications for tailoring governance intensity.
operationalisation_hint: Before applying a uniform LCNC (or broader decentralized-development) governance policy, segment initiatives along two axes -- developer technical background and process criticality/risk -- and calibrate guardrail intensity (environment separation, mandatory feature defaults, harmonization requirements) accordingly, reserving the heaviest standardisation requirements for citizen-developer-built, mission-critical/cross-functional initiatives.

finding_statement: Early-maturity organizations benefit most from adhering closely to platform standards ("quick wins," foundational competency-building), while advanced-maturity organizations can productively shift toward proactive vendor co-design and greater customization; moreover, pursuing flexibility (e.g. adopting LCNC to move fast) itself often exposes and forces the harmonization of previously fragmented/outdated processes, meaning standardisation and flexibility reinforce rather than oppose each other over time -- treating either pole as a fixed, permanent policy choice is a governance failure mode.
mechanism: Cross-case comparison of SoftCo (advanced maturity, design-partnership stage) versus TechCo (earlier stage, standard-feature-reliant) plus the authors' concluding theoretical reflection explicitly reframing the flexibility-standardisation "paradox" as a dynamic, evolving "both-and" relationship rather than a static trade-off.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating or designing governance for decentralized/citizen-led technology initiatives, revisit and update the flexibility/standardisation balance periodically as organizational and platform maturity increases, rather than fixing a governance policy at initial rollout and treating deviations from it as permanent violations to be suppressed.

finding_statement: Rather than periodically re-running a full maturity assessment (COBIT, CMMI, etc.), an organization can track a compact panel of 36 sub-indicators (3 per each of 12 IT areas: percentage of work completed; percentage completed on schedule/budget; percentage completed, on schedule/budget, AND formally accepted by the customer) calculated via a standardized percentage formula against organization-set maximum/minimum goals, enabling continuous, low-overhead monitoring between full maturity assessments.
mechanism: Design Science Research methodology (Wieringa's process): problem investigation (bibliographic gap analysis across 9 databases), solution design (synthesis of 26 maturity models into 12 non-redundant IT monitoring areas), and validation via three simulation rounds within one real organization, culminating in reusable spreadsheet and guideline artefacts.
operationalisation_hint: For organizations needing continuous, lightweight visibility into ITG execution between full periodic maturity assessments, consider adopting a compact indicator panel (work-completion rate, on-schedule/on-budget delivery rate, and formally-accepted-delivery rate) per governance-relevant IT area, rather than relying solely on infrequent, resource-intensive full maturity-model audits.

finding_statement: The authors note that different sectors should weight the 12 IT monitoring areas differently (e.g. a financial-sector company should weight security KMIs more heavily, a media company should weight knowledge-management KMIs more heavily); moreover, the real-world pilot at the Brazilian Government Agency documented concrete scoring anomalies requiring human interpretation -- a security-area KMI could not be evaluated because the security team was mid-review of its internal processes, and a customer-satisfaction sub-indicator showed an anomalously low score explained by unrelated staff-leave patterns rather than true service failure.
mechanism: Documented findings from the three-round implementation-assessment case study at a single Brazilian Government Agency undergoing organizational restructuring, including explicit reviewer comments recorded in the validation spreadsheet explaining anomalous scores.
operationalisation_hint: When deploying a standardized IT-governance indicator panel across sectors or organizational contexts, apply sector-appropriate significance weighting rather than a uniform scheme, and build in a human-review step to catch and explain data-availability gaps or context-confounded scores (e.g. a bad score driven by unrelated organizational events) before treating raw indicator output as an accurate governance signal.

finding_statement: Risk appetite is modeled as an association from the Risk_Appetite class to specific Strategic_Objective instances, allowing an organization to hold near-zero risk tolerance for one objective (e.g. patient safety) while accepting much higher risk for another (e.g. pursuing innovation/reputational opportunities) within the same governance model.
mechanism: Meta-model extension (UML class diagram, Fig. 1) of the MoDrIGo framework, illustrated (not empirically tested) via the fictional Saint-Romain hospital cloud-adoption scenario.
operationalisation_hint: When modeling or assessing an organization's risk governance, do not treat "risk appetite" as a single scalar setting -- represent it per strategic objective, since a board may rationally tolerate very different risk levels for safety-critical objectives versus innovation/reputation-oriented objectives within the same portfolio of decisions.
page_or_section: Section 5.1 (Risk-Aware MoDrIGo Meta-Model), item 7 "Risk appetite", pp. 511-532

finding_statement: Digital context (e.g. cloud computing, IoT, big data, blockchain, AI) is modeled with explicit "help"/"hurt" contribution links to both hazard and opportunity risks at the strategic level -- e.g. cloud adoption can aggravate data-loss risk (hurt) while simultaneously improving real-time information sharing (help) -- rather than being assessed only for its alignment/value contribution to strategic objectives.
mechanism: Meta-model extension illustrated via the Saint-Romain cloud-adoption example, where the same digital-context element (cloud computing) is shown simultaneously helping one risk/opportunity pair and hurting another.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing the adoption of a new technology at the governance level, explicitly trace both its value-alignment contribution AND its help/hurt effect on existing strategic risks -- a purely capability- or alignment-focused technology assessment (as in most BITA models) will miss the risk-profile changes that same technology introduces.
page_or_section: Section 5.2 (Model-based Representation of Risk), Fig. 2, pp. 540-661

finding_statement: The ten-organization pilot reports similar awareness and COBIT-based maturity patterns across surveyed organizations. It does not independently validate awareness as a leading proxy through statistical testing.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The authors identify that the standard approach to determining ITG implementation success (COBIT-based maturity-level calculation) evaluates only the artifacts/objects of governance, while the parties involved (stakeholders) have "a very significant influence in determining the success rate of implementing IT Governance practices, especially in awareness" -- a gap this paper's awareness formula was specifically designed to address, motivated by prior research showing a positive correlation between awareness and governance implementation success.
mechanism: Motivating problem statement grounded in a literature review of prior ITG-awareness research (including a Malaysian senior-manager study establishing the awareness-implementation correlation) and the authors' own prior published work on ITG critical success factors and barriers.
operationalisation_hint: When evaluating why an organization's IT governance implementation stalled despite passing artifact/process-based maturity checks (COBIT, ITIL, etc.), check whether stakeholder awareness (knowledge, attitude, and enacted behavior toward governance rules) was ever assessed -- a governance program can look mature on paper (controls, processes documented) while lacking the subject-side awareness needed to sustain it.

finding_statement: Across 157 surveyed IT leaders, the direct path from environmental turbulence to IT organisational resilience was statistically insignificant (beta=0.034, p>0.05), contradicting the researchers' own a priori expectation -- meaning organizations that merely experience turbulence do not thereby become more resilient; resilience only follows if that turbulence is channeled into strengthening IT service quality (beta=0.156, p<0.05) and IT governance maturity (beta=0.331, p<0.01), which in turn drive resilience.
mechanism: PLS-SEM structural model estimated on cross-sectional survey data from 157 IT leaders/executives across industries, using validated multi-item scales for each construct with reported path coefficients and significance levels.
operationalisation_hint: Do not assume that surviving a crisis or disruption automatically builds organizational resilience for the next one -- "reacting" to turbulence is not the resilience mechanism; the mechanism is turbulence prompting deliberate investment in IT governance maturity and IT service quality, which are the actual, measurable resilience-building levers.

finding_statement: IT governance maturity has a strong, statistically significant, direct positive effect on IT service quality (beta=0.258, p<0.01) -- mature governance (clear decision rights, accountability, and COBIT-domain practices: value delivery, risk optimisation, resource optimisation, stakeholder engagement) is a validated causal driver of better IT service delivery outcomes (tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy), not merely a parallel, independent capability.
mechanism: PLS-SEM path analysis across 157 respondents, corroborated by CIO follow-up interview quotes explicitly linking IT governance maturity to downstream service-quality outcomes ("better IT governance is at the core of most IT capabilities").
operationalisation_hint: When seeking to improve IT service quality (customer satisfaction, responsiveness, reliability), prioritize maturing IT governance structures and processes as a primary lever, tying governance practices directly to service-quality outcome metrics (response times, uptime, user satisfaction) -- rather than treating governance maturity and service-quality improvement as separate initiatives.
page_or_section: Section 4.2 (Finding 2: Mastering IT Governance Drives IT Service Quality), pp. 560-599

finding_statement: Both IT service quality (beta=0.406, p<0.01) and IT governance maturity (beta=0.212, p<0.01) show direct, statistically significant, positive effects on IT organisational resilience -- confirming both are necessary, non-redundant building blocks (a people-side and a process-side pillar) rather than one being a proxy or subset of the other, with the people-side (service quality) showing the numerically stronger direct path.
mechanism: PLS-SEM structural model results across 157 respondents, with both paths remaining significant when estimated simultaneously in the full structural model (ruling out one construct fully mediating or subsuming the other's effect).
operationalisation_hint: When building organizational resilience against disruption, invest in both dimensions in parallel rather than treating one as sufficient -- IT service quality (staff training, customer-service skills, empathetic/responsive support) and IT governance maturity (COBIT-domain practices) contribute independently and should be tracked/resourced as separate resilience-building programs.

finding_statement: Practitioner accounts (CIO interviews) describe modifying, not discarding, existing governance frameworks during disruption -- e.g. biweekly reassessment of priorities and governance-framework adjustments, and re-evaluating stakeholder-engagement committee composition and meeting more frequently -- enabling response to emerging demands "without being hindered by bureaucracy," consistent with the quantitative finding that turbulence drives governance maturity.
mechanism: Qualitative CIO follow-up interviews conducted to contextualize and validate the quantitative PLS-SEM findings, explicitly designed as an exploratory (not full qualitative) supplementary component.
operationalisation_hint: When adapting IT governance during a period of disruption, do not treat governance structures as fixed -- increase the frequency of governance-committee reassessment (composition, priorities, meeting cadence) as a deliberate practice, since this adaptive-adjustment behavior (not wholesale replacement of governance) is what practitioners credit with maintaining continuity without bureaucratic drag.

finding_statement: In a documented CIO account of responding to generative-AI-driven disruption, the CIO found that "many of their existing policies address most of the new needs due to generative AI. Most policies in their organisation […]" -- reinforcing the paper's broader finding that foundational, already-established IT governance and service-quality mechanisms (not novel disruption-specific frameworks) are the more reliable resilience-building investment.
mechanism: Illustrative practitioner case (CIO at a mid-sized higher-education institution) documented as a "from concept to practice" application of the paper's quantitatively-derived framework to the 2022-2023 generative-AI disruption.
operationalisation_hint: When a genuinely new type of technological disruption emerges (e.g. a new AI capability), resist the urge to build an entirely new bespoke governance framework for it first -- audit whether existing IT governance policies (data privacy, ethical use, strategic alignment) already cover most of the new risk surface with only minor tailoring needed, reserving novel framework-building for genuine gaps.
page_or_section: Section 5.4 (From Concept to Practice, Generative AI), pp. 795-846

finding_statement: Formalizing business objectives, IT resources, governance processes, risks, and security requirements -- along with their dependency, alignment, ownership, and mitigation relationships -- as a single OWL ontology (validated for RDF syntax/semantic consistency via the W3C RDF validator) allows automated reasoning (SPARQL/OWL/SWRL) to check that security controls and governance decisions remain traceably linked to strategic objectives, rather than relying on manually-maintained, siloed documentation across three separate frameworks.
mechanism: Ontological modeling methodology (UML class diagram to OWL to RDF/Turtle, validated for syntactic/semantic RDF conformance only -- not organizationally validated in the reported text).
operationalisation_hint: When strategic alignment, IT governance, and information security are managed via three separate frameworks/teams (as is typical), consider whether a shared, formally-modeled ontology linking their core concepts could reduce the specific failure modes documented in the literature (overlapping responsibilities, gaps between security investment and business value, misalignment between strategic intent and security practice) -- while noting this specific paper has not yet reported empirical evidence that its own ontology achieves this in a real organization.

finding_statement: Synthesizing prior literature, the authors note that governance frameworks and security standards "provide comprehensive guidelines... respectively. Yet, their application often remains fragmented, leading to inefficiencies, overlapping responsibilities, and gaps in organizational processes," and that IT governance mechanisms are frequently implemented without integration with security management, "resulting in limited effectiveness."
mechanism: Literature synthesis (not this paper's own empirical finding) citing prior systematic reviews (e.g. AlGhamdi, Win & Vlahu-Gjorgievska 2020 on information security governance critical success factors) and theory-practice gap studies (e.g. Ko & Fink 2010).
operationalisation_hint: When auditing an organization's governance maturity, check specifically whether IT governance (COBIT-based) and information security (ISO 27001/NIST-based) programs operate from a shared conceptual model of business objectives and risk, or as independently-run compliance exercises -- the literature synthesized here suggests the latter pattern is common and produces measurable inefficiency and misalignment.

finding_statement: Senior management awareness of how IT is governed -- not any particular governance structure -- was the single best predictor of governance effectiveness in the study: on average only 38% of senior managers knew how IT was governed at their company, but top-performing firms had 60-80% awareness, and governance performance correlates with three-year average financial performance (ROE, market capitalization growth).
mechanism: Statistical and qualitative analysis of survey responses from 256+ enterprises (300 total across combined studies) plus 40 interview-based case studies, using a weighted-average governance-performance self-assessment instrument (cost-effective IT use, asset utilization, growth, business flexibility) benchmarked against three-year financial performance.
operationalisation_hint: Before redesigning IT governance structures, first measure and invest in raising senior-management awareness and understanding of however IT is currently governed -- communicating and making governance transparent may be a higher-leverage intervention than any specific structural redesign, since awareness itself is the strongest observed predictor of effectiveness.
page_or_section: Section "A Quick Assessment of Your IT Governance," pp. 185-257 (of source PDF text)

finding_statement: The "IT governance on one page" 5x6 matrix (five decision domains -- IT principles, IT architecture, IT infrastructure, business application needs, IT investment/prioritization -- crossed with six decision archetypes ranging from centralized business/IT monarchy to federal/duopoly hybrids to decentralized feudal/anarchy) lets an organization deliberately assign different decision rights to different archetypes per domain, rather than uniformly centralizing or decentralizing all IT decisions -- enabling federal/duopoly hybrid designs that explicitly balance synergy (standardization, shared services) against business-unit autonomy.
mechanism: Cross-case comparative analysis (UPS: centralized; Manheim: initially decentralized then blended; ING DIRECT and Carlson Companies: hybrid duopoly/federal designs with named coordinating bodies) demonstrating that firms leading on asset utilization specifically favor duopoly/federal hybrid governance to balance enterprise-wide and local control.
operationalisation_hint: When designing IT governance for a multi-business-unit organization, do not default to a single archetype across all five decision domains -- map each domain (principles, architecture, infrastructure, application needs, investment) separately and assign the archetype (monarchy, federal, duopoly, feudal) that fits that specific domain's synergy/autonomy tradeoff, as top performers like Carlson and ING DIRECT do.
page_or_section: Section "IT Governance on One Page," Figures 2-3, and hybrid-approach case studies (ING DIRECT, Carlson Companies), pp. 297-720

finding_statement: Firms leading on profit favor centralized mechanisms (executive committees, centralized capital-approval and architecture-compliance processes, formal post-implementation project assessments) to standardize business processes and IT; firms leading on growth favor decentralized mechanisms (few mandated standards, local accountability, an investment process focused only on risk management) to maximize innovation speed and business-unit autonomy; firms leading on asset utilization favor hybrid mechanisms (business/IT relationship managers, SLAs, chargeback, cross-unit process teams with IT members) to balance shared-service efficiency with responsiveness.
mechanism: Analysis of firms with statistically significantly higher three-year industry-adjusted performance on each of three dimensions (ROI/ROE for profit, ROA for asset utilization, revenue growth for growth), cross-tabulated against their governance mechanism portfolios (Figure 5).
operationalisation_hint: Before selecting IT governance mechanisms, first clarify which financial/strategic outcome the organization is primarily optimizing for (cost/profit efficiency, asset utilization/shared-service efficiency, or growth/innovation speed) -- then select the mechanism portfolio empirically associated with top performers on that specific dimension, rather than adopting a generic "best practice" mechanism set.
page_or_section: Section "How Top Performers Govern," Figure 5, pp. 509-690

finding_statement: Governance stability (rather than frequent redesign) is empirically associated with governance effectiveness: firms that had achieved effective governance made incremental adjustments roughly annually, while firms struggling with governance effectiveness churned through governance changes up to three times per year, suggesting that frequent restructuring reflects unresolved uncertainty rather than adaptive improvement.
mechanism: Cross-firm comparison within the combined 300-enterprise/40-case-study research base, contrasting the frequency of governance-design changes between firms rated as effective versus less-effective governors.
operationalisation_hint: When an organization is on its second or third governance redesign within a year, treat this as a warning sign rather than evidence of admirable adaptiveness -- diagnose whether the underlying synergy/autonomy tradeoffs and organizational structure have actually been resolved, since effective governance design is typically stable at roughly an annual cadence of adjustment.
page_or_section: Footnote 9 (governance change frequency) and closing section, pp. 906-943

finding_statement: Because organizational structure alone cannot enforce every desired IT-related behavior (e.g. an autonomous business-unit structure can still be paired with enterprise-wide IT architecture principles or centrally-vetted investment approval to achieve enterprise cost/synergy objectives without reorganizing), firms can achieve conflicting synergy and autonomy objectives simultaneously by using IT governance mechanisms to fill the specific gaps left by organizational structure, rather than repeatedly restructuring.
mechanism: Synthesized design methodology derived from cross-case analysis (Dow Corning's governance evolution from large executive-committee involvement to a smaller steering committee as organizational learning matured is given as a worked example).
operationalisation_hint: When designing or redesigning IT governance, do not start by asking "how should we reorganize?" -- first clarify the firm's synergy/autonomy needs, take the current organizational structure as a given baseline, identify precisely which desirable behaviors that structure does NOT already produce, and design targeted governance mechanisms (not restructuring) to close exactly that gap.
page_or_section: Section "Recommendations to Guide Effective IT Governance Design," pp. 856-936

finding_statement: Digital maturity requires BOTH technology-adoption intensity AND management capability jointly, not either alone: organizations that adopt technology aggressively but lack coordinating management skill ("Fashionistas") and organizations with strong management but slow technology adoption ("Conservatives") both underperform organizations strong on both dimensions ("Digirati"), which achieved +9% revenue, +26% profitability, and +12% market valuation versus negative performance for "Beginner" (weak on both) organizations; only 15% of surveyed organizations reached the Digirati category.
mechanism: Digital maturity index (developed by MIT Center for Digital Business and Capgemini Consulting from prior 450-company interview research) applied via self-assessment to 1,559 survey respondents across 106 countries, cross-tabulated against self-reported revenue, profitability, and market-valuation trends.
operationalisation_hint: When assessing an organization's digital-transformation readiness, evaluate technology adoption and management capability as two independent, jointly-necessary axes -- do not credit an organization with high digital maturity based on impressive technology adoption alone (or strong management alone); only the combination predicts superior financial performance.
page_or_section: Section "Digital Immaturity: A Widespread Problem," Figures 1 and 3, pp. 172-443

finding_statement: In the reported survey, employees whose senior leaders had shared a digital-transformation vision showed high agreement that transformation was the right priority; only 36% of respondents reported such a shared vision. The report also includes an attributed practitioner observation favouring top-down leadership.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: The survey reports the prevalence of cross-functional digital-governance mechanisms and greater investment-decision authority among Digirati organizations. It does not establish that mechanism authority causes reduced political resistance or higher maturity.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.

finding_statement: A clear perception gap by hierarchy level was found: 53% of CEOs rated the pace of digital transformation as adequate, fast, or very fast, versus only 25% of managers and 22% of staff -- with satisfaction dropping consistently the further down the organizational ladder respondents were, indicating that senior leaders systematically overestimate transformation progress relative to those actually executing it.
mechanism: Survey cross-tabulation (1,559 respondents) of self-rated transformation pace by organizational role/level (C-level/board, CEO/President, managers, staff), corroborated by open-text respondent comments describing leadership as out of touch ("clueless management").
operationalisation_hint: When a CEO or senior leadership team believes digital transformation is proceeding at an adequate pace, treat this belief as unverified until corroborated by manager- and staff-level perception surveys -- the evidence here shows a large, consistent gap by hierarchy level, meaning leadership self-assessment alone risks masking a stalled transformation at the operational level.

finding_statement: 68% of Digirati (top-maturity) organizations tie reward structures to digital-transformation goals, compared to only 39% of Beginner (lowest-maturity) organizations -- and even among Digirati, personal advancement (65%) and awards/recognition (48%) are more commonly used incentive levers than direct financial incentives (39%), suggesting incentive-alignment (not necessarily monetary) is itself a distinguishing driver of top-tier digital-transformation performance, separate from governance structure or leadership vision.
mechanism: Survey cross-tabulation (1,559 respondents) of reward-structure alignment with digital-transformation goals, segmented by digital-maturity category (Figure 9).
operationalisation_hint: When designing a digital-transformation program, explicitly build recognition- and advancement-based incentive mechanisms tied to transformation goals (not only monetary bonuses) -- the evidence indicates this is a distinguishing practice of the highest-performing organizations, and is currently absent in the majority of lower-maturity organizations.

finding_statement: Four typical EA-organization placements were compared: (1) EA embedded as one team within IT -- simplest to set up, but structurally disconnected from business departments, limited to an IT-centric view of business capabilities, and easily becomes a bottleneck with no authority to compel business-side data or collaboration; (2) EA as a staff department to the CIO -- shifts EA toward strategic IT activities and allows delegating data-collection to IT teams, but remains business-disconnected; (3) EA as a corporate-level division on par with IT and business departments -- improves business relevance and collaboration but has only advisory (not enforcement) power over peer departments; (4) EA as a corporate staff department reporting directly to the CEO -- enables a genuine corporate governance approach with enforcement authority across all departments, but requires enabling/training people company-wide and setting proper incentives, representing the largest organizational change.
mechanism: Comparative framework synthesized from the lead author's first-hand professional experience in EA organizations of types (1)-(3) at a major logistics company, cross-referenced against practitioner literature and the general EAM literature on organizational placement.
operationalisation_hint: When advising on where to place a newly-formed (or restructuring) EA function, do not treat organizational placement as a minor implementation detail -- map the intended placement against this four-level hierarchy first, since the authority to compel business-side collaboration and enforce architecture standards (not just produce artifacts) scales directly with how close EA sits to the CEO, and each step up this hierarchy requires a correspondingly larger change-management and incentive-design investment.

finding_statement: The masterclass and cited literature describe communication, collaboration, brokering, and avoidance of siloed or ivory-tower EA as important EA success conditions. The sources do not compare these with all alternative explanations for failure.
mechanism: The cited evidence supports the bounded pattern stated above. Its documented scope does not establish a universal, comparative, or causal relationship beyond the source context.
operationalisation_hint: Use this finding as a context-sensitive consideration when designing or assessing transformation initiatives; do not treat it as an unconditional requirement.
